title: Algebra 1
intro: Algebra is arithmetic with letters standing in for numbers you do not know yet. Learn one move at a time and check each one.

lessons.title: Collect like terms
lessons.goal: Spot terms with the same letter part and add or subtract the numbers in front of them, called the coefficients.

steps.title: Sort by type
steps.text: Each sign belongs to the term that follows it. Sort the terms into three groups: x² terms, x terms and plain numbers, called constants.
steps.why: A term is a number, its letters and its sign together. When you move a term, its sign moves with it.

steps.title: Combine the squared terms
steps.text: Six lots of x² take away two lots of x² leaves four lots of x². The power stays as 2.
steps.why: You are counting x² tiles, not multiplying them. Counting tiles does not change the kind of tile.

steps.title: Combine the linear terms
steps.text: A term −x means one x taken away, so the number in front, called the coefficient, is −1. Three x take away one x leaves two x.
steps.why: Only terms with exactly the same letter part can be combined into one term.

steps.title: Keep the constant and check
steps.text: The 5 has no partner, so it stays as it is. Check with x = 2: the long expression and the short one both give 25.
steps.why: If the two values were different, a term or a sign was lost on the way.

quiz.question: Simplify 7a + 4 − 2a.
quiz.hint: Group the a terms; keep the constant.
quiz.explanation: 7a + 4 − 2a = 7a − 2a + 4 = 5a + 4. The 4 has no letter, so it stays on its own.

quiz.question: Which term is like 3x²?
quiz.hint: The letter and the power must both match.
quiz.explanation: −7x² has the same letter part, x². The number in front and the sign can be different.

lessons.takeaway: Add or subtract the numbers in front only when the letter parts match exactly.
lessons.mistake: Writing x² + x as x³. Adding does not change powers, so x² + x stays as x² + x. Only x² × x gives x³.

lessons.title: Multiply two brackets: every pair
lessons.goal: Multiply two brackets with a grid so that no product is missed, even when a term is negative.

steps.title: Give every term a place
steps.text: Expand (2x − 3)(x + 4), which means multiply it out. Put one bracket down the side of a grid and the other across the top.
steps.why: Each box in the grid holds one multiplication, so nothing gets missed.

steps.title: Multiply the first pair
steps.text: Multiply 2x by x. A plain x means 1x. Do the numbers first, 2 × 1 = 2, then the letters, x × x = x².
steps.why: x times x is x squared.

steps.title: Finish the first row
steps.text: Now multiply 2x by 4. This is a different product, so it needs its own box.
steps.why: 2x must multiply every term in the second bracket, not only the first one.

steps.title: Start the negative row
steps.text: Multiply −3 by x. Carry the minus sign with the 3.
steps.why: A negative times a positive is negative.

steps.text: Multiply −3 by 4. Count the four filled boxes before simplifying.
steps.why: Two terms times two terms always gives four products.

quiz.question: Expand (x + 3)(x + 2).
quiz.hint: There are four products; combine the two middle terms.
quiz.explanation: (x + 3)(x + 2) = x² + 2x + 3x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6. The answer x² + 6 leaves out the two middle products.

quiz.question: What is the constant term in (2x − 5)(x − 3)?
quiz.hint: The number on its own comes from multiplying the two numbers, signs included.
quiz.explanation: (−5) × (−3) = 15. A negative times a negative is positive.

lessons.takeaway: Every term in one bracket multiplies every term in the other.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying only first by first and last by last, so (x + 3)(x + 2) becomes x² + 6. The middle products 2x and 3x are missing. The correct answer is x² + 5x + 6.

lessons.title: Multiply a binomial by a trinomial
lessons.goal: Use the same grid when one bracket has three terms. You get six products and an x³ term.

steps.title: Build a two-by-three grid
steps.text: Expand (x + 2)(x² − 3x + 4). Treat −3x as one term with its minus sign attached.
steps.why: Two terms times three terms gives six products, so the grid needs six boxes.

steps.why: x² means x × x. One more x makes x × x × x, which is x³.

steps.text: Combine −3x² with 2x² to get −x². Combine 4x with −6x to get −2x. Write the answer from the highest power down.
steps.why: Like terms have the same letter and the same power.

quiz.question: How many pairwise products come from (a + b)(c + d + e)?
quiz.hint: Count rows times columns.
quiz.explanation: There are two rows and three columns: 2 × 3 = 6 products.

quiz.question: What is x multiplied by −4x²?
quiz.hint: Multiply the numbers, keep the minus sign, then add the powers of x.
quiz.explanation: x × (−4x²) = −4x³. Keep the minus sign and add the powers: 1 + 2 = 3.

lessons.takeaway: A bigger bracket needs a bigger grid, not a different rule.
lessons.mistake: Stopping after the first row. In (x + 2)(x² − 3x + 4) the 2 must also multiply all three terms, giving 2x² − 6x + 8.

lessons.title: Substitute without losing signs
lessons.goal: Swap each letter for its value, minus sign included, before you calculate anything.

steps.title: Write the given values
steps.text: Find the value of 2a² − 3b when a = −2 and b = 3. Write the expression down first, before any arithmetic.
steps.why: Each value belongs to one letter. Writing them down stops you mixing them up.

steps.title: Use brackets around the input
steps.text: Replace a with (−2) and b with (3). The brackets show that the whole of −2 is squared.
steps.why: Brackets keep the minus sign and the number together as one value.

steps.title: Use the order of operations
steps.text: Square −2 first, then multiply. Negative two times negative two is positive four.
steps.why: Order of operations: powers first, then multiplying, then adding and subtracting.

steps.title: Finish and compare
steps.text: Subtract: 8 − 9 = −1. Notice that −2² without brackets means −4, because only the 2 is squared.
steps.why: (−2)² = 4 but −2² = −4. The brackets decide whether the minus sign is squared too.

quiz.question: For a = −3, evaluate a² + 2a.
quiz.hint: Write (−3) in place of a, then square it first.
quiz.explanation: (−3)² + 2(−3) = 9 − 6 = 3. Remember that (−3)² is 9, not −9.

quiz.question: Which replacement is correct for x² when x = −4?
quiz.hint: The whole value, minus sign included, takes the place of x.
quiz.explanation: x² becomes (−4)² = 16. Without brackets, −4² means −16.

lessons.takeaway: Substitute first, with brackets. Calculate second.
lessons.mistake: Writing (−3)² as −9. A negative times a negative is positive, so (−3)² = 9. Only −3² without brackets is −9.

lessons.title: Solve a linear equation
lessons.goal: Find x by doing the same thing to both sides until x is on its own.

steps.title: Read the equality
steps.text: Solve 3(2x − 1) = 15. The two sides are the same amount, like the two pans of a balanced scale.
steps.why: The equals sign says both sides weigh the same. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

steps.title: Undo the outside multiplication
steps.text: The whole bracket is multiplied by 3. Divide both sides by 3 to undo that: 15 ÷ 3 = 5.
steps.why: Both sides are equal. A third of each side is still equal, like sharing each pan of a balanced scale into three.

steps.title: Undo subtraction, then multiplication
steps.text: Add 1 to both sides, giving 2x = 6. Then divide both sides by 2.
steps.why: x was doubled, then 1 was taken away. Undo these in reverse order: add 1, then halve.

steps.title: Check in the original equation
steps.text: Put x = 3 back into the equation you started with. The left side comes to 15, the same as the right side.
steps.why: x = 3 is correct only if it makes the first equation true. This check catches slips.

quiz.question: Solve 4x − 7 = 9.
quiz.hint: Add 7 to both sides first.
quiz.explanation: 4x − 7 = 9 → 4x = 16 → x = 4. Add 7 to both sides, then divide both sides by 4.

quiz.question: What should you do to both sides of x/5 = 3?
quiz.hint: x is divided by 5. Which operation undoes dividing?
quiz.explanation: x is divided by 5, so multiply both sides by 5. This gives x = 3 × 5 = 15.

lessons.takeaway: Undo one operation at a time on both sides. Then put your answer back into the first equation to check.
lessons.mistake: Saying "move it across and change the sign" without knowing why. You are really adding or subtracting the same amount on both sides.

lessons.title: Turn a word problem into an equation
lessons.goal: Name the unknown with a letter, write each amount using that letter, then join them with the fact the question gives.

steps.title: Label the unknown lengths
steps.text: A rectangle has length 2x + 3 centimetres and width x + 1 centimetres. Its perimeter is 32 centimetres. Find its length and width.
steps.why: The letter x stands for one number. It is the same number in the length and in the width.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="rectangle" x="150" y="90" width="440" height="210" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

steps.title: Translate the perimeter
steps.text: Perimeter is the distance around all four sides. Add two lengths and two widths.
steps.why: A rectangle has two equal pairs of opposite sides.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="rectangle" x="150" y="90" width="440" height="210" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="length" x="370" y="335" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">2x + 3</text><text id="width" x="645" y="205" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">x + 1</text></svg>

steps.title: Simplify and solve
steps.text: Multiply out both brackets and collect: 4x + 6 + 2x + 2 becomes 6x + 8. Subtract 8 from both sides, then divide both sides by 6.
steps.why: Each move is done to both sides, so the two sides stay equal.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="rectangle" x="150" y="90" width="440" height="210" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="length" x="370" y="335" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">2x + 3</text><text id="width" x="645" y="205" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">x + 1</text></svg>

steps.title: Answer the question in context
steps.text: x = 4 is not the answer yet. The length is 2 × 4 + 3 = 11 centimetres and the width is 4 + 1 = 5 centimetres. Check: 22 + 10 = 32.
steps.why: The question asks for lengths, not for x. Use x to work out what was asked.
steps.math: L = 11 cm; W = 5 cm; P = 32 cm

quiz.question: A rectangle has width x and length x + 2. Its perimeter is 20. Which equation fits?
quiz.hint: Perimeter adds all four sides.
quiz.explanation: Two widths plus two lengths gives 2x + 2(x + 2) = 20. The option x(x + 2) would be the area, not the perimeter.

quiz.question: Three identical tickets plus a €4 booking fee cost €25. What is one ticket?
quiz.hint: Remove the fee before splitting the ticket total.
quiz.explanation: Let t be the price of one ticket in euro. 3t + 4 = 25 → 3t = 21 → t = 7. One ticket costs €7. Adding the fee instead of removing it gives €9.67.

lessons.takeaway: Name the unknown, write the equation, solve it, then answer the question that was asked, with units.
lessons.mistake: Stopping at x = 4 when the question asks for a length or a price. Read the question again and use x to find what it asks for.

lessons.title: Divide polynomials with a reverse grid
lessons.goal: Divide by finding the missing bracket: the one that multiplies the bracket you divide by, called the divisor, to give the expression on top.

steps.title: Think of division as a missing bracket
steps.text: Divide x² + 5x + 6 by x + 2. Ask which bracket multiplies x + 2 to make x² + 5x + 6.
steps.why: Division undoes multiplication, just as 12 ÷ 3 asks what times 3 makes 12.

steps.title: Fill the leading product
steps.text: The first box must hold x². One bracket starts with x, so the missing bracket must start with x too.
steps.why: x squared divided by x gives x.

steps.title: Account for the other product in that row
steps.text: The x you just found also multiplies the 2, which makes 2x. You need 5x in total, so 3x is still missing.
steps.why: Each term of the answer multiplies both the x and the 2 in the divisor.

steps.text: To make the missing 3x from x, the next term must be +3. Check the last box: 3 × 2 = 6, which is the number you need.
steps.why: The x term and the plain number must both match the original.

steps.text: The answer, called the quotient, is x + 3. The original bottom line, x + 2, is zero when x = −2, so x cannot be −2.
steps.why: You can never divide by zero. Simplifying does not remove that rule.

quiz.question: Divide x² + 7x + 10 by x + 5.
quiz.hint: Which bracket multiplies x + 5 to give the constant 10 and the middle term 7x?
quiz.explanation: (x + 5)(x + 2) = x² + 7x + 10, so dividing by x + 5 leaves x + 2. This needs x ≠ −5.

quiz.question: Which input is excluded from (x² − 9)/(x − 3)?
quiz.hint: Look at the original bottom line, the denominator.
quiz.explanation: The bottom line x − 3 is zero when x = 3. That value stays excluded, even after you simplify to x + 3.

lessons.takeaway: Use a multiplication grid in reverse, then multiply back.
lessons.mistake: Cancelling single terms across a plus sign, such as crossing out the x in (x + 6)/(x + 2) to get 3. You can cancel only something that multiplies the whole top and the whole bottom, such as a whole bracket.

lessons.title: Place number types on a number line
lessons.goal: Tell integers, rationals and irrationals apart, and put each one in the right place on a number line.

steps.title: Start with the integers
steps.text: Integers are the whole numbers: negative ones, zero and positive ones. The ticks are evenly spaced, so each step is a jump of 1.
steps.why: A number line shows order and distance.

steps.text: Negative three halves is negative one and a half. Place it halfway between −2 and −1.
steps.why: A rational number can be written as one whole number over another, with the bottom not zero.

steps.text: The square root of 2 lies between 1 and 2, at about 1.414. It cannot be written exactly as one whole number over another, so it is irrational.
steps.why: The decimal 1.414 only shows where √2 sits. The exact value is still √2.

steps.title: Read direction and inclusion
steps.text: Follow one number through the families. The number 3 is natural, an integer, rational (3/1), and real. But the reverse does not always work: 1/2 is rational without being an integer.
steps.why: A bigger family contains more numbers. Belonging to the bigger family does not guarantee belonging to the smaller one.

quiz.question: Which number lies between −2 and −1?
quiz.hint: Convert the fractions to decimals.
quiz.explanation: −3/2 = −1.5, halfway between −2 and −1.

quiz.question: Which number is irrational?
quiz.hint: A rational number can be written exactly as one whole number over another.
quiz.explanation: √2 is irrational; 0.25 = 1/4, −4 = −4/1 and 7/3 are rational.

lessons.takeaway: Integers sit inside the rationals and the rationals inside the reals; place any number by its decimal value.
lessons.mistake: Thinking every decimal is irrational. 0.25 is 1/4 and 0.333… is 1/3, so both are rational. Only decimals that never end and never repeat are irrational.

lessons.title: Solve and graph an inequality
lessons.goal: Solve an inequality like an equation, with one extra rule: turn the sign around when you multiply or divide by a negative number.

steps.title: Read the inequality
steps.text: Solve −3x + 4 < 13. You want every value of x that makes the left side smaller than 13.
steps.why: An equation such as −3x + 4 = 13 has one answer. An inequality has a whole stretch of the number line.

steps.text: Subtract 4 from both sides. The inequality sign stays the way it is.
steps.why: Taking the same amount from both sides does not change which side is smaller.

steps.title: Divide by a negative
steps.text: Divide both sides by −3. Because −3 is negative, turn the sign around: less than becomes greater than. The result is x > −3.
steps.why: 2 is less than 5, but −2 is greater than −5. A negative multiplier flips the order, so the sign must flip too.

steps.why: x cannot equal −3 itself, so the circle is open. The arrow shows that every larger number works.

quiz.question: Solve −2x ≤ 8.
quiz.hint: You divide by −2. What must happen to the sign?
quiz.explanation: −2x ≤ 8 → x ≥ −4. Dividing both sides by −2 turns the sign around. Check x = 0: 0 ≤ 8 is true, and 0 ≥ −4.

quiz.question: How should x < 2 be shown?
quiz.hint: 2 itself is not included. Which numbers are less than 2?
quiz.explanation: Use an open dot at 2 and shade all values smaller than 2, to the left.

lessons.takeaway: Multiply or divide by a negative number: turn the inequality sign around. Adding or subtracting never turns it.
lessons.mistake: Turning the sign around just because a negative number appears. In x − 5 < 2 you add 5 and the sign stays: x < 7. Only multiplying or dividing by a negative turns it.

reference.name: Like terms
reference.note: The letter part, including the power, must match.

reference.name: Distributive law
reference.note: Multiply every term inside the bracket.

reference.name: Multiplying polynomials
reference.formula: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd
reference.note: A grid makes missing products easier to spot.

reference.name: Equation balance
reference.formula: Do the same operation to both sides
reference.note: Division by zero is never allowed.

reference.name: Inequalities
reference.formula: Multiply or divide by a negative → reverse <, >, ≤, ≥
reference.note: Adding or subtracting does not reverse the sign.

toolkit.strategy: First decide what the question wants: simplify an expression, find its value, solve an equation, or solve an inequality. Keep each sign with its term. Pick a grid, a balance or a number line before you calculate.

methods.title: Collect by variable and power
methods.when: Several terms are added or subtracted and you are asked to simplify.
methods.rule: axⁿ + bxⁿ = (a+b)xⁿ; variable parts must match.
steps: Read each sign as part of the term that follows it.
Group the terms whose letter parts match exactly.
Add or subtract the numbers in front. Terms with no partner stay as they are.
methods.check: At x = 1, both forms give 9.
methods.trap: x² + x is not x³. Adding never changes a power.

methods.title: Multiply out a single term or two brackets
methods.when: A term multiplies a bracket, or one bracket multiplies another.
methods.rule: a(b+c)=ab+ac; x^m × x^n=x^(m+n) for non-negative integer powers; m terms × n terms gives mn products.
steps: Draw one row or one column for each term, with its sign.
Fill every box: multiply the numbers in front and add the powers of x.
Collect like terms only after every box is filled.
Write the answer from the highest power down.
methods.check: At x = 2, the original and expanded expressions both give 0.
methods.trap: Do not stop after the first row. The second term of the first bracket multiplies everything too.

methods.title: Substitute into powers and fractions
methods.when: Values are given for the letters, including negative values or a denominator.
methods.rule: Replace the whole variable with its signed value; denominator ≠ 0.
steps: Write the expression down before putting any values in.
Put each negative value in brackets.
Work out powers first, then multiplying, then adding and subtracting.
For a fraction, work out the whole top and the whole bottom separately.
methods.check: The top is −6 and the bottom is −5. A negative divided by a negative is positive.
methods.trap: −3² means −9; (−3)² means 9.

methods.title: Solve an equation with brackets or fractions
methods.when: There is an equals sign and you are asked to find the unknown.
methods.rule: Apply the same valid operation to both sides; never divide by zero.
steps: Multiply out the brackets, or divide both sides by a number that multiplies a whole side.
If there are fractions, multiply every term on both sides by a common multiple of the bottom numbers.
Get the x terms on one side and the plain numbers on the other.
Divide to leave x on its own, then put your answer back into the first equation.
methods.trap: When you clear fractions, multiply every term, including the number on the other side.

methods.title: Translate shared perimeters
methods.when: Two shapes have equal perimeters or share a total boundary condition.
methods.rule: Rectangle P=2L+2W; equal perimeters need not mean equal areas.
steps: Use the same letter for the same unknown in both shapes.
Write the full perimeter of each shape.
Set the two perimeters equal and solve.
Use x to find the real lengths and check that each one is positive.
methods.example: Rectangles (2 x+1) by (x−1), and (x+4) by (x+1), have equal perimeters: 6 x=4 x+10 → x=5.
methods.check: The dimensions 11 by 4 and 9 by 6 both give perimeter 30.
methods.trap: Do not equate areas when the condition says perimeters.

methods.title: Model an unshaded area
methods.when: A rectangle or other region has a piece removed.
methods.rule: Unshaded area = whole area − shaded area, in square units.
steps: Label the sides of the whole shape and of the removed piece.
Write both areas as products before you subtract.
Put brackets around the whole area you are taking away.
Multiply out, solve for x using the area given, and check that the lengths make sense.
methods.example: (x+5)(x+2)−x(x+1)=6 x+10; if the area is 46, then x=6.
methods.trap: A minus sign before a bracket changes every sign inside.

methods.title: Divide by a single term
methods.when: You are dividing by a single term, such as 4x.
methods.rule: (A+B−C)/d=A/d+B/d−C/d, d≠0; x^m/x^n=x^(m−n) for x≠0.
steps: Divide every term on the top by the divisor.
Divide the numbers in front and subtract the powers of x.
State any value that would make the original bottom line zero.
methods.check: Multiplying 4 x(3 x²−2 x) recovers the numerator.
methods.trap: Do not divide only the first term. Every term on the top is divided.

methods.title: Divide by a binomial using a reverse grid
methods.when: You are dividing by a bracket such as x + 3.
methods.rule: Dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder; divisor ≠ 0.
steps: Find the first term of the answer: ask what x must be multiplied by to make the first term on the top.
Multiply that term by the whole divisor and take the product away from the top.
Use what is left to find the next term of the answer in the same way.
Carry on down to the plain number. Then multiply back to check, and state the value x cannot take.
methods.example: (x³+3 x²−4 x−12)/(x+3)=x²−4, x≠−3, because (x+3)(x²−4) gives the numerator.
methods.trap: Zero coefficients still need places: x³+0 x²−4 x cannot skip the x² position.

methods.title: Identify numbers and locate them
methods.when: A task asks about integer, rational, irrational or real values.
methods.rule: ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ; a rational is p/q with integers p,q and q≠0; the irrationals are ℝ\ℚ.
steps: Keep exact forms, such as a fraction or a square root, while you work.
Place a negative fraction between the two integers on either side of it, such as −7/4 between −2 and −1.
Place a square root by finding the square numbers (such as 4 and 9) on either side of the number under the root.
methods.check: −1.75 × 4 = −7, and 2² = 4 < 7 < 9 = 3² confirms both placements.
methods.trap: A decimal that goes on for ever but repeats, such as 0.333…, is rational.

methods.title: Solve and display an inequality
methods.when: The question has an inequality sign instead of an equals sign.
methods.rule: Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality; other balance operations preserve it.
steps: Simplify both sides.
Get x on its own. Turn the sign around each time you multiply or divide by a negative.
Draw an open circle for less than or greater than. Draw a filled circle when "or equal to" is included.
Keep only the values the question allows, such as whole numbers or positive lengths.
methods.example: 5−2 x≥11 → −2 x≥6 → x≤−3. Integer solutions include −3,−4,−5,…
methods.check: x=−4 gives 13≥11, while x=0 fails.
methods.trap: Do not turn the sign around just because a negative number is added or subtracted.

checks: Every box in the grid is filled and every term has been divided.
Negative values went in with brackets, and no bottom line is zero.
Your answer makes the original equation true and makes sense in the story, for example no negative lengths.
The inequality sign points the right way, and the circle is open or filled correctly.

challenges.title: Six products, then a fraction
challenges.question: Let P(x)=(2 x−1)(x²+3 x−2). (a) Expand and simplify P(x). (b) Find P(−2). (c) Set a=P(−2) and b=−5. Find ab/(a−b), and state the condition needed for this fraction to be defined.
hints: Draw a grid with two rows and three columns. Keep the minus signs with −1 and −2.
Once you know a, work out the top ab and the bottom a − b separately, then divide.

solution.title: Fill all six cells
solution.reason: Each term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second.

solution.title: Collect by degree
solution.reason: Only terms with the same power of x combine: 6x² − x² = 5x² and −4x − 3x = −7x.

solution.title: Substitute the signed input
solution.reason: With brackets, (−2)³ = −8 and (−2)² = 4. An odd power stays negative and an even power turns positive.

solution.title: Evaluate the fraction
solution.reason: The bottom is 20 − (−5) = 25, which is not zero. The fraction only makes sense when a and b are different.

challenges.answer: P(x)=2 x³+5 x²−7 x+2; P(−2)=20; the fraction is −4, requiring a≠b.
challenges.check: Directly in the brackets, P(−2)=(−5)(−4)=20; multiplying −4 by the denominator 25 returns the numerator −100.

challenges.title: Reverse a cubic multiplication
challenges.question: For x≠−3, let Q(x)=(2 x³+5 x²−4 x−3)/(x+3). (a) Find the quadratic quotient using a reverse grid or division. (b) Verify every coefficient by multiplication. (c) Find Q(2) from both forms.
hints: The first term of the answer must be 2x², because x × 2x² = 2x³.
Multiplying x + 3 by 2x² uses up 2x³ + 6x². You only have 5x², so −x² is left over to deal with next.

solution.title: Find the leading term
solution.reason: x times what gives 2x³? It must be 2x². Take 2x² lots of (x + 3) away from the top to see what is left.

solution.title: Continue with the remaining polynomial
solution.reason: x times what gives −x²? It must be −x. Take away the whole of −x lots of (x + 3), both terms.

solution.title: Complete the quotient
solution.reason: What is left is exactly −1 lot of (x + 3). Nothing remains, so the division is exact.

solution.title: Verify all terms
solution.reason: Multiplying back should rebuild every term of the top line. That checks the whole division.

solution.title: Evaluate and keep the restriction
solution.reason: Both forms give 5. The value x = −3 is still not allowed, because the original bottom line would be zero.

challenges.check: Coefficient-by-coefficient multiplication gives the original numerator; the independent numerical evaluation also agrees.

challenges.title: Equal fencing, different playing areas
challenges.question: Two rectangular training areas have dimensions in metres. Area A is (2 x+1) by (x−1); area B is (x+4) by (x+1). Their perimeters are equal. (a) Write and solve an equation for x. (b) Find each perimeter and area. (c) Decide which offers more playing space and by how much. Check that all lengths are physically possible.
hints: A rectangle's perimeter is two lengths plus two widths.
Solve 6x = 4x + 10 first. Then put x into each side length before finding the areas.

solution.title: Translate both perimeters
solution.math: Perimeter of A=2(2 x+1)+2(x−1)=6 x; perimeter of B=2(x+4)+2(x+1)=4 x+10
solution.reason: The question says the perimeters are equal, so write each perimeter first.

solution.title: Solve the shared condition
solution.reason: Subtract 4x from both sides to get 2x = 10, then divide both sides by 2.

solution.title: Find actual dimensions
solution.math: A:11 m by 4 m; B:9 m by 6 m
solution.reason: x = 5 is not the answer. Put it into each side length to get real measurements.

solution.title: Compare the areas
solution.math: Both perimeters are 30 m; area of A=44 m²; area of B=54 m²
solution.reason: Area is length times width.

solution.title: Interpret the result
solution.math: B offers 10 m² more; all four lengths are positive
solution.reason: The same amount of fencing can enclose different areas. Here the rectangle closer to a square holds more.

challenges.answer: x=5; both perimeters 30 m; areas 44 m² and 54 m²; B has 10 m² more.
challenges.check: Direct sums give 11+4+11+4=30 and 9+6+9+6=30; direct products give the two areas.

challenges.title: An area equation with cancelling squares
challenges.question: A rectangle is (x+6) cm wide and (x+2) cm high, with x>0. A shaded rectangle of width x cm and height (x+1) cm sits in its bottom-left corner. (a) Simplify the unshaded area. (b) Find x when this area is 68 cm². (c) Find all allowed x for which the unshaded area is at most 82 cm².
hints: Unshaded area = big rectangle − shaded rectangle. Put the shaded area in brackets when you subtract it.
The x² terms cancel, so the unshaded area has no x². The second part is an equation. The third part is an inequality, because "at most" allows equal or less.

solution.title: Write the area difference
solution.reason: The shaded piece sits inside the big rectangle, so take its area away from the whole.

solution.title: Expand and subtract
solution.reason: The minus sign in front of the bracket changes both signs inside: −x² and −x.

solution.title: Solve the specified area
solution.reason: Subtract 12 from both sides to get 7x = 56, then divide both sides by 7.

solution.title: Solve the upper bound
solution.reason: Subtract 12 to get 7x ≤ 70. Dividing by positive 7 leaves the sign as it is.

solution.title: Apply the physical restriction
solution.reason: A length cannot be zero or negative, and the question says x > 0. Combine that with x ≤ 10.

challenges.answer: U=(7 x+12) cm²; x=8 for U=68; the permitted range is 0<x≤10.
challenges.check: At x=8, the outer area is 14×10=140 and the shaded area is 8×9=72, leaving 68. At x=10 the unshaded area is exactly 82.

title: Factors
intro: Factorising is multiplying out brackets in reverse. You start with the expanded expression and find the brackets that made it. You can always check by multiplying back.

lessons.title: Take out the highest common factor
lessons.goal: Find the biggest number and the letters that divide into every term, and take them outside a bracket.

steps.title: Compare the coefficients
steps.text: Factorise 12x²y + 18xy². Start with the numbers. The biggest number that divides into both 12 and 18 is 6. This is their highest common factor, or HCF.
steps.why: A common factor has to divide into every term, not just one of them.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Compare the coefficients</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">12x²y + 18xy²</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Compare the coefficients</text></svg>

steps.title: Include shared variable factors
steps.text: Now the letters. Both terms have at least one x and at least one y. Take the smaller power of each letter: one x and one y.
steps.why: If you took x² outside, the second term has only one x to give. You would be left with a fraction inside the bracket.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Include shared variable factors</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">12x²y + 18xy²</text><rect id="row1" x="30" y="97" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num1" x="48" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">02</text><text id="math1" x="95" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">HCF = 6xy</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Include shared variable factors</text></svg>

steps.title: Divide each term by the HCF
steps.text: Divide each term by 6xy. The first term leaves 2x and the second leaves 3y. What is left goes inside the bracket.
steps.why: The outside factor times each term inside must give back the term you started with.

steps.title: Expand to check
steps.text: Multiply 6xy by each term inside the bracket. You get the two terms you started with, so the answer is right.
steps.why: Factorising and multiplying out are opposites, so multiplying out is always the check.

quiz.question: Factorise 8x² + 12x fully.
quiz.hint: Find the biggest number that divides 8 and 12. Then check whether both terms also share an x.
quiz.explanation: 8x² + 12x = 4x(2x + 3). The biggest shared factor is 4x. The answers 4(2x² + 3x) and 2x(4x + 6) are true but not finished, because their brackets still share a factor.

quiz.question: Factorise 5x + 15.
quiz.hint: The terms share the number 5 but not the letter x.
quiz.explanation: 5x + 15 = 5(x + 3). Both terms share the factor 5. Check: 5 × x = 5x and 5 × 3 = 15.

lessons.takeaway: Take out the biggest shared number and the lowest shared power of each letter. Then multiply back to check.
lessons.mistake: Leaving a gap or a 0 when a whole term is taken out. 6xy ÷ 6xy is 1, not 0, so 18x³y − 24x²y² + 6xy = 6xy(3x² − 4xy + 1).

lessons.title: Factorise by grouping
lessons.goal: Factorise four terms in two pairs so that the same bracket appears twice, then take that bracket out.

steps.title: Choose helpful groups
steps.text: Factorise ax + ay + 3x + 3y. No factor is shared by all four terms. But the first two terms share the letter a, and the last two share 3.
steps.why: You pair the terms hoping that both pairs leave the same bracket behind.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Choose helpful groups</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">(ax + ay) + (3x + 3y)</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Choose helpful groups</text></svg>

steps.title: Factorise each pair
steps.text: Take the letter a out of the first pair and 3 out of the second. Both brackets are x + y.
steps.why: Each pair is a small common-factor question, like the ones in lesson 2.1.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Factorise each pair</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">(ax + ay) + (3x + 3y)</text><rect id="row1" x="30" y="97" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num1" x="48" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">02</text><text id="math1" x="95" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">a(x + y) + 3(x + y)</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Factorise each pair</text></svg>

steps.title: Collect the repeated bracket
steps.text: The first part is a times (x + y). The second part is 3 times (x + y). Altogether that is (a + 3) times (x + y).
steps.why: Treat the whole bracket like a single letter. 5k + 3k = (5 + 3)k works the same way.

steps.title: Check the four products
steps.text: Multiply out (a + 3)(x + y). You should get all four terms back, each with the right sign.
steps.why: One correct term does not prove the answer. All four must match.

quiz.question: Factorise bx + by + 2x + 2y.
quiz.hint: Take a common factor out of each pair and look for a repeated bracket.

quiz.question: Factorise ax − ay + 4x − 4y.
quiz.hint: Take the letter a out of the first pair and 4 out of the second. What bracket is left each time?

lessons.takeaway: Factorise each pair, make the two brackets match exactly, then take the matching bracket out.
lessons.mistake: Treating x − y and y − x as the same bracket. They are opposites: y − x = −(x − y). Take out a negative factor to make the brackets match.

lessons.title: Difference of two squares
lessons.goal: Spot a square minus a square and write it as two brackets, one with minus and one with plus.

steps.title: Look for the special pattern
steps.text: Factorise 9x² − 25. Both terms are squares, and there is a minus between them.
steps.why: Without two squares, or without the minus, this pattern cannot be used.

steps.title: Find the two building blocks
steps.text: Ask what was squared to make each term. 3x squared is 9x² and 5 squared is 25. So 3x and 5 go in both brackets.
steps.why: Squaring 3x gives 9x², and squaring 5 gives 25.

steps.text: Write (3x − 5)(3x + 5). One bracket has minus and the other has plus.
steps.why: The opposite signs make the two middle terms cancel when you multiply out.

steps.text: Multiply out to check. The middle terms are +15x and −15x, which add to zero. The last term is −5 × 5 = −25.
steps.why: This is why the pattern always works: the middle terms always cancel.

quiz.question: Factorise x² − 49.
quiz.hint: 49 is 7 squared.

quiz.question: Which expression is a difference of two squares?
quiz.hint: Look for two squares with a minus between them.
quiz.explanation: x² − 16 = x² − 4², a square minus a square. x² + 16 has a plus, so the pattern does not apply. x² − 8x + 16 has three terms, so it is a different pattern.

lessons.takeaway: A square minus a square becomes (first − second)(first + second).
lessons.mistake: Using this pattern on a sum such as x² + 9. The pattern needs a minus. x² + 9 does not factorise into brackets with real numbers.

lessons.title: Factorise x² + bx + c: sum and product
lessons.goal: Find two numbers that multiply to the last number and add to the number in front of x.

steps.title: Read both clues
steps.text: Factorise x² + x − 12. The number in front of x² (its coefficient) is 1. You need two numbers that multiply to −12 and add to +1, because x means 1x.
steps.why: Multiply out (x + p)(x + q) and you get x² + (p + q)x + pq. The sum lands in the middle and the product at the end.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Read both clues</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">pq = −12; p + q = 1</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Read both clues</text></svg>

steps.title: Choose signs and test pairs
steps.text: The product is negative, so one number is positive and one is negative. Try the pairs that make 12: 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4. Only +4 and −3 add to +1.
steps.why: Plenty of pairs multiply to −12. Only one pair also adds to +1.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Choose signs and test pairs</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">pq = −12; p + q = 1</text><rect id="row1" x="30" y="97" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num1" x="48" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">02</text><text id="math1" x="95" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">4×(−3) = −12; 4 − 3 = 1</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Choose signs and test pairs</text></svg>

steps.title: Build the brackets
steps.text: Put +4 in one bracket and −3 in the other. It does not matter which bracket you write first.
steps.why: 3 × 5 and 5 × 3 are equal. Brackets multiply in either order too.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Build the brackets</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">pq = −12; p + q = 1</text><rect id="row1" x="30" y="97" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num1" x="48" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">02</text><text id="math1" x="95" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">4×(−3) = −12; 4 − 3 = 1</text><rect id="row2" x="30" y="169" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num2" x="48" y="208" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">03</text><text id="math2" x="95" y="208" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">x² + x − 12 = (x + 4)(x − 3)</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Build the brackets</text></svg>

steps.title: Expand as a check
steps.text: Multiply out to check. The middle terms −3x and +4x add to +x. The last term is 4 × (−3) = −12.
steps.why: Every term must match the one you started with, signs included.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Expand as a check</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">pq = −12; p + q = 1</text><rect id="row1" x="30" y="97" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num1" x="48" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">02</text><text id="math1" x="95" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">4×(−3) = −12; 4 − 3 = 1</text><rect id="row2" x="30" y="169" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num2" x="48" y="208" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">03</text><text id="math2" x="95" y="208" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">x² + x − 12 = (x + 4)(x − 3)</text><rect id="row3" x="30" y="241" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num3" x="48" y="280" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">04</text><text id="math3" x="95" y="280" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">x² − 3x + 4x − 12 = x² + x − 12</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Expand as a check</text></svg>

quiz.question: Factorise x² + 7x + 12.
quiz.hint: Find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7.

quiz.question: Factorise x² − 2x − 15.
quiz.hint: The product −15 is negative, so the signs are different. The sum −2 is negative, so the bigger number gets the minus.

lessons.takeaway: The two numbers multiply to the last number and add to the number in front of x. Check both.
lessons.mistake: Choosing a pair with the right product but the wrong sum. For x² + x − 12, the pair −4 and +3 multiplies to −12 but adds to −1. You need +4 and −3.

lessons.title: Factorise ax² + bx + c when a ≠ 1
lessons.goal: When the number in front of x² is not 1, split the middle term in two and then factorise by grouping.

steps.title: Multiply the outer coefficients
steps.text: Factorise 2x² + 7x + 3. Multiply the first number by the last: 2 × 3 = 6. Now find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 7. They are 6 and 1.
steps.why: These two numbers tell you how to split 7x so that grouping will work.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Multiply the outer coefficients</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">2×3 = 6; 6 + 1 = 7</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Multiply the outer coefficients</text></svg>

steps.title: Split the middle term
steps.text: Write 7x as 6x + x. Nothing has changed in value, because 6x + x is still 7x.
steps.why: You usually add like terms together. Here you do the opposite, and it is just as allowed.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Split the middle term</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">2×3 = 6; 6 + 1 = 7</text><rect id="row1" x="30" y="97" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num1" x="48" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">02</text><text id="math1" x="95" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">2x² + 6x + x + 3</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Split the middle term</text></svg>

steps.title: Factorise both groups
steps.text: Factorise each pair. The first pair shares 2x and leaves x + 3. The second pair, x + 3, has no shared factor, so write it as 1(x + 3).
steps.why: Both pairs now show the same bracket, x + 3. That tells you the split was right.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Factorise both groups</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">2×3 = 6; 6 + 1 = 7</text><rect id="row1" x="30" y="97" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num1" x="48" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">02</text><text id="math1" x="95" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">2x² + 6x + x + 3</text><rect id="row2" x="30" y="169" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num2" x="48" y="208" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">03</text><text id="math2" x="95" y="208" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3)</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Factorise both groups</text></svg>

steps.title: Finish and multiply back
steps.text: Take out the bracket x + 3 to get (2x + 1)(x + 3). Multiply out to check: 2x², 6x, x and 3. The middle terms add to 7x.
steps.why: Multiplying back takes seconds and catches sign slips.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Finish and multiply back</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">2×3 = 6; 6 + 1 = 7</text><rect id="row1" x="30" y="97" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num1" x="48" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">02</text><text id="math1" x="95" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">2x² + 6x + x + 3</text><rect id="row2" x="30" y="169" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num2" x="48" y="208" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">03</text><text id="math2" x="95" y="208" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3)</text><rect id="row3" x="30" y="241" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num3" x="48" y="280" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">04</text><text id="math3" x="95" y="280" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">2x² + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3)</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Finish and multiply back</text></svg>

quiz.question: Factorise 3x² + 7x + 2.
quiz.hint: First × last is 3 × 2 = 6. Which two numbers multiply to 6 and add to 7?

quiz.question: For 2x² + 9x + 4, which split is useful?
quiz.hint: The split numbers multiply to 8 and add to 9.

lessons.takeaway: Multiply the first and last numbers, find the pair, split the middle term, group, then multiply back to check.
lessons.mistake: Looking for numbers that multiply to the last number only. When the number in front of x² is not 1, they must multiply to first × last. For 2x² + 7x + 3 that is 6, not 3.

lessons.title: Cancel factors, not terms
lessons.goal: Simplify an algebraic fraction by cancelling a whole factor, and keep a note of any value x is not allowed to take.

steps.title: Find the excluded value
steps.text: Simplify (x² − 4)/(x − 2). First look at the bottom (the denominator). It is zero when x = 2, and you cannot divide by zero. So write x ≠ 2 straight away.
steps.why: Dividing by zero has no answer, so x = 2 is not allowed.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Cancel a whole common factor, retaining the original restriction.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><text id="restriction" x="380" y="70" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">Original restriction: x ≠ 2</text><text id="numerator" x="380" y="160" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="34" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">x² − 4</text><line id="bar" x1="255" y1="180" x2="505" y2="180" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text id="denominator" x="380" y="230" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="34" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">x − 2</text></svg>

steps.title: Factorise the numerator
steps.text: The top (the numerator) is a square minus a square, so it factorises as (x − 2)(x + 2). Leave the bottom as it is.
steps.why: You can only cancel something that multiplies the whole top and the whole bottom. Factorising shows you what that is.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Cancel a whole common factor, retaining the original restriction.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><text id="restriction" x="380" y="70" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">Original restriction: x ≠ 2</text><rect id="commonTop" x="180" y="110" width="170" height="65" rx="10" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text id="factor1" x="265" y="153" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">(x − 2)</text><text id="factor2" x="465" y="153" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">(x + 2)</text><line id="bar" x1="160" y1="195" x2="610" y2="195" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><rect id="commonBottom" x="180" y="220" width="170" height="65" rx="10" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text id="factor3" x="265" y="263" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">(x − 2)</text></svg>

steps.title: Cancel the common non-zero factor
steps.text: The bracket x − 2 is a factor of the top, and it is the whole bottom. Dividing it by itself gives 1, so x + 2 is left.
steps.why: Any number except zero divided by itself is 1, like 7 ÷ 7.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Cancel a whole common factor, retaining the original restriction.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff" /><text id="restriction" x="380" y="70" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">Original restriction: x ≠ 2</text><rect id="commonTop" x="180" y="110" width="170" height="65" rx="10" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="factor1" x="265" y="153" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">(x − 2)</text><text id="factor2" x="465" y="153" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">(x + 2)</text><line id="bar" x1="160" y1="195" x2="610" y2="195" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3" /><rect id="commonBottom" x="180" y="220" width="170" height="65" rx="10" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="factor3" x="265" y="263" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">(x − 2)</text><text id="why" x="380" y="340" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">common factor ÷ itself = 1</text><line data-cancel-target="factor1" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linecap="round" aria-hidden="true" x1="204.200" y1="153.708" x2="325.800" y2="134.010" /><line data-cancel-target="factor3" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linecap="round" aria-hidden="true" x1="204.200" y1="263.708" x2="325.800" y2="244.010" /></svg>

steps.title: Keep the original restriction
steps.text: Write the answer as x + 2, with x ≠ 2 beside it. Put x = 2 into the fraction you started with and the bottom is zero. Cancelling does not make that division possible.
steps.why: x + 2 matches the original fraction for every x except 2, where the original has no value.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Cancel a whole common factor, retaining the original restriction.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><text id="restriction" x="380" y="70" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">Original restriction: x ≠ 2</text><text id="result" x="380" y="200" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="44" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">x + 2</text><text id="keep" x="380" y="285" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">Still exclude x = 2.</text></svg>

quiz.question: Simplify (x² − 9)/(x + 3).
quiz.hint: Factorise the top as a square minus a square. Then ask which x makes the bottom, x + 3, equal to zero.
quiz.explanation: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3)(x + 3)/(x + 3) = x − 3. The original bottom, x + 3, is zero when x = −3, so x ≠ −3.

quiz.question: Which cancellation is valid?
quiz.hint: You can only cancel something that multiplies the whole top and the whole bottom.
quiz.explanation: 3x means 3 × x, so x is a factor and cancels: 3x/x = 3 when x ≠ 0. In the others the top is a sum, such as x + 3, and part of a sum cannot be cancelled.

lessons.takeaway: Note the values that make the bottom zero, factorise, cancel whole factors, and keep the note with your answer.
lessons.mistake: Crossing out single terms joined by plus or minus. (x + 3)/x is not 3. Test x = 1: (1 + 3)/1 = 4, not 3.

reference.name: Common factor
reference.note: Divide every original term by the outside factor.

reference.name: Grouping
reference.formula: ax + ay + bx + by = (a + b)(x + y)
reference.note: The grouped brackets must match.

reference.name: Difference of squares
reference.note: Two squares separated by subtraction.

reference.name: Quadratic factors
reference.note: The two numbers add to the middle coefficient and multiply to the constant.

reference.name: Cancel factors
reference.note: B and C must be non-zero. Never cancel terms of a sum.

toolkit.strategy: Look for a common factor first. Then inspect the number of terms: two squares, a quadratic, or four terms that can be grouped. In a fraction, finish factorising both numerator and denominator before cancelling.

methods.title: Extract the highest common factor first
methods.when: All terms share a number, letter or power.
methods.rule: HCF = numerical HCF × lowest power shared by every term.
steps: Find the numerical HCF.
Take the lowest shared power of each letter.
Divide every term by this factor.
Inspect the remaining bracket for another pattern.
methods.check: Multiply the three factors to recover 12 x³−48 x.
methods.trap: Stopping after the common factor. Check the bracket that is left: here x² − 4 is a square minus a square and factorises again.

methods.title: Group terms, including negative groups
methods.when: Four terms can produce a repeated bracket.
methods.rule: ap+aq+bp+bq=(a+b)(p+q); a negative factor reverses signs inside its bracket.
steps: Group pairs that can share the same bracket.
Factorise each pair, choosing a negative factor if needed.
Treat the matching bracket as one factor.
Check whether either factor can be factorised further.
methods.check: At x=4, both original and factorised forms are zero; expansion checks all coefficients.
methods.trap: x−4 and 4−x are opposites, not the same bracket.

methods.title: Recognise a difference of squares
methods.when: Two square terms are separated by subtraction.
methods.rule: a²−b²=(a−b)(a+b), over the reals.
steps: Take out any common factor first.
Ask what was squared to give each term.
Write a minus bracket and a plus bracket.
methods.check: The cross-products +20 x and −20 x cancel.
methods.trap: a² + b² has a plus between the squares, so this rule does not apply to it.

methods.title: Factorise x² + bx + c
methods.when: The quadratic begins with x².
methods.rule: x²+bx+c=(x+p)(x+q) if p+q=b, pq=c. Special cases: x²±2 ax+a²=(x±a)².
steps: List factor pairs of c.
Use the sign of c and b to choose signs.
Check both the sum and the product.
methods.check: Expand the middle terms: 4 x−5 x=−x.
methods.trap: A correct product alone is not enough.

methods.title: Factorise ax² + bx + c when a ≠ 1
methods.when: The coefficient of x² is not 1.
methods.rule: For ax²+bx+c, split bx using m+n=b and mn=ac.
steps: Check for an HCF first.
Multiply a by c and find the split pair.
Split only the middle term.
Factorise by grouping and multiply back.
methods.check: The first, middle and last coefficients are 6, 9−2=7 and −3.
methods.trap: Do not use c alone when searching for the split pair.

methods.title: Simplify a fraction with full restrictions
methods.when: The top and the bottom of a fraction are both sums that can be factorised.
methods.rule: N/D may cancel a common factor only where the original D≠0.
steps: Factorise the bottom of the original fraction and list every value that makes it zero.
Factorise the numerator fully.
Cancel entire common factors.
Write the simplified answer together with every excluded value.
methods.check: At x=0 both forms give 2; x=4 remains excluded although the simplified formula has a value there.
methods.trap: The simplified bottom does not show every excluded value. Take them from the original fraction.

methods.title: Handle a cubic denominator or numerator
methods.when: A fraction has an x³ term on the top or the bottom.
methods.rule: Use HCF or grouping to reduce the cubic to a linear factor times a quadratic.
steps: Look for a shared x or a common bracket.
Factorise the remaining quadratic fully.
Before cancelling, list the value that makes each factor on the bottom zero.
methods.check: Multiplying x(x+1)(x+3) gives x³+4 x²+3 x.
methods.trap: Do not cancel an x from a sum such as x³ + 4x² + 3x until you have factorised it.

checks: No common factor remains hidden inside the brackets.
Multiplication reproduces every original coefficient and sign.
Every original denominator zero is excluded, even after cancellation.
Cancellation removed whole factors, never parts of sums.

challenges.title: Choose the pattern, then finish it
challenges.question: (a) Factorise 6 x³−54 x completely. (b) Factorise 3 x²+8 x+4 completely. (c) For each expression, verify your factors by expansion and by substituting x=1.
hints: In the first expression, take out 6x first. Then look at the bracket: is it a square minus a square?
For the second expression, split 8 x into 6 x+2 x.

solution.title: Remove the common factor
solution.reason: Both terms contain 6 x.

solution.title: Complete the square pattern
solution.reason: x² − 9 is a square minus a square, because 9 = 3².

solution.title: Split the middle term when a ≠ 1
solution.reason: The split numbers 6 and 2 multiply to 12 and add to 8.

solution.title: Finish and check coefficients
solution.reason: Multiplying out gives 3x² + 6x + 2x + 4, and the middle terms add to 8x.

solution.title: Check at one
solution.reason: Putting in a number is a second way to catch a wrong sign or a wrong coefficient.

challenges.answer: (a) 6 x(x−3)(x+3). (b) (3 x+2)(x+2). At x=1 the values are −48 and 15.
challenges.check: Multiplying out the factors gives back both expressions exactly, so the factorisations are right for every value of x.

challenges.title: A cubic denominator with a hidden exclusion
challenges.question: Consider F(x)=(2 x²+7 x+3)/(x³+4 x²+3 x). (a) State every excluded input. (b) Simplify completely. (c) Find F(2). (d) Is x=−3 permitted after cancellation? Explain.
hints: Take x out of the denominator, then factorise the quadratic left behind.
The top factorises as (2x + 1)(x + 3). Keep all three excluded values after you cancel.

solution.title: Factorise the original denominator
solution.reason: Every term on the bottom has an x. Take it out and a simpler quadratic, x² + 4x + 3, is left to factorise.

solution.title: Record the original domain
solution.reason: If any factor on the bottom is zero, the whole bottom is zero, and you cannot divide by zero.

solution.title: Factorise the numerator and cancel
solution.reason: The bracket x + 3 multiplies the whole top and the whole bottom, so it cancels. The three excluded values stay.

solution.title: Evaluate a valid input
solution.reason: x = 2 is not one of the excluded values, so you can put it in.

solution.title: Retain the hidden exclusion
solution.reason: At x = −3 the original fraction is 0 ÷ 0, which has no value. Cancelling does not change that.

challenges.answer: Excluded inputs: 0,−1,−3. F(x)=(2 x+1)/(x(x+1)) on that domain; F(2)=5/6; −3 remains excluded.
challenges.check: At x=2 the original numerator is 25 and denominator is 30, also giving 5/6.

challenges.title: Grouping, cancellation and an output condition
challenges.question: Let G(x)=(x³−2 x²−9 x+18)/(x²−5 x+6). (a) Factorise both polynomials completely and state the excluded inputs. (b) Simplify G(x). (c) Solve G(x)=10. (d) Explain why substituting x=2 into the simplified expression does not give G(2).
hints: Group the cubic as x²(x−2)−9(x−2).
The denominator factors as (x−2)(x−3).

solution.title: Expose the repeated bracket
solution.reason: Group the top as x²(x − 2) − 9(x − 2). The bracket x − 2 comes out and leaves x² − 9.

solution.title: Factorise the denominator
solution.reason: x² − 9 is a square minus a square. The bottom is zero at x = 2 and x = 3, so those values are not allowed.

solution.title: Cancel only common factors
solution.reason: Each matching bracket divided by itself is 1, as long as x is not 2 or 3.

solution.title: Solve the output condition
solution.reason: 7 is not one of the excluded values, so it is allowed as an answer.

solution.title: Explain the excluded input
solution.math: At x=2, the original expression is 0/0, not 5
solution.reason: x + 3 equals the original fraction only where the original has a value. At x = 2 it has none.

challenges.answer: Numerator (x−2)(x−3)(x+3); denominator (x−2)(x−3); G=x+3 for x≠2,3; G(x)=10 gives x=7.

challenges.title: Recover the side of a rectangle
challenges.question: A rectangle has area 6 x²−x−2 square units and one side 2 x+1 units. (a) Factorise the area and find the other side. (b) Determine the allowed real values of x for a genuine rectangle with both sides positive. (c) Find x when the rectangle is a square, and find its area then.
hints: First × last is 6 × (−2) = −12. Find two numbers that multiply to −12 and add to −1.
The other factor is 3 x−2. A square needs the two positive side lengths to be equal.

solution.title: Split and group the area
solution.reason: 3 and −4 have product −12 and sum −1.

solution.title: Read off the other side
solution.math: A=(3 x−2)(2 x+1), so the other side is 3 x−2
solution.reason: Area is the product of the side lengths.

solution.title: Use both positivity conditions
solution.reason: Both sides must be longer than zero. The first needs x > −1/2 and the second needs x > 2/3. Both are true only when x > 2/3.

solution.title: Impose the square condition
solution.reason: A square has all sides equal, so set the two sides equal to each other.

solution.title: Find the actual size
solution.math: Both sides are 7; area=49 square units
solution.reason: x = 3 is bigger than 2/3, so both sides are positive. Each side is 7 units.

challenges.answer: Other side 3 x−2; allowed x>2/3; square at x=3, with side 7 and area 49.
challenges.check: The original area at x=3 is 54−3−2=49; dividing it by the known side 7 gives 7.

title: Sets
intro: A set is a collection of things, called its elements. A Venn diagram sorts people into regions so that you count each person once.

lessons.title: Membership, subsets and number families
lessons.goal: Read set symbols as plain sentences: belongs to, does not belong to, is a subset of.

steps.title: Decide membership
steps.text: Let A = {2, 4, 6}. The number 4 belongs to A, but 5 does not. A has three different elements, so n(A) = 3. Irish exam papers write this as #A = 3.
steps.why: For any number, you must be able to say clearly whether it is in the set or not.

steps.title: Tell an element from a subset
steps.text: The number 2 is an element of A. The set {2, 4} is a subset because every one of its elements belongs to A.
steps.why: An element is one member. A subset is a set, so it needs its own curly brackets.
