steps.title: Nest the number families
steps.text: The natural numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on lie inside the integers. The integers lie inside the rationals, which are the fractions. The rationals lie inside the reals. Zero is an integer but not a natural number.
steps.why: Every integer is also a fraction, because you can write it over 1. For example, 5 = 5/1.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Number families nest; real numbers also include irrationals.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="set0" x="45" y="45" width="670" height="310" rx="13" fill="#fff" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text id="setlabel0" x="60" y="77" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">Real ℝ</text><rect id="set1" x="80" y="100" width="490" height="230" rx="13" fill="#fff" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="setlabel1" x="95" y="132" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Rational ℚ</text><rect id="set2" x="120" y="155" width="300" height="150" rx="13" fill="#fff" stroke="#7650a0" stroke-width="2"/><text id="setlabel2" x="135" y="187" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#7650a0" text-anchor="start">Integer ℤ</text><rect id="set3" x="155" y="210" width="150" height="70" rx="13" fill="#fff" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="2"/><text id="setlabel3" x="170" y="242" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">Natural ℕ</text><text id="integer" x="350" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#7650a0" text-anchor="start">−2</text><text id="rational" x="470" y="230" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">1/2</text><text id="irrational" x="635" y="210" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">√2</text></svg>

steps.title: Ignore order and repeated entries
steps.text: The sets {2, 4, 6} and {6, 2, 4} are equal. The empty set has no elements, while {0} has one.
steps.why: Only the members matter, not the order. The set {0} is not empty, because it contains the number 0.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>An empty set differs from a set whose one element is zero.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><circle id="empty" cx="230" cy="190" r="90" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><circle id="zero-set" cx="530" cy="190" r="90" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="zero" x="530" y="200" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="36" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">0</text><text id="empty-label" x="230" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">∅: no elements</text><text id="zero-label" x="530" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">{0}: one element</text></svg>

quiz.question: For A = {1,3,5}, which statement is correct?
quiz.hint: A subset is a set, so look for curly brackets on the left of the subset sign.
quiz.explanation: 1 and 5 are both in A, so {1,5} is a subset of A. The statement 3 ⊂ A is wrong because 3 is an element, not a set. Write 3 ∈ A.

quiz.question: Which inclusion is correct?
quiz.hint: Every integer can be written over 1.
quiz.explanation: Every integer is a fraction over 1, so the integers sit inside the rationals. The reverse fails: 1/2 is rational but not an integer.

lessons.takeaway: An element belongs to a set: 4 ∈ A. A subset is a whole set inside another set: {2, 4} ⊂ A.
lessons.mistake: Thinking {0} is the empty set. {0} has one element, the number 0. The empty set has none.

lessons.title: Union, intersection and complement
lessons.goal: Find the region that union, intersection and complement each describe.

steps.title: Find the overlap
steps.text: Use U = {1,2,3,4,5,6}, A = {1,2,3}, B = {3,4}. Only 3 belongs to both A and B.
steps.why: 3 is in A and in B, so it goes once in the overlap, not once in each circle.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Intersection: in both</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="universal" x="25" y="20" width="710" height="330" rx="5" fill="#f7fafc" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="2"/><circle id="set0" cx="290" cy="165" r="100" fill="#087f75" fill-opacity="0.10" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="setlabel0" x="290" y="65" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">A</text><circle id="set1" cx="465" cy="165" r="100" fill="#3175ba" fill-opacity="0.10" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="setlabel1" x="465" y="65" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">B</text><circle id="pick1" cx="378" cy="165" r="21" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="tick1" x="378" y="173" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">✓</text><text id="label0" x="35" y="365" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Intersection: in both</text></svg>

steps.title: Gather the union
steps.text: Union means in either set, including both. Combine the members without repeating 3.
steps.why: In maths, “or” includes the case where both are true, so the overlap belongs to the union.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Union: either or both</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="universal" x="25" y="20" width="710" height="330" rx="5" fill="#f7fafc" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="2"/><circle id="set0" cx="290" cy="165" r="100" fill="#087f75" fill-opacity="0.10" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="setlabel0" x="290" y="65" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">A</text><circle id="set1" cx="465" cy="165" r="100" fill="#3175ba" fill-opacity="0.10" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="setlabel1" x="465" y="65" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">B</text><circle id="pick0" cx="245" cy="165" r="21" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="tick0" x="245" y="173" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">✓</text><circle id="pick1" cx="378" cy="165" r="21" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="tick1" x="378" y="173" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">✓</text><circle id="pick2" cx="510" cy="165" r="21" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="tick2" x="510" y="173" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">✓</text><text id="label0" x="35" y="365" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Union: either or both</text></svg>

steps.title: Take the complement
steps.text: The complement of A consists of the elements in U but not in A. Keep 4, 5 and 6.
steps.why: The complement is everything else in the universal set U. Change U and the complement changes too.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Complement: outside A, inside U</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="universal" x="25" y="20" width="710" height="330" rx="5" fill="#f7fafc" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="2"/><circle id="set0" cx="290" cy="165" r="100" fill="#087f75" fill-opacity="0.10" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="setlabel0" x="290" y="65" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">A</text><circle id="set1" cx="465" cy="165" r="100" fill="#3175ba" fill-opacity="0.10" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="setlabel1" x="465" y="65" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">B</text><circle id="pick2" cx="510" cy="165" r="21" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="tick2" x="510" y="173" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">✓</text><circle id="pick3" cx="655" cy="285" r="21" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="tick3" x="655" y="293" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">✓</text><text id="label0" x="35" y="365" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Complement: outside A, inside U</text></svg>

steps.title: Use commutativity and associativity
steps.text: You can swap the order in a union or an intersection. This is called commutative. You can also move the brackets. This is called associative. The answer stays the same.
steps.why: Union asks “in at least one set” and intersection asks “in all of them”. Neither depends on the order.
steps.math: A ∪ B = B ∪ A; (A ∩ B) ∩ C = A ∩ (B ∩ C)
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Union and intersection ignore set order</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="universal" x="25" y="20" width="710" height="330" rx="5" fill="#f7fafc" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="2"/><circle id="set0" cx="290" cy="165" r="100" fill="#087f75" fill-opacity="0.10" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="setlabel0" x="290" y="65" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">A</text><circle id="set1" cx="465" cy="165" r="100" fill="#3175ba" fill-opacity="0.10" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="setlabel1" x="465" y="65" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">B</text><circle id="pick0" cx="245" cy="165" r="21" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="tick0" x="245" y="173" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">✓</text><circle id="pick1" cx="378" cy="165" r="21" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="tick1" x="378" y="173" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">✓</text><circle id="pick2" cx="510" cy="165" r="21" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="tick2" x="510" y="173" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">✓</text><text id="label0" x="35" y="365" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Union and intersection ignore set order</text></svg>

quiz.question: If A = {1,2,3} and B = {3,4,5}, find A ∩ B.
quiz.hint: Intersection means in both sets.
quiz.explanation: Only 3 belongs to both sets. {1,2,3,4,5} is the union, which is the usual mix-up.

quiz.question: U = {1,2,3,4,5}; A = {2,4}. Find A′.
quiz.hint: Remove A from the universal set.
quiz.explanation: The elements outside A but inside U are 1, 3 and 5.

lessons.takeaway: Union means in either set or both. Intersection means in both. Complement means everything else in the universal set.
lessons.mistake: Leaving the overlap out of a union. “A or B” includes the elements that are in both.

lessons.title: Set difference has a direction
lessons.goal: Find A \ B: keep the elements of the first set that are not in the second.

steps.title: Start with the first set
steps.text: For A = {1,2,3} and B = {3,4}, A \ B means “in A but not in B”. Start by writing out A.
steps.why: Only elements of the first set can be in the answer.

steps.text: Remove 3 because it belongs to B as well. Keep 1 and 2.
steps.why: Difference means in the first set and not the second.

quiz.question: A = {a,b,c}; B = {b,d}. Find A \ B.
quiz.hint: Start with A and remove the overlap.
quiz.explanation: b is in both sets, so remove it from A. That leaves {a,c}. The d never appears because it was not in A.

quiz.question: Which operation is not commutative?
quiz.hint: Swapping the first and second sets may change this answer.
quiz.explanation: Set difference depends on order; union and intersection do not.

lessons.takeaway: A \ B means start with A and remove anything that is also in B.
lessons.mistake: Treating A \ B and B \ A as the same. With A = {1,2,3} and B = {3,4}, A \ B = {1,2} but B \ A = {4}.

lessons.title: Fill three-set diagrams from the centre
lessons.goal: Fill a three-circle Venn diagram in the right order, starting from the centre.

steps.title: Fill the centre
steps.text: There are 2 elements in all three sets. Put 2 in the middle first.
steps.why: The centre lies inside every pair overlap. Fill it first so you can take it out of each pair total.

steps.text: The pair totals are n(A ∩ B) = 5, n(A ∩ C) = 4 and n(B ∩ C) = 3. Each includes the centre, so subtract the central 2 from each.
steps.why: “A and B only” means in A and B but not in C. So the centre must come out.
steps.math: AB only = 3; AC only = 2; BC only = 1

quiz.question: 12 people are in A ∩ B, including 4 in all three sets. How many are in A and B only?
quiz.hint: The pair total already includes the centre.
quiz.explanation: The 12 includes the 4 in all three. Take them out: 12 − 4 = 8.

quiz.question: Set A has 20 elements. AB-only is 5, AC-only is 3 and the centre is 2. Find A-only.
quiz.hint: Remove all three overlap regions inside A.
quiz.explanation: Take all three overlap regions out of A: 20 − 5 − 3 − 2 = 10.

lessons.takeaway: Fill in this order: centre, pair-only regions, single-only regions, then outside.
lessons.mistake: Writing a whole pair total in the pair-only region. If n(A ∩ B) = 5 and the centre is 2, the pair-only region is 5 − 2 = 3, not 5.

lessons.title: Solve a three-club survey
lessons.goal: Turn a survey in words into separate regions of a Venn diagram. Then make sure the totals fit.

steps.title: Record the full club totals
steps.text: 40 students choose clubs. Totals: rugby 22, maths 18, music 12. Pair totals: rugby and maths 10, rugby and music 6, maths and music 5. Three students join all three, so put 3 in the centre first. A, B and C stand for rugby, maths and music.
steps.why: An overlap total is not an extra group. It includes everyone in that overlap, including the centre.

steps.text: Subtract the triple 3 from each pair total. Rugby and maths only is 7, rugby and music only is 3, maths and music only is 2.
steps.why: Students in exactly two clubs are not in the centre, so take the 3 out of each pair total.

steps.why: If a circle does not add back to its club total, one of its regions is wrong.

quiz.question: The three pair-only club regions contain 7, 3 and 2 students; another 3 join all three. How many join exactly two clubs?
quiz.hint: Add the three pair-only regions.
quiz.explanation: 7 + 3 + 2 = 12. The all-three group is excluded.

quiz.question: The three pair-only club regions contain 7, 3 and 2 students; another 3 join all three. How many join at least two clubs?
quiz.hint: Include exactly two and all three.
quiz.explanation: 12 join exactly two and 3 join all three: 15 altogether.

lessons.takeaway: Exactly two leaves out the centre. At least two includes it.
lessons.mistake: Adding the three club totals to count the students. 22 + 18 + 12 = 52, but only 34 students are in a club. Those in two or three clubs were counted more than once.

reference.name: Union
reference.note: In A or B or both.

reference.name: Intersection
reference.note: In both sets.

reference.name: Difference
reference.note: In A but not B. Irish exam papers write set difference with a backslash: A \ B.

reference.name: Complement
reference.note: Inside the universal set, outside A.

reference.name: Two-set counting
reference.formula: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
reference.note: Adding the two totals counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once.

reference.name: Three-set counting
reference.note: Each pair total includes the centre. That is why the centre is added back once.

reference.name: Number families
reference.note: In Irish exams ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …}: 0 is an integer but not a natural number.

toolkit.strategy: Decide whether each number in the question is one region or a whole set. Fill the overlaps first, then use the totals. Count people, not memberships: a person in two clubs is still one person. No region can be negative.

methods.title: Read membership, cardinality and subset symbols
methods.when: The question asks about members, sizes or relationships between sets.
methods.rule: a∈A is membership; B⊂A means every member of B is in A; n(A), written #A on exam papers, counts distinct elements.
steps: Decide whether the item is an element or a set.
Ignore order and repeats when counting a set.
Use the stated universal set for complements.
methods.check: List all members of a proposed subset and check each lies in A.
methods.trap: {0} has one element; ∅ has none.

methods.title: Locate number families
methods.when: A set contains natural, integer, rational or real numbers.
methods.rule: ℕ⊂ℤ⊂ℚ⊂ℝ; the irrationals ℝ\ℚ are in ℝ but not ℚ.
steps: Remember ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …}: 0 is not a natural number.
A rational number can be written as an integer over a non-zero integer.
To show one family is not inside another, find one number that breaks the claim.
methods.example: −6∈ℤ and −6=−6/1∈ℚ, while √3∉ℚ.
methods.check: 1/2 is rational but not an integer, so ℚ is not a subset of ℤ.
methods.trap: Every integer is rational, but not every rational is an integer.

methods.title: Apply union, intersection, complement and their properties
methods.when: A statement uses “either”, “both”, “outside”, or regrouped set operations.
methods.rule: A∪B=B∪A; A∩B=B∩A; (A∪B)∪C=A∪(B∪C); (A∩B)∩C=A∩(B∩C). A′=U\A; n(A′)=n(U)−n(A).
steps: Read union as “in either or both” and intersection as “in all the sets named”.
Work inside brackets first.
Swapping or regrouping ∪ or ∩ does not change the result. Test a few elements to see this.
methods.check: Take each element in turn. Ask whether it is in the left-hand set and in the right-hand set.
methods.trap: A union includes its overlap.

methods.title: Respect the direction of set difference
methods.when: The task asks for A but not B.
methods.rule: A\B=A∩B′; in general, set difference is not commutative and not associative.
steps: Start with the first set.
Remove members that also lie in the second.
If there are brackets, work them out first, exactly as written.
methods.check: The element 3 is in one answer but not the other, so the two groupings differ.
methods.trap: Do not swap or regroup difference as if it were union.

methods.title: Fill three-set regions and inclusive intersections
methods.when: Three overlapping sets are described.
methods.rule: AB-only=n(A∩B)−n(A∩B∩C). n(A∪B∪C)=n(A)+n(B)+n(C)−n(A∩B)−n(A∩C)−n(B∩C)+n(A∩B∩C).
steps: Fill the centre, the region in all three sets.
Subtract it from each pair total to get the pair-only regions.
Subtract the three filled regions in each circle from that set’s total.
Add the seven regions for the union, then subtract from U for outside.
methods.example: If AB=11, triple=3, then AB-only=8; if A=25, AC-only=4, then A-only=25−8−4−3=10.
methods.check: Add the four regions in each set to recover its original total.
methods.trap: Writing the whole pair total in the pair-only region counts the centre twice.

methods.title: Find an unknown region or total
methods.when: Regions contain x, or the total of a set or of the union is missing.
methods.rule: Disjoint regions add without overlap; union = universal total − outside.
steps: Label each separate region once.
Pick a given total that includes the unknown region.
Form and solve the equation.
Make sure every region is a whole number that is not negative.
methods.example: Regions x, x+3 and 9 fill a universe of 30: 2 x+12=30 → x=9.
methods.check: The regions 9,12,9 add to 30.
methods.trap: A negative or fractional number of people means something was read or solved wrongly.

methods.title: Find feasible two-set bounds
methods.when: A set size, the overlap or the number outside is not fixed, so you need the smallest and largest possible values.
methods.rule: max(0,a+b−N)≤n(A∩B)≤min(a,b); n(A∪B)=a+b−overlap.
steps: Write union = a + b − overlap.
No region can be negative, including the outside region.
Turn those conditions into a smallest and a largest value.
Show an arrangement that reaches each of those values.
methods.example: In U of 50 with n(A)=32 and n(B)=27, overlap lies from 9 to 27; outside lies from 0 to 18.
methods.check: At overlap 9 the union is 50; at overlap 27 the union is 32.
methods.trap: The overlap can never be bigger than the smaller set.

methods.title: Combine percentages, ratios and memberships
methods.when: A Venn problem gives a percentage, a region ratio or total memberships.
methods.rule: Membership total = E₁+2 E₂+3 E₃; union = E₁+E₂+E₃.
steps: Turn each percentage into a count, using the total it is a percentage of.
Take out the known overlaps before sharing the “only” regions in a ratio.
Keep “exactly two” separate from “at least two”.
For memberships, count a person once for each set they are in.
methods.example: If 80 join at least one, 20 join both, and A-only:B-only=2:3, then the 60 single-only people split into 24 and 36.
methods.check: Set totals are 44 and 56; their sum 100 equals union 80 plus overlap 20.
methods.trap: A ratio of the “only” regions is not the ratio of the whole-set totals.

checks: Each person appears in exactly one separate Venn region.
Each pair total includes the centre region.
No region is negative, and all the regions add to the universal total.
A total of memberships can exceed the number of distinct people.

challenges.title: Solve a three-club region equation
challenges.question: A survey contains 50 students. For clubs A, B and C, the disjoint regions are: A-only=x, B-only=x+2, C-only=5, AB-only=4, AC-only=3, BC-only=2, all three=1, none=7. (a) Find x. (b) Find n(A), n(B), n(C) and n(A∩B). (c) Find the number joining at least one club and the total number of club memberships. Explain why those two totals differ.
hints: The eight regions do not overlap, so together they must add to 50.
A whole-circle total includes its single region, two pair-only regions and the centre.

solution.title: Use the universal total
solution.reason: The eight regions do not overlap and cover all 50 students. Add them and set the total equal to 50.

solution.title: Find the unknown
solution.reason: Take 24 from both sides, then divide both sides by 2. So A-only is 13 and B-only is 13 + 2 = 15.

solution.title: Recover whole-set totals
solution.reason: A whole circle is four regions: its single region, two pair-only regions and the centre.

solution.title: Read the inclusive pair and union
solution.reason: A ∩ B is AB-only plus the centre. At least one club means everyone except the 7 in none.

solution.title: Count memberships
solution.reason: Memberships count a student once for each club. The 9 students in exactly two clubs each add one extra, and the student in all three adds two extra: 9 + 2 = 11.

challenges.answer: x=13; n(A)=21, n(B)=22, n(C)=11; n(A∩B)=5; union 43 people, membership total 54.
challenges.check: Exactly one=33, exactly two=9, exactly three=1: 33+9+1=43 people, but 33+18+3=54 memberships.

challenges.title: Find the smallest and largest possible set
challenges.question: In a group of 80 students, 46 belong to A and 18 belong to neither A nor B. Write b=n(B). (a) Express n(A∩B) in terms of b. (b) Find the smallest and largest possible b, explaining how each can occur. (c) If 12 students belong to both, find all four disjoint region counts.
hints: You know how many are in A or B: everyone except the 18 in neither.
Write 46 + b − overlap = 62. The overlap cannot be negative and cannot be bigger than A, which has 46.

solution.title: Fix the union
solution.reason: Everyone except the 18 in neither is in A or B.

solution.title: Express the overlap
solution.reason: Adding 46 and b counts the overlap t twice, so subtract it once. Then solve for t.

solution.title: Apply feasibility
solution.reason: The overlap cannot be negative and cannot be bigger than A. Add 16 to each part to find the range for b.

solution.title: Show the extremes can occur
solution.math: b=16: B disjoint from A. b=62: B contains all of A and 16 further students.
solution.reason: A smallest or largest value only counts if it can really happen. Each of these can.

solution.title: Use the specified overlap
solution.math: t=12 → b=28; A-only=34, B-only=16, both=12, neither=18
solution.reason: With t = 12, b = 12 + 16 = 28. Take the 12 out of each set total: 46 − 12 = 34 and 28 − 12 = 16.

challenges.answer: Overlap=b−16; minimum b=16, maximum b=62. With overlap 12: A-only 34, B-only 16, both 12, neither 18.

challenges.title: Percentages and ratios in two clubs
challenges.question: Of 120 students, 25% join neither rugby nor music. Exactly 18 join both. The numbers in rugby-only and music-only are in the ratio 3:5. (a) Find all four regions. (b) Find each whole club total. (c) What percentage joins exactly one club? (d) Find the total memberships and explain how to check it.
hints: Take out the students in neither, then take out the 18 in both. Share what is left in the ratio 3:5.
The students in exactly one club are split into 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts.

solution.title: Convert the percentage
solution.reason: The 25% is a quarter of all 120 students. The other 90 are in at least one club.

solution.title: Find the exclusive total
solution.reason: The 90 includes the 18 in both. Take them out to leave the students in exactly one club.

solution.title: Apply the ratio
solution.reason: 3 + 5 = 8 parts share the 72 students, so one part is 9.

solution.title: Recover club totals and percentage
solution.reason: Each club total is its “only” region plus the 18 in both: 27 + 18 and 45 + 18.

solution.title: Count memberships
solution.reason: The 18 in both clubs are counted in each club total. So there are 18 more memberships than the 90 people.

challenges.answer: Rugby-only 27, music-only 45, both 18, neither 30; club totals 45 and 63; exactly one 60%; memberships 108.
challenges.check: 27+45+18+30=120 and 27:45=3:5; the membership identity gives 90+18=108.

challenges.title: Recover how many joined two or three
challenges.question: There are 100 students and three clubs. Ten students join none, 46 join exactly one, and the sum of the three whole-club totals is 142 memberships. (a) Find how many join exactly two clubs and all three clubs. (b) Decide whether the three individual club totals are uniquely determined. Support your answer by constructing two different valid arrangements.
hints: Let E₂ be the number in exactly two clubs and E₃ the number in all three. Count the people first. Then count memberships: 1, 2 or 3 for each person.
Use E₂+E₃=44 and 46+2 E₂+3 E₃=142.

solution.title: Count distinct people
solution.reason: 90 students join at least one club. 46 of them join exactly one, so the other 44 join two or three.

solution.title: Count memberships
solution.reason: A student in one club adds 1 membership, in two clubs adds 2 and in three clubs adds 3. The total is 142.

solution.title: Eliminate the double count
solution.reason: Double the first equation so both have 2E₂. Subtract to leave E₃ = 96 − 88 = 8. Then E₂ = 44 − 8 = 36.

solution.title: Construct one valid arrangement
solution.math: Single-only (A,B,C)=(20,16,10); pair-only (AB,AC,BC)=(12,14,10); triple=8; none=10. Club totals=(54,46,42).
solution.reason: Choose region sizes that fit every fact: 46 in exactly one, 36 in exactly two, 8 in all three and 10 in none.

solution.title: Construct a different arrangement
solution.math: Change single-only to (21,15,10), keeping all other regions. Club totals become (55,45,42).
solution.reason: Moving one student from B-only to A-only keeps every given fact true but changes two club totals. So the club totals are not fixed.

challenges.answer: Exactly two=36; all three=8. Individual club totals are not unique, as the two displayed arrangements demonstrate.
challenges.check: Both arrangements have 46+36+8+10=100 people and 46+2×36+3×8=142 memberships.

title: Applied Arithmetic
intro: Every percentage is a percentage of something. Find that starting amount first, turn the percentage into a multiplier, and keep an eye on the units.

lessons.title: Use and reverse percentage multipliers
lessons.goal: Increase or decrease an amount by a percentage. Work back to the original amount after a change.

steps.title: Name the base amount
steps.text: A price is €80 before VAT. Use an example VAT rate of 23%. The 23% is worked out on the €80, so €80 is the starting amount (the base).
steps.why: A percentage is always a percentage of something. Here it is 23% of the original €80.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Example rate: 23%</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="block0" x="50" y="100" width="533.5853658536585" height="130" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value0" x="318.29268292682923" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">80</text><text id="blocklabel0" x="318.29268292682923" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">original</text><line id="whole" x1="50" y1="83" x2="710" y2="83" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text id="total" x="380" y="60" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">Whole = ?</text><text id="label0" x="50" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Example rate: 23%</text></svg>

steps.title: Combine the whole and the percentage into one multiplier
steps.text: The original price is 100%. Adding 23% VAT makes 123% of €80. As a decimal, 123% is 1.23, so multiply once by 1.23.
steps.why: Multiplying by 1.23 keeps the whole €80 and adds 23% of it in one move.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>100% + 23% = 123%</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="block0" x="50" y="100" width="533.5853658536585" height="130" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value0" x="318.29268292682923" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">80</text><text id="blocklabel0" x="318.29268292682923" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">original</text><rect id="block1" x="586.5853658536585" y="100" width="120.41463414634144" height="130" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value1" x="648.2926829268292" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">18.4</text><text id="blocklabel1" x="648.2926829268292" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">VAT</text><line id="whole" x1="50" y1="83" x2="710" y2="83" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text id="total" x="380" y="60" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">Whole = €98.40</text><text id="label0" x="50" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">100% + 23% = 123%</text></svg>

steps.title: Reverse with division
steps.text: Think forwards first: original price × 1.23 = €98.40. To get back to the original, undo × 1.23 with ÷ 1.23. This gives €80.
steps.why: The 23% was calculated on €80. Taking 23% off €98.40 would use a different base, so it cannot undo the increase.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Reverse: divide the whole €98.40 by 1.23</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="block0" x="50" y="100" width="533.5853658536585" height="130" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value0" x="318.29268292682923" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">80</text><text id="blocklabel0" x="318.29268292682923" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">original</text><rect id="block1" x="586.5853658536585" y="100" width="120.41463414634144" height="130" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value1" x="648.2926829268292" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">18.4</text><text id="blocklabel1" x="648.2926829268292" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">VAT</text><line id="whole" x1="50" y1="83" x2="710" y2="83" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text id="total" x="380" y="60" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">Whole = €98.40</text><text id="label0" x="50" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Reverse: divide the whole €98.40 by 1.23</text></svg>

steps.title: Transfer the method to a discount
steps.text: A 15% discount takes 15% away, so you pay the other 85%. For a €60 item, multiply by 0.85 to get €51.
steps.why: 100% − 15% = 85%, and 85% as a decimal is 0.85. A decrease multiplier is always less than 1.

quiz.question: Using an example VAT rate of 20%, what is the price of an €80 item including VAT?
quiz.hint: 100% + 20% = 120%: write that as a decimal multiplier.
quiz.explanation: The price with VAT is 120% of €80. 80 × 1.20 = €96. Check: 20% of €80 is €16, and 80 + 16 = 96.

quiz.question: A price after a 10% discount is €72. What was the original?
quiz.hint: The sale price is 90% of the original. It is not the original.
quiz.explanation: Original × 0.90 = 72, so original = 72 ÷ 0.90 = €80. Adding 10% of €72 gives €79.20, which is wrong, because the 10% was taken from the original.

lessons.takeaway: Write the multiplier first. Multiply to go forwards. Divide by the same multiplier to go back.
lessons.mistake: Undoing a 23% increase by taking 23% off the new price. The 23% was of the original, so divide by 1.23 instead.

lessons.title: Distinguish markup from profit margin
lessons.goal: Find profit as a percentage of the cost (markup) or of the selling price (margin).

steps.title: Find the profit amount
steps.text: A shop buys an item for €80 and sells it for €100. The profit is the difference, €20.
steps.why: Profit is selling price minus cost price.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Selling price: €100</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="block0" x="50" y="100" width="525.0" height="130" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value0" x="314.0" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">80</text><text id="blocklabel0" x="314.0" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">cost</text><line id="whole" x1="50" y1="83" x2="710" y2="83" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text id="total" x="380" y="60" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">Whole = 100</text><text id="label0" x="50" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Selling price: €100</text></svg>

steps.title: Measure markup against cost
steps.text: Markup compares the profit with what the shop paid. Divide the €20 profit by the €80 cost, then multiply by 100.
steps.why: Markup is profit as a percentage of the cost, so the cost goes on the bottom of the fraction.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Markup: profit ÷ €80</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="block0" x="50" y="100" width="525.0" height="130" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value0" x="314.0" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">80</text><text id="blocklabel0" x="314.0" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">cost</text><rect id="block1" x="578.0" y="100" width="129.0" height="130" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value1" x="644.0" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">20</text><text id="blocklabel1" x="644.0" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">profit</text><line id="whole" x1="50" y1="83" x2="710" y2="83" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text id="total" x="380" y="60" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">Whole = 100</text><text id="label0" x="50" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Markup: profit ÷ €80</text></svg>

steps.title: Measure margin against sales
steps.text: Margin compares the profit with what the customer paid. Divide the €20 profit by the €100 selling price, then multiply by 100.
steps.why: Margin is profit as a percentage of the selling price, so the selling price goes on the bottom.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Margin: profit ÷ €100</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="block0" x="50" y="100" width="525.0" height="130" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value0" x="314.0" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">80</text><text id="blocklabel0" x="314.0" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">cost</text><rect id="block1" x="578.0" y="100" width="129.0" height="130" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value1" x="644.0" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">20</text><text id="blocklabel1" x="644.0" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">profit</text><line id="whole" x1="50" y1="83" x2="710" y2="83" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text id="total" x="380" y="60" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">Whole = 100</text><text id="label0" x="50" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Margin: profit ÷ €100</text></svg>

steps.title: Check which percentage the question names
steps.text: The same €20 profit gives 25% or 20%. It depends on what you compare it with. If the shop makes a loss, compare the loss with the cost.
steps.why: A percentage only means something when you know what it is a percentage of. Read which one the question names.

quiz.question: An item costs €60 and sells for €75. What is the markup?
quiz.hint: Markup compares the profit with the cost. Find the profit first.

quiz.question: An item costs €60 and sells for €75. What is the profit margin?
quiz.hint: Margin compares the profit with the selling price.

lessons.takeaway: Markup is profit ÷ cost. Margin is profit ÷ selling price. Multiply by 100 to get the percentage.
lessons.mistake: Dividing by the cost for both. Markup divides by the cost, but margin divides by the selling price.

lessons.title: Build a household bill
lessons.goal: Work out a bill in parts: the fixed charge, the charge for what you used, and then the tax.

steps.title: Read units and rates
steps.text: A bill has a €25 standing charge. That is a fixed amount you pay whatever you use. You also used 180 units at €0.20 per unit.
steps.why: Only the usage charge changes with the number of units.

steps.text: 180 × 0.20 = €36 for the units. Add the €25 standing charge to get €61 before tax.
steps.why: Both amounts are now in euro, so you can add them. Never add 180 units to €25.

steps.text: Use an example tax of 10% on the €61 subtotal. The tax is €6.10, so the total is €67.10. One multiplier does it: 61 × 1.10.
steps.why: Tax here is charged on the whole subtotal. Always check in the question which amounts are taxed.

quiz.question: A bill has a €12 fixed charge and 50 units at €0.30 each. Find the pre-tax subtotal.
quiz.hint: Find the cost of the 50 units first. Then add the fixed charge once.

quiz.question: A rate is 18 cents per unit. What is its euro value?
quiz.hint: There are 100 cents in one euro.

lessons.takeaway: Bill = fixed charge + units × rate. Then apply the tax the question gives.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying the standing charge by the number of units. You pay the standing charge once only.

lessons.title: Calculate net pay from supplied bands
lessons.goal: Tax each slice of pay at its own rate. Then take off the tax credit and the other deductions.

steps.title: Use the question’s classroom rates
steps.text: Assume annual pay of €40,000. In this invented example, the first €30,000 (the standard rate cut-off point) is taxed at 20% and the remaining €10,000 at 40%.
steps.why: Each rate applies only to its own slice of the pay. The 40% is charged on the top €10,000, not on all €40,000.

steps.title: Apply tax credits
steps.text: The example tax credit is €2,000. Subtract it from the gross income tax, giving €8,000 net income tax (the tax payable).
steps.why: A tax credit comes off the tax, not off the pay. Work out the tax on the full pay first.

steps.text: For this exercise only, USC is 1% of the first €10,000 plus 3% of the other €30,000. That is €100 + €900 = €1,000. PRSI is an example flat 4% of €40,000, which is €1,600.
steps.why: USC and PRSI each have their own rules, so work them out separately. These are not real current rates.

quiz.question: In an invented tax system, the first €20,000 is taxed at 10% and the next €5,000 at 20%. What is gross tax on €25,000?
quiz.hint: Tax the first €20,000 at 10% and only the next €5,000 at 20%. Then add.

quiz.question: Gross income tax is €3,000 and the supplied credit is €800. What is net income tax?
quiz.hint: A credit is taken off the tax. Does the tax go up or down?

lessons.takeaway: Split the pay into bands and tax each slice. Take credits off the tax. Then take every deduction off the gross pay.
lessons.mistake: Taxing all the pay at the highest rate. Only the slice above the cut-off pays the higher rate. Use the rates in the question, not real ones.

lessons.title: Choose the direction of currency conversion
lessons.goal: Decide whether to multiply or divide by an exchange rate by reading its units.

steps.title: Read the rate as a statement
steps.text: Suppose the example rate is €1 = £0.85. One euro buys 0.85 pounds.
steps.why: Read the rate as a sentence: every €1 becomes £0.85. It tells you which way the rate goes: from euro to pounds.

steps.title: Convert euro to pounds
steps.text: You have €240. Each euro becomes £0.85, so you get 240 lots of £0.85. Multiply: €240 becomes £204.
steps.why: Going the same way as the rate, from euro to pounds, you multiply.

steps.text: Now go the other way. You have £170 and want euro. Divide by 0.85 to get €200.
steps.why: Each €1 is worth £0.85. Dividing asks how many lots of £0.85 fit into £170.

steps.text: A €5 fee is taken before €240 is changed. Only €235 is left to convert, which gives £199.75.
steps.why: The fee is in euro and comes first, so subtract it from the euro before you multiply.

quiz.question: At the example rate €1 = $1.10, how many dollars are €50?
quiz.hint: Each €1 becomes $1.10. You are going the same way as the rate.
quiz.explanation: Each euro becomes $1.10, so 50 × 1.10 = $55. Dividing gives $45.45, which is fewer dollars than euro, so it cannot be right.

quiz.question: At €1 = £0.80, how many euro are £64?
quiz.hint: The rate goes from euro to pounds. You are going back from pounds to euro.
quiz.explanation: Going back against the rate, divide: 64 ÷ 0.80 = €80. Check forwards: 80 × 0.80 = £64.

lessons.takeaway: Going the same way as the rate, multiply. Going back the other way, divide.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying by the rate in both directions. Going back, you must divide.

lessons.title: Grow by compound interest
lessons.goal: Add interest each year to the new balance, not to the starting amount.

steps.title: Find the multiplier
steps.text: An example deposit of €1,200 grows at 5% per year for two years. The yearly multiplier is 1.05.
steps.why: A 5% rise means 105% of the balance, which is 1.05 as a decimal. Use it once for every year.

quiz.question: €500 grows by 10% per year for two years. What is the final balance?
quiz.hint: The multiplier is 1.10. Use it once for each year.
quiz.explanation: Year one: 500 × 1.10 = €550. Year two: 550 × 1.10 = €605. €600 would be simple interest, with no interest earned on the first €50.

quiz.question: Why is the second year’s interest larger at a fixed positive compound rate?
options: Interest is earned on the updated balance
quiz.hint: What amount is in the account at the start of the second year?
quiz.explanation: The second year earns interest on the starting amount and on the first year’s interest as well.

lessons.takeaway: Compound interest means multiplying the new balance by the same multiplier each year.
lessons.mistake: Adding the first year’s interest again each year. With compound interest, each year’s interest is worked out on the new balance.

lessons.title: Reverse growth and model depreciation
lessons.goal: Work back to a starting amount or a rate. Use a multiplier below 1 when a value falls each year.

steps.title: Recover the original principal
steps.text: A balance reaches €1,323 after two years at 5%. Going forwards you multiplied by 1.05 twice. To go back, divide by 1.05 twice, which is dividing by 1.05².
steps.why: Two years of growth need two divisions. Dividing by 1.05 only once takes you back one year.

steps.title: Recover a repeated rate
steps.text: A value grows from €1,200 to €1,323 in two years at the same rate. Divide final by start to get the two-year multiplier. Its square root is the one-year multiplier, 1.05. So the rate is 5%.
steps.why: The same multiplier was used twice, so it was squared. A square root undoes squaring.

steps.title: Use a reduction multiplier
steps.text: An €800 device loses 10% of its value each year (depreciation). It keeps 90%, so multiply by 0.90 once for every year.
steps.why: Each year’s 10% is taken from the value at that time, which keeps getting smaller.

steps.title: Interpret the depreciated value
steps.text: After three years the value is €583.20. The total loss is €216.80. That is less than 3 × €80 = €240, because each year’s loss is smaller than the last.
steps.why: The yearly losses are €80, then €72, then €64.80. Each one is 10% of a smaller value.

quiz.question: An item is worth €810 after two years of 10% annual depreciation. What was its initial value?
quiz.hint: Two years of keeping 90% give one combined multiplier; undo that multiplier.

quiz.question: A value increases from €100 to €121 in two years at a fixed annual compound rate. Find the rate.
quiz.hint: Find the two-year multiplier first. The same yearly multiplier was used twice.
quiz.explanation: The two-year multiplier is 121 ÷ 100 = 1.21. The yearly multiplier is √1.21 = 1.1, so the rate is 10%. Halving 21% does not work.

lessons.takeaway: To go back, divide by the multiplier once for every year. For depreciation, the multiplier is below 1.
lessons.mistake: Taking the same euro amount off every year. A percentage loss gets smaller each year, because the value it is taken from gets smaller.

reference.name: Percentage
reference.note: First find the amount the percentage is of (the base).

reference.name: Increase or decrease
reference.note: Use plus for increase and minus for decrease.

reference.name: Reverse a percentage
reference.note: Divide by the multiplier. Do not take the percentage off the final amount.

reference.name: Markup and margin
reference.note: Markup divides by the cost. Margin divides by the selling price.

reference.name: Compound growth
reference.note: Fixed rate r per period, n matching periods. The Formulae and Tables booklet writes this as F = P(1 + i)ᵗ with i = r/100.

reference.name: Depreciation
reference.note: A fixed percentage of the reducing value (the reducing-balance method).

reference.name: Income-tax calculation
reference.formula: Net income tax = max(0, gross income tax − credits)
reference.note: Use the rates, bands, credits and deductions given in the question. The tax due cannot be less than zero.

toolkit.strategy: Write the events in order first. For every percentage, ask what it is a percentage of. Note the currency and the time period. Then use one multiplier for each stage. All rates in these worked examples are invented classroom figures, not current financial rules.

methods.title: Percentages, VAT and reverse prices
methods.when: A price changes by a stated percentage.
methods.rule: New=old(1±r/100); old=new/(1±r/100), with a non-zero multiplier.
steps: Find the amount the percentage is of (the base).
Turn the percentage into a decimal multiplier, such as 1.12 for a 12% rise.
Multiply to go forwards or divide to go back.
Round only the final money answer, not the steps on the way.
methods.example: An invented 12% tax turns €75 into €84; reversing gives 84/1.12=€75.
methods.trap: Taking 12% off €84 gives €73.92, not €75. The 12% was a percentage of the original price.

methods.title: Profit, loss, markup and margin
methods.when: A question compares buying and selling prices.
methods.rule: Profit=S−C; markup%=profit/C×100; margin%=profit/S×100; loss%=loss/C×100.
steps: Find the euro profit or loss first.
Divide by the amount the question names: cost for markup, selling price for margin.
To work backwards, write S=C(1+markup rate) or C=S(1−margin rate).
methods.example: Cost €120 and sales €150 give profit €30, markup 25% and margin 20%.
methods.trap: Markup and margin are different percentages of the same profit. Do not swap them.

methods.title: Tiered bills and fixed charges
methods.when: Units are charged at different rates in different bands.
methods.rule: Subtotal=fixed charge+Σ(units in each band × band rate).
steps: Split the units at every band limit.
Charge each slice once, at its own rate.
Add the fixed charges.
Apply any tax to the subtotal the question names, then check the units.
methods.example: Invented bill: fixed €12; first 100 units at €0.20, next units at €0.30. For 160 units: 12+20+18=€50 before tax.
methods.check: The band quantities 100+60 recover all 160 units.
methods.trap: The higher rate applies only to units above the threshold, unless the question says otherwise.

methods.title: Gross pay, overtime and tiered commission
methods.when: Pay is made of basic earnings plus overtime hours or commission on sales.
methods.rule: Gross pay=basic+overtime+commission; each band uses only its own quantity.
steps: Separate the basic pay from the extra pay.
Use each overtime or commission rate only on its own hours or sales.
Add all the parts of the pay before taking any deductions.
If the sales are unknown, first work out which commission band they reach.
methods.example: Invented weekly pay €400 plus 3% of first €2,000 sales and 5% above: sales €2,600 give 400+60+30=€490.
methods.check: The €90 commission is 3% of €2,000 plus 5% of €600.
methods.trap: Do not apply the highest commission rate to all sales.

methods.title: Income bands, credits, USC and PRSI structure
methods.when: The question gives tax bands, credits and other deductions.
methods.rule: Gross tax=Σ(band income×rate); net income tax=max(0,gross tax−credits); net pay=gross pay−all deductions.
steps: Keep all amounts for the same time period, such as a year.
Work out the income tax band by band.
Take tax credits off the tax, not off the income.
Work out each other deduction by its own rule, then subtract it.
methods.example: Invented €30,000 annual pay: first €20,000 at 10%, rest at 20% gives gross tax €4,000; credit €700 gives net income tax €3,300 before any separately stated deductions.
methods.check: 20,000+10,000=30,000; gross tax − net tax equals the credit used.
methods.trap: USC and PRSI are separate calculations; do not assume they share income-tax bands or credits.

methods.title: Recover gross pay or a tax credit
methods.when: Net pay or tax paid is known, but gross income or a credit is missing.
methods.rule: Within one tax band, write net pay as an expression in gross pay G and solve. If some tax is actually paid, credit=gross tax−net income tax. If the tax bill is zero, the credit could be anything at least as large as the gross tax, so it cannot be found exactly.
steps: Call the gross pay G. Write each deduction using G.
Use the right band and include any fixed deductions.
Solve the net-pay equation.
Check your answer lies in the band you used. If the tax bill is zero, you can only say the credit is at least the gross tax.
methods.example: Invented flat tax 20%, credit €30 and other deduction €10: N=G−(0.2 G−30)−10=0.8 G+20. If N=500, G=600.
methods.trap: Your answer may land in a different band from the one you assumed, so check it. A zero tax bill alone cannot tell you the exact credit.

methods.title: Currency conversion and fees
methods.when: A rate is quoted in one currency per unit of another.
methods.rule: If €1=£r, pounds=euro×r and euro=pounds/r, r>0.
steps: Write the rate as a sentence with both currencies, such as €1=£0.80.
Apply a fee in its stated currency and at its stated stage.
Going the same way as the rate, multiply. Going back, divide.
methods.example: With an invented €1=£0.80 and a €4 fee before exchange, €104 yields (104−4)×0.80=£80.
methods.check: £80/0.80=€100; adding the €4 fee restores €104.
methods.trap: A €4 fee is not a £4 fee. Take the fee off in the currency and at the stage the question states.

methods.title: Compound growth or depreciation
methods.when: A fixed percentage applies repeatedly to the current amount.
methods.rule: A=P(1+r/100)ⁿ; depreciation A=P(1−r/100)ⁿ, using matching periods.
steps: Choose the multiplier: above 1 for growth, below 1 for depreciation.
Apply it once for each period.
Check whether the question wants the final amount, or the interest or loss.
methods.example: €900 losing an invented 20% a year for two years becomes 900×0.8²=€576; loss=€324.
methods.check: The successive values are 900,720,576.
methods.trap: Percentage depreciation is not a fixed euro deduction each year.

methods.title: Changing rates and intermediate transactions
methods.when: Rates differ by year or money is deposited or withdrawn between years.
methods.rule: A=(P m₁−W+D)m₂ for a withdrawal W and deposit D after period 1.
steps: Draw a timeline with the transaction between the correct periods.
Update the balance by the first multiplier.
Apply the cash transaction.
Apply the next multiplier to the new balance.
methods.example: €1,000 grows 4%, then €100 is withdrawn, then it grows 5%: (1000×1.04−100)×1.05=€987.
methods.check: Without the withdrawal the final amount is €1,092; the withdrawal reduces it by 100×1.05=€105.
methods.trap: Do not add 4% and 5% to make 9%. Each rate acts on the balance at that time.

methods.title: Reverse a principal or a repeated rate
methods.when: The final amount is given.
methods.rule: P=A/(m₁m₂…); for n equal periods, m=(A/P)^(1/n). Growth r%=100(m−1); depreciation r%=100(1−m).
steps: Work backwards: undo the last change first.
If the same unknown rate repeats, divide final by start and take the matching root.
Turn the multiplier into a percentage increase or decrease.
methods.example: An item worth €1,152 after two 20% falls began at 1152/0.8²=€1,800.
methods.trap: Adding the lost percentage back onto the final value does not give the original. Divide by the multipliers instead.

methods.title: Tax deducted from interest
methods.when: A tax (called DIRT in Ireland) is charged on interest, rather than the whole balance.
methods.rule: Net interest=P×r×(1−t), when r and t are decimal interest and interest-tax rates.
steps: Work out the full interest on the balance (the gross interest).
Take the tax from that interest only.
Add the interest you keep to the balance.
For an unknown rate, divide the net increase by P(1−t).
methods.example: Invented principal €2,000, gross rate 4%, tax on interest 25%: gross interest €80, tax €20, closing balance €2,060.
methods.trap: Do not take interest tax from the whole balance. Do not subtract the tax rate from the interest rate either.

checks: Each percentage is taken of the right starting amount.
Every fee, withdrawal and tax happens in the order the question states.
Rates and time periods match, and all amounts use the same units.
Keep exact values in the working. Round only the final money answer.
After working backwards, check by running the steps forwards.

challenges.title: A withdrawal between two different rates
challenges.question: Use these invented classroom rates and assume no tax or fees. €1,500 earns 4% in year 1. Immediately afterwards €200 is withdrawn. The remaining money earns 5% in year 2. (a) Find the balance after each event. (b) Find the total interest earned over the two years. (c) How much lower is the final balance than if no withdrawal had been made? Explain why the difference is not just €200.
hints: Write a timeline with four points: start, after year 1, after the withdrawal, after year 2.
Total interest equals final balance plus the withdrawal minus the initial deposit.

solution.title: Apply the first rate
solution.reason: A 4% rise is a multiplier of 1.04. The first year earns €60 interest.

solution.title: Make the transaction at the stated time
solution.reason: The withdrawal happens before year 2. Only the €1,360 left earns year-2 interest.

solution.title: Apply the second rate
solution.reason: A 5% rise is a multiplier of 1.05, used on the balance after the withdrawal. The second year earns €68.

solution.title: Find total interest
solution.reason: You put in €1,500 and got back €200 plus €1,428. The extra is the interest.

solution.title: Compare with no withdrawal
solution.reason: The €200 withdrawn also misses €10 of second-year interest.

challenges.answer: After year 1 €1,560; after withdrawal €1,360; final €1,428; interest €128; final-balance difference €210.
challenges.check: The separate interest amounts €60+€68 equal €128; the withdrawal effect is 200×1.05=€210.

challenges.title: Reverse two different depreciations
challenges.question: A device loses 20% of its value in year 1 and 15% of its value at that time in year 2. Its value afterwards is €1,360. Treat these as invented classroom rates. (a) Find the original value. (b) Find each year’s euro loss. (c) Find the overall percentage loss and explain why adding 20% and 15% is wrong.
hints: Losing 20% keeps 80%. Losing 15% keeps 85%. Write both as decimal multipliers.
Original × 0.80 × 0.85 = 1,360. Divide to undo the multiplying.

solution.title: Form the full retained multiplier
solution.reason: Each year the device keeps part of its value. The second multiplier acts on the value already reduced.

solution.title: Recover the original
solution.reason: Dividing by 0.68 undoes both years of multiplying in one move.

solution.title: Calculate each loss
solution.reason: Year 1 loses 20% of €2,000. Year 2 loses 15% of the €1,600 that is left.

solution.title: Find the combined rate
solution.reason: The device keeps 68% of its value, so it loses 32%.

solution.title: Explain the non-additivity
solution.reason: Adding 20% and 15% treats both losses as percentages of €2,000. The second loss is 15% of only €1,600.

challenges.answer: Original €2,000; losses €400 and €240; overall loss 32%.
challenges.check: Forward calculation gives 2000×0.80×0.85=1360 exactly.

challenges.title: Find an interest rate after interest tax
challenges.question: Use invented classroom figures. A €2,000 balance earns gross interest of 5% in year 1. Tax of 20% is deducted from the interest only. In year 2 the gross interest rate changes to r%, and the same 20% interest tax applies. With no deposits or withdrawals, the final balance is €2,184. (a) Find the year-1 closing balance. (b) Find the year-2 gross interest and r. (c) Find the total interest tax deducted over both years.
hints: The tax takes 20% of the interest, so you keep 80% of the interest.
In year 2, the balance rose by the interest you kept. Divide that rise by 0.80 to get the full interest before tax.

solution.title: Calculate year-1 interest and tax
solution.reason: The tax is 20% of the €100 interest, not 20% of the €2,000.

solution.title: Find the next principal
solution.reason: The €80 you keep is added to the balance. Year 2 interest is worked out on €2,080.

solution.title: Reverse the year-2 tax
solution.reason: The €104 rise is the 80% of the interest that you kept. Dividing by 0.80 gives the full interest.

solution.title: Find the unknown rate
solution.reason: The rate is the interest as a percentage of the balance at the start of year 2, which is €2,080.

solution.title: Add the tax amounts
solution.reason: Each year’s tax is 20% of that year’s full interest.

challenges.answer: Year-1 closing balance €2,080; year-2 gross interest €130; r=6.25%; total tax €46.
challenges.check: 2080×(1+0.0625×0.80)=2184; total gross interest €230 minus tax €46 gives net growth €184.

challenges.title: Recover sales from net pay
challenges.question: Use this invented weekly pay system. Basic pay is €500. Commission is 3% of the first €4,000 sales and 5% of sales above €4,000. Income tax is 20% of gross pay minus a €40 credit; a separate fixed deduction is €20. Net pay is €540. (a) Find gross pay. (b) Find the commission. (c) Find the sales amount, checking which commission band applies. (d) Verify the net pay from the recovered sales.
hints: Call the gross pay G. Write the tax and the fixed deduction using G before you solve.
Net=G−(0.20 G−40)−20. The first commission band can contribute at most €120.

solution.title: Write the net-pay equation
solution.reason: The credit is taken off the tax. The fixed deduction is separate.

solution.title: Recover gross pay
solution.reason: Take 20 from both sides, then divide by 0.80. The tax, 130 − 40 = €90, is above zero, so the equation holds.

solution.title: Recover commission
solution.reason: Gross pay is basic pay plus commission. Basic pay is €500 of the €650.

solution.title: Locate the correct commission band
solution.reason: The first band can give at most €120. The commission is €150, so sales must be above €4,000.

solution.title: Recover and verify sales
solution.reason: The extra €30 is 5% of the sales above €4,000. Then run the pay forwards to check the €540.

challenges.answer: Gross €650; commission €150; sales €4,600; tax €90 and other deduction €20 give net €540.
challenges.check: Forward commission is 0.03×4000+0.05×600=150, and every later deduction reproduces €540.

title: Statistics 1: Collecting data
intro: Good statistics starts before any calculating. Learn to ask a clear question, collect the answers fairly and say honestly what the results can and cannot tell you.

lessons.title: Ask a question that data can answer
lessons.goal: Before you collect anything, decide who you are asking (the population), what you will record (the variable) and what kind of data it is.

steps.title: Expect different answers
steps.text: Ask how many minutes students in this year group spend travelling to school. Students will have different travel times.
steps.why: A statistical question is one where you expect different answers from different people.
steps.math: Population: all students in the year
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Read across one row at a time.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="headbg0" x="40.0" y="40" width="338.0" height="48" rx="10" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="head0" x="210.0" y="72" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">Planning decision</text><rect id="headbg1" x="380.0" y="40" width="338.0" height="48" rx="10" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="head1" x="550.0" y="72" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">Our example</text><rect id="tablebg0-0" x="40.0" y="100" width="338.0" height="44" rx="3" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="table0-0" x="210.0" y="130" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">Population</text><rect id="tablebg0-1" x="380.0" y="100" width="338.0" height="44" rx="3" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="table0-1" x="550.0" y="130" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">Students in one year</text><text id="label0" x="40" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Read across one row at a time.</text></svg>

steps.title: Define exactly what to measure
steps.text: Say exactly what to measure: the time from leaving home to arriving at school on a normal school morning, in minutes.
steps.why: If everyone measures the same thing in the same way, their answers can be compared fairly.
steps.math: Variable: morning journey time, in minutes

steps.title: Classify the data
steps.text: Travel time is measured, so it is numerical continuous data. Number of siblings is counted, so it is numerical discrete. Travel method is a word, so it is categorical.
steps.why: A measurement can fall anywhere on a scale, such as 12.5 minutes. A count goes up in whole steps: 0, 1, 2.
steps.math: Time: continuous; siblings: discrete; method: categorical

steps.text: Ask “How many minutes did your journey take?” rather than suggesting it was too long. Give sensible answer choices when they are needed.
steps.why: A question that hints at the answer you want (a leading question) can change what people say.

quiz.question: Which is a statistical question?
options: How many pets do students in this class have?
How many sides has a triangle?
quiz.hint: Which question would get different answers from different people?
quiz.explanation: Students may have different numbers of pets, so data are needed to describe the group.

quiz.question: Which variable is numerical continuous?
quiz.hint: Continuous data are measured, not counted. Which of these is a measurement?
quiz.explanation: Height is measured and can fall between whole numbers, such as 161.5 cm. Tries and players are counted in whole numbers, so they are discrete.

lessons.takeaway: Name the group you are asking. Say exactly what you will record and in what units. Word the question so it does not push people towards an answer.
lessons.mistake: Treating a question with one fixed answer, such as “What is 7 × 8?”, as a statistical question. A statistical question expects different answers.

lessons.title: Collect and organise reliable data
lessons.goal: Tell primary data from secondary data, and build a frequency table that counts every answer exactly once.

steps.title: Identify the source
steps.text: Recording your own class survey gives primary data. Using a published survey gives secondary data.
steps.why: The only difference is who collected the data: you (primary) or someone else (secondary).

steps.why: Data can be trustworthy and still be about the wrong people. Check both.
steps.math: Who collected it? When? How? From which population?

quiz.question: You use a report published by a sports organisation. What kind of data source is this for you?
options: Primary, because you are the one analysing it
quiz.hint: You did not collect the original observations.
quiz.explanation: Someone else collected the data, so it is secondary for you. You still need to check how good it is.

quiz.question: For 2,1,2,3,2,1, what is the frequency of 2?
quiz.hint: Count how many times the value 2 appears in the list.
quiz.explanation: The value 2 appears three times, so its frequency is 3. The answer 6 is the number of values in the whole list.

lessons.takeaway: The frequencies in a table must add up to the number of answers you collected.
lessons.mistake: Deciding a secondary source is good, or bad, without checking. Ask who collected it, when, how and from whom.

lessons.title: Choose a sample fairly
lessons.goal: Spot a sample that is unfair (biased), choose a fairer one, and say what a sample can and cannot prove.

steps.title: Name the target population
steps.text: To study all students’ sports preferences, the population is all students in the school. A sample is the smaller group actually surveyed.
steps.why: Your conclusion will be about the whole population, so be clear who that is before you choose a sample.

steps.title: Choose a fairer sample
steps.text: Give every student a chance to be picked. One approach is to choose randomly within each year group. If a year contains one quarter of the school, give it one quarter of the sample.
steps.why: This includes the different years in the right proportions. Random choice within each year reduces the risk of only asking your friends.

steps.title: Do not claim too much
steps.text: A sample gives an estimate, not a guarantee about every student. A bigger sample is steadier, but making it bigger does not fix an unfair way of choosing.
steps.why: Chance differences and unfair selection are two separate problems. Sample size only helps with the first.
