quiz.question: Which sample best supports a claim about the whole school?
options: Students randomly selected across all year groups
quiz.hint: Who has a fair chance of being included?
quiz.explanation: Random selection across all year groups gives every student a fair chance. The other three samples leave out most students.

quiz.question: Why might 5,000 votes on a fan-page poll still be misleading?
options: Only 5,000 votes is too small a sample
Online votes cannot be turned into percentages
The poll should have been repeated on another day
quiz.hint: Think about who chooses to vote on a fan page.
quiz.explanation: The people who vote on a fan page are mostly fans who chose to answer. They may not think like everyone else, however many votes there are.

lessons.takeaway: Ask who was included, who was missed and how people were selected.
lessons.mistake: Thinking a large sample must be a fair one. 5,000 votes from fans still only tell you what fans think.

reference.name: Statistical question
reference.note: Name the population and the quantity being measured.

reference.name: Data types
reference.note: Categories describe groups; discrete values count; continuous values measure.

reference.name: Frequency
reference.note: Frequencies should add to the number of observations.

reference.name: Sources
reference.formula: Primary: collect it yourself; secondary: already collected
reference.note: Judge both relevance and reliability.

reference.name: Sampling
reference.formula: Representative selection matters as well as sample size
reference.note: A larger biased sample can still be misleading.

toolkit.strategy: Before calculating, ask what population, variable and sampling method produced the data. A useful answer explains both the numbers and the limits of the conclusion.

methods.title: Define an investigation and data type
methods.when: You must write a question or classify its answers.
methods.rule: Population=target group; variable=recorded characteristic. Categorical data are labels; numerical discrete data are counts; numerical continuous data are measurements.
steps: Name the target population.
Specify one variable and any measurement unit.
Distinguish counts, measurements and categories.
Fix a time period or other ambiguous wording.
methods.example: “How many minutes did your journey to school take this morning?” measures continuous numerical data for the surveyed students.
methods.check: Two readers should know the same start, finish and units.
methods.trap: Rounding a measured time to minutes does not make time itself a count variable.

methods.title: Critique and repair questionnaire wording
methods.when: A questionnaire may steer answers or combine questions.
methods.rule: Use neutral wording, one idea at a time, and a precise reference period.
steps: Underline judgemental or leading words.
Separate double questions.
Replace vague words with a defined measure or category.
Write the improved question, not just a criticism.
methods.example: Replace “Don’t you agree that the bus is too slow?” with “How many minutes did your bus journey to school take this morning?”
methods.check: The rewritten question allows short and long journeys without favouring either.
methods.trap: A friendly tone does not automatically make a question unbiased.

methods.title: Make response options exhaustive and exclusive
methods.when: Answers are grouped into intervals or categories.
methods.rule: Each permitted response should fit exactly one option.
steps: Test boundary values against adjacent options.
Use consistent non-overlapping interval notation.
Include the largest possible values or an open-ended last group.
Include “other” or an appropriate non-applicable option when needed.
methods.example: For non-negative time t: 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20, 20≤t<30, t≥30.
methods.check: Exactly 10 minutes belongs only to the second group; 65 minutes still has a group.
methods.trap: “0 to 10, 10 to 20, 20 to 30” does not say which group owns 10 or 20 unless a note fixes it. Exam papers often add a note such as “10 to 20 means 10 or more but less than 20”.

methods.title: Turn raw data into frequencies and percentages
methods.when: A list of observations must be summarised.
methods.rule: Relative frequency=f/N; percentage=100 f/N, with N the number of observations.
steps: List all values or valid categories.
Tally each observation once.
Add frequencies to verify N.
Calculate the requested percentage using the correct combined frequency.
methods.example: Data 0,1,1,2,2,2 have frequencies 1,2,3. A value of at least one occurs 5 times out of 6, so its percentage is 5/6 × 100% = 83⅓%.
methods.check: Frequencies sum to 6; exact category percentages sum to 100%.
methods.trap: The denominator is the observation count, not the number of distinct categories.

methods.title: Compare sources and samples
methods.when: You must decide whether results support a population claim.
methods.rule: Primary data are collected for your investigation; secondary data were already collected. Representativeness depends on selection, not simply sample size.
steps: Name who could enter each sample and who was missed.
Identify who was convenient to ask, who volunteered and who was left out.
Compare the method with the intended population.
Give a cautious conclusion; random selection reduces selection bias but does not remove uncertainty.
methods.example: A random sample across year groups better represents a whole school than a larger poll of the rugby team.
methods.check: Ask whether every relevant student had a fair route into the sample.
methods.trap: A large sample can precisely describe the wrong group.

methods.title: Allocate a proportional sample
methods.when: The population contains known groups of different sizes.
methods.rule: Group sample size = total sample size × group population / total population.
steps: Calculate each group’s share of the population.
Allocate the requested sample in those proportions.
Check the allocations add to the total sample.
Select randomly within each group rather than taking volunteers only.
methods.example: Groups of 60,90,150 in a population of 300 receive 6,9,15 places in a sample of 30.
methods.check: 6+9+15=30, and each group supplies 10% of its members.
methods.trap: Correct quotas do not cure biased selection within each group.

checks: The question is neutral, clear and about one variable.
Response options do not overlap and cover every permitted response.
Frequencies match the number of observations; percentages use that count.
The conclusion names the population and acknowledges sampling limitations.

challenges.title: Repair a journey-time questionnaire
challenges.question: A survey asks: “How many minutes do you waste on your journey to school?” Its choices are “0 to 20”, “20 to 40” and “40 to 60”. (a) Identify three distinct weaknesses. (b) Rewrite the question neutrally for this morning’s journey. (c) Give a complete set of non-overlapping numerical options for any non-negative journey time. (d) Classify the data type.
hints: Consider the tone, exactly 20 or 40 minutes, and journeys longer than an hour.
Let each group include its lower end but not its upper end, and give the last group no upper end.

solution.title: Identify the wording problem
solution.math: “Waste” suggests a negative judgement about travel time.
solution.reason: A loaded word such as “waste” can push people towards a negative answer.

solution.title: Check boundaries and coverage
solution.math: 20 and 40 have ambiguous groups; times over 60 have no group.
solution.reason: Every possible answer should fit exactly one option, with none left out.

solution.title: Rewrite the question
solution.math: “How many minutes did your journey from home to school take this morning?”
solution.reason: The new question has no loaded word. It says where the journey starts and ends, and which day.

solution.title: Rewrite the options
solution.math: 0≤t<20; 20≤t<40; 40≤t<60; t≥60. If needed, add “I did not make this journey today.”
solution.reason: Every possible time now fits exactly one group. Someone who did not travel has a separate option.

solution.title: Classify the variable
solution.reason: Time is measured, and a journey can take any value in between, such as 12.5 minutes.

challenges.answer: Weaknesses: leading word, ambiguous boundaries, missing long journeys. The displayed neutral question and four half-open/open-ended intervals repair them; time is continuous numerical data.
challenges.check: Test 0,20,40,60 and 75 minutes: each falls into exactly one interval. A non-traveller is not forced to invent a time.

challenges.title: From pet counts to an honest conclusion
challenges.question: Twelve volunteers report these pet counts: 0,1,2,2,0,3,1,2,4,1,0,2. (a) Make a frequency table for 0 through 4 pets. (b) Give each category percentage, retaining exact fractions where helpful. (c) Find the percentage with at least two pets. (d) Explain why the result alone does not establish that same percentage for the entire school.
hints: Tally each answer once, then check that the frequencies add to twelve.
For “at least two”, combine the frequencies of 2, 3 and 4 before dividing.

solution.title: Count each category
solution.reason: Each of the twelve answers goes into exactly one row.

solution.title: Convert to percentages
solution.reason: Divide each frequency by 12 and multiply by 100.

solution.title: Combine the requested categories
solution.math: Fraction with at least two pets = (4 + 1 + 1)/12 = 1/2, or 50%
solution.reason: “At least two” means 2 or more, so add the frequencies for 2, 3 and 4 pets.

solution.title: State the population limit
solution.math: 50% describes these twelve volunteers; a school-wide claim needs a suitable sampling method
solution.reason: Volunteers may not be like other students, and twelve people are too few to speak for a whole school.

challenges.answer: Frequencies 3,3,4,1,1; percentages 25,25,33⅓,8⅓,8⅓; at least two pets 50%; a whole-school conclusion is unsupported by this sample alone.
challenges.check: The frequencies sum to 12 and exact percentages sum to 100%; six listed observations have at least two pets.

challenges.title: Build a better school sample
challenges.question: A school has year-group populations 120,200,180 and 300. A poll of 50 sports-team members finds 40 favour more sports time. A random sample of 80 students across the school finds 46 favour it. (a) Find both percentages. (b) Explain which sampling approach better supports a whole-school claim and why. (c) Allocate a new sample of 80 proportionally across the four year groups and describe how students should be chosen within each group. (d) Does this guarantee the exact school percentage?
hints: The school population is 800, so an 80-person proportional sample uses one tenth of each group.
Unfair selection is one problem. Chance differences between samples are another. Keep them apart.

solution.title: Calculate the observed percentages
solution.reason: Divide by the number of people in that poll: 50 for the team poll and 80 for the random sample.

solution.title: Evaluate selection
solution.math: The school-wide random approach is better aligned to the target population
solution.reason: Sports-team members are likely to want more sports time, and everyone else is left out.

solution.title: Allocate proportionally
solution.reason: The sample of 80 is one tenth of the 800 students, so take one tenth of each year group.

solution.title: Specify a fair procedure
solution.math: Use a random selection from each complete year-group list
solution.reason: If you only took willing friends to fill each number, the unfair selection would come back.

solution.title: Limit the claim
solution.math: The result remains an estimate, not a guarantee
solution.reason: A fair sample can still differ from the whole population by chance.

challenges.answer: 80% and 57.5%; the random school sample is better aligned. Proportional allocations:12,20,18,30, with random selection within groups. No exact percentage is guaranteed.
challenges.check: 12+20+18+30=80; each allocation divided by its population is 0.10. The claim concerns the whole school, not just sports-team members.

challenges.title: Compare a large voluntary poll with a small random sample
challenges.question: A school of 1,000 students posts an optional travel poll online. Of 300 respondents, 210 report travelling by bus. A separate random sample of 40 students reports bus 18, walking 10, cycling 6 and car 6. (a) Calculate the online bus percentage and the random sample’s four category percentages. (b) Find the difference between the two bus percentages in percentage points. (c) Assess the claim “Exactly 70% of the school travel by bus.” (d) Explain why the larger response count does not settle which estimate is better.
hints: Who chooses to answer matters. That is a separate question from how many answer.
Use 40 as the denominator for the second set of category percentages.

solution.title: Summarise the online respondents
solution.reason: This percentage describes respondents to the optional online poll.

solution.title: Summarise the random sample
solution.reason: The counts total 40 and each is divided by 40.

solution.title: Compare the bus results
solution.reason: A difference between percentages is stated in percentage points.

solution.title: Assess the exact claim
solution.math: The claim about exactly 70% of all 1,000 students is not established
solution.reason: The optional poll counts only those who chose to answer, so it may be biased; neither sample is a count of every one of the 1,000 students.

solution.title: Compare the methods
solution.math: The random sample gives a better route to representation, although it is smaller and has sampling variability
solution.reason: More replies do not fix an unfair way of choosing who replies.

challenges.answer: Online bus 70%; random sample 45%,25%,15%,15%; difference 25 percentage points. The exact whole-school claim is unsupported.
challenges.check: The random-sample percentages sum to 100%. Distinguishing the 300 respondents from all 1,000 students prevents an unjustified change of population.

title: Perimeter, Area, Volume
intro: Every question here asks for one of three things: the distance around a shape, the space inside a flat shape, or the space that fills a solid. Decide which one first, then choose the formula.

lessons.title: Separate perimeter from area
lessons.goal: Tell the distance around a shape, called the perimeter, from the space inside it, called the area, and find each one.

steps.title: Choose what is being measured
steps.text: An 8 cm by 5 cm rectangle has perimeter 26 cm and area 40 square centimetres. These measure different things.
steps.why: Perimeter is a walk around the edge. Area counts the 1 cm squares that fit inside.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="rectangle" x="180" y="55" width="400" height="250" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="length" x="380" y="340" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">8 cm</text><text id="width" x="635" y="188" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">5 cm</text></svg>

steps.title: Split a compound shape
steps.text: Now cut a 3 cm by 2 cm rectangle out of one corner. Take its area away from the area of the big rectangle.
steps.why: The cut piece held 6 squares. Those squares are gone, so 40 − 6 are left.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="rectangle" x="180" y="55" width="400" height="250" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="length" x="380" y="340" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">8 cm</text><text id="width" x="635" y="188" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">5 cm</text><rect id="cutout" x="430" y="55" width="150" height="100" rx="0" fill="#fff" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="2"/><text id="cutsize" x="505" y="113" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">3 × 2</text></svg>

steps.title: Trace the new boundary
steps.text: Cutting the corner removes 3 cm and 2 cm of outside edge. It adds new inside edges of 3 cm and 2 cm. So the perimeter is still 26 cm.
steps.why: Less area does not always mean less edge. Here the cut adds exactly as much edge as it removes.

steps.title: Square the unit conversion too
steps.text: Picture a square 1 metre wide and 1 metre tall. In centimetres it is 100 by 100. That is 10,000 little squares of 1 cm², not 100.
steps.why: Changing both width and height multiplies the area by 100 twice. For an area conversion, square the length conversion factor.

quiz.question: Find the area of a 7 cm by 4 cm rectangle.
quiz.hint: Multiply length by width and use square units.
quiz.explanation: 7 × 4 = 28 cm². The answer 22 is the perimeter. Area needs square units, so 28 cm is not correct either.

quiz.question: Convert 2 m² to cm².
quiz.hint: 1 m² is a square 100 cm wide and 100 cm tall. How many cm² is that?
quiz.explanation: 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10,000 cm², so 2 m² = 20,000 cm². Multiplying by 100 only once gives 200, which is far too small.

lessons.takeaway: Around the edge is perimeter, measured in cm. Inside is area, measured in cm².
lessons.mistake: Saying 1 m² is 100 cm² because 1 m is 100 cm. A square metre is 100 cm by 100 cm, so it is 10,000 cm².

lessons.title: See why a parallelogram has area base times height
lessons.goal: Find the area of a parallelogram or a triangle using the height that meets the base at a right angle, not the sloping side.

steps.title: Identify base and height
steps.text: A parallelogram has base 9 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm. The sloping side is not the height.
steps.why: The height is the straight distance from the base to the opposite side, measured at a right angle to the base.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Cut and translate a triangle to turn the parallelogram into a rectangle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="remaining" points="240,126 610,126 490,290 240,290" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="cutpiece" points="120,290 240,290 240,126" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="height" x1="240" y1="126" x2="240" y2="290" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><text id="height-label" x="280" y="216" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">4 cm</text><text id="base-label" x="300" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">9 cm</text></svg>

steps.title: Cut a corner triangle
steps.text: Imagine cutting a triangle off one end, with the cut at a right angle to the base. Nothing is thrown away.
steps.why: Cutting a shape and moving the pieces does not change the total area.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Cut and translate a triangle to turn the parallelogram into a rectangle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="remaining" points="240,126 610,126 490,290 240,290" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="cutpiece" points="120,290 240,290 240,126" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><line id="height" x1="240" y1="126" x2="240" y2="290" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><text id="height-label" x="280" y="216" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">4 cm</text><text id="base-label" x="300" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">9 cm</text></svg>

steps.title: Slide it to the other side
steps.text: Move that triangle into the gap on the other side. The pieces now form a rectangle with the same base and height.
steps.why: The rearranged pieces cover exactly the same area; nothing is stretched or lost.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Cut and translate a triangle to turn the parallelogram into a rectangle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="remaining" points="240,126 610,126 490,290 240,290" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="cutpiece" points="490,290 610,290 610,126" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><line id="height" x1="240" y1="126" x2="240" y2="290" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><text id="height-label" x="280" y="216" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">4 cm</text><text id="base-label" x="425" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">9 cm</text><line id="move" x1="290" y1="92" x2="560" y2="92" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text id="move-label" x="425" y="75" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">slide the cut piece</text></svg>

steps.title: Calculate and transfer
steps.text: The area is 36 square centimetres. A triangle with the same base and height is half this area.
steps.why: A diagonal cuts a parallelogram into two identical triangles, so each triangle is half of it.
steps.math: A = bh = 36 cm²; triangle area = 18 cm²
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Cut and translate a triangle to turn the parallelogram into a rectangle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="remaining" points="240,126 610,126 490,290 240,290" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="cutpiece" points="490,290 610,290 610,126" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><line id="height" x1="240" y1="126" x2="240" y2="290" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><text id="height-label" x="280" y="216" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">4 cm</text><text id="base-label" x="425" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">9 cm</text><text id="area" x="380" y="380" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">Same area: 9 × 4 = 36 cm²</text></svg>

quiz.question: A parallelogram has base 12 cm, perpendicular height 5 cm and sloping side 7 cm. Find its area.
quiz.hint: Use the perpendicular height.
quiz.explanation: 12 × 5 = 60 cm². Using the sloping side instead, 12 × 7 = 84, is the usual mistake.

quiz.question: A triangle has base 10 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm. Find its area.
quiz.hint: A triangle is half of a parallelogram with the same base and height.
quiz.explanation: ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm². The answer 60 forgets to halve.

lessons.takeaway: Parallelogram: base × perpendicular height. Triangle: half of that.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying the base by the sloping side because it looks like a height. The height must meet the base at a right angle.

lessons.title: Circles, sectors and curved boundaries
lessons.goal: Use the radius, not the diameter, in circle formulas, and find the part of a circle that a sector covers.

steps.title: Identify radius and diameter
steps.text: A circle has radius 6 cm, so its diameter is 12 cm. Use the radius, not the diameter, in the area formula.
steps.why: The diameter goes right across the circle through the centre. It is twice the radius.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><circle id="circle" cx="300" cy="190" r="115" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="300" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text id="r" x="350" y="177" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">r</text></svg>

steps.title: Find a whole circle’s measures
steps.text: The circumference is 12π cm and the area is 36π square centimetres. Leave π exact unless a decimal is requested.
steps.why: Circumference is the distance around the edge. Area is the space inside.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><circle id="circle" cx="300" cy="190" r="115" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="300" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text id="r" x="350" y="177" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">r</text><line id="diameter" x1="185" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="diam" x="300" y="340" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">d = 2r</text></svg>

steps.title: Take the sector fraction
steps.text: A 90-degree sector is one quarter of a full turn. Its arc is 3π cm and its area is 9π square centimetres.
steps.why: Divide the angle by 360 degrees to find the fraction of the circle.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><circle id="circle" cx="300" cy="190" r="115" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="300" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text id="r" x="350" y="177" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">r</text><line id="diameter" x1="185" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="diam" x="300" y="340" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">d = 2r</text><path id="sector" d="M300 190 L415 190 A115 115 0 0 0 300 75 Z" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

steps.title: Add straight edges when finding perimeter
steps.text: The sector’s boundary contains the curved arc and two radii. Its perimeter is 3π + 12 cm.
steps.why: Walk around the sector: out along one radius, around the arc, and back along the other radius.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><circle id="circle" cx="300" cy="190" r="115" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="300" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text id="r" x="350" y="177" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">r</text><line id="diameter" x1="185" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="diam" x="300" y="340" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">d = 2r</text><path id="sector" d="M300 190 L415 190 A115 115 0 0 0 300 75 Z" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="quarter" x="515" y="180" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">90° = ¼ turn</text></svg>

quiz.question: A circle has diameter 10 cm. What is its area?
quiz.hint: Halve the diameter before squaring.
quiz.explanation: r = 5, so area = π × 5² = 25π cm². Using 10 as the radius gives 100π, which is four times too big.

quiz.question: What fraction of a circle is a 120° sector?
quiz.hint: Divide the central angle by 360.

lessons.takeaway: A sector is angle ÷ 360 of the whole circle. Its perimeter is the arc plus the two straight radii.
lessons.mistake: Putting the diameter into a formula that needs the radius, or leaving the two radii out of a sector’s perimeter.

lessons.title: Count faces and layers in rectangular solids
lessons.goal: Tell apart the space inside a box, called its volume, the area of its outside faces, called its surface area, and the liquid it holds, called its capacity.

steps.title: Think in layers for volume
steps.text: A cuboid is 6 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. Each one-centimetre layer holds 24 unit cubes.
steps.why: Base area counts the cubes in one layer.

steps.title: Stack the layers
steps.text: Three layers give 72 unit cubes, so the volume is 72 cubic centimetres.
steps.why: Volume counts the 1 cm cubes that fill the solid.

steps.title: Count the six exterior faces
steps.text: There are two 6-by-4 faces, two 6-by-3 faces and two 4-by-3 faces. Their total area is 108 square centimetres.
steps.why: Surface area counts only the exterior faces, not the interior volume.

steps.title: Connect volume and capacity
steps.text: One cubic centimetre holds one millilitre, so 1,000 cubic centimetres hold one litre. For a box with no lid, leave the top face out of the surface area.
steps.why: Read the question carefully: is the box closed, or is one face missing?

quiz.question: Find the volume of a 5 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm cuboid.
quiz.hint: Multiply all three dimensions.
quiz.explanation: 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cm³. Adding the three lengths gives 10, which is not a volume.

quiz.question: A cube has side 4 cm. What is its total surface area?
quiz.hint: A cube has six square faces, all the same size.
quiz.explanation: 6 × 4² = 96 cm². The answer 64 is the volume, 4³, not the surface area.

lessons.takeaway: Volume fills the solid; surface area covers its exposed faces.
lessons.mistake: Giving a surface area in cm³ instead of cm², or counting a lid on a box that has no lid.

lessons.title: Use the constant cross-section of a prism
lessons.goal: Find the area of the end face of a prism, called the cross-section, then multiply by the length.

steps.title: Find the repeated face
steps.text: A triangular prism has a triangular cross-section with base 6 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm. Its length is 10 cm.
steps.why: A prism has the same cross-section all along its length.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="front" points="120,285 340,285 230,105" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="top" points="340,285 600,210 490,30 230,105" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="hidden" x1="120" y1="285" x2="380" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/><line id="backbase" x1="380" y1="210" x2="600" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

steps.title: Calculate the cross-sectional area
steps.text: The triangle’s area is half of 6 times 4, giving 12 square centimetres.
steps.why: The end face is a triangle, so use the triangle area formula first.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="front" points="120,285 340,285 230,105" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="top" points="340,285 600,210 490,30 230,105" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="hidden" x1="120" y1="285" x2="380" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/><line id="backbase" x1="380" y1="210" x2="600" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="cross" x="230" y="250" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">cross-section A</text></svg>

steps.title: Extend it through the prism
steps.text: Multiply 12 square centimetres by the 10 cm length. The volume is 120 cubic centimetres.
steps.why: Picture 10 slices, each 1 cm thick. Each slice holds 12 cm³.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="front" points="120,285 340,285 230,105" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="top" points="340,285 600,210 490,30 230,105" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="hidden" x1="120" y1="285" x2="380" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/><line id="backbase" x1="380" y1="210" x2="600" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="cross" x="230" y="250" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">cross-section A</text><text id="length" x="500" y="300" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">length L</text></svg>

steps.title: Do not confuse the two heights
steps.text: The triangle’s perpendicular height was 4 cm; the prism’s length was 10 cm. Draw and label both before calculating. The net of this prism has two triangular ends and three rectangles, each 10 cm long.
steps.why: The 4 cm belongs to the triangle. The 10 cm runs along the prism. Keep them apart.

quiz.question: A prism has cross-sectional area 18 cm² and length 7 cm. Find its volume.
quiz.hint: Multiply cross-sectional area by length.
quiz.explanation: 18 × 7 = 126 cm³. Adding 18 and 7 gives 25, which mixes an area with a length.

quiz.question: A prism has volume 150 cm³ and cross-sectional area 25 cm². Find its length.
quiz.hint: Undo multiplying by the cross-sectional area.
quiz.explanation: Length = 150 ÷ 25 = 6 cm. Multiplying instead gives 3,750 cm, which is far too long.

lessons.takeaway: Find the area of one repeated slice, then multiply by length.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying the three lengths you can see. For a triangular end you must halve first: ½ × base × height.

lessons.title: Read a scale drawing
lessons.goal: Change a length on a drawing into the real length, and back again, keeping the units the same.

steps.title: Read the scale as a ratio
steps.text: A scale of 1:200 means one unit on the drawing represents 200 of the same units in reality.
steps.why: Both numbers in a scale use the same unit, so 1 cm stands for 200 cm.
steps.math: 1 cm on plan = 200 cm in reality

steps.title: Convert a drawing length
steps.text: A wall measuring 4.5 cm on the plan is 900 cm long in reality. Convert that to 9 m.
steps.why: The real wall is 200 times longer than the drawn one, so multiply by 200.

steps.title: Reverse for drawing a real object
steps.text: A real 12 m length is 1,200 cm. Divide by 200 to draw it as 6 cm.
steps.why: Change metres to centimetres first. Then divide, because the drawing is 200 times smaller.

steps.title: Scale areas and volumes differently
steps.text: Doubling every length multiplies area by 4 and volume by 8. So the scale for lengths is not the scale for areas.
steps.why: Area uses two lengths, so the factor is used twice. Volume uses three lengths, so it is used three times.

quiz.question: At scale 1:100, how long is a real 7 m wall on the drawing?
quiz.hint: Put both lengths in the same unit before applying 1:100.
quiz.explanation: 7 m = 700 cm, and 700 cm ÷ 100 = 7 cm. Change the units before you divide.

quiz.question: A shape is enlarged with length scale factor 3. What is its area scale factor?
quiz.hint: Area uses two lengths, so the factor is used twice.
quiz.explanation: Area uses two lengths, so the factor is 3 × 3 = 9. The answer 27 is the volume factor.

lessons.takeaway: Same units first; multiply to enlarge, divide to reduce.
lessons.mistake: Using the length scale for an area. If every length is 3 times bigger, the area is 9 times bigger, not 3.

reference.name: Rectangle
reference.note: Perimeter uses length units; area uses square units.

reference.name: Triangle and parallelogram
reference.formula: Triangle A = ½bh; parallelogram A = bh
reference.note: h is perpendicular to the base.

reference.name: Circle
reference.note: Radius is half the diameter.

reference.name: Sector
reference.note: Sector perimeter also includes two radii.

reference.name: Cuboid
reference.note: Count exposed faces carefully.

reference.name: Prism
reference.note: The end face is the same all the way along.

reference.name: Scale factors
reference.formula: Length: k; area: k²; volume: k³
reference.note: Convert units before comparing lengths.

reference.name: Sector perimeter
reference.note: Add both exposed radii to the arc length. θ is measured in degrees; use this for a sector with two radial boundary edges.

toolkit.strategy: Decide what the question measures: an edge, a flat face, a filled solid or a scale drawing. Label the lengths and units before you choose a formula. When solids are joined, take hidden faces off the surface area only, never off the volume.

methods.title: Composite perimeter and area
methods.when: A shape is built from rectangles, triangles or other familiar shapes.
methods.rule: Rectangle A=lw, P=2(l+w); trapezium A=(a+b)h/2 for parallel sides a,b and perpendicular h; rhombus/kite A=d₁d₂/2 for perpendicular diagonals. Add/subtract non-overlapping areas; trace the external boundary.
steps: Split the figure into standard shapes.
Find any missing lengths.
Add or subtract areas.
Trace the outer boundary separately, excluding internal joins.
methods.example: An 8 by 6 rectangle with a 3 by 2 corner removed has area 48−6=42 square units.
methods.check: Adding back the removed 6 restores the full 48; the area must lie between 0 and 48.
methods.trap: Cutting a piece off the area does not always shorten the perimeter. Trace the new edge instead.

methods.title: Parallelogram and triangle height
methods.when: A sloping shape has a stated base and perpendicular height.
methods.rule: Parallelogram A=bh; triangle A=½bh.
steps: Choose a base.
Identify the perpendicular distance to the opposite vertex or parallel side.
Apply the correct whole or half product.
methods.example: A triangle with base 14 cm and perpendicular height 9 cm has area 63 cm².
methods.check: Two congruent copies form a parallelogram of area 126 cm².
methods.trap: The sloping side is not the height. Use the height that meets the base at a right angle.

methods.title: Circle, sector and semicircle measures
methods.when: A figure contains circular area or curved boundary.
methods.rule: C=2πr; A=πr²; arc=(θ/360)2πr; sector area=(θ/360)πr²; sector perimeter=2 r+arc for 0<θ<360°. Semicircle area=πr²/2; standalone perimeter=πr+2 r.
steps: Convert diameter to radius when needed.
Take the correct fraction of a full circle.
Add any straight radii or diameter needed for perimeter.
Exclude a shared diameter if it lies inside a composite region.
methods.example: A semicircle of radius 5 has area 25π/2 and a standalone perimeter 5π+10.
methods.check: Its curved boundary is half of 2π×5.
methods.trap: A semicircle’s perimeter includes the diameter only when that diameter is on the outside.

methods.title: Cuboid volume, nets and surface area
methods.when: A rectangular solid or its net is given.
methods.rule: V=lwh; closed SA=2(lw+lh+wh); 1 cm³=1 ml, 1000 cm³=1 litre.
steps: Identify the three perpendicular dimensions.
For volume, count base area times height.
For surface area, list every exposed face.
Remove a missing lid or opening if the object is not closed.
methods.example: A closed 7 by 4 by 3 cuboid has V=84 and SA=2(28+21+12)=122 in the corresponding cubic and square units.
methods.check: A net must have two faces of each area 28,21,12.
methods.trap: Material to cover a box is a surface area, in cm². Do not give it in cm³.

methods.title: Join solids and remove shared faces
methods.when: Two solids are glued face to face.
methods.rule: Exposed SA=SA₁+SA₂−2×(shared face area), for one full shared face; volumes add if there is no overlap.
steps: Calculate each separate surface area.
Identify the actual contact area.
Subtract it twice because one face from each solid becomes hidden.
For minimum or maximum exposed area, compare permitted contact areas.
methods.example: Two identical cubes of side 2 joined on a full face have exposed SA=24+24−2×4=40; volume=8+8=16.
methods.check: The result is a 4 by 2 by 2 cuboid with SA=2(8+8+4)=40.
methods.trap: Subtracting the contact area only once leaves one hidden face counted.

methods.title: Prism volume and reverse dimensions
methods.when: A solid has the same end face all the way along.
methods.rule: V=A×L and L=V/A, where A is the cross-section area, A>0.
steps: Identify the repeated cross-sectional shape.
Find its area using the correct 2 D formula.
Multiply by prism length, or divide volume by the area to reverse.
Distinguish the cross-section’s height from prism length.
methods.example: A triangular section with base 8 and height 5 has area 20; volume 300 therefore needs length 15.
methods.trap: Multiplying all three lengths and forgetting the ½ for a triangular end. That doubles the volume.

methods.title: Surface area of a right prism
methods.when: A closed prism has end faces that are not rectangles, such as triangles.
methods.rule: SA=2A+P×L for a closed right prism, where A and P are the area and perimeter of one end.
steps: Calculate one end area.
Find the full perimeter of that end, using any required side calculation.
Multiply its perimeter by prism length for lateral faces.
Add both ends, or omit any explicitly open face.
methods.example: A prism whose cross-section is a right-angled triangle with perpendicular sides 3, 4 and hypotenuse 5, length 10, has SA=2×6+(3+4+5)×10=132.
methods.check: The rectangular side faces have areas 30,40,50; adding the two 6-unit ends gives 132.
methods.trap: Mixing up the perimeter of the end face with its area. The side faces need the perimeter.

methods.title: Map scales in both directions
methods.when: Drawing and real lengths are connected by a scale 1:n.
methods.rule: Real length=n×drawing length; drawing length=real length/n, using the same units.
steps: Convert all lengths to one unit system.
Multiply from drawing to reality, divide in reverse.
If changing map scale, pass through the real length.
methods.example: At 1:20,000, 3 cm represents 60,000 cm=600 m; at 1:10,000 the same length is 6 cm.
methods.check: 6 cm×10,000=60,000 cm, the same real length; the less reduced map shows the object larger.
methods.trap: Both sides of a scale use the same unit. Change metres or kilometres to centimetres before using it.

methods.title: Scale area, volume and a cost decision
methods.when: A scale drawing is used to find real area or a practical cost.
methods.rule: Length factor k gives area factor k² and volume factor k³; cost=quantity×unit price.
steps: Find real dimensions before calculating a physical area.
Use square or cube scale factors only for matching types of measurement.
Apply the cost rate to the correct quantity.
Compare the final cost with the budget, keeping exact intermediate values.
methods.example: A 2 cm by 3 cm rectangle at 1:100 represents 2 m by 3 m, area 6 m², not 0.06 m².
methods.check: The real lengths are 100 times larger, so area is 10,000 times larger in matching square units.
methods.trap: Using the length scale for an area. Find the real lengths first, then multiply them.

checks: Perimeter uses length units, area square units, volume cubic units.
All lengths are in compatible units before substitution.
Shared interior faces are excluded from exposed surface area.
Curved formulas use radius, not diameter, and exact π is retained until the end.
The final result answers the requested cost, size or decision, not only an intermediate area.

challenges.title: Recover the length and cover a prism
challenges.question: A closed triangular prism has a right-angled triangular cross-section with perpendicular sides 6 cm and 8 cm. Its volume is 360 cm³. (a) Find its length. (b) Find the third side of the triangular cross-section. (c) Find the total surface area needed to cover all five faces.
hints: Find the triangular area before using the volume.
For surface area, use two triangular ends and one rectangular face for each side of the triangle.

solution.title: Find the cross-sectional area
solution.reason: The cross-section is a right-angled triangle.

solution.title: Reverse the volume
solution.reason: Volume is the repeated cross-sectional area times length.

solution.title: Find the missing edge
solution.reason: Pythagoras applies to the given right-angled triangle.

solution.title: Count every exterior face
solution.reason: There are two triangular ends and three rectangular lateral faces.

challenges.answer: Prism length 15 cm; third triangle side 10 cm; total surface area 408 cm².
challenges.check: The separate lateral areas 90,120,150 plus triangular areas 24 and 24 sum to 408; volume 24×15 returns 360.

challenges.title: A field purchase and fencing decision
challenges.question: A field consists of a 60 m by 40 m rectangle with a semicircle attached externally along one complete 40 m side. The shared diameter is inside the field. Land costs €2 per square metre and fencing costs €15 per metre around the outer boundary; these are invented classroom prices. (a) Find the exact area and outer perimeter. (b) Find the combined land-and-fencing cost. (c) Is a €9,400 budget sufficient? Keep π exact until the final money rounding.
hints: The semicircle’s radius is 20 m. Only three rectangle sides remain on the outside.
The area is the rectangle plus half a circle. The fence follows two 60 m sides, one 40 m side and the curved half circle.

solution.title: Find the combined area
solution.reason: The two regions do not overlap.

solution.title: Trace the external boundary
solution.reason: The shared 40 m diameter is internal and is not fenced.

solution.title: Apply both prices
solution.reason: Area and length are charged at different unit prices.

solution.title: Round and decide
solution.reason: The total is just under €9,400, so the budget is enough, with about 89 cents left.

challenges.answer: Area 2400+200π m²; perimeter 160+20π m; total €7200+700π≈€9,399.11; the stated budget is sufficient by about €0.89.
challenges.check: Using A≈3028.3185307 and P≈222.8318531 gives 2 A+15 P≈9399.114858, independently matching the exact expression.

challenges.title: Choose the least or most exposed joined solid
challenges.question: Two identical closed cuboids each measure 6 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm. They are joined flush along one complete matching face, with no overlap of volume and no gaps. (a) Find each separate surface area and volume. (b) Find the exposed surface area for each possible matching face size. (c) State which join gives the minimum and maximum exposed area, and give the resulting overall dimensions in each case. (d) Find the combined volume.
hints: The possible contact areas are 6×4, 6×3 and 4×3.
Subtract twice the contact area from the sum of the two separate surface areas.

solution.title: Measure one cuboid
solution.reason: Opposite faces form three equal pairs.

solution.title: Remove each possible shared pair
solution.reason: The two touching faces end up inside the solid, so take the contact area away twice.

solution.title: Choose the minimum
solution.math: Largest contact 24 gives minimum 168 cm²; joined dimensions 6×4×6 cm
solution.reason: The more area you hide in the join, the less is left showing.

solution.title: Choose the maximum
solution.math: Smallest contact 12 gives maximum 192 cm²; joined dimensions 12×4×3 cm
solution.reason: Hiding the smallest face leaves the most area showing.

solution.title: Add the volumes
solution.reason: The solids share a boundary face but no interior volume.

challenges.answer: One cuboid:108 cm²,72 cm³. Joined areas 168,180,192 cm². Minimum 168 for a 6×4 face; maximum 192 for a 4×3 face. Combined volume 144 cm³.
challenges.check: Direct cuboid formulas give SA(6,4,6)=168 and SA(12,4,3)=192, and both overall volumes are 144.

challenges.title: Redraw a field at a different map scale
challenges.question: On a 1:25,000 map, a rectangular field measures 3.2 cm by 2.0 cm. (a) Find its actual dimensions in metres, perimeter in metres and area in hectares, using 1 hectare=10,000 m². (b) Find the dimensions of the same field on a 1:10,000 map. (c) A separate 900 m route is drawn on the original map. Find its map length.
hints: Convert the real lengths from centimetres to metres after multiplying by 25,000.
For the new map, divide the real centimetre lengths by 10,000.

solution.title: Recover real dimensions
solution.reason: Scale ratios use the same units on both sides.

solution.title: Calculate the field measures
solution.reason: Perimeter and area use different formulas and units.

solution.title: Redraw at the new scale
solution.reason: The less reduced map displays larger lengths.

solution.title: Reverse the route scale
solution.reason: Divide the real length by the original scale denominator.

challenges.answer: Actual 800 m by 500 m; perimeter 2600 m; area 40 ha. New map 8 cm by 5 cm; route 3.6 cm on the original map.
challenges.check: The new drawing lengths are 2.5 times the old because 25000/10000=2.5; 3.6×25000 cm=900 m.

title: Statistics 2: Averages and Variability
intro: An average is one number that stands for a whole list. Learn the three averages (mean, median and mode), then use the range to show how spread out the list is.

lessons.title: Find mode and median
lessons.goal: Find the mode by counting repeats. Find the median by putting the list in order and taking the middle value.

steps.title: Order the data
steps.text: Use the values 2, 3, 3, 4 and 8. They are already in order from smallest to largest. Keep both 3s.
steps.why: The median is the middle of the ordered list, so the order must be right first.

quiz.question: Find the median of 9, 1, 7, 4, 3.
quiz.hint: Write the list in order from smallest to largest first.
quiz.explanation: In order the list is 1, 3, 4, 7, 9. The third of the five values is 4. The 7 is only the middle of the list as it was written.

quiz.question: Find the mode of 2,2,3,4,4,4,8.
quiz.hint: Count how many times each value appears.
quiz.explanation: 4 appears three times, more than any other value.

lessons.takeaway: Mode: the value that appears most often. Median: the middle value once the list is in order.
lessons.mistake: Taking the middle of the list as it is written. Put the values in order first, then find the middle.

lessons.title: Understand mean as fair sharing
lessons.goal: Find the mean by adding the values and sharing the total equally. Work backwards from a mean to find a missing value.

quiz.question: Find the mean of 4, 8, 9, 11.
quiz.hint: Add the four values, then divide the total by 4.

quiz.question: Four values have mean 7. Three values are 4, 6 and 8. Find the fourth.
quiz.hint: Four values with mean 7 must add to 4 × 7. Find that total first.

lessons.takeaway: Mean = total ÷ number of values. Working backwards, mean × number of values = total.
lessons.mistake: Dividing by the number of different values. For 5, 5 and 8 divide by 3, not by 2, because there are three values.

lessons.title: Choose an average that fits the question
lessons.goal: Choose the mean, median or mode to suit the data. See how one very different value (an outlier) pulls the mean.

steps.title: Use mode for categories
steps.text: You cannot add shirt colours or put them in order, so they have no mean or median. You can still say which colour is most common. That is the mode.
steps.why: Words (categories) cannot be added. The mode, the one that appears most often, is the only average that works.

quiz.question: Which summary is usually least affected by one extreme numerical value?
quiz.hint: Which one only looks at the middle of the ordered list?
quiz.explanation: The median is the middle of the ordered list. One extreme value changes the total, and so the mean, but usually leaves the middle value alone.

quiz.question: Which summary describes the most popular shirt colour?
quiz.hint: Colours are words, not numbers. You cannot add them or put them in order.
quiz.explanation: The mode is the most frequent category.

lessons.takeaway: Pick the average that suits the data and say why. An outlier favours the median. Categories need the mode.
lessons.mistake: Saying one average is always best. An outlier pulls the mean, and only the mode works for categories.

lessons.title: Use a frequency table for the mean
lessons.goal: Find the mean from a frequency table by counting each value as many times as it occurs.

steps.title: Read values and frequencies separately
steps.text: The score 1 occurs twice, the score 2 occurs three times and the score 3 occurs once. That makes six scores, not three.
steps.why: The frequency tells you how many times each score appears. Add the frequencies to count all the scores.

quiz.question: Values 2 and 5 have frequencies 3 and 1. Find the mean.
quiz.hint: The value 2 appears three times. Find the total of all four values first.
quiz.explanation: (2 × 3 + 5 × 1)/(3 + 1) = 11/4 = 2.75. The answer 3.5 comes from averaging 2 and 5 and forgetting the frequencies.

quiz.question: Why is a mean calculated from grouped intervals usually an estimate?
options: The individual values inside each interval are unknown
quiz.hint: A midpoint stands in for several values you cannot see.
quiz.explanation: The table tells you how many values are in each interval, but not what they are. The midpoint is a sensible stand-in, so the mean is an estimate.

lessons.takeaway: Multiply value × frequency, add the results, then divide by the total frequency.
lessons.mistake: Averaging only the values in the first column. Each value must be counted as many times as its frequency says.

lessons.title: Compare spread, not just averages
lessons.goal: Find the range and say what it tells you about how spread out the data are.

steps.why: The range only needs the smallest and the largest value.

steps.text: One unusual value can make the range large even when the other values sit close together. Look at all the values before you say the data are widely spread.
steps.why: The range ignores every value between the smallest and the largest.

quiz.question: Find the range of −3, 1, 4, 8.
quiz.hint: The smallest value is −3. Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding.
quiz.explanation: Range = 8 − (−3) = 8 + 3 = 11. On a number line, −3 to 8 is 11 steps.

quiz.question: Two players have the same mean score. Which extra measure helps compare consistency?
options: The number of games each played
quiz.hint: Consistent scores stay close together. Which measure shows how far apart they are?
quiz.explanation: The range shows how far apart the highest and lowest scores are. The player with the smaller range is the more consistent.

lessons.takeaway: Give an average for the centre and the range for the spread. You need both to compare two sets of data.
lessons.mistake: Thinking two sets with the same mean are equally consistent. 4, 5, 6 and 0, 5, 10 both have mean 5, but their ranges are 2 and 10.

reference.name: Mean
reference.formula: Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values
reference.note: Use all observations, including repetitions.

reference.name: Frequency-table mean
reference.note: Multiply each value by its frequency first.

reference.name: Grouped-data mean
reference.note: Mid-interval values (midpoints) replace the unknown individual values, so this is an estimate.

reference.name: Median
reference.note: For an even count, average the two middle values.

reference.name: Mode
reference.note: There may be more than one mode or no useful unique mode.

reference.name: Range
reference.note: A simple spread measure that is sensitive to extreme values.

toolkit.strategy: Decide whether you need frequency, position, total or spread. Recover totals before combining means, order the data before using a median, and check whether missing-value answers satisfy every stated condition.

methods.title: Mode and ordered median
methods.when: A question asks for the most common or middle observation.
methods.rule: Mode=most frequent; there may be several modes or no unique mode. Ordered odd N: median at position (N+1)/2. Even N: average positions N/2 and N/2+1.
steps: Keep all repeated observations.
Order the list.
Identify the middle position or pair.
For mode, compare frequencies rather than positions.
methods.example: For 2,4,4,7,9,12 the median is (4+7)/2=5.5 and the mode is 4.
methods.check: Three observations lie on either side of the middle gap.
methods.trap: The median need not be an observed value when N is even.

methods.title: Mean and a missing observation
methods.when: A total or mean is given with one unknown value.
methods.rule: Mean=total/N; required total=N×mean; missing value=required total−known total.
steps: Count the observations, including the missing one.
Recover the required total.
Subtract all known values.
Check the result is permitted in context.
methods.example: Five values have mean 12; four total 47. The missing value is 5×12−47=13.
methods.trap: Do not multiply by the number of known observations only.

methods.title: Combine means using group sizes
methods.when: Two or more groups have known means and counts.
methods.rule: Combined mean=(n₁m₁+n₂m₂+…)/(n₁+n₂+…).
steps: Recover each group total using count×mean.
Add those totals.
Divide by the combined count.
Use a direct average of means only when group sizes are equal.
methods.example: A group of 6 with mean 8 and a group of 4 with mean 13 have combined mean (48+52)/10=10.
methods.check: The result lies between 8 and 13 and nearer 8 because that group is larger.
methods.trap: (8+13)/2=10.5 ignores the unequal weights.

methods.title: Choose and justify a representative average
methods.when: The task asks for a typical value or compares summaries.
methods.rule: Mean uses all values; median resists a distant extreme; mode describes the most common value or category.
steps: Identify the data type and the question being answered.
Check for an outlier or uneven distribution.
Calculate the plausible summaries.
Choose one and give a reason connected to this data, not a universal slogan.
methods.example: For journey times 8,9,10,11,62, mean=20 but median=10. Median better describes the middle journey in this small sample.
methods.check: The chosen representative should be interpreted alongside the distribution.
methods.trap: “Median is always best” is not a valid general rule.

methods.title: Use a frequency-weighted mean
methods.when: Repeated values are organised into a frequency table.
methods.rule: Mean=Σfx/Σf.
steps: Multiply each value by its frequency.
Add products for the data total.
Add frequencies for the observation count.
Divide the two totals.
methods.example: Values 1,3,5 with frequencies 2,4,1 give mean (2+12+5)/7=19/7.
methods.check: Expanding the data list gives 1,1,3,3,3,3,5 with total 19.
methods.trap: Averaging 1,3,5 without weights loses repeated observations.

methods.title: Estimate a mean from grouped intervals
methods.when: Only interval frequencies are known.
methods.rule: Mid-interval value (midpoint)=(lower+upper)/2; estimated mean=Σ(f×midpoint)/Σf.
steps: Use consistent non-overlapping intervals.
Find each midpoint.
Multiply midpoint by frequency and add.
Divide by total frequency and label the result an estimate.
methods.example: Intervals 0≤t<10 and 10≤t<20 with frequencies 3 and 7 give estimated mean (3×5+7×15)/10=12.
methods.check: The estimate should lie inside the overall interval range.
methods.trap: The midpoint is a stand-in; the actual observations are not known.

methods.title: Range and missing extremes
methods.when: The smallest or largest value is unknown.
methods.rule: Range=max−min; max=min+range.
steps: Identify which entries really are the extremes.
Write the range equation.
Combine it with any mean-total equation.
Check the solved values keep the list ordered.
methods.example: Ordered a,5,8,10,b have range 14 and mean 9: b−a=14 and a+b=22, so a=4,b=18.
methods.check: The sum 45 gives mean 9, the extremes differ by 14, and 4≤5≤8≤10≤18.
methods.trap: A solution to the equations may fail the required order.

methods.title: Test whether statistics are possible together
methods.when: A problem claims a mean, median, range or integer condition.
methods.rule: All constraints must hold simultaneously; one contradiction makes a claim impossible.
steps: Translate each statistic into a total, position or difference condition.
Use the data type: whole-number observations require integer totals and entries.
Solve or construct an example.
For impossibility, state the exact contradiction.
methods.example: Three integer observations cannot have mean 2.5, because their required total would be 7.5.
methods.check: If a claim is said to be possible, exhibit a complete list satisfying every condition.
methods.trap: A plausible-looking average is not a proof that a data set exists.

checks: Mean uses all observations or their frequencies, not just distinct values.
Median is taken from the ordered list; an even count uses two middle values.
Grouped-data means are labelled estimates.
Missing values preserve the required ordering, range and data type.
The chosen average answers the contextual question, with outliers considered.

challenges.title: Combine two training groups correctly
challenges.question: Group A has 12 training scores with mean 14. Group B has 8 scores with mean 19. (a) Find the combined mean. (b) Explain why averaging 14 and 19 directly gives the wrong result. (c) One further score of 30 is added to the combined group. Find the new mean exactly and to two decimal places.
hints: Find each group’s total first: number of scores × mean.
The first combined count is 20; after the extra score it is 21.

solution.title: Recover the group totals
solution.reason: A mean multiplied by its count gives its total.

solution.title: Combine totals and counts
solution.reason: Add the two totals and share them among all 20 scores. Every score counts once.

solution.title: Explain the incorrect shortcut
solution.math: (14+19)/2=16.5 weights the two unequal groups equally
solution.reason: The group of 12 should influence the mean more than the group of 8.

solution.title: Add the extra observation
solution.reason: Both the total and the count change.

challenges.answer: Combined mean 16; a direct average of group means is inappropriate because counts differ; new mean 50/3≈16.67.
challenges.check: 12(14−16)+8(19−16)=−24+24=0, confirming the combined mean. The added score 30 is above 16, so the new mean must increase.

challenges.title: Estimate a grouped mean without inventing exact data
challenges.question: Eighteen journey times t minutes are grouped as follows: 0≤t<10 has frequency 4; 10≤t<20 has frequency 8; 20≤t<30 has frequency 6. (a) Estimate the mean using mid-interval values. (b) State the modal class. (c) Locate the median within a class and explain why its exact value cannot be recovered from this table. (d) Can the exact range be calculated?
hints: The midpoints are 5,15 and 25; weight them by their frequencies.
With 18 observations, the median uses positions 9 and 10 in the ordered list.

solution.title: Calculate midpoint contributions
solution.reason: Each midpoint stands in for the unknown values inside its group.

solution.title: Find the estimate
solution.reason: Divide by the 18 journey times, not by the 3 groups.

solution.title: Identify the modal class
solution.reason: This interval has the greatest frequency, 8.

solution.title: Locate the median positions
solution.math: Cumulative frequencies are 4,12,18, so positions 9 and 10 are both in 10≤t<20
solution.reason: The 9th and 10th values are somewhere in this interval, but the table does not say where. So the median lies in this interval and its exact value is unknown.

solution.title: Explain the range limitation
solution.math: The exact minimum and maximum are not given, so the exact range is unknown
solution.reason: The table only gives intervals. The smallest time could be anywhere from 0 up to 10, so the exact range cannot be found.

challenges.answer: Estimated mean 145/9≈16.11 min; modal class 10≤t<20; median lies in that class but is not exact; exact range cannot be recovered.
challenges.check: The midpoint-based total is 290 and 290/18≈16.11. Changing an observation within its interval leaves the table unchanged but can change the exact mean, median or range.

challenges.title: Find missing extremes and reject an impossible claim
challenges.question: Five whole-number journey times, in minutes, are ordered as a,4,7,9,b. Their mean is 8 and range is 12. (a) Find a and b. (b) Find the median and explain why the mean exceeds it. (c) Could a different pair of whole-number extremes in the same ordered pattern have mean 7 and range 12? Give a mathematical reason.
hints: The three middle values total 20; mean 8 fixes the complete total at 40.
For part (c), use a+b=15 and b−a=12, then check the whole-number condition.

solution.title: Translate mean and range
solution.reason: Mean 8 for five values gives a total of 40. The middle three add to 20, so a + b = 20. The range links the two end values.

solution.title: Solve both conditions
solution.math: 2b = 32 and a + b = 20 → b = 16 and a = 4
solution.reason: Add the two equations. The a and the −a cancel, leaving 2b = 32.

solution.title: Check order and median
solution.reason: The third of five observations is the middle one; the high 16 raises the mean above it.

solution.title: Test the alternate mean
solution.reason: Use the same two equations with the new total. They give only one possible pair of end values.

solution.title: Use the data-type restriction
solution.math: That alternative is impossible for whole-number times
solution.reason: Journey times here are whole numbers, and 13.5 and 1.5 are not. They would only be allowed if fractions of a minute could be used.

challenges.answer: a=4,b=16; median 7, mean 8. Mean 7 with the same middle values and range 12 is impossible under the whole-number condition.
challenges.check: 4+4+7+9+16=40 and 16−4=12. In part (c), integer extremes with an even difference must have an even sum, contradicting the required sum 15.

challenges.title: Choose a useful summary when one time is extreme
challenges.question: Seven completion times in minutes are 5,6,7,7,8,9,70. (a) Find the mean, median, mode and range. (b) Choose a useful summary for a typical middle participant and justify it. (c) Replace 70 by 140 and recalculate the four summaries. (d) Explain why the mean may still be relevant if an organiser wants to estimate total participant-minutes.
hints: The first six times sum to 42.
An extreme replacement changes totals and endpoints, but not the ordered middle positions.

solution.title: Calculate the original summaries
solution.reason: The mean uses the total. The median is the fourth of the seven ordered values. The mode is the most frequent value. The range uses the two ends.

solution.title: Choose a contextual centre
solution.math: Median 7 minutes is a useful middle-participant summary here
solution.reason: Six times cluster from 5 to 9 while 70 is far away; the median is not pulled by its distance.

solution.title: Replace the extreme value
solution.reason: Changing 70 to 140 changes the total and the largest value. The middle value and the most frequent value stay the same.

solution.title: Explain the total-based purpose
solution.math: For a specified participant count, count×mean gives total participant-minutes
solution.reason: Which average is useful depends on the job. Only the mean keeps the total, so it is the one to use for total minutes.

challenges.answer: Original: mean 16, median 7, mode 7, range 65. After replacement: mean 26, median 7, mode 7, range 135. Median suits the middle participant; mean relates to total participant-minutes.
challenges.check: 7×16=112 and 7×26=182. Both ordered lists still have 7 in position 4 and 7 as the only repeated value.

title: Geometry 1: Triangles, Quadrilaterals and Theorems
intro: Geometry is about saying why. Find the fact that links the angles or lengths, name it, then calculate. You need to follow proofs and explain your reasons; full formal proofs are not examinable at Junior Cycle. Chapter 16 explains the proofs of Theorems 4, 6, 9, 14 and 19 step by step.

lessons.title: Recognise lines and angle relationships
lessons.goal: Name the fact that links two angles before you calculate anything.

steps.title: Name the objects
steps.text: A line goes on for ever in both directions. A segment is the piece between two endpoints. A ray starts at one point and goes on for ever. Parallel lines never meet.
steps.why: The exact name tells you which facts you are allowed to use.
steps.math: Line AB; segment [AB]; ray from A through B

steps.title: Use a straight-line total
steps.text: Two angles side by side on a straight line add to 180 degrees. If one is 125 degrees, the other is 55 degrees.
steps.why: Together they make a half turn, which is 180 degrees.

steps.title: Identify parallel-line angles
steps.text: A line that crosses two parallel lines is called a transversal. Corresponding angles, in the same corner at each crossing, are equal. Alternate angles, in a Z shape, are equal. Interior angles on the same side, called co-interior angles, add to 180 degrees.
steps.why: These facts are true only when the two lines are parallel.

steps.title: Match the picture to the reason
steps.text: Mark the pair of angles you are using, then write the fact beside your answer. Lines that only look parallel are not enough. You need arrow marks, a statement or a proof.
steps.why: A stated reason shows your answer is true, not just likely.

quiz.question: An angle adjacent to 132° on a straight line is…
quiz.hint: Angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees.
quiz.explanation: The two angles add to 180 degrees, so the other is 180 − 132 = 48 degrees.

quiz.question: For parallel lines cut by a transversal, which pair is equal?
options: An acute and an obtuse angle
quiz.hint: Look for angles in the same corner at each crossing.
quiz.explanation: Corresponding angles are equal when the lines are parallel.

lessons.takeaway: Name the fact first, then calculate.
lessons.mistake: Assuming lines are parallel because they look parallel. Use parallel-line facts only when the lines are marked or stated as parallel.

lessons.title: Use triangle and exterior angles
lessons.goal: Use the 180-degree total of a triangle to find an outside angle, called an exterior angle.

steps.title: Start with the triangle total
steps.text: Two interior angles of a triangle are 55 and 65 degrees. Their total is 120 degrees.
steps.why: The three interior angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Interior angle plus its adjacent exterior angle makes a straight angle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="190,285 470,285 344,66" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="angle0" x="245" y="262" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">55°</text><text id="angle1" x="320" y="152" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">65°</text><text id="angle2" x="383" y="262" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">?</text></svg>

steps.title: Find the missing interior angle
steps.text: Subtract 120 from 180. The third angle is 60 degrees.
steps.why: The three angles must add to 180 degrees, so the third makes up the difference.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Interior angle plus its adjacent exterior angle makes a straight angle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="190,285 470,285 344,66" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="angle0" x="245" y="262" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">55°</text><text id="angle1" x="320" y="152" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">65°</text><text id="angle2" x="383" y="262" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">60°</text></svg>

steps.title: Extend a side
steps.text: Extend one side past the 60-degree corner. The outside angle made there is called an exterior angle. It sits on a straight line with the 60-degree angle, so it is 120 degrees.
steps.why: The inside angle and the outside angle beside it add to 180 degrees.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Interior angle plus its adjacent exterior angle makes a straight angle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="190,285 470,285 344,66" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="angle0" x="245" y="262" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">55°</text><text id="angle1" x="320" y="152" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">65°</text><text id="angle2" x="383" y="262" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">60°</text><line id="extension" x1="470" y1="285" x2="700" y2="285" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="4"/><text id="exterior" x="500" y="228" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">120°</text><path id="exterior-arc" d="M525 285 A55 55 0 0 0 442.5 237.4" fill="none" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

steps.title: See the exterior-angle rule
steps.text: The exterior angle also equals the two inside angles that do not touch it, added together. These are called the interior opposite angles. You get the same 120 degrees.
steps.why: Both 60 + 120 and 60 + 55 + 65 make 180. Take away the shared 60 and the rest must match.

quiz.question: A triangle has angles 42° and 71°. Find the third.
quiz.hint: The total is 180 degrees.
quiz.explanation: The three angles add to 180 degrees, so the third is 180 − 42 − 71 = 67 degrees.

quiz.question: An exterior angle is 110° and one interior opposite angle is 45°. Find the other interior opposite angle.
quiz.hint: The two interior opposite angles add to the exterior angle.
quiz.explanation: The two interior opposite angles add to 110 degrees, so the other is 110 − 45 = 65 degrees.

lessons.takeaway: The three inside angles add to 180°. An exterior angle equals the two interior opposite angles added together.
lessons.mistake: Adding the inside angle that touches the exterior angle. Add the two inside angles that do not touch it.

lessons.title: Use quadrilateral properties
lessons.goal: Use only the facts that the named shape guarantees. Do not add extra ones from the picture.

steps.title: Split a quadrilateral
steps.text: A quadrilateral is a shape with four straight sides. Draw a diagonal, a line joining two opposite corners. It splits the shape into two triangles, and their angle totals add.
steps.why: Each triangle gives 180 degrees.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="quad" points="140,285 590,285 650,105 250,80" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

steps.title: Solve a missing angle
steps.text: If three angles are 80, 95 and 105 degrees, their sum is 280. The fourth is 80 degrees.
steps.why: The four interior angles must total 360 degrees.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="quad" points="140,285 590,285 650,105 250,80" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="diagonal" x1="140" y1="285" x2="650" y2="105" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/></svg>

steps.title: Use a parallelogram’s extra structure
steps.text: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are parallel and equal. Opposite angles are equal. Angles next to each other add to 180 degrees.
steps.why: The parallel sides make co-interior angles, and those add to 180 degrees.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="quad" points="140,285 590,285 650,105 250,80" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="diagonal" x1="140" y1="285" x2="650" y2="105" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text id="one" x="350" y="155" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">180°</text><text id="two" x="440" y="255" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">180°</text></svg>

steps.title: Separate special cases
steps.text: A rectangle has four right angles. A rhombus has four equal sides. A square has both. An ordinary parallelogram may have neither.
steps.why: Each special shape is a parallelogram with one extra rule added.

quiz.question: A parallelogram has one angle 70°. What is an adjacent angle?
quiz.hint: In a parallelogram, angles next to each other add to 180 degrees.
quiz.explanation: Angles next to each other add to 180 degrees, so the adjacent angle is 180 − 70 = 110 degrees.

quiz.question: Which property is guaranteed for every rectangle?
options: Exactly one pair of parallel sides
quiz.hint: Think about what makes a shape a rectangle.
quiz.explanation: Every rectangle has four right angles. Equal sides are guaranteed only for a square.

lessons.takeaway: Use only the facts guaranteed by the named shape.
lessons.mistake: Treating every parallelogram as a rectangle, or every rhombus as a square. A slanted parallelogram has no right angles.

lessons.title: Decide whether triangles are congruent
lessons.goal: Decide whether two triangles are identical in shape and size, and name the test that proves it.

steps.title: Understand congruent
steps.text: Congruent triangles have the same shape and size. One can fit exactly over the other after moving, rotating or reflecting it.
steps.why: Turning or flipping a triangle does not change its sides or angles.
steps.math: Congruent → matching sides and angles equal

steps.title: Use SSS or SAS
steps.text: SSS matches all three sides. SAS matches two sides and the included angle between them.
steps.why: The angle must sit between the two sides. With any other angle, two different triangles can sometimes be drawn.

steps.title: Use ASA or RHS
steps.text: ASA matches two angles and the side between them. RHS is for right-angled triangles: a right angle, equal hypotenuses and one other equal side.
steps.why: With that information, only one triangle can be drawn.
