steps.title: Reject tempting shortcuts
steps.text: Three equal angles give the same shape, but one triangle can be bigger. Two sides and an angle that is not between them is not a test either.
steps.why: A test only counts if no other size or shape of triangle fits the same facts.
steps.math: AAA: similarity only; SSA: not a general test

quiz.question: Which information guarantees congruence?
options: Two equal corresponding sides and their included angle
quiz.hint: Look for one of SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS.
quiz.explanation: Two sides and the angle between them is the SAS test.

quiz.question: Two right-angled triangles have equal hypotenuses and one other equal corresponding side. Which test applies?
options: ASA, because the right angle counts as an angle
quiz.hint: The right angle is already known.
quiz.explanation: RHS uses a right angle, equal hypotenuses and one other pair of equal sides.

lessons.takeaway: Name the test, and match each part of one triangle with the same part of the other.
lessons.mistake: Using three equal angles, AAA, to claim equal size. AAA gives the same shape only.

lessons.title: Choose the correct side in Pythagoras
lessons.goal: Find the hypotenuse first. Add squares to find it, and subtract squares to find a shorter side.

steps.title: Identify the hypotenuse
steps.text: A right-angled triangle has perpendicular sides 6 cm and 8 cm. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side.
steps.why: Pythagoras applies only to a right-angled triangle.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>The hypotenuse is opposite the marked right angle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="150,300 470,300 150,60" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="vertex0" x="125" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><text id="vertex1" x="485" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="vertex2" x="124" y="58" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><line id="right1" x1="150" y1="276" x2="174" y2="276" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="right2" x1="174" y1="276" x2="174" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="side0" x="115" y="180" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">6</text><text id="side1" x="310" y="335" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">8</text><text id="side2" x="335" y="165" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">c</text></svg>

steps.title: Add the two smaller squares
steps.text: Square each perpendicular side, then add. This gives 100, the square of the hypotenuse.
steps.why: Pythagoras is a fact about the squares of the sides, not the sides themselves.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>The hypotenuse is opposite the marked right angle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="150,300 470,300 150,60" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="vertex0" x="125" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><text id="vertex1" x="485" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="vertex2" x="124" y="58" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><line id="right1" x1="150" y1="276" x2="174" y2="276" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="right2" x1="174" y1="276" x2="174" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="side0" x="115" y="180" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">6</text><text id="side1" x="310" y="335" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">8</text><text id="side2" x="335" y="165" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">c</text></svg>

steps.title: Return to a length
steps.text: Take the positive square root because a length is positive. The hypotenuse is 10 cm.
steps.why: 100 is the square of the side. The square root brings you back to the side itself.

steps.title: Reverse for a missing shorter side
steps.text: If the hypotenuse is 13 cm and one shorter side is 5 cm, subtract squares and then take the root.
steps.why: It is the same rule turned around. A shorter side must come out smaller than the hypotenuse.

quiz.question: A right-angled triangle has perpendicular sides 5 cm and 12 cm. Find the hypotenuse.
quiz.hint: Square the two shorter sides, add them, then take the square root.
quiz.explanation: Add the squares, then take the square root: √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 cm.

quiz.question: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 10 cm and one perpendicular side 6 cm. Find the other perpendicular side.
quiz.hint: Square the hypotenuse, subtract the square of the known side, then take the square root.
quiz.explanation: Subtract the squares, then take the square root: √(100 − 36) = √64 = 8 cm.

lessons.takeaway: The hypotenuse squared equals the other two sides squared and added.
lessons.mistake: Adding the squares when you want a shorter side, or forgetting the final square root. For a shorter side, subtract: 13² − 5², not 13² + 5².

lessons.title: Know what a proof is doing
lessons.goal: Know what you are given, what you must show, and give a reason for every step between.

steps.title: Separate definitions and axioms
steps.text: A definition says what a word means. An axiom is a starting fact that everyone accepts without proof. Neither one comes from measuring a drawing.
steps.why: A proof needs agreed meanings and starting facts.
steps.math: Definition → meaning; axiom → accepted starting fact
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Separate definitions and axioms</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">Definition → meaning; axiom → accepted starting fact</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Separate definitions and axioms</text></svg>

steps.title: State the theorem precisely
steps.text: A theorem is a statement that has been proved by reasoning. Before you start, pick out what is given and what you must show.
steps.why: You cannot use the thing you are trying to prove as one of your reasons.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>State the theorem precisely</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">Definition → meaning; axiom → accepted starting fact</text><rect id="row1" x="30" y="97" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num1" x="48" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">02</text><text id="math1" x="95" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">Given → justified steps → conclusion</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">State the theorem precisely</text></svg>

steps.title: Recognise converse and corollary
steps.text: A converse swaps the two halves of a statement, so it needs its own proof. A corollary is a fact that follows quickly from a theorem already proved.
steps.why: Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square. A converse can be false.
steps.math: If P then Q; converse: if Q then P

steps.title: Write a reason beside every claim
steps.text: For an angle calculation, a reason might be “straight-line angles total 180 degrees” or “alternate angles on parallel lines”.
steps.why: A diagram shows one case. A reason covers every case.

quiz.question: What is a converse?
options: The statement with “not” added to its conclusion
The statement with condition and conclusion swapped
A theorem that has already been proved
quiz.hint: Think “if P then Q” changed to “if Q then P”.
quiz.explanation: A converse swaps the “if” part and the “then” part. It needs its own proof.

quiz.question: Which is a valid proof reason?
options: The protractor reads 40° on the sketch
It worked in the previous question
quiz.hint: Pick the reason that is true for every diagram, not just this one.
quiz.explanation: That vertically opposite angles are equal is a proved theorem. The other three are only observations.

lessons.takeaway: A proof explains why the result is true in every possible case, not just in one drawing.
lessons.mistake: Treating one accurate drawing as a proof. A drawing checks one case; a proof must cover them all.

lessons.title: Prove vertically opposite angles equal
lessons.goal: Use two straight-line totals that share one angle to show the opposite angles are equal.

steps.title: Label the angles at a crossing
steps.text: Two straight lines intersect. Name one angle α, its neighbour β, and the angle opposite α as γ.
steps.why: The crossing gives two useful straight-line pairs.
steps.math: α next to β; γ opposite α
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Two straight-line equations share β.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><line id="ab" x1="150" y1="90" x2="610" y2="310" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="cd" x1="150" y1="310" x2="610" y2="90" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="4"/><text id="o" x="380" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text id="alpha" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">α</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Two straight-line equations share β.</text></svg>

steps.title: Use the first straight line
steps.text: Angles α and β together make 180 degrees.
steps.why: Angles side by side on a straight line add to 180 degrees.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Two straight-line equations share β.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><line id="ab" x1="150" y1="90" x2="610" y2="310" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="cd" x1="150" y1="310" x2="610" y2="90" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="4"/><text id="o" x="380" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text id="alpha" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">α</text><text id="beta" x="490" y="210" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">β</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Two straight-line equations share β.</text></svg>

steps.title: Use the second straight line
steps.text: Angles β and γ also make 180 degrees. The same β appears in both equations.
steps.why: The other straight line gives a second total of 180 degrees.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Two straight-line equations share β.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><line id="ab" x1="150" y1="90" x2="610" y2="310" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="cd" x1="150" y1="310" x2="610" y2="90" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="4"/><text id="o" x="380" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text id="alpha" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">α</text><text id="beta" x="490" y="210" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">β</text><text id="gamma" x="380" y="285" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">γ</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Two straight-line equations share β.</text></svg>

steps.title: Subtract the shared angle
steps.text: Both α and γ equal 180 degrees minus β. So they are equal, however the two lines are drawn.
steps.why: Take the same amount from two equal totals and what is left is still equal.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Two straight-line equations share β.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><line id="ab" x1="150" y1="90" x2="610" y2="310" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="cd" x1="150" y1="310" x2="610" y2="90" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="4"/><text id="o" x="380" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text id="alpha" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">α</text><text id="beta" x="490" y="210" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">β</text><text id="gamma" x="380" y="285" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">γ</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Two straight-line equations share β.</text></svg>

quiz.question: Two vertically opposite angles are labelled 3x + 5 and 65 degrees. Find x.
quiz.hint: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so write an equation.
quiz.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are equal: 3x + 5 = 65 → 3x = 60 → x = 20.

quiz.question: Which fact starts a proof that vertically opposite angles are equal?
options: Opposite angles are equal by definition
The two angles look the same size
Adjacent angles at the crossing are equal
quiz.hint: The proof uses two pairs of angles that each lie on a straight line.
quiz.explanation: Both pairs form straight angles, so each total is 180 degrees.

lessons.takeaway: Both opposite angles are 180° minus the same neighbour, so they are equal.
lessons.mistake: Mixing up vertically opposite angles with angles side by side. Opposite angles are equal; angles side by side add to 180°.

lessons.title: Prove the isosceles angle rule and its converse
lessons.goal: Show that equal sides in a triangle face equal angles, and the reverse.

steps.title: State the equal-side assumption
steps.text: In triangle ABC, suppose AB = AC. The angles opposite those equal sides are angle C and angle B.
steps.why: Each side faces one angle. Match a side with the angle across from it, not one that touches it.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Read the marked sides and angles, not the apparent shape.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="150,300 610,300 380,70" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="vertex0" x="125" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="vertex1" x="625" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><text id="vertex2" x="395" y="90" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text></svg>

steps.title: Compare the triangle with reversed labels
steps.text: Compare ABC with the same triangle read backwards, ACB. Matching sides in that order: AB with AC, AC with AB, and BC with CB, all equal. So the triangles are congruent by SSS.
steps.why: All three corresponding sides are equal.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Read the marked sides and angles, not the apparent shape.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="150,300 610,300 380,70" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="vertex0" x="125" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="vertex1" x="625" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><text id="vertex2" x="395" y="90" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><line id="equal1" x1="220" y1="225" x2="230" y2="235" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="equal2" x1="530" y1="225" x2="540" y2="235" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

steps.title: Read the corresponding angles
steps.text: The congruence matches corner B with corner C, so the base angles are equal. That proves the first half: equal sides give equal angles.
steps.why: Corresponding angles of congruent triangles are equal.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Read the marked sides and angles, not the apparent shape.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="150,300 610,300 380,70" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="vertex0" x="125" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="vertex1" x="625" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><text id="vertex2" x="395" y="90" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><line id="equal1" x1="220" y1="225" x2="230" y2="235" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="equal2" x1="530" y1="225" x2="540" y2="235" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="base1" x="255" y="278" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">equal</text><text id="base2" x="450" y="278" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">equal</text></svg>

steps.title: Prove the converse separately
steps.text: Now start from the other end: the two base angles are equal. Compare ABC with ACB again, using those two angles and the side BC between them. ASA gives AB = AC.
steps.why: The converse is a new statement, so it needs its own proof. Swapping the words is not enough.
steps.math: Equal base angles → equal opposite sides
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Read the marked sides and angles, not the apparent shape.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="150,300 610,300 380,70" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="vertex0" x="125" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="vertex1" x="625" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><text id="vertex2" x="395" y="90" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><line id="equal1" x1="220" y1="225" x2="230" y2="235" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="equal2" x1="530" y1="225" x2="540" y2="235" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="base1" x="255" y="278" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">equal</text><text id="base2" x="450" y="278" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">equal</text></svg>

quiz.question: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and angle A = 40°. Find angle B.
quiz.hint: Subtract the vertex angle from 180 degrees, then share what is left equally between the two base angles.
quiz.explanation: The two base angles share what is left: (180 − 40)/2 = 70 degrees.

quiz.question: In triangle ABC, if angle B equals angle C, which sides are equal?
quiz.hint: Match each angle with the side opposite it.
quiz.explanation: The side opposite B is AC and the side opposite C is AB. Equal angles face equal sides, so AB = AC.

lessons.takeaway: Equal sides face equal angles; equal angles face equal sides.
lessons.mistake: Pairing an equal side with the angle touching it. The equal angles are the ones opposite the equal sides.

lessons.title: Connect parallel lines and equal angles
lessons.goal: Use parallel lines to get equal angles, and equal angles to prove lines are parallel.

steps.title: Start with parallel lines
steps.text: A transversal crosses parallel lines l and m. The alternate angles, the pair in the Z shape, are equal. Theorem 3 covers this.
steps.why: Here we are told the lines are parallel. That is our starting fact.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><line id="line1" x1="75" y1="110" x2="690" y2="110" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="line2" x1="75" y1="260" x2="690" y2="260" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="transversal" x1="210" y1="350" x2="490" y2="30" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="4"/><text id="l" x="710" y="118" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">l</text><text id="m" x="710" y="268" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">m</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Use a stated fact to justify each step.</text></svg>

steps.title: Connect alternate and corresponding positions
steps.text: At each crossing, vertically opposite angles are equal. Put that together with the equal alternate angles and the corresponding angles must be equal too.
steps.why: If two angles both equal a third angle, they equal each other.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><line id="line1" x1="75" y1="110" x2="690" y2="110" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="line2" x1="75" y1="260" x2="690" y2="260" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="transversal" x1="210" y1="350" x2="490" y2="30" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="4"/><text id="l" x="710" y="118" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">l</text><text id="m" x="710" y="268" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">m</text><circle id="angle1" cx="454" cy="85" r="24" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="alpha" x="454" y="94" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">α</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Use a stated fact to justify each step.</text></svg>

steps.title: Use the converse test
steps.text: Now go the other way. The alternate angles are equal and we must show the lines are parallel. Through the crossing on m, draw a line parallel to l. It makes the same alternate angle as m does. So that line is m itself.
steps.why: Only one line through that point can make that angle on that side. So the parallel line and m are the same line.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><line id="line1" x1="75" y1="110" x2="690" y2="110" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="line2" x1="75" y1="260" x2="690" y2="260" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="transversal" x1="210" y1="350" x2="490" y2="30" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="4"/><text id="l" x="710" y="118" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">l</text><text id="m" x="710" y="268" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">m</text><circle id="angle1" cx="454" cy="85" r="24" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="alpha" x="454" y="94" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">α</text><circle id="angle2" cx="323" cy="235" r="24" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="alpha2" x="323" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">α</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Use a stated fact to justify each step.</text></svg>

steps.title: Get the corresponding-angle converse
steps.text: Suppose two corresponding angles are equal. Swap one for its vertically opposite angle. Now you have equal alternate angles, so the converse test shows the lines are parallel.
steps.why: This is Theorem 5. It rests on Theorem 3 for alternate angles and Theorem 1 for vertically opposite angles.

quiz.question: A transversal makes equal corresponding angles with two lines. What follows?
quiz.hint: Equal corresponding angles tell you something about the two lines.
quiz.explanation: Equal corresponding angles show that the two lines are parallel.

quiz.question: To infer equality of alternate angles, what fact must be given or proved?
options: The lines are the same length
The diagram is drawn to scale
quiz.hint: The rule only works for a special pair of lines.
quiz.explanation: Alternate angles are equal only when the two crossed lines are parallel.

lessons.takeaway: Parallel lines give equal angles. Equal angles in the right positions prove lines are parallel.
lessons.mistake: Using parallel-line angle facts before you know the lines are parallel. Look for arrow marks or a statement first.

lessons.title: Prove parallelogram diagonals bisect each other
lessons.goal: Show that each diagonal of a parallelogram cuts the other exactly in half.

steps.title: Name the intersection
steps.text: In parallelogram ABCD, diagonals AC and BD meet at E. We want to prove AE = CE and BE = DE.
steps.why: Bisect means cut into two equal parts.
steps.math: Goal: AE = CE and BE = DE
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="quad" points="140,275 500,275 620,105 260,105" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="p0" x="115" y="290" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><text id="p1" x="515" y="290" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="p2" x="635" y="120" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><text id="p3" x="235" y="120" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">D</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Use a stated fact to justify each step.</text></svg>

steps.title: Choose opposite small triangles
steps.text: Compare triangles AEB and CED. AB = CD because opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.
steps.why: Choose triangles containing the half-diagonals you want to compare.

steps.title: Match two angle pairs
steps.text: AB is parallel to CD. The diagonal AC crosses them, so ∠EAB = ∠ECD, alternate angles. The diagonal BD gives ∠EBA = ∠EDC the same way. The equal sides AB and CD lie between these angles, so ASA applies.
steps.why: The equal side lies between the two matched angles.

steps.title: Read off the half-diagonals
steps.text: Corresponding sides now give AE = CE and BE = DE. This proves both diagonals are bisected at E.
steps.why: Congruent triangles match in every part, so their matching sides are equal.

quiz.question: A parallelogram diagonal AC is 18 cm long and meets the other diagonal at E. Find AE.
quiz.hint: The diagonals of a parallelogram cut each other in half.
quiz.explanation: AE is half of AC, so 18/2 = 9 cm.

quiz.question: Does a general parallelogram necessarily have equal diagonals?
options: No; bisection does not imply equal total lengths
Yes, because the diagonals bisect each other
Yes, because its opposite sides are parallel
quiz.hint: Equal halves of one diagonal say nothing about the other diagonal.
quiz.explanation: Each diagonal is cut in half, but one diagonal can be longer than the other.

lessons.takeaway: Each diagonal is cut in half by the other. The two diagonals need not be the same length.
lessons.mistake: Confusing “bisect each other” with “are equal”.

lessons.title: Why similar triangles have proportional sides
lessons.goal: See why triangles with the same angles have sides in the same ratio.

steps.title: Match the equal angles
steps.text: Triangles ABC and PQR have equal matching angles: A with P, B with Q, C with R. Suppose AB is longer than PQ.
steps.why: The matching corners tell you which side pairs with which.
steps.math: AB ↔ PQ; AC ↔ PR; BC ↔ QR
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="large" points="100,300 400,300 220,70" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="small" points="490,300 700,300 574,139" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="a" x="80" y="325" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><text id="b" x="405" y="325" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="c" x="210" y="55" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><text id="p" x="470" y="325" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">P</text><text id="q" x="705" y="325" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">Q</text><text id="r" x="570" y="120" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">R</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Use a stated fact to justify each step.</text></svg>

steps.title: Make a matching small triangle
steps.text: Choose D on AB so that AD = PQ. Through D draw DE parallel to BC, meeting AC at E.
steps.why: Because DE is parallel to BC, the small triangle ADE has the same angles as ABC.

steps.title: Use congruence for the constructed triangle
steps.text: In triangles ADE and PQR, ∠A = ∠P is given and AD = PQ by construction. Also ∠ADE = ∠ABC = ∠Q, corresponding angles because DE is parallel to BC. ASA gives AE = PR and DE = QR.
steps.why: Same angles and one equal matching side make the triangles identical.

steps.title: Apply parallel-line proportionality
steps.text: Theorem 12 says a line parallel to one side cuts the other two sides in the same ratio, so AD/AB = AE/AC. The same argument from vertex B brings in DE/BC. Now swap AD, AE and DE for PQ, PR and QR.
steps.why: Theorem 12 is used here as a tool. Chapter 16 works with it in more detail.

quiz.question: Two similar triangles have matching sides 4 and 10. Another side in the smaller triangle is 6. Find its matching larger side.
quiz.hint: The length scale factor is 10/4.
quiz.explanation: The scale factor is 10/4 = 2.5, so the matching side is 6 × 2.5 = 15.

quiz.question: Why must corresponding sides be matched in the same order?
options: The larger triangle must always be on top of the ratio
Every ratio must compare matching sides in the same direction
Ratios only work for right-angled triangles
quiz.hint: Put the larger triangle on top in every ratio, or the smaller on top in every ratio.
quiz.explanation: If one ratio is large over small and another is small over large, they will not match.

lessons.takeaway: Equal matching angles mean every side is multiplied by the same scale factor.
lessons.mistake: Pairing sides by where they sit on the page. Pair each side with the side opposite the equal angle.

lessons.title: Prove the converse of Pythagoras
lessons.goal: Use the three side lengths alone to decide whether a triangle has a right angle.

steps.title: Put the longest side in the correct role
steps.text: Suppose a triangle has sides a, b and longest side c, with c² = a² + b². We want to show it is right-angled.
steps.why: We do not know yet that there is a right angle. That is what we must prove.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Begin with a triangle whose angle has not yet been proved right.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="original" points="145,300 590,300 275,80" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="given-a" x="175" y="180" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">a</text><text id="given-b" x="460" y="180" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">b</text><text id="given-c" x="365" y="340" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">c</text><text id="unknown" x="380" y="45" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">Angle unknown: do not assume 90°.</text></svg>

steps.title: Construct a comparison triangle
steps.text: Construct a right-angled triangle whose perpendicular sides have lengths a and b. Call its hypotenuse d.
steps.why: You can always draw a right angle and mark lengths a and b along its arms.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>A comparison triangle supplies the right angle without assuming the conclusion.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="comparison" points="170,290 570,290 170,100" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="square1" x1="170" y1="265" x2="195" y2="265" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><line id="square2" x1="195" y1="265" x2="195" y2="290" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="perpendicular side-a" x="125" y="205" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">a</text><text id="perpendicular side-b" x="365" y="335" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">b</text><text id="hyp" x="370" y="170" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">d</text><text id="reason" x="380" y="50" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">Constructed right-angled triangle</text></svg>

steps.title: Compare all three lengths
steps.text: We are given c² = a² + b², and Pythagoras gives d² = a² + b². So d² = c², and since lengths are positive, d = c. The two triangles now have all three sides equal.
steps.why: Two positive lengths with the same square are equal. Three equal sides give congruence by SSS.
steps.math: d = c → triangles congruent by SSS
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>A comparison triangle supplies the right angle without assuming the conclusion.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="comparison" points="170,290 570,290 170,100" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="square1" x1="170" y1="265" x2="195" y2="265" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><line id="square2" x1="195" y1="265" x2="195" y2="290" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="perpendicular side-a" x="125" y="205" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">a</text><text id="perpendicular side-b" x="365" y="335" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">b</text><text id="hyp" x="370" y="170" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">d = c</text><text id="reason" x="380" y="50" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">SSS transfers the 90° angle to the original</text></svg>

steps.title: Transfer the right angle
steps.text: The angle opposite c in the original triangle matches the right angle of the constructed triangle, so it is 90°. For sides 5, 12 and 13: 25 + 144 = 169 = 13², so the angle opposite 13 is a right angle.
steps.why: Corresponding angles of congruent triangles are equal.

quiz.question: Which side lengths make a right-angled triangle?
quiz.hint: Square the longest side and compare with the other two squares.
quiz.explanation: The longest side is 10, and 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10². The other sets do not match.

quiz.question: For sides 7, 8 and 10, which calculation tests for a right angle?
quiz.hint: Only the longest side could be the hypotenuse.
quiz.explanation: Compare 100 with 49 + 64 = 113. They differ, so the triangle is not right-angled.

lessons.takeaway: To test for a right angle, square the longest side and compare it with the sum of the other two squares.
lessons.mistake: Using Pythagoras to find a side before you know the triangle is right-angled. Test the three sides first.

reference.name: Angle totals
reference.note: Vertically opposite angles are equal.

reference.name: Triangle
reference.note: Theorem 6: an exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.

reference.name: Quadrilateral
reference.note: A diagonal splits a simple quadrilateral into two triangles.

reference.name: Congruence
reference.note: AAA gives similarity, not necessarily equal size; SSA is not a general test.

reference.name: Pythagoras
reference.note: Only for a right-angled triangle, with c the hypotenuse.

reference.name: Converse of Pythagoras
reference.formula: If longest side c satisfies c² = a² + b², the triangle is right-angled
reference.note: Compare the largest side’s square with the sum of the other two.

reference.name: Proof habit
reference.note: Distinguish given information, established facts and the conclusion.

toolkit.strategy: Mark only given or proved facts. For an angle, name the relationship; for congruence, match parts in order; for a length, establish a right-angled triangle before using Pythagoras. A proof is a chain of claims with reasons, not a measurement of a picture.

methods.title: Lines, transversals and angle totals
methods.when: A figure contains intersecting or parallel lines.
methods.rule: Straight angle 180°; full turn 360°; vertically opposite angles equal; parallel lines give equal corresponding and alternate angles, and supplementary same-side interiors.
steps: Identify the exact angle pair by position.
Check parallelism is given or has been proved.
Write the equality or sum before calculating.
Use the matching converse when angle data must prove parallelism.
methods.example: If parallel-line corresponding angles are 3x+8 and 74 degrees, then 3x+8=74 → x=22.
methods.check: Substitution gives both angles 74°.
methods.trap: An F or Z appearance is not enough without the parallel-line condition.

methods.title: Triangle and exterior-angle chains
methods.when: A triangle is mixed with parallel lines or an extended side.
methods.rule: Interior sum 180°; exterior angle=sum of the two non-adjacent interiors.
steps: Transfer any valid parallel-line angle into the triangle.
Use equal sides to identify equal opposite angles when given.
Use the 180° total.
For an exterior angle, use either the adjacent straight-line pair or the two interior opposite angles.
methods.example: An isosceles triangle with a base angle 68° has the other base angle 68°, vertex angle 44° and a vertex exterior angle 136°.
methods.trap: The adjacent interior angle is not one of the two interior opposite angles in the exterior-angle sum.

methods.title: Quadrilateral properties without extra assumptions
methods.when: The figure is a quadrilateral, parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus or square.
methods.rule: Simple quadrilateral interior sum 360°; parallelogram opposite sides/angles equal and adjacent angles supplementary.
steps: Split a simple quadrilateral by an interior diagonal to obtain the angle sum.
Use only the properties of the named shape.
Distinguish bisection of diagonals from equality of their lengths.
methods.example: A parallelogram with one angle 112° has angles 112°,68°,112°,68°.
methods.check: All four sum 360°. A parallelogram has equal diagonals only when it is a rectangle.
methods.trap: A rhombus has equal sides, but its angles need not all be 90°.

methods.title: Write a complete triangle congruence argument
methods.when: Two triangles must have equal corresponding lengths or angles.
methods.rule: Valid tests:SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS; SAS uses the included angle; RHS requires right-angled triangles.
steps: Choose and order the two triangles to match corresponding vertices.
List the three equal parts and give a reason for each.
Name the applicable test.
State the required corresponding consequence.
methods.example: If AB=AD, AC is common and ∠BAC=∠CAD, then △BAC≅△DAC by SAS; hence BC=DC.
methods.check: The equal angle lies between the two listed equal sides in each triangle.
methods.trap: AAA proves similarity, not equal size; SSA is not a general congruence test.

methods.title: Pythagoras, reverse sides and overhang
methods.when: A right-angled triangle determines a sloping distance or a missing shorter side.
methods.rule: c²=a²+b², where c is the hypotenuse; a=√(c²−b²).
steps: Identify the right angle and opposite hypotenuse.
Add squares for the hypotenuse or subtract for a shorter side.
Take the positive root to return to a length.
Only then add or subtract any extra length asked for.
methods.example: A 5 m sloping section spanning horizontal 4 m rises √(25−16)=3 m; a 7 m pole with that 5 m section has 2 m overhang.
methods.trap: The squared result is not the length, and overhang is measured along the pole unless specified otherwise.

methods.title: Use two right-angled triangles in a cuboid
methods.when: A distance runs between opposite vertices of a rectangular solid.
methods.rule: Floor diagonal d=√(l²+w²); space diagonal D=√(d²+h²)=√(l²+w²+h²).
steps: Find a diagonal in one rectangular face.
Use that diagonal with the perpendicular height in a second right-angled triangle.
Retain exact intermediate values.
Compare the final diagonal with the stated cable or rod length.
methods.example: A 2 by 3 by 6 cuboid has face diagonal √13 and space diagonal √(13+36)=7.
methods.check: Squaring 7 gives 49=4+9+36.
methods.trap: Adding edge lengths measures an edge route, not a straight diagonal.

methods.title: Proof language and vertically opposite angles
methods.when: A question asks for a reasoned proof, especially theorem 1.
methods.rule: Definition:meaning; axiom:accepted starting fact; theorem:proved statement; converse:reversed implication; corollary:direct consequence.
steps: State the givens and desired conclusion separately.
At a crossing label opposite angles α,γ and their common neighbour β.
Write α+β=180° and β+γ=180° using straight-line angles.
Subtract the same β to obtain α=γ.
methods.example: If two crossing-line angles are opposite, each equals 180° minus the same adjacent angle; therefore they are equal.
methods.check: The argument uses no special measured angle, so it applies to every crossing.
methods.trap: A diagram looking equal is not a proof.

methods.title: Prove the isosceles rule and its converse
methods.when: Theorem 2 connects equal sides and equal opposite angles.
methods.rule: AB=AC ⇔ ∠ABC=∠ACB in triangle ABC.
steps: For the forward direction compare ABC with ACB.
AB=AC, AC=AB and BC=CB give SSS, hence the base angles match.
For the converse assume the two base angles equal.
Use those two angles and the shared included side BC to compare BCA with CBA by ASA; conclude AB=AC.
methods.example: In a triangle with AB=AC and vertex angle 36°, the equal base angles each equal (180−36)/2=72°.
methods.check: Each equal side is opposite one of the equal angles.
methods.trap: The converse needs its own reasoning; it is not automatic just because the forward statement is true.

methods.title: Prove the parallel-line angle tests in both directions
methods.when: Theorems 3 and 5 connect alternate/corresponding angle equality with parallelism.
methods.rule: Parallel lines ⇔ equal alternate angles (Theorem 3); parallel lines ⇔ equal corresponding angles (Theorem 5).
steps: For parallel lines, use equal alternate angles and vertically opposite angles to obtain equal corresponding angles.
For the alternate-angle converse, draw through the second crossing the parallel to the first line.
Its alternate angle equals the given angle; uniqueness of a ray on the chosen side with that angle makes it coincide with the second line.
Convert equal corresponding angles into equal alternate angles using a vertically opposite pair, then apply the converse.
methods.example: Two corresponding angles of (4x−10)° and 70° imply parallelism when x=20, since both then equal 70°.
methods.check: The angle pair must occupy the required positions on the same transversal.
methods.trap: Equal arbitrary angles somewhere in a diagram do not establish parallel lines.

methods.title: Prove diagonals of a parallelogram bisect
methods.when: Theorem 10: diagonals AC and BD meet at E in parallelogram ABCD.
methods.rule: AE=CE and BE=DE.
steps: Compare triangles AEB and CED.
AB=CD because opposite parallelogram sides are equal.
Parallel AB and CD give equal angle pairs at A,C and at B,D by alternate angles.
ASA gives congruence; corresponding half-diagonals are equal.
methods.example: If AC=18 and BD=14, then AE=CE=9 and BE=DE=7.
methods.check: The two halves recombine to each original diagonal.
methods.trap: The theorem does not say that AC and BD have the same total length.

methods.title: Proportional sides of similar triangles: proof route
methods.when: Theorem 13 starts from equal corresponding angles.
methods.rule: AB/PQ=AC/PR=BC/QR, with correspondence A↔P,B↔Q,C↔R.
steps: If AB=PQ, ASA gives congruence at once. Otherwise swap the triangle names if needed so that AB>PQ.
Take D on AB with AD=PQ and E on AC with AE=PR. SAS (angle A equals angle P between them) gives △ADE≅△PQR, so ∠ADE=∠PQR=∠ABC.
Equal corresponding angles at D and B give DE∥BC (Theorem 5).
Theorem 12, a line parallel to one side cuts the other two sides in the same ratio, gives AD/AB=AE/AC; the same argument from vertex B gives DE/BC=AD/AB.
Substitute AD=PQ, AE=PR and DE=QR from the congruence, then invert the positive ratios: AB/PQ=AC/PR=BC/QR.
methods.example: If corresponding bases are 8 and 12, the larger/smaller scale factor is 3/2; a matching side of 10 becomes 15.
methods.check: The route uses Theorem 12 as a tool, which is how the Junior Cycle course treats it; its formal proof is not required at Higher Level.
methods.trap: Match sides by corresponding vertices or opposite angles, not where they sit on the page.

methods.title: Prove the converse of Pythagoras
methods.when: Theorem 15 tests whether a triangle with known sides is right-angled.
methods.rule: If c is the longest side and c²=a²+b², the opposite angle is 90°.
steps: Construct a separate right-angled triangle with perpendicular sides a and b, and hypotenuse d.
Pythagoras gives d²=a²+b²=c².
Positive lengths imply d=c, so the comparison triangle and original are congruent by SSS.
Transfer the comparison triangle’s right angle to the original.
methods.example: For sides 8,15,17:64+225=289=17², so the angle opposite 17 is right.
methods.check: The constructed triangle supplies the right angle; the original one was not assumed right.
methods.trap: Putting a shorter side in the hypotenuse role invalidates the test.

checks: Parallel, equal-side and right-angle assumptions are stated or proved.
The hypotenuse is opposite the established right angle.
A congruence test matches corresponding parts and includes its required angle or side.
Every proof step has a valid reason and does not assume the conclusion.
The final length has units and any requested overhang or extra distance is handled after the geometric length.

challenges.title: Parallel lines, equal sides and an SAS proof
challenges.question: In triangle ABC, AB=AC. A point D lies on the line through A parallel to BC, on the side for which ∠DAB=65°. Also AD=BC. The segments form the non-crossing quadrilateral D-A-C-B, with AB as a diagonal. (a) Find ∠ABC, ∠BCA and ∠BAC. (b) Prove △DAB≅△CBA, giving a reason for each matching part. (c) Deduce DB=CA and find ∠DBA.
hints: First transfer the 65° angle using the parallel lines, then use the equal sides.
For SAS, match DA with CB, AB with BA and the angles between those sides.

solution.title: Transfer the parallel-line angle
solution.reason: AD is parallel to BC and AB crosses both. D and C are on opposite sides of AB, so these are alternate angles.

solution.title: Use the isosceles triangle
solution.reason: Equal sides AB and AC face equal base angles; triangle angles total 180°.

solution.title: List the congruence data
solution.reason: The equal angle sits between the two equal sides in each triangle, as SAS needs.

solution.title: Conclude congruence
solution.reason: The order of the letters shows which corners match: D with C, A with B and B with A.

solution.title: Read corresponding consequences
solution.reason: Corresponding sides and angles of congruent triangles are equal.

challenges.answer: ∠ABC=65°, ∠BCA=65°, ∠BAC=50°. The triangles are congruent by SAS; DB=CA and ∠DBA=50°.
challenges.check: Triangle DAB has angles 65°, 65°, 50° at D, A, B, which total 180° and match the angles of triangle CBA at C, B, A.

challenges.title: A pole over a fence
challenges.question: An 8 m straight pole rests on level ground with its lower end 4.8 m horizontally from a vertical fence. It passes over the fence’s top at height 3.6 m. Assume the pole continues along the same straight line and ignore thickness. (a) Find the length from the lower end to the fence top. (b) Find the overhang measured along the pole. (c) Use similar right-angled triangles to find the height of the pole’s upper end above the ground.
hints: The ground and vertical fence create the first right-angled triangle.
The full pole is 8/6 times the lower sloping segment; use the same scale factor for the vertical rise.

solution.title: Identify the right-angled triangle
solution.reason: Horizontal ground and vertical fence are perpendicular.

solution.title: Return to a length
solution.reason: A length is positive, so take the positive square root.

solution.title: Subtract along the same straight pole
solution.reason: The overhang is measured along the pole, so subtract lengths along the pole.

solution.title: Scale the similar triangles
solution.reason: The small and full right-angled triangles share the pole’s angle with the ground.

challenges.answer: Lower-end-to-fence length 6 m; overhang 2 m; upper-end height 4.8 m.
challenges.check: The full horizontal run is 4.8×8/6=6.4 m, and 6.4²+4.8²=64=8².

challenges.title: Find a straight cable through a cuboid
challenges.question: A rectangular hall is 6 m wide, 8 m long and 24 m high. A straight cable is to run from a lower corner to the opposite upper corner. (a) Find the floor diagonal. (b) Find the required straight cable length. (c) A 30 m cable is available: how much remains after the straight span? (d) Compare the straight span with a route following one width edge, one length edge and one height edge.
hints: The first right-angled triangle lies on the floor.
The second right-angled triangle has the floor diagonal as one perpendicular side and the vertical height as the other.

solution.title: Find the floor diagonal
solution.reason: The floor is a rectangle with perpendicular sides.

solution.title: Build the second right-angled triangle
solution.reason: The upright edge meets the floor at a right angle, so it meets the floor diagonal at a right angle too.

solution.title: Find the cable and spare length
solution.reason: Take the root before comparing lengths.

solution.title: Compare an edge route
solution.math: Edge route=6+8+24=38 m; it is 12 m longer
solution.reason: Following the edges is a longer path than the straight line between the two corners.

challenges.answer: Floor diagonal 10 m; straight cable 26 m; 4 m spare; edge route 38 m, which is 12 m longer.
challenges.check: 26²=6²+8²+24²=676. The straight span is longer than each individual edge but shorter than the 38 m edge route.

challenges.title: Prove a right angle from three equal segments
challenges.question: In triangle ABC, X lies strictly between A and C on the straight side AC, and AX=XC=BX. (a) Name the two isosceles triangles and write their equal base-angle pairs. (b) Prove ∠ABC=90° without assuming a right angle from the drawing. (c) If AC=20 cm and AB=12 cm, find BC and BX.
hints: Let ∠ABX=α and ∠XBC=β. Equal sides make the angle at A equal to α and the angle at C equal to β.
In the whole triangle ABC, the three angles are α, α+β and β.

solution.title: Use the equal lengths
solution.math: AX=BX makes △ABX isosceles; BX=XC makes △BXC isosceles
solution.reason: Equal sides face equal base angles.

solution.title: Name the angle pairs
solution.reason: X lies on AC, so these are also the angles at A and C of the whole triangle ABC.

solution.title: Use the whole triangle total
solution.reason: The two adjacent angles at B add to ∠ABC.

solution.title: Conclude the proof
solution.reason: The right angle is now proved by reasoning, not read from the diagram.

solution.title: Calculate the requested lengths
solution.reason: The right angle is proved, so Pythagoras may be used. X is the midpoint of AC because AX = XC.

challenges.answer: The isosceles triangles are ABX and BXC; the angle sum proves ∠ABC=90°. BC=16 cm and BX=10 cm.
challenges.check: 12²+16²=20². Also AX=XC=10 and the given equality BX=AX independently gives BX=10.

title: Probability
intro: Probability is a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely something is. List everything that could happen, then count the outcomes you want.

lessons.title: List outcomes without missing any
lessons.goal: List every possible outcome in an organised way. This list is called the sample space. Then count the outcomes quickly by multiplying.

steps.title: Choose the stages
steps.text: A rugby kit has two shirt colours and three shorts colours. A complete outfit needs one choice from each list.
steps.why: Decide the order first: shirt, then shorts. A fixed order helps you list every outfit once, with none missing.

columns = six outcomes.</text></svg>

steps.title: Use the fundamental principle of counting
steps.text: Two shirts with three shorts each is 2 × 3 = 6. This shortcut is the fundamental principle of counting: multiply the number of choices at each stage. Adding four sock colours would give 24 outfits.
steps.why: Each of the six outfits can go with four sock colours, so 6 × 4 = 24.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="One decision at a time"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">One decision at a time</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">2 shirts</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">2 × 3 = 6 shirt and shorts pairs</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">2 × 3 × 4 = 24 complete outfits</text></svg>

quiz.question: There are 3 starters and 4 main courses. You choose one starter and one main. How many different combinations are possible?
quiz.hint: For each starter, list all four mains.
quiz.explanation: Each of the 3 starters can go with 4 mains, so 3 × 4 = 12 combinations. Adding to get 7 is the usual mistake.

quiz.question: One letter, A or B, is followed by one digit 1, 2 or 3. Which complete list is correct?
quiz.hint: Keep the letter fixed while running through all three digits.
quiz.explanation: A must be paired with 1, 2 and 3, and so must B. That gives six outcomes.

lessons.takeaway: List outcomes in a fixed order, or use a table. To count them quickly, multiply the number of choices at each stage.
lessons.mistake: Adding the choices, 2 + 3 = 5, when an outfit needs one from each list. Each shirt goes with every shorts colour, so multiply: 2 × 3 = 6.

lessons.title: Place chance on a probability scale
lessons.goal: Read a probability as a place on a scale from 0 to 1. Find the chance that something does not happen.

steps.title: Mark the endpoints
steps.text: Zero means impossible and one means certain. All probabilities lie between these endpoints.
steps.why: You cannot have fewer than none of the outcomes, or more than all of them.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="A scale for uncertainty"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">A scale for uncertainty</text><line id="line-auto-1" x1="95" y1="210" x2="665" y2="210" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3" /><circle id="circle-auto-1" cx="95" cy="210" r="6" fill="#087f75" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><circle id="circle-auto-2" cx="665" cy="210" r="6" fill="#087f75" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="95" y="250" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">0</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="665" y="250" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">1</text><text id="text-auto-3" x="95" y="170" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Impossible</text><text id="text-auto-4" x="665" y="170" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Certain</text></svg>

steps.title: Locate an even chance
steps.text: A fair coin has probability one half of landing heads. One half is halfway along the scale.
steps.why: Heads and tails are equally likely, so they share the whole probability of 1 equally.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Halfway means an even chance"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Halfway means an even chance</text><line id="line-auto-1" x1="95" y1="210" x2="665" y2="210" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3" /><circle id="circle-auto-1" cx="380" cy="210" r="11" fill="#087f75" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="380" y="260" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">1/2</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="380" y="150" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Even chance</text><text id="text-auto-3" x="95" y="250" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">0</text><text id="text-auto-4" x="665" y="250" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">1</text></svg>

steps.title: Read likely and unlikely
steps.text: A probability of 0.8 is likely, but it does not promise success on the next attempt. The chance of not succeeding, called the complement, is 1 − 0.8 = 0.2.
steps.why: Success or failure is certain to happen, so the two chances add to 1.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Two complementary regions"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Two complementary regions</text><rect id="success" x="80" y="150" width="480" height="95" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><rect id="failure" x="560" y="150" width="120" height="95" rx="12" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="2" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="320" y="206" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Success: 0.8</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="620" y="206" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">0.2</text><text id="text-auto-3" x="380" y="310" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Whole bar = 1</text></svg>

steps.title: Check the meaning, not only the number
steps.text: If the chance of rain is three tenths, the chance of no rain is seven tenths. Neither outcome is guaranteed.
steps.why: Rain and no rain cannot both happen, and one of them must. So their chances add to 1.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Complement check"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Complement check</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Rain: 3/10</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">No rain: 1 − 3/10 = 7/10</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">3/10 + 7/10 = 1</text></svg>

quiz.question: Which value cannot be a probability?
quiz.hint: Compare each number with the endpoints zero and one.
quiz.explanation: 1.2 is greater than one, so it cannot be a probability.

quiz.question: P(win) = 0.35. What is P(not win)?
quiz.hint: Winning and not winning together make 1.
quiz.explanation: 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. The two chances, 0.35 and 0.65, add back to 1.

lessons.takeaway: A probability tells you how likely something is. It does not promise what happens next.
lessons.mistake: Treating likely as certain. A chance of 0.8 still leaves a chance of 0.2 that it does not happen.

lessons.title: Count equally likely outcomes
lessons.goal: Find a probability by counting: the outcomes you want, divided by all the outcomes. First make sure every outcome is equally likely.

steps.title: Name the sample space
steps.text: A fair six-sided die has outcomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Fair means each face is equally likely.
steps.why: The bottom of the fraction, called the denominator, counts every outcome that could happen.

font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Each individual face has probability 1/6.</text></svg>

steps.title: Identify the event
steps.text: The event “greater than four” contains faces 5 and 6. Circle only those outcomes.
steps.why: An event is the group of outcomes that fit what the question asks for.

font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Favourable count = 2.</text></svg>

steps.title: Divide and simplify
steps.text: Two outcomes fit the event. These are called favourable outcomes. Divide them by all six equally likely outcomes, then simplify the fraction.
steps.why: 2 out of 6 and 1 out of 3 are the same chance. The simpler fraction is easier to read.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Favourable ÷ total"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Favourable ÷ total</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Favourable faces: 2</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">All equally likely faces: 6</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">P(greater than 4) = 2/6 = 1/3</text></svg>

steps.title: Check that the outcomes are equally likely
steps.text: Two colours on a spinner are not automatically equally likely. If blue covers three quarters of the circle, its probability is three quarters.
steps.why: On a spinner, a bigger sector is hit more often. The angle decides the chance, not the number of colours.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Two colours do not mean equal chances"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Two colours do not mean equal chances</text><circle id="circle-auto-1" cx="220" cy="210" r="110" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" /><path id="quarter" d="M220 210 L220 100 A110 110 0 0 1 330 210 Z" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="475" y="185" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Blue: 270°</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="475" y="235" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Amber: 90°</text></svg>

quiz.question: A fair die is rolled. What is P(an odd number)?
quiz.hint: List the odd faces.
quiz.explanation: The odd faces are 1, 3 and 5: 3/6 = 1/2.

quiz.question: A fair spinner has a red 90° sector and a blue 270° sector. What is P(red)?
quiz.hint: Compare the red angle with a full turn.
quiz.explanation: 90/360 = 1/4. Saying 1/2 because there are two colours ignores that the sectors are different sizes.

lessons.takeaway: Divide the outcomes you want by all the outcomes. This works only when every outcome is equally likely.
lessons.mistake: Giving each colour or label the same chance without looking. Two colours have probability 1/2 each only when their sectors are the same size.

lessons.title: Build a two-event sample space
lessons.goal: Use a table or a tree diagram to list every result when two things happen, such as two coin tosses.

steps.title: Keep the first and second results separate
steps.text: Toss a fair coin twice. HT means heads first, then tails. TH means tails first, then heads, so it is a different outcome.
steps.why: The order tells you which toss gave which result.

steps.text: After either first toss, the second toss can be heads or tails. This creates four endpoints.
steps.why: Each branch is one thing that could happen next.

steps.text: Exactly one head occurs on HT and TH. Two of the four equally likely paths fit.
steps.why: Exactly one head rules out TT, which has no heads, and HH, which has two.

steps.text: The second toss does not depend on the first, so the tosses are independent. Each path has probability one half times one half. Add the probabilities of the paths you want.
steps.why: Multiply along one path. Add separate paths, because only one of them can happen.
