quiz.question: Two fair dice are rolled. How many ordered outcomes are in the sample space?
quiz.hint: Each number on the first die can go with six numbers on the second.
quiz.explanation: 6 × 6 = 36 ordered outcomes. A 2 then a 5 is a different outcome from a 5 then a 2.

quiz.question: Two independent fair coin tosses are made. What is P(two heads)?
quiz.hint: Multiply the branch probabilities along the H-then-H path.
quiz.explanation: P(HH) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. HH is one of four equally likely outcomes.

lessons.takeaway: A table and a tree show the same list of outcomes. Use whichever you find easier to fill in.
lessons.mistake: Counting HT and TH as one outcome. They are two different outcomes, so one head can happen in two ways.

lessons.title: Estimate probability from experiments
lessons.goal: Use the results of an experiment to estimate a probability. This estimate is called relative frequency. Then predict how often something should happen.

steps.title: Record actual trials
steps.text: A player makes 36 successful kicks in 60 practice attempts. This is data from an experiment, not a promise about the next kick.
steps.why: You estimate the chance from what really happened: successes out of attempts.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Observed practice results"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Observed practice results</text><line id="line-auto-1" x1="65" y1="320" x2="700" y2="320" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="2" /><line id="line-auto-2" x1="65" y1="76" x2="65" y2="320" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="2" /><rect id="bar0" x="90.0" y="188.0" width="220.0" height="132.0" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="value0" x="200.0" y="179.0" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">36</text><text id="text-auto-1" x="200.0" y="348" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Scored</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="495.0" y="348" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Missed</text><text id="text-auto-3" x="53" y="325" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="end" font-weight="400">0</text><text id="text-auto-4" x="53" y="104" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="end" font-weight="400">60</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">60 attempts in total.</text></svg>

steps.title: Find relative frequency
steps.text: Divide successes by attempts: 36 divided by 60 is 0.6. You can also write this as 60%.
steps.why: The fraction of kicks that scored is your best estimate of the chance of scoring.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Convert counts into a proportion"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Convert counts into a proportion</text><line id="line-auto-1" x1="65" y1="320" x2="700" y2="320" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="2" /><line id="line-auto-2" x1="65" y1="76" x2="65" y2="320" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="2" /><rect id="bar0" x="90.0" y="188.0" width="220.0" height="132.0" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="value0" x="200.0" y="179.0" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">36</text><text id="text-auto-1" x="200.0" y="348" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Scored</text><rect id="bar1" x="385.0" y="232.0" width="220.0" height="88.0" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="value1" x="495.0" y="223.0" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">24</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="495.0" y="348" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Missed</text><text id="text-auto-3" x="53" y="325" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="end" font-weight="400">0</text><text id="text-auto-4" x="53" y="104" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="end" font-weight="400">60</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">36/60 = 0.6 = 60%</text></svg>

steps.title: Predict an expected frequency
steps.text: Suppose the player takes 150 more kicks at the same success rate. You would expect about 90 scores. This number is called the expected frequency.
steps.why: 0.6 means 6 scores in every 10 kicks. In 150 kicks that pattern gives 90.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Probability → expected count"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Probability → expected count</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Estimated chance: 0.6</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Future attempts: 150</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">Expected scores: 150 × 0.6 = 90</text></svg>

steps.title: Explain variation and reliability
steps.text: The calculation predicts 90, but a real set of kicks might give 86 or 94. More trials give a better estimate. If the conditions change, such as the wind or the distance, the old estimate may not fit.
steps.why: A prediction describes what to expect, not a guaranteed count. Random results vary.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Expectation is the centre of a prediction"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Expectation is the centre of a prediction</text><line id="line-auto-1" x1="100" y1="225" x2="660" y2="225" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="140" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">80</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="380" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">90</text><text id="text-auto-3" x="620" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">100</text><circle id="circle-auto-1" cx="380" cy="225" r="11" fill="#087f75" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-4" x="380" y="160" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Expected: 90</text><text id="text-auto-5" x="380" y="315" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Actual outcomes can vary</text></svg>

quiz.question: A spinner lands green 27 times in 90 trials. What is the estimated P(green)?
quiz.hint: Divide green results by all trials.

quiz.question: An event has probability 0.2. What is its expected frequency in 250 trials?
quiz.hint: Multiply the number of trials by the probability.
quiz.explanation: 250 × 0.2 = 50. The actual count may differ.

lessons.takeaway: Relative frequency is successes divided by trials. It estimates a chance. Expected frequency is trials times the chance. It predicts a count.
lessons.mistake: Saying the expected count will definitely happen. Say “about 90 scores”, not “exactly 90 scores”.

lessons.title: Read probabilities from a Venn diagram
lessons.goal: Fill in each separate region of a Venn diagram first. Then count the people the question asks about.

steps.title: Put the overlap in first
steps.text: In a group of 30 pupils, 16 play rugby, 14 play football and 6 play both. Start with the six in the overlap.
steps.why: Those 6 pupils are counted in the 16 and again in the 14. Placing them first stops you counting them twice.

steps.title: Find the single-sport regions
steps.text: Rugby only is 16 minus 6, or 10. Football only is 14 minus 6, or 8.
steps.why: The 16 rugby players include the 6 who play both. Take them away to leave rugby only.

steps.title: Complete the universal set
steps.text: There are 10 plus 6 plus 8, or 24, inside at least one circle. The remaining 6 play neither sport.
steps.why: Every pupil sits in exactly one region, so the four regions must add to 30.

steps.title: Choose the right event
steps.text: For rugby or football, count all 24 inside the union. For rugby and football, count only the overlap of 6.
steps.why: “Or” means at least one here; “and” means both.

quiz.question: In a class of 20, 12 like A, 9 like B and 5 like both. How many like A or B?
quiz.hint: Add both totals, then remove the double-counted overlap.
quiz.explanation: 12 + 9 = 21 counts the 5 who like both twice. Subtract them once: 21 − 5 = 16.

quiz.question: Of 40 people, 8 belong to both A and B. What is P(A and B) for a randomly selected person?
quiz.hint: “A and B” means the people in both. Put that number over the total.
quiz.explanation: 8 of the 40 people are in both, so the probability is 8/40 = 1/5.

lessons.takeaway: Fill in every separate region first. Then add only the regions that match the words in the question.
lessons.mistake: Adding 16 + 14 = 30 for rugby or football. That counts the 6 who play both twice. The correct count is 16 + 14 − 6 = 24.

lessons.title: Update probabilities along a tree
lessons.goal: Find probabilities for two draws when the first draw changes what is left for the second.

steps.title: Describe the first draw
steps.text: A bag contains 3 red and 2 blue counters. Draw two, without putting the first one back. This is called without replacement. The chance of red first is three fifths.
steps.why: At the start all five counters are in the bag, and three of them are red.

steps.why: The first counter stays out, so the second draw depends on which colour was taken.

steps.why: You need red first and then red again. For “and then”, multiply along the path.

steps.title: Add paths when either order works
steps.text: One of each colour can be RB or BR. Add three fifths times two fourths to two fifths times three fourths, giving three fifths.
steps.why: Red then blue and blue then red cannot both happen in one pair of draws. So you add the two paths.

quiz.question: A bag has 4 red and 2 blue counters. One red is drawn and kept out. What is P(red next)?
quiz.hint: Update both the red count and the total count.
quiz.explanation: Three red remain among five counters, giving 3/5.

quiz.question: Two independent events have probabilities 1/3 and 1/2. What is P(both)?
quiz.hint: Independent means the first event does not change the chance of the second. Multiply the two chances.
quiz.explanation: 1/3 × 1/2 = 1/6. Adding to get 5/6 is the usual mistake. If the first event changed the second chance, you would use the updated chance instead.

lessons.takeaway: Multiply along a path. If the first counter is not put back, change the numbers on the second branches.
lessons.mistake: Using 3/5 again for the second red when the first counter was not put back. One red is gone and only four counters remain, so the chance is 2/4.

reference.name: Equally likely outcomes
reference.note: Use this counting rule only when the individual outcomes are equally likely.

reference.name: Complement
reference.note: Either the event happens or it does not, so the two chances add to 1.

reference.name: Expected frequency
reference.formula: Expected count = number of trials × P(E)
reference.note: An expectation is a prediction, not a guarantee.

reference.name: Either event
reference.formula: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)
reference.note: The overlap is counted in both totals, so subtract it once.

reference.name: Two-stage path
reference.formula: P(A then B) = P(A) × P(B given A)
reference.note: For the second stage, use the chance that applies after the first event has happened.

toolkit.strategy: First decide what kind of question it is: counting equally likely outcomes, using data from an experiment, filling Venn regions or following a tree. Say exactly which outcomes you want before you write any fraction.

methods.title: Organise a sample space
methods.when: Several choices or stages form one outcome.
methods.rule: Total = n₁ × n₂ × … when every first choice has the same number of next choices.
steps: Name each stage and keep the order where order matters.
Fill in a table or tree in a fixed order.
Multiply the numbers of choices only if no choice is ruled out.
methods.example: 3 badge colours and 4 numbers give 12 badges; if two colours allow only 2 numbers, count 4 + 2 + 2 = 8.
methods.check: Count the complete list and check that no outcome is repeated.
methods.trap: If some choices are not allowed, multiplying counts too many. Count those cases separately.

methods.title: Use the probability scale and complement
methods.when: The opposite event is easier to count.
steps: Say exactly what the event E is.
Say everything that counts as not E.
Subtract from 1 and simplify.
methods.example: If P(at least one success) = 7/12, P(no successes) = 5/12.
methods.trap: “Not both” means exactly one or neither. It does not mean neither only.

methods.title: Count equally likely outcomes
methods.when: The question has a fair die, an item chosen at random or sectors of equal size.
methods.rule: P(E) = favourable outcomes / total equally likely outcomes.
steps: List all the individual outcomes.
Pick out the ones that fit every condition.
Write the fraction and simplify it.
methods.example: Choose an integer from 1 to 12 at random: P(multiple of 3) = 4/12 = 1/3.
methods.check: The favourable list is 3, 6, 9, 12.
methods.trap: Two named groups are not always equally likely. Count the outcomes inside each.

methods.title: Change a mixture and its denominator
methods.when: Counts are given as a ratio, then objects are added or removed.
methods.rule: A:B = a:b ⇒ A = ak, B = bk. After adding g, new total = old total + g.
steps: Write each count as its ratio number times one multiplier.
Use the given total or share to find the multiplier.
Write the new probability with the new total.
Find how many were added before you work out any other chance.
methods.example: 18 red and 30 blue; add g green with green probability 1/4: g/(48 + g) = 1/4, so g = 16 and P(blue) = 30/64.
methods.check: 16/64 = 1/4; all three counts total 64.
methods.trap: A new 25% share means g is one quarter of the final total, not the original total.

methods.title: Combine weighted independent events
methods.when: The same trial is repeated, each one independent, and the outcomes may not be equally likely.
methods.rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) when the events are independent. Add the products of separate complete paths.
steps: Label each branch with its real probability. Do not assume 1/2.
Keep the order and list every path you want.
Multiply along each path, then add separate paths.
For “at least one”, try 1 − P(none).
methods.example: If independent tosses have P(H)=3/5, exactly two heads in three tosses uses HHT, HTH, THH: 3(3/5)²(2/5)=54/125.
methods.check: All eight complete path probabilities add to 1.
methods.trap: Independent does not mean fair. Different numbers of heads are not equally likely.

methods.title: Count repeated faces, not just distinct labels
methods.when: A die repeats numbers or a spinner has unequal sectors.
methods.rule: Probability follows equally likely physical faces or sector angles, not the number of different names.
steps: Count how many faces carry each label.
Use those counts for the branch probabilities.
For independent rolls, multiply. For “at least one”, use 1 − P(none).
methods.example: A fair die labelled 1,1,2,2,2,6 has P(6)=1/6 and P(2)=1/2. In two independent rolls, P(at least one 2)=1−(1/2)²=3/4.
methods.check: The label probabilities 2/6+3/6+1/6 total 1.
methods.trap: There are three different labels, but they do not each have probability 1/3.

methods.title: Estimate and predict from data
methods.when: Results from past trials are used to predict future counts.
methods.rule: Estimated probability = successes/trials; expected count = future trials × probability.
steps: Use all recorded trials as the denominator.
Turn the count into a proportion.
Multiply by the number of future trials, if conditions stay the same.
Call the result an expected count, not a certain one.
methods.example: 42 successes in 70 trials give 0.6; expected successes in 150 comparable trials = 90.
methods.check: 90 lies between 0 and 150, and 90/150 = 0.6, the same proportion.
methods.trap: An expected count is not a promise. It also assumes that conditions stay the same.

methods.title: Fill two- and three-set regions
methods.when: Totals overlap, and the question says only, both, exactly or neither.
methods.rule: n(A∪B)=n(A)+n(B)−n(A∩B). For three sets: n(A∪B∪C)=n(A)+n(B)+n(C)−n(A∩B)−n(A∩C)−n(B∩C)+n(A∩B∩C).
steps: Put the number in all three sets in the centre first.
Subtract it from each pair total to get the pair-only regions.
Subtract the filled regions from each set total to get the single-set regions.
Add all the regions inside the circles. Subtract from the whole group to find neither.
methods.example: If n(A)=18, n(A∩B)=7, n(A∩C)=6 and the triple is 2: A∩B only = 5, A∩C only = 4, so A only = 18−5−4−2 = 7.
methods.check: Add the regions inside each set. You should get back that set’s total.
methods.trap: A pair total such as “A and B” includes those in all three, unless the question says “A and B only”.

methods.title: Read logical words as events
methods.when: The question uses words such as at least one, exactly one, both or neither.
methods.rule: “Or” means union; “and” means intersection; “exactly one” selects only single-set regions.
steps: Translate the words into regions.
Add only those separate regions.
Divide by the number of people who could be chosen.
methods.example: In three sets, “at least two” includes all three pair-only regions plus the triple region.
methods.check: Compare the chosen region list with the wording before calculating.
methods.trap: Adding the three pair totals counts the centre region three times.

methods.title: Update conditional tree branches
methods.when: Items are chosen without replacement, or the first event changes the chance of the second.
methods.rule: P(A then B) = P(A) × P(B given A).
steps: Write the first-stage counts.
On each second branch, change both the colour count and the total.
Multiply along a complete path.
Add the separate paths you want. Use the complement if that is quicker.
methods.example: 4 red and 3 blue, two draws without replacement: P(RB or BR) = (4/7)(3/6)+(3/7)(4/6)=4/7.
methods.trap: Do not keep the original denominator after removing a counter.

checks: Every probability lies from 0 to 1; complementary probabilities total 1.
Every person or outcome belongs to exactly one separate region.
At each split in a tree, the branch probabilities add to 1.
Say whether the choice is random, whether outcomes are equally likely and whether items are put back.
Use the updated total after objects are removed or added.

challenges.title: Three clubs, eight separate regions
challenges.question: A group has 60 pupils. Rugby R has 30, music M has 25 and chess C has 20. The inclusive pair counts are R∩M = 12, R∩C = 8 and M∩C = 7; 4 pupils do all three. A pupil is chosen at random. (a) Find all seven regions inside the sets and the number outside. (b) Find the probability of exactly one activity. (c) Find the probability of at least two activities.
hints: Start with the 4 pupils who do all three. Subtract 4 from each pair total to get the pair-only regions.
Exactly one uses the three single-activity regions. At least two uses the three pair-only regions and the centre, counted once.

solution.title: Separate the pairs
solution.math: RM only = 12 − 4 = 8; RC only = 8 − 4 = 4; MC only = 7 − 4 = 3; triple = 4
solution.reason: Each pair total includes the 4 pupils who do all three. Take them out to leave the pair-only regions.

solution.title: Find single activities
solution.reason: Rugby’s 30 includes three overlap regions. Subtract them to leave rugby only. Do the same for music and chess.

solution.title: Complete the population
solution.reason: The seven regions do not overlap, so adding them counts each pupil once. The rest of the 60 do none of the activities.

solution.title: Find exactly one
solution.reason: Exactly one activity means the three single-activity regions only.

solution.title: Find at least two
solution.reason: At least two means two or three activities. The centre region is counted once, not three times.

challenges.answer: R only 14, M only 10, C only 9; RM only 8, RC only 4, MC only 3, triple 4, outside 8. Probabilities: 11/20 and 19/60.
challenges.check: The eight regions total 60; reconstruct R = 14+8+4+4 = 30, M = 10+8+3+4 = 25 and C = 9+4+3+4 = 20.

challenges.title: Add a new colour without losing the old counts
challenges.question: A bag initially contains 48 counters, red and blue in ratio 3:5. Green counters are then added until the probability that a counter chosen at random is green is 25%. (a) Find the original red and blue counts. (b) Find the number of green counters added. (c) Find the new probability of blue and compare it with the original probability.
hints: Find the size of one ratio part first.
Let g be the number of green counters added. Green is then g out of 48 + g, and that fraction equals 1/4.

solution.title: Recover the counts
solution.reason: 3 + 5 = 8 parts share the 48 counters, so one part is 6. Red is 3 parts and blue is 5 parts.

solution.title: Model the final share
solution.reason: Green is g out of the new total, 48 + g. Multiply both sides by 4 and by 48 + g to clear the fractions.

solution.title: Solve the addition
solution.reason: Subtract g from both sides, then divide both sides by 3. The bag now holds 48 + 16 = 64 counters.

solution.title: Compare blue chances
solution.reason: Blue is still 30 counters, but the total has grown from 48 to 64. So the chance of blue falls.

solution.title: Measure the change
solution.reason: Write 5/8 as 20/32 to subtract. The fall is 5/32, about 15.6 percentage points. Blue does not lose the whole 25% that green now holds.

challenges.answer: 18 red, 30 blue; add 16 green. Blue probability changes from 5/8 to 15/32, a decrease of 5/32.
challenges.check: The final probabilities are 18/64+30/64+16/64=1 and green is exactly 1/4.

challenges.title: Compare replacement rules
challenges.question: A bag contains 4 red and 3 blue counters. Two are selected randomly. (a) Without replacement, find the probability of one of each colour and of two matching colours. (b) With replacement and remixing, find the probability of one of each. (c) Which procedure makes one of each more likely, and by how much? (d) For 140 repetitions of the without-replacement experiment, resetting the bag each time, predict the number with one of each.
hints: Use two paths for one of each: RB and BR.
Without replacement the second denominator is 6; with replacement it is 7.

solution.title: Use the updated branches
solution.reason: The first counter is not put back, so the second fraction is out of 6. Red then blue and blue then red both count.

solution.title: Add and complement
solution.reason: The two counters either match or they do not. So the two chances add to 1.

solution.title: Replace and remix
solution.reason: The first counter goes back, so both draws use sevenths. Red then blue and blue then red have the same chance, so double it.

solution.title: Compare exactly
solution.reason: Write 4/7 as 28/49 so both fractions have the same denominator. Without replacement is the higher one.

solution.title: Predict a count
solution.reason: Expected count = number of repetitions × probability. It is a prediction, not a promise.

challenges.answer: Without replacement: one of each 4/7, matching 3/7. With replacement: one of each 24/49. Without replacement is higher by 4/49. Expected count 80.
challenges.check: Directly count matching paths without replacement: (4/7)(3/6)+(3/7)(2/6)=3/7, agreeing with the complement.

challenges.title: A biased coin: paths and a shortcut
challenges.question: A biased coin has P(heads)=3/5 on every toss; successive tosses are independent. (a) Find P(exactly one head in two tosses). (b) List the favourable paths and find P(exactly two heads in three tosses). (c) Find P(at least one head in three tosses) using a complement. (d) Predict the number of exactly-two-heads results in 250 independent repetitions of the three-toss experiment.
hints: Use 3/5 for H and 2/5 for T at every branch.
For part b, list HHT, HTH and THH. For part c, the only path with no heads is TTT.

solution.title: Two-toss paths
solution.reason: HT and TH are separate paths with the same chance, 3/5 × 2/5. Add them, which is the same as doubling.

solution.title: List three-toss paths
solution.math: Exactly two heads: HHT, HTH, THH
solution.reason: The one tail can come third, second or first. That gives three different paths.

solution.title: Add their products
solution.reason: Each path has two heads and one tail, so each has chance (3/5)² × 2/5. There are three such paths, so multiply by 3.

solution.title: Use the complement
solution.reason: The only way to get no heads is TTT. Take its chance away from 1.

solution.title: Predict a count
solution.reason: Expected count = repetitions × probability. The real count may be a little more or less.

challenges.answer: 12/25; favourable paths HHT, HTH, THH with total 54/125; at least one head 117/125; expected exactly-two-heads count 108.
challenges.check: For three tosses, P(0H), P(1H), P(2H), P(3H) are 8/125, 36/125, 54/125, 27/125; their sum is 1.

title: Simultaneous equations
intro: Find the values that make two equations true at the same time.
prerequisites: Multiplying every term in an equation

lessons.title: Eliminate one unknown, then find the other
lessons.goal: Multiply whole equations so that one letter cancels, solve for the letter that is left, then find the other and check both.

steps.title: Read the pair together
steps.text: Solve 2x + 3y = 17 and 3x − 2y = 6. You need one value of x and one value of y that make both equations true.
steps.why: Each equation is one clue about the same two numbers. You need both clues to find them.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the entire equation balanced"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the entire equation balanced</text><rect id="equation0" x="65" y="95" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row0" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">2x + 3y = 17</text><rect id="equation1" x="65" y="195" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row1" x="380" y="245" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">3x − 2y = 6</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Two unknowns need two independent equations.</text></svg>

steps.title: Scale the whole equations
steps.text: Aim to make the y terms +6y and −6y, so they will cancel. Multiply the first equation by 2 and the second by 3. Multiply the whole left side and the right side.
steps.why: Double both pans of a balanced scale and it still balances. The same is true of an equation.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the entire equation balanced"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the entire equation balanced</text><rect id="equation0" x="65" y="95" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row0" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">2(2x + 3y) = 2(17)</text><rect id="equation1" x="65" y="195" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row1" x="380" y="245" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">3(3x − 2y) = 3(6)</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Scale BOTH sides: first equation ×2, second equation ×3.</text></svg>

steps.title: Make opposite y-coefficients
steps.text: Multiply out. Every term changes, including the numbers on the right: 17 becomes 34 and 6 becomes 18. The y terms are now +6y and −6y.
steps.why: +6y and −6y add to zero, so adding the equations will remove y.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the entire equation balanced"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the entire equation balanced</text><rect id="equation0" x="65" y="95" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row0" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">4x + 6y = 34</text><rect id="equation1" x="65" y="195" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row1" x="380" y="245" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">9x − 6y = 18</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">EVERY term is multiplied, including the right-hand sides.</text></svg>

steps.title: Add the complete equations
steps.text: Add the two equations, left sides together and right sides together. The y terms cancel and leave 13x = 52. Divide both sides by 13 to get x = 4.
steps.why: You are adding equal amounts to both sides, so the result is still balanced.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the entire equation balanced"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the entire equation balanced</text><rect id="equation0" x="65" y="95" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row0" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">13x + 0y = 52</text><rect id="equation1" x="65" y="195" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row1" x="380" y="245" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">x = 4</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Add the two rows: +6y and −6y cancel.</text></svg>

steps.title: Back-substitute
steps.text: Put x = 4 into the first original equation. 2 × 4 is 8, so 8 + 3y = 17. Subtract 8 and divide by 3 to get y = 3.
steps.why: Once you know x, the equation has only one unknown left, and you can solve it.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the entire equation balanced"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the entire equation balanced</text><rect id="equation0" x="65" y="95" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row0" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">2(4) + 3y = 17</text><rect id="equation1" x="65" y="195" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row1" x="380" y="245" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">3y = 9 → y = 3</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Back-substitute x = 4 into an original equation.</text></svg>

steps.title: Check both original equations
steps.text: Check x = 4 and y = 3 in both original equations. 8 + 9 = 17 and 12 − 6 = 6. Checking only one equation is not enough.
steps.why: The answer is only right if the same pair works in both equations.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the entire equation balanced"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the entire equation balanced</text><rect id="equation0" x="65" y="95" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row0" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">2(4) + 3(3) = 17 ✓</text><rect id="equation1" x="65" y="195" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row1" x="380" y="245" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">3(4) − 2(3) = 6 ✓</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">The same pair works in BOTH original equations.</text></svg>

quiz.question: Solve x + y = 9 and x − y = 3. What is (x, y)?
quiz.hint: Add the two equations. The +y and −y cancel.
quiz.explanation: x + y = 9 and x − y = 3 → 2x = 12 and x − y = 3 → x = 6 and y = 3. Both original equations check.

quiz.question: Multiply 2x − 3y = 7 by 4. Which equation results?
quiz.hint: The multiplier applies to every term on both sides.

lessons.takeaway: Make one letter's terms match, add or subtract to remove it, solve, put the value back, then check both original equations.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying only the term you want to cancel. Multiply every term on both sides. Doubling 2x + 3y = 17 gives 4x + 6y = 34, not 2x + 6y = 17.

lessons.title: See the solution where lines meet
lessons.goal: Turn a story into two equations and see the solution as the point where their two lines cross.

steps.title: Turn a story into two equations
steps.text: At a school event, an adult ticket costs x euro and a child ticket y euro. One adult plus one child costs €11; two adults plus one child cost €18.
steps.why: The same ticket prices must fit both purchases.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="The story sets two constraints"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">The story sets two constraints</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">1 adult + 1 child = €11</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">2 adults + 1 child = €18</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">x + y = 11; 2x + y = 18</text></svg>

steps.title: Plot the first equation
steps.text: Rearrange the first equation to y = 11 − x. Choose x = 3 to get y = 8, and x = 9 to get y = 2. Plot (3, 8) and (9, 2) and join them with a straight line.
steps.why: Every point on this line is a pair of prices that fits the first purchase.

steps.title: Add the second line
steps.text: The second equation is y = 18 − 2x. Plot (4, 10) and (8, 2) and join them. The two lines cross at (7, 4), so x = 7 and y = 4.
steps.why: The crossing point is on both lines, so it is the one pair of prices that fits both purchases.

steps.title: Know what other graph shapes mean
steps.text: Imagine trying to stand on both lines at once. If they are separate and parallel, there is nowhere to stand: no solution. If one lies exactly on top of the other, every point on the line works: infinitely many solutions.
steps.why: A solution is a point on both lines. Count how many points the lines share.
steps.math: Crossing: one; parallel: none; same line: infinitely many
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Count common points, not just equations"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Count common points, not just equations</text><line id="line-auto-1" x1="65" y1="145" x2="235" y2="285" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><line id="line-auto-2" x1="65" y1="285" x2="235" y2="145" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" /><circle id="circle-auto-1" cx="150" cy="215" r="6" fill="#b96a12" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="150" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">One solution</text><line id="line-auto-3" x1="295" y1="145" x2="455" y2="265" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><line id="line-auto-4" x1="295" y1="190" x2="455" y2="310" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-2" x="375" y="350" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">No solution</text><line id="line-auto-5" x1="525" y1="145" x2="695" y2="285" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="8" /><line id="line-auto-6" x1="525" y1="145" x2="695" y2="285" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-3" x="610" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Same line</text></svg>

quiz.question: A pair of line graphs intersects at (−2, 5). What is the simultaneous solution?
quiz.hint: Coordinates are ordered as x then y.
quiz.explanation: The intersection gives x = −2 and y = 5.

quiz.question: How many solutions do y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 have?
quiz.hint: Both lines have slope 2. Do they cross the y-axis at the same place?
quiz.explanation: Both lines have slope 2, but one crosses the y-axis at 1 and the other at −3. They are parallel and never meet, so there is no solution.

lessons.takeaway: On a graph, the solution is the point that lies on both lines.
lessons.mistake: Trusting a crossing point read from a graph. A graph reading can be slightly off, so put the values into both equations to confirm them.

reference.name: Equivalent equations
reference.formula: Multiply both sides, and every term, by the same non-zero number.
reference.note: The answers do not change.

reference.name: Elimination
reference.formula: Match coefficients, then add or subtract whole equations.
reference.note: Choose the operation that cancels one unknown.

reference.name: Graphical solution
reference.note: Parallel distinct lines have no common solution; the same line has infinitely many.

toolkit.strategy: Say what your two letters stand for, with units. Write one equation for each fact in the story. Solve by elimination or substitution, then check that the answer makes sense in the story.

methods.title: Clear fractions before elimination
methods.when: Each equation contains fractional terms.
methods.rule: Multiply each whole equation by the least common multiple of its denominators; denominators must be non-zero.
steps: Choose an LCM separately for each equation.
Multiply every term, including constants.
Match one coefficient, add or subtract, then back-substitute.
methods.check: Original checks: 4+1=5 and 2−1/2=3/2.
methods.trap: Multiplying only the fraction terms changes the equation. Multiply the whole numbers too.

methods.title: Choose elimination or substitution
methods.when: One variable is easy to isolate, or coefficients can be matched simply.
methods.rule: Doing the same thing to both sides of each equation keeps the same solution.
steps: Use substitution when a variable has coefficient 1 or is already isolated.
Use elimination when the numbers in front of a letter are equal, opposite or easy to match.
Find the second unknown in an original equation.
Check both.
methods.example: x+y=11 and 2x+y=18: subtract to obtain x=7, then y=4.
methods.trap: A value that satisfies only one equation is not a simultaneous solution.

methods.title: Model wages and two kinds of items
methods.when: Two purchases or shifts use the same two unknown rates.
methods.rule: Total = quantity₁ × rate₁ + quantity₂ × rate₂.
steps: Define each unknown rate and its units.
Translate each total separately.
Solve and interpret the rates.
methods.example: Example wages: 6r+2s=108, 4r+5s=138 ⇒ r=€12/h, s=€18/h.
methods.check: Both wage totals recompute correctly.
methods.trap: The numbers of hours are coefficients, not the unknown rates.

methods.title: Recover fixed and daily costs
methods.when: A price has a one-off part and a repeating daily/unit part.
methods.rule: C=F+nd; two distinct n-values identify F and d.
steps: Subtract two totals to remove F.
Divide the cost difference by the unit difference.
Back-substitute for F.
Use the rule for a new number of days. For a budget, round the number of days down.
methods.example: Example hire: 3 days €86 and 7 days €158 ⇒ d=€18/day, F=€32; 10 days €212.
methods.trap: Do not charge the fixed cost once per day.

methods.title: Translate ages and changed fractions
methods.when: The story changes the same quantities by adding or subtracting fixed amounts.
methods.rule: Age k years ago: x−k. Changed fraction: (n+a)/(d+b), with d+b≠0.
steps: Define present ages or original numerator and denominator.
Apply each change to the correct quantity.
Cross-multiply valid fractions or expand age relations.
Solve, then check the changed situations.
methods.example: Ages x+y=42 and x−6=2(y−6) give x=26, y=16. A changed denominator affects the whole denominator.
methods.check: Six years ago the ages were 20 and 10, and their current sum is 42.
methods.trap: “Twice the age six years ago” means 2(y−6), not 2y−6.

methods.title: Model folded rectangles
methods.when: A fold halves one dimension and a new perimeter is supplied.
methods.rule: P=2(L+W); after halving W, the folded perimeter is 2L+W.
steps: Name the original dimensions.
State which dimension the fold halves.
Write each perimeter using its actual dimensions.
Solve and check the original and folded rectangles.
methods.example: Original perimeter 50 and W-halved perimeter 40: 2L+2W=50, 2L+W=40 ⇒ W=10, L=15.
methods.trap: A fold does not generally halve the perimeter.

methods.title: Interpret intersections and exceptional systems
methods.when: A question asks about a common point or number of solutions.
methods.rule: Crossing lines: one pair; distinct parallel lines: none; coincident lines: infinitely many.
steps: Rearrange where useful to compare slopes and intercepts.
Solve algebraically for an exact point.
If elimination leaves something false, such as 0 = −2, there is no solution. If it leaves 0 = 0, the two equations give the same line.
methods.example: 2x+2y=8 and x+y=5 give 0=−2, so no common point.
methods.check: The two equivalent slope forms have equal slopes but different intercepts.
methods.trap: Two written equations do not automatically give a unique answer.

checks: Multiply every term on both sides when clearing fractions or matching coefficients.
Use the same unknown consistently in both equations.
Check both original equations, including their original fractions.
Reject impossible ages, lengths, counts or denominators.
State units and whether an answer must be a whole number.

challenges.title: Fractions first, simultaneous equations second
challenges.question: Solve x/2 + y/3 = 5 and x/4 − y/6 = 3/2. (a) Clear the denominators, showing what multiplies every term. (b) Solve the system. (c) Verify the answer in the two original fractional equations.
hints: Multiply the first equation by 6 and the second by 12. These are the smallest numbers that clear all the fractions.
After clearing, the y terms are +2y and −2y, so adding removes y.

solution.title: Clear the first equation
solution.reason: The multiplier applies to every term.

solution.title: Clear the second
solution.reason: The constant is multiplied too.

solution.title: Eliminate
solution.reason: Adding cancels y.

solution.title: Back-substitute
solution.reason: Put x = 8 into 3x + 2y = 30. Either cleared equation would do.

solution.title: Check originals
solution.reason: Both fractional equations are satisfied.

challenges.answer: x=8 and y=3; cleared equations 3x+2y=30 and 3x−2y=18.
challenges.check: Putting x = 8 and y = 3 into the original equations gives 5 and 3/2, so the cleared equations were right too.

challenges.title: Find ordinary and overtime rates
challenges.question: A part-time job pays one hourly rate for ordinary hours and a higher rate for overtime hours. A shift of 6 ordinary hours and 2 overtime hours pays €108. Another shift of 4 ordinary hours and 5 overtime hours pays €138. (a) Define the rates and form two equations. (b) Find both rates. (c) Calculate the pay for 9 ordinary hours and 3 overtime hours.
hints: Let r be the ordinary hourly rate and s the overtime hourly rate.
Multiply the first equation by 5 and the second by 2 to eliminate s.

solution.title: Model both shifts
solution.reason: Pay is hours times rate. Add the ordinary pay and the overtime pay for each shift.

solution.title: Match overtime
solution.reason: Multiply the first equation by 5 and the second by 2, every term, so that both have 10s.

solution.title: Subtract
solution.reason: Both equations have 10s, so subtracting removes s.

solution.title: Find overtime
solution.reason: Put r = 12 into the first shift's equation to find s.

solution.title: Price the new shift
solution.reason: Apply the same two rates.

challenges.answer: Ordinary €12/hour; overtime €18/hour; new shift €162.
challenges.check: 4×12+5×18=138 and 6×12+2×18=108, checking both supplied shifts.

challenges.title: A hire quote and a maximum budget
challenges.question: A bicycle-hire company charges a fixed fee plus a constant fee per complete day. Three days cost €86 and seven days cost €158. (a) Find the fixed and daily fees. (b) Price ten days. (c) Find the greatest number of complete days affordable with €250 and prove the next day is unaffordable.
hints: Subtract the three-day quote from the seven-day quote. The fixed fee cancels and four daily fees are left.
After finding the fixed fee, subtract it from the budget before dividing by the daily fee.

solution.title: Write the model
solution.reason: The fixed fee is paid once in each quote.

solution.title: Find the repeating fee
solution.reason: Both quotes include the fixed fee once. Subtracting removes it and leaves four daily fees.

solution.title: Find the fixed fee
solution.reason: Put d = 18 into the three-day quote to find F.

solution.title: Extrapolate
solution.reason: Ten days use ten daily fees.

solution.title: Use the budget
solution.reason: The number of days must be a whole number, so round 109/9, about 12.1, down to 12.

solution.title: Check the boundary
solution.reason: 12 days fits inside €250 and 13 days does not, so 12 is the most.

challenges.answer: Fixed fee €32; daily fee €18; ten days €212; maximum 12 complete days.
challenges.check: The rule also gives €158 for 7 days. Testing 12 days and 13 days proves that 12 is the most you can afford.

challenges.title: Recover an original fraction
challenges.question: An original fraction has positive integer numerator n and denominator d. Increasing only the numerator by 2 makes the fraction 1/2. Increasing only the denominator of the original fraction by 4 makes the fraction 1/3. (a) Form two equations. (b) Find n and d. (c) Simplify the original fraction and check both changes using the original counts.
hints: Cross-multiplication gives d=2n+4 and d=3n−4.

solution.title: Translate the changes
solution.reason: In each case only one part changes: first the numerator, then the denominator.

solution.title: Clear valid denominators
solution.reason: Multiply both sides by the denominators to clear the fractions. They are positive, so this is safe.

solution.title: Eliminate d
solution.reason: Both expressions describe the same denominator.

solution.title: Recover d
solution.reason: Substitute and then simplify the original fraction.

solution.title: Check both changes
solution.reason: Use 8 and 20, the original numbers, in the checks. The simplified 2 and 5 would not work.

challenges.answer: n=8, d=20; original fraction 8/20=2/5.
challenges.check: Using the reduced counts 2 and 5 would fail the stated changes; 8 and 20 pass both.

title: Coordinate Geometry: The Line
intro: Every point on a grid has two numbers: x across and y up. With them you can measure a line, say how steep it is and write its equation.

lessons.title: Measure a segment and locate its midpoint
lessons.goal: Find the length of a line segment by subtracting coordinates, and its midpoint by averaging them.

steps.title: Plot the endpoints
steps.text: Take A(−2, 1) and B(4, 9). The first number is x, how far across. The second is y, how far up. Do not swap them.
steps.why: Coordinates tell you where a point is. They do not yet tell you how far apart two points are.

steps.title: Make a right-angled triangle
steps.text: Walk along the grid from the first point to the second. Go 6 units across: 4 − (−2) = 6. Then go 8 units up: 9 − 1 = 8. The direct distance is the sloping side of that right-angled triangle.
steps.why: Across and up meet at 90°. That is what lets us use Pythagoras for the direct distance.

steps.text: Square both changes, add, and take the positive square root. The length is 10 units.
steps.why: The segment AB is the longest side, called the hypotenuse, of the triangle you made.

steps.title: Average for the midpoint
steps.text: The midpoint has x-coordinate (−2 + 4)/2 = 1 and y-coordinate (1 + 9)/2 = 5. It lies halfway along the segment.
steps.why: The average of two numbers is the number exactly halfway between them.

quiz.question: Find the midpoint of (−4, 2) and (6, 8).
quiz.hint: Average each coordinate separately.
quiz.explanation: ((−4 + 6)/2, (2 + 8)/2) = (1, 5). Add each pair, then halve. Forgetting to halve gives (2, 10).

quiz.question: Find the distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6).
quiz.hint: The horizontal and vertical changes are 3 and 4.
quiz.explanation: √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. Adding 3 and 4 gives 7, which is the walk along the grid, not the direct distance.

lessons.takeaway: Subtract to measure a change. Average to find a midpoint.
lessons.mistake: Mixing up the two jobs. Distance subtracts the coordinates and then uses Pythagoras. Midpoint adds the coordinates and halves.

lessons.title: Read slope as rise over run
lessons.goal: Work out how steep a line is, and tell apart rising, falling, flat and vertical lines.

steps.title: Choose a consistent direction
steps.text: Use points A(1, 2) and B(5, 4). Go from A to B both times: B’s y minus A’s y on top, B’s x minus A’s x underneath.
steps.why: If you start from B on top, start from B underneath too. Mixing the order flips the sign.

steps.title: Connect sign with direction
steps.text: Reading left to right, a rising line has positive slope and a falling line negative slope. A horizontal line has no rise.
steps.why: As you move right, y goes up for a positive slope and down for a negative slope.

steps.title: Handle the vertical exception
steps.text: A vertical line goes up but not across, so its run is zero. You cannot divide by zero. Say the slope is “undefined”, not zero.
steps.why: No number answers a division by zero, so the slope has no value.

quiz.question: Find the slope through (2, 7) and (6, −1).
quiz.hint: Change in y over change in x. Take the points in the same order both times.
quiz.explanation: (−1 − 7)/(6 − 2) = −8/4 = −2. The line falls from left to right, so the slope is negative.

quiz.question: Which statement about x = 4 is correct?
quiz.hint: Every point on this line has x = 4. Which way does the line run?
quiz.explanation: The line is vertical. Its run is zero, so its slope is undefined.

lessons.takeaway: Slope is rise over run: how far the line goes up for each 1 unit across.
lessons.mistake: Subtracting the y-values in one order and the x-values in the other. That flips the sign, for example 2 where the answer is −2.

lessons.title: Build a line from a point and slope
lessons.goal: Write the equation of a line when you know one point on it and its slope.

steps.why: From P, you reach every other point on the line by rising 3 for each 1 across.

steps.text: Put 5 in place of y₁, 2 in place of x₁ and 3 in place of m. Keep the bracket around x − 2.
steps.why: The slope multiplies the whole change in x, not just the x.

steps.title: Expand and rearrange
steps.text: Multiply 3 by both terms in the bracket, then add 5 to both sides. The result is y = 3x − 1.
steps.why: Doing the same thing to both sides changes how the equation looks, not which line it is.

steps.title: Check point and slope
steps.text: At x = 2 the equation gives y = 5, so P is on the line. The number in front of x is 3, the slope you were given.
steps.why: You built the line from a point and a slope, so test both.

quiz.question: A line has slope 2 and passes through (1, 4). Which equation is correct?
quiz.hint: Put the point and the slope into y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
quiz.explanation: y − 4 = 2(x − 1) → y − 4 = 2x − 2 → y = 2x + 2. The 4 is the y-value at x = 1, not the y-intercept.

quiz.question: Which substitution uses slope −1 and point (−3, 2)?
quiz.hint: Taking away −3 is the same as adding 3.

lessons.takeaway: One point and a slope are enough. Put them into y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
lessons.mistake: Writing x − 3 when the point has x = −3. Taking away −3 gives x + 3.

lessons.title: Read y = mx + c
lessons.goal: Read the slope and the y-intercept straight from an equation, after getting y on its own.

steps.title: Separate slope and starting value
steps.text: In y = 2x + 3, the number in front of x is 2. That is the slope. The number on its own, 3, is the value of y when x is zero.
steps.why: When x = 0, the 2x part is zero, so only the 3 is left.

steps.title: Use slope to move from the intercept
steps.text: Starting at (0, 3), move right 1 and up 2 to (1, 5). Repeat to get (2, 7).
steps.why: Slope 2 means a rise of 2 for a run of 1.

steps.title: Rearrange before reading
steps.text: For 2x + 3y = 12, first get y on its own. Subtract 2x from both sides, then divide every term by 3.
steps.why: The number in front of x is the slope only when the equation starts with y =.

steps.title: Check intercept and direction
steps.text: This line crosses the y-axis at (0, 4) and falls from left to right. Moving right 3 lowers y by 2.
steps.why: Negative slope matches a falling graph.

quiz.question: What are the slope and y-intercept of y = −4x + 7?
quiz.hint: Match with y = mx + c.
quiz.explanation: The number in front of x is −4, so m = −4. The number on its own is 7, so c = 7.

quiz.question: What is the slope of 3x + 2y = 8?
quiz.hint: Get y on its own first.
quiz.explanation: 3x + 2y = 8 → 2y = −3x + 8 → y = −(3/2)x + 4. The slope is −3/2. The 3 in front of x is not the slope until y is on its own, and the minus sign matters.

lessons.takeaway: Get y on its own. Then the number in front of x is the slope and the number on its own is the y-intercept.
lessons.mistake: Reading 3 as the slope of 3x + 2y = 8. Get y on its own first: y = −(3/2)x + 4, so the slope is −3/2.

lessons.title: Recognise parallel and perpendicular lines
lessons.goal: Use slopes to tell when two lines are parallel or meet at a right angle.

steps.title: Compare slopes
steps.text: The lines y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 both rise 2 for each 1 across. They cross the y-axis at different points, 1 and −3, so they never meet.
steps.why: Parallel lines point the same way, so they have the same slope.

steps.title: Take a negative reciprocal
steps.text: A line at right angles to a line of slope 2 has slope −1/2. Turn 2 upside down and change its sign. The two slopes multiply to −1.
steps.why: For perpendicular lines that are not vertical, m₁m₂ = −1.

steps.title: Use a known point
steps.text: Now build the perpendicular line through (4, 1). Use slope −1/2: y − 1 = −(1/2)(x − 4). This simplifies to y = −x/2 + 3.
steps.why: One point and a slope fix exactly one line.

steps.text: A horizontal line meets a vertical line at a right angle. You can see that from the picture. The product rule cannot be used, because a vertical slope is undefined.
steps.why: The right angle is still there, even though one slope has no value to multiply.

quiz.question: Which slope is perpendicular to 3/4?
quiz.hint: Turn the fraction upside down and change its sign.
quiz.explanation: Flip 3/4 to get 4/3, then change the sign: −4/3. The two slopes multiply to −1: (3/4)(−4/3) = −1.

quiz.question: Which pair is parallel and distinct?
quiz.hint: Look for equal slopes and different intercepts.
quiz.explanation: Both have slope 3, and they cross the y-axis at different points, 1 and −2. Each of the other pairs meets at a right angle.

lessons.takeaway: Parallel lines have equal slopes. Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1: flip the fraction and change the sign.
lessons.mistake: Changing the sign but forgetting to flip. The slope perpendicular to 3/4 is −4/3, not −3/4.

lessons.title: Draw a line from reliable points
lessons.goal: Draw a line by finding where it crosses each axis, then test a third point.

steps.title: Join and check
steps.text: Join the two points with a straight line. Check (1, 4): two times one plus four equals six.
steps.why: Only one straight line passes through two different points.

steps.title: Read special equations
steps.text: The equation x = 3 says x is always 3 and y can be anything, so the line is vertical. The equation y = −2 says y is always −2, so the line is horizontal.
steps.why: When only one letter appears, that coordinate never changes along the line.

quiz.question: What is the x-intercept of 3x + 2y = 12?
quiz.hint: Set y = 0.
quiz.explanation: At y = 0: 3x + 2(0) = 12 → 3x = 12 → x = 4. The intercept is (4, 0).

quiz.question: Which point is on y = −3?
quiz.hint: The second number in each pair is y.
quiz.explanation: (7, −3) has y-coordinate −3. On the line y = −3, x can be any number.

lessons.takeaway: Use two exact points and check a third.
lessons.mistake: Drawing x = 3 as a flat line. x = 3 is vertical, through 3 on the x-axis. y = 3 is the horizontal one.

lessons.title: Find where two lines intersect
lessons.goal: Find the point where two lines cross by making their y-values equal.

steps.title: Set the rules equal
steps.text: At the point where y = x + 2 and y = −2x + 8 cross, both rules give the same y. So make the two right-hand sides equal.
steps.why: The crossing point, called the intersection, is on both lines.

steps.title: Find the shared x
steps.text: Add 2x to both sides and subtract 2. This gives 3x = 6, so x = 2.
steps.why: Do the same thing to both sides and they stay equal, like a balanced scale.

steps.title: Complete the coordinate pair
steps.text: Substitute x = 2 into y = x + 2. Then y = 4 and the intersection is (2, 4).
steps.why: A point needs both an x and a y.

steps.title: Verify with the other rule
steps.text: The second rule gives −2(2) + 8 = 4. Both original equations agree.
steps.why: Checking both originals catches sign errors.

quiz.question: Where do y = 2x and y = x + 3 intersect?
quiz.hint: At the crossing both rules give the same y, so make them equal.
quiz.explanation: y = 2x and y = x + 3 → 2x = x + 3 and y = 2x → x = 3 and y = 6. Intersection: (3, 6).

quiz.question: Why is it not enough to find only x?
options: The y-value is always equal to the x-value.
quiz.hint: Think about how a point is written.
quiz.explanation: An intersection is written (x, y), so both values are needed.

lessons.takeaway: Make the two y-values equal to find x. Then put x into either equation to find y.
lessons.mistake: Stopping at x = 2. The question asks for a point, so find y as well and write (2, 4).

lessons.title: Give a slope real-world units
lessons.goal: Say what the slope and the y-intercept mean in a real situation, with their units.

steps.text: A taxi fare of C euro follows C = 2d + 5, where d is the distance in kilometres. The slope 2 is measured in euro per kilometre.
steps.why: The units tell you what the slope means: €2 more for every kilometre.

steps.title: Interpret the intercept
steps.text: At zero kilometres, the model gives a cost of €5. This is the fixed starting charge.
steps.why: When d = 0, the 2d part is zero, so only the 5 is left.

steps.title: Calculate the rate
steps.text: Cost rises from €7 to €13 as distance rises from 1 km to 4 km. Six euro over three kilometres gives €2 per kilometre.
steps.why: On a straight line, each extra kilometre adds the same amount.

steps.title: Use the model
steps.text: A journey of 6 km costs 2(6) + 5 = €17. The €12 pays for the distance and the €5 is the fixed charge.
steps.why: Total cost is the starting charge plus the cost of the kilometres travelled.

quiz.question: Volume falls from 80 L to 50 L in 6 min. What is the rate of change?
quiz.hint: Take the final volume minus the starting volume, then divide by the time.
quiz.explanation: (50 − 80)/6 = −30/6 = −5 L/min. The minus sign shows that the volume is falling.

quiz.question: For C = 4n + 12, what does 12 represent?
quiz.hint: Set n to zero.
quiz.explanation: When n = 0, C = 12. It is the fixed cost, paid before any items are counted. The 4 is the cost per item.

lessons.takeaway: The slope is a rate, such as euro per kilometre. The intercept is the starting value, when the input is zero.
lessons.mistake: Mixing up the total cost with the cost per kilometre. In C = 2d + 5, the 2 is the cost per kilometre and C is the total.

reference.name: Distance
reference.note: A distance is never negative.

reference.name: Midpoint
reference.note: Average each coordinate separately.

reference.name: Slope
reference.note: A vertical line has undefined slope.

reference.name: Point-slope equation
reference.note: Use one known point and the slope. A vertical line has an undefined slope, so write x = k for it.

reference.name: Slope-intercept form
reference.note: c is the y-value when x = 0.

reference.name: General form
reference.note: Rearrange to y = mx + c to read the slope −a/b and the y-intercept −c/b, provided b ≠ 0. Multiply through to clear fractions so that a, b and c are whole numbers.

reference.name: Parallel / perpendicular
reference.note: The product rule works only when neither line is vertical. A horizontal line and a vertical line are also perpendicular.

toolkit.strategy: Mark the points you know and the thing you must find. Use differences for lengths and slopes, averages for midpoints, an equation for a whole line, and two equations together for a crossing point.

methods.title: Measure a direct or multi-leg route
methods.when: A map question asks for the distance straight from A to B, or by way of other points.
methods.rule: AB=√((x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²); via C means AC+CB.
steps: Find the change across and the change up for each leg.
Use Pythagoras on each straight leg separately.
Add the leg lengths for a route, then compare with the direct distance.
methods.check: A route with a bend cannot be shorter than the straight segment joining its ends.
methods.trap: Do not add the changes across and up and call the result the direct distance.

methods.title: Find or reverse a midpoint
methods.when: You need the centre of a segment, or one end when you know the centre and the other end.
methods.rule: M=((x₁+x₂)/2,(y₁+y₂)/2); missing endpoint B=2M−A coordinate by coordinate.
steps: For a midpoint, average the two x-values and average the two y-values.
For a missing end, double each midpoint coordinate and subtract the matching coordinate of the known end.
Check by finding the midpoint of your two ends.
methods.trap: Distance subtracts the coordinates; midpoint adds them and halves.

methods.title: Calculate a slope and classify exceptions
methods.when: Two points are given and you need the direction of the line through them.
methods.rule: m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), provided x₂≠x₁; horizontal m=0; vertical slope undefined.
steps: Choose which point comes first and keep that order on the top and the bottom.
Look at the bottom of the fraction before dividing: if it is 0, the line is vertical.
Read the sign from left to right: positive rises, negative falls.
methods.check: Swapping the order of the points in both subtractions gives the same slope.
methods.trap: A vertical line has undefined slope, not zero.

methods.title: Build a line from one point and slope
methods.when: You know a point and a slope. The slope may come from other information.
methods.rule: y−y₁=m(x−x₁).
steps: Put the point into the formula, keeping the brackets.
Multiply out the bracket and tidy up into the form the question asks for.
Check that the original point fits your equation.
methods.check: At x=−1 the equation gives y=5.
methods.trap: Subtracting a negative coordinate becomes addition: x − (−1) is x + 1.

methods.title: Read slope and intercept only after isolating y
methods.when: A line is given as ax+by+c=0 or y=mx+c.
methods.rule: For b≠0, ax+by+c=0 ⇒ m=−a/b and y-intercept −c/b.
steps: Get y on its own before reading the number in front of x.
Set x=0 for the y-intercept.
If b=0 the line is vertical: handle it separately.
methods.check: The point (0,4) fits the original equation: 3(0)+2(4)−8=0.
methods.trap: The number in front of x is the slope only after y is on its own.

methods.title: Construct parallel and perpendicular lines
methods.when: You need a new line that is parallel or perpendicular to a given line.
methods.rule: Parallel: m₁=m₂. Perpendicular: m₁m₂=−1. Horizontal y=k has slope 0; vertical x=k has undefined slope; a horizontal line and a vertical line are perpendicular.
steps: Find the original slope.
Use the same slope for a parallel line, or flip it and change the sign for a perpendicular line.
Put the new point into the point-slope form.
For a horizontal or vertical line, write y=k or x=k directly.
methods.example: Perpendicular to y=−2x+3 through (4,5): m=1/2, y=x/2+3.
methods.check: (−2)(1/2)=−1 and (4,5) lies on the new line.
methods.trap: The product test cannot be used when one line is vertical, because its slope is undefined.

methods.title: Plot a line with checks
methods.when: You are asked to draw a line or to find where it crosses the axes.
methods.rule: x-intercept: y=0; y-intercept: x=0.
steps: Find two different points, using the intercepts if they are easy.
Plot them on axes marked in equal steps.
Join with a straight line and check a third point.
methods.example: 2x+y=8 has intercepts (4,0),(0,8), with check point (1,6).
methods.trap: If both intercept calculations give the origin, choose another point instead of plotting one point twice.

methods.title: Find an exact intersection
methods.when: You need the exact point where two lines cross.
methods.rule: At the intersection, both line equations hold.
steps: Make the two expressions for y equal, or add or subtract the equations to remove one letter.
Solve for x, then find y.
Check the point in both equations.
methods.example: y=−2x+3 and y=x/2+3 meet at (0,3).
methods.check: Both give y=3 at x=0.
methods.trap: A reading from a graph is only approximate until you confirm the coordinates with algebra.

methods.title: Interpret a linear rate and its domain
methods.when: Coordinates represent cost, time, volume or another measured quantity.
methods.rule: y=mx+c: m=change in y/change in x; c is the value at x=0.
steps: Name both quantities and units.
Find the slope from two known pairs of values.
Find c, the starting value, and say which inputs make sense.
Say what each answer means in the situation, with units.
methods.example: A tank changes from 80 L at 0 min to 50 L at 6 min: V=80−5t; V=20 at t=12 min.
methods.check: The slope has units L/min, and both observed points fit.
methods.trap: Do not extend a straight-line model to values that cannot happen, such as a negative volume.

checks: Keep the same subtraction order on the top and the bottom of a slope.
A point is written (x,y), x first. An intercept is a point too, with one coordinate equal to zero.
Keep square roots exact until the final rounding the question asks for.
Check a line you have found against both its slope and a point it must pass through.
Put a crossing point into both line equations, and give map distances with their units.

challenges.title: Direct route or the boundary path?
challenges.question: On a coordinate map, one unit represents 100 m. A=(−2,1), B=(4,9) and C=(4,1). (a) Find the direct distance AB and the route AC then CB, in metres. (b) What percentage longer is the route via C than the direct route? (c) Find the midpoint of AB. (d) At a constant 5 km/h, how many minutes would each route take?
hints: The horizontal and vertical changes from A to B are 6 and 8.
For the percentage, divide the extra distance by the direct distance, not by the longer route.

solution.title: Calculate the direct distance
solution.reason: The changes across and up are the two short sides of a right-angled triangle.

solution.title: Add the boundary legs
solution.reason: A route through C is two straight legs, so add their lengths.

solution.title: Compare percentages
solution.reason: The question asks how much longer than the direct route, so divide the extra 400 m by the direct 1000 m.

solution.title: Locate the midpoint
solution.reason: Average the two x-values and the two y-values.

solution.title: Convert distance to time
solution.reason: Change metres to kilometres to match km/h. Then multiply the hours by 60 to get minutes.

challenges.answer: 1000 m direct; 1400 m via C; 40% longer; midpoint (1,5); times 12 min and 16.8 min.

challenges.title: Find a line, its perpendicular and their meeting point
challenges.question: Line l passes through A=(−1,5) and B=(3,−3). A second line k passes through P=(4,5) and is perpendicular to l. (a) Find the equation of l. (b) Find the equation of k. (c) Find their intersection I. (d) Find the exact length PI.
hints: Find the slope of l from A and B. For k, flip that slope and change its sign.
Make the two expressions for y equal to find I. Then use the distance formula from P to I.

solution.title: Find the first slope
solution.reason: Use the same point order in both differences.

solution.title: Build l
solution.reason: Put the slope −2 and the point A into the point-slope formula.

solution.title: Build k
solution.reason: Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1, and (−2) × (1/2) = −1.

solution.title: Solve the intersection
solution.reason: The point I is on both lines, so both equations must be true there.

solution.title: Measure the segment
solution.reason: √20 = √4 × √5 = 2√5. Leave it as a surd, because the question asks for the exact length.

challenges.check: A and B satisfy l, P satisfies k, I satisfies both, and the slope product is −1.

challenges.title: Use coordinates to verify a midpoint connection
challenges.question: A=(0,0), B=(6,0), C=(2,4). M is the midpoint of AB and N is the midpoint of AC. (a) Find M and N. (b) Calculate the slopes of MN and BC and state what they show. (c) Find MN and BC exactly and compare their lengths. (d) Find an equation of MN and check both its endpoints.
hints: Find the midpoints before using slope or distance.
The two slopes should be equal. Compare the exact square roots, not rounded decimals.

solution.title: Find midpoints
solution.reason: Average the endpoint coordinates.

solution.title: Compare slopes
solution.reason: Equal slopes mean the lines are parallel, so MN is parallel to BC.

solution.title: Calculate lengths
solution.reason: Use the distance formula once for each segment. √8 = 2√2 and √32 = 4√2.

solution.title: Compare lengths
solution.reason: Using the exact surds, the √2 cancels and no rounding is needed.

solution.title: Find and check the line
solution.reason: The slope is −1 and M(3, 0) is on the line. Both end points fit the equation.

challenges.answer: M=(3,0), N=(1,2); MN ∥ BC; MN=2√2 and BC=4√2, so MN is half BC; line MN is y=−x+3.
challenges.check: The changes M→N=(−2,2) and B→C=(−4,4) give a second check: one is exactly half the other.

challenges.title: A perpendicular access route
challenges.question: A straight path passes through T=(−2,5) and U=(4,−1). A base is at P=(4,5). A direct access route from P meets the path perpendicularly at I. One coordinate unit is 200 m. (a) Find equations of the path and the access line. (b) Find I. (c) Compare the exact distance PI with the alternative route P→U→I, in metres. (d) State the extra distance of the alternative route.
hints: The path has slope −1, so the access line has slope 1.
After finding I, calculate PU and UI separately for the alternative route.

solution.title: Find the path
solution.reason: Find the slope from T and U, then use T in the point-slope formula.

solution.title: Find the access line
solution.reason: A perpendicular to slope −1 has slope 1. The access line passes through P.

solution.title: Find the foot
solution.reason: I is on both lines, so solve the two equations together.

solution.title: Find exact lengths
solution.math: PI=3√2 units; PU=6 units; UI=3√2 units
solution.reason: Use the distance formula on each segment. PI and UI are each 3 across and 3 up or down.

solution.title: Convert and compare
solution.reason: Multiply each length by 200, because one unit is 200 m.

solution.title: Find the extra distance
solution.reason: Both routes contain 600√2 m, so it cancels when you subtract.

challenges.answer: Path y=−x+3; access y=x+1; I=(1,2); direct 600√2 m; via U 1200+600√2 m; extra 1200 m.
challenges.check: I satisfies both lines and the slopes multiply to −1. PU is a vertical segment 6 units long, which is 1200 m, the extra distance.

title: Ratio, Time, Speed
intro: A ratio splits a total into equal parts. Find what one part is worth, then build each share. For time and speed, put everything into the same units first.

lessons.title: Share a total in a ratio
lessons.goal: Share an amount in a ratio by finding one equal part first. Tell direct proportion from inverse proportion.

steps.title: Match the units
steps.text: Put both lengths into the same unit before comparing them. Here 2 m is 200 cm. So the comparison is 200 cm to 50 cm: four lots of 50 cm to one lot.
steps.why: Comparing 2 with 50 would compare metres with centimetres. The same unit makes the ratio meaningful.

steps.title: Count all the parts
steps.text: Share €150 in the ratio 2:3. Picture five identical envelopes. One person gets 2 envelopes and the other gets 3. So 2 + 3 = 5 equal parts hold the whole €150.
steps.why: The 2 and the 3 count parts, not euro. Add them first, so you know how many equal parts share the money.

steps.text: One part is €150 ÷ 5 = €30, so put €30 in each envelope. Two envelopes hold €60 and three hold €90. Check: €60 + €90 = €150, so all the money is shared.
steps.why: Always find one equal part first. Then each share is one part times that person’s number of parts.

steps.text: Ask what stays fixed. Tickets at €3 each: twice the tickets means twice the bill. A fixed journey: twice the speed means half the time. Try both stories in the interactive model above.
steps.why: Direct: both rise together. Cost ÷ tickets stays the same: the price of one ticket. Inverse: one rises as the other falls. Speed × time stays the same: the distance.
steps.math: Direct: y/x = k. Inverse: xy = k.
