quiz.question: Share €84 in the ratio 3:4. What is the smaller share?
quiz.hint: Draw 3 boxes for one share and 4 for the other. How many boxes share the €84 altogether?
quiz.explanation: There are 3 + 4 = 7 equal parts. One part is €84 ÷ 7 = €12. The smaller share has 3 parts: 3 × €12 = €36. €12 is only one part, and €48 is the larger share. Check: €36 + €48 = €84.

quiz.question: For a fixed distance, speed doubles. What happens to time?
quiz.hint: Picture the same road. If you go twice as fast, do you need more time or less?
quiz.explanation: Picture the same road travelled twice as fast. In each hour you cover twice as much, so you need half as many hours. The distance stays fixed: speed × time is unchanged.

lessons.takeaway: Add the ratio numbers to count the parts. Find one part. Build each share. Then check what the question asks for: one share, the difference or the total.
lessons.mistake: Dividing the total by 2 or by 3 instead of by 5. A 2:3 split has 2 + 3 = 5 equal parts, so the shares are two fifths and three fifths.

lessons.title: Work with clock time and elapsed time
lessons.goal: Change minutes to hours correctly. Find how long something lasts, even when it passes an hour or midnight.

steps.title: Separate a reading from a duration
steps.text: 18:45 is a clock time: it says when. A duration says how long. 1 hour 30 minutes is 90 minutes, or 1.5 hours, because 30 minutes is half an hour.
steps.why: An hour has 60 minutes, not 100. So half an hour is 0.5 hours, not 0.30.

steps.text: From 15:00 to 16:00 is 60 minutes; then add 12 minutes. Total: 13 + 60 + 12 = 85 minutes.
steps.why: The three chunks sit end to end with no gaps, so adding them gives the whole journey time.

steps.title: Cross midnight deliberately
steps.text: From 23:40 to 00:15 the next day is 20 minutes to midnight and 15 minutes afterwards. The duration is 35 minutes.
steps.why: The clock goes back to zero at midnight, but time keeps going. Count up to midnight, then count on.

quiz.question: Express 2 h 45 min in decimal hours.
quiz.hint: 45 minutes is what fraction of an hour? Divide the minutes by 60.
quiz.explanation: 45 minutes is 45/60 = 0.75 of an hour. So 2 h 45 min = 2.75 hours. Writing 2.45 would treat an hour as 100 minutes.

quiz.question: A train leaves at 09:38 and arrives at 11:05. How long is the journey?
quiz.hint: Count to 10:00, then 11:00, then five more minutes.
quiz.explanation: 09:38 to 10:00 is 22 minutes. 10:00 to 11:00 is 60 minutes. 11:00 to 11:05 is 5 minutes. 22 + 60 + 5 = 87 minutes.

lessons.takeaway: Divide minutes by 60 to get hours. For a duration, count up to the next whole hour or midnight, then count on.
lessons.mistake: Writing 1 h 30 min as 1.30 hours. It is 1.5 hours, because 30 minutes is half of 60.

lessons.title: Choose speed, distance or time
lessons.goal: Find speed, distance or time when you know the other two. Find the average speed for a whole journey.

steps.title: Match the units
steps.text: A cyclist covers 18 km in 45 minutes. You want kilometres per hour, so change the time to hours first: 45 minutes is 0.75 hours.
steps.why: The answer is in km per hour, so the time must be in hours. 45 minutes is 0.75 hours, not 0.45.

steps.title: Divide distance by time
steps.text: Speed is distance divided by time: 18 ÷ 0.75 = 24 km/h. Always write the unit.
steps.why: Speed tells you how far you go in one hour. 18 km in three quarters of an hour is 24 km in a full hour.

steps.title: Rearrange for other unknowns
steps.text: Start from distance = speed × time. At 8 m/s for 15 s you cover 8 × 15 = 120 m. Going back, 120 m at 8 m/s takes 120 ÷ 8 = 15 s. To change m/s to km/h, multiply by 3.6.
steps.why: Multiplying gives distance. Dividing undoes it: distance ÷ speed gives time, and distance ÷ time gives speed.
steps.math: d = vt; t = d/v; 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h

steps.title: Average the whole journey
steps.text: A 60 km trip has two legs. The first 30 km at 30 km/h takes 1 hour. The next 30 km at 60 km/h takes half an hour. Altogether: 60 km in 1.5 hours, so 60 ÷ 1.5 = 40 km/h.
steps.why: You spent longer at 30 km/h than at 60 km/h, so the average is nearer 30. It is 40 km/h, not 45. Divide the whole distance by the whole time.

quiz.question: A runner covers 400 m in 80 s. What is the average speed?
quiz.hint: Speed is distance divided by time. Which number is the distance?
quiz.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time = 400 ÷ 80 = 5 m/s. That means 5 metres every second.

quiz.question: Convert 10 m/s to km/h.
quiz.hint: One hour has 3,600 seconds and one kilometre has 1,000 metres. Together they give the multiplier 3.6.
quiz.explanation: 10 × 3.6 = 36 km/h. Check: 10 m every second is 36,000 m in an hour, which is 36 km.

lessons.takeaway: Average speed is the whole distance divided by the whole time.
lessons.mistake: Adding two speeds and halving. That only works when you spend the same time at each speed. Use the whole distance ÷ the whole time.

reference.name: Share in ratio a:b
reference.note: Add the ratio numbers to count the equal parts. One part = total ÷ (a + b).

reference.name: Direct proportion
reference.note: Double x and y doubles. y ÷ x always gives the same number k.

reference.name: Inverse proportion
reference.note: Double x and y halves. x × y always gives the same number k.

reference.name: Journey formulae
reference.formula: v = d/t; d = vt; t = d/v
reference.note: The units must match: km with hours, or metres with seconds.

toolkit.strategy: Put everything into the same units first. Then ask what stays the same: the size of one part, a rate, the total work or the distance. That tells you which calculation to use.

methods.title: Share a total or reconstruct it from one share
methods.when: You know a ratio, and either the total or one person’s share.
methods.rule: Total known: one part=total÷(a+b). One share known: one part=that share÷its own ratio number. Each share=one part×its ratio number.
steps: Ask what the given amount is: the whole total, or only one share.
Find one part. Divide a total by all the parts. Divide one share by its own number of parts.
Multiply one part by the number of parts the question asks for.
methods.example: A:B=3:5 and A=€72. The €72 fills A’s 3 parts, so one part is 72÷3=€24. B=5×24=€120 and the total is 8×24=€192.
methods.check: 72:120 simplifies to 3:5, and 72+120=192.
methods.trap: Do not divide €72 by 8. The €72 is only A’s share, so it fills 3 parts, not all 8.

methods.title: Mix quantities with different ratios
methods.when: Two jugs or batches are different sizes and are mixed in different ratios.
methods.rule: Ingredient amount = batch volume × ingredient parts/total parts.
steps: Convert every volume to the same unit.
For each batch, count its parts, find one part, then find the real amount of each ingredient.
Add juice to juice and water to water, then simplify the final ratio.
methods.example: 1.5 L at juice:water=2:3 has 5 parts of 0.3 L, so 0.6 L juice. 2 L at 3:7 has 10 parts of 0.2 L, so 0.6 L juice. Mixed juice:water=1.2:2.3=12:23.
methods.check: Juice 1.2 L plus water 2.3 L gives the combined volume 3.5 L.
methods.trap: Do not add or average the ratio numbers. Do not add or average the ratio numbers. One part is 0.3 L in the first jug and 0.2 L in the second, so the parts are different sizes.

methods.title: Identify direct or inverse proportion
methods.when: One quantity changes and another changes with it, while something else stays fixed.
methods.rule: Direct: y=kx. Inverse: xy=k. For identical workers, workers × time = fixed work.
steps: Name what stays fixed.
Direct: divide to find the amount for one. Inverse: multiply to find the fixed total.
Use that same number in the new situation.
methods.example: Direct: 5 tickets cost €15, so one ticket costs €3 and 8 tickets cost €24. Inverse: 6 equal workers need 15 days, so the job is 6×15=90 worker-days and 9 such workers need 90÷9=10 days.
methods.trap: More workers means fewer days, not more. This only works if every worker does the same amount each day.

methods.title: Update a partly completed work problem
methods.when: The number of workers changes after some work is done.
methods.rule: Remaining worker-days = total worker-days − completed worker-days.
steps: Calculate the total work in worker-days.
Subtract work already completed.
Divide the remainder by the new number of equal workers.
Add the days already worked if the question asks for the total time.
methods.example: 6 workers need 15 days. After 4 days, 66 worker-days remain; 11 workers need 6 more days, 10 days total.
methods.trap: Do not start the whole job again when the team changes. Only the unfinished work is left.

methods.title: Read durations across midnight
methods.when: A journey passes an hour boundary, midnight or a connection.
methods.rule: 1 h=60 min; 1 day=24 h. Duration=finish−start on one continuous timeline; add 24 h to a next-day clock time before subtracting.
steps: Separate clock times from durations.
Count up to midnight, then count on past it. Or put both times on one long minute timeline.
Include waiting times once.
methods.check: Adding 95 minutes to 23:42 reaches 01:17.
methods.trap: 01:17 is not earlier in the journey just because its clock number is smaller.

methods.title: Use compatible speed units
methods.when: A distance, speed or time is unknown.
methods.rule: v=d/t; d=vt; t=d/v; 1 m/s=3.6 km/h.
steps: Decide what you are asked for: speed, distance or time.
Make the units match before you put numbers in.
Calculate, and write the unit, such as km/h.
methods.check: 24 km/h for 3/4 h gives 18 km.
methods.trap: 45 minutes is 0.75 hours, not 0.45 hours.

methods.title: Average a whole journey
methods.when: A journey has parts at different speeds, or includes a stop.
methods.rule: Average speed = total distance / total elapsed time; use moving time only if explicitly asked.
steps: Find each leg’s distance or time as needed.
Add all the distances.
Add all the times. Include stops for an overall average.
Divide the total distance by the total time.
methods.example: 72 km/h for 40 min and 48 km/h for 35 min: 76 km in 1.25 h gives 60.8 km/h.
methods.check: 60.8×1.25=76 km, which is the total distance.
methods.trap: Adding the speeds and halving works only when the same time is spent at each speed.

checks: The shares add back to the total, and both sides of a ratio use the same unit.
When mixing, work with the real amount of each ingredient, not the ratio numbers.
Convert minutes to hours by dividing by 60, not 100.
Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Include stops for an overall average.
In worker questions, every worker does the same amount each day.

challenges.title: Unequal legs and a rest stop
challenges.question: A coach travels at 72 km/h for 40 minutes and then 48 km/h for 35 minutes. (a) Find the total distance. (b) Find its average speed while moving. (c) If a 15-minute stop occurs between the two legs, find the overall average speed including the stop. Explain why averaging 72 and 48 is unsuitable.
hints: Turn each duration into hours before finding its distance.
The stop adds time but no distance.

solution.title: Find leg distances
solution.reason: Each distance is speed times its own duration.

solution.title: Combine distance
solution.reason: Add the two legs.

solution.title: Average while moving
solution.reason: Moving time is 40 + 35 = 75 minutes. Divide the whole distance by that whole time.

solution.title: Include the stop
solution.reason: The 15-minute stop adds time but no distance, so the overall average is lower.

solution.title: Explain the weighting
solution.math: (72+48)/2=60 km/h is not the moving average
solution.reason: The coach spent longer at 72 km/h than at 48 km/h, so a plain average of the two speeds is wrong.

challenges.answer: 76 km; moving average 60.8 km/h; overall average 50⅔ km/h with the stop.
challenges.check: 60.8×1.25=76 and (152/3)×1.5=76; including a stop lowers the average as expected.

challenges.title: Mix two different jugs
challenges.question: Jug A contains 1500 ml of juice and water in ratio 2:3. Jug B contains 2 L in ratio 3:7. They are mixed. (a) Find the amount of juice and water in each jug, in litres. (b) Find the ratio of juice to water in the mixture. (c) How much pure juice must be added to make the final mixture half juice?
hints: Find the real litres of juice and of water in each jug before you combine anything.
For part (c), call the added juice x litres. It increases the juice and the total, but not the water.

solution.title: Convert and split A
solution.math: 1500 ml=1.5 L; juice=0.6 L, water=0.9 L
solution.reason: Jug A has 2 + 3 = 5 equal parts of 0.3 L. Juice is 2 parts and water is 3 parts.

solution.title: Split B
solution.reason: Jug B has 3 + 7 = 10 equal parts of 0.2 L. Juice is 3 parts and water is 7 parts.

solution.title: Combine
solution.reason: Add juice to juice and water to water. Never add the ratio numbers themselves.

solution.title: Model added juice
solution.reason: The extra juice joins the juice and the total. Half juice means juice ÷ total = 1/2.

solution.title: Solve and check
solution.math: x=1.1 L; final juice=2.3 L and water=2.3 L
solution.reason: Juice and water are now equal, so the mixture is half juice.

challenges.answer: A: 0.6 L juice, 0.9 L water; B: 0.6 L juice, 1.4 L water. Mixed ratio 12:23. Add 1.1 L pure juice.
challenges.check: The initial component volumes total 3.5 L; after adding, 2.3/4.6=1/2.

challenges.title: A team changes after work has begun
challenges.question: Six equally productive workers can complete a job in 15 working days. Assume the work can be shared out and every worker does the same amount each day. (a) How long would nine workers need from the start? (b) Instead, six workers work for four days, then eleven workers take over the remaining work. Find the remaining time and the total completion time. (c) Explain which assumption makes this method valid.
hints: Measure the job in worker-days. One worker-day is one worker working for one day.
Subtract 6×4 from the total before dividing by 11.

solution.title: Quantify the job
solution.reason: Six workers for 15 days do 6 × 15 worker-days of work. That number is the size of the job.

solution.title: Change the starting team
solution.reason: The job is the same size. Nine workers share it, so it takes fewer days.

solution.title: Find the remainder
solution.reason: Six workers for 4 days finish 24 worker-days. Only the unfinished work is left for the new team.

solution.title: Find completion time
solution.reason: Share the remaining work between 11 workers. Then add the 4 days already worked.

solution.title: State the model condition
solution.math: Constant equal productivity and divisible work
solution.reason: The method works only if every worker does the same amount each day and extra workers do not slow each other down.

challenges.answer: Nine workers: 10 days. Changed-team plan: 6 further days, 10 days total, under the stated constant-productivity assumptions.
challenges.check: The changed-team output is 6×4+11×6=90 worker-days, exactly the original workload.

challenges.title: A midnight connection and two averages
challenges.question: A bus leaves at 23:42 and reaches a connection at 01:17 the next day after 114 km. After an 18-minute wait, a second bus travels 78 km in 65 minutes. (a) Find the first journey duration and the final arrival time. (b) Find each bus’s average speed. (c) Find the overall average speed for the 192 km journey, including waiting, correct to one decimal place. (d) Compare it with the average while travelling only.
hints: Count the first duration through midnight; put the second departure at 01:35.
Elapsed time includes both journeys plus 18 minutes; moving time excludes the wait.

solution.title: Read the timeline
solution.math: First leg=95 min; second departure=01:35; arrival=02:40
solution.reason: Count 18 minutes to midnight and 77 minutes after it. The clock resets at midnight, but the journey keeps going.

solution.title: Find each speed
solution.reason: Speed is in km/h, so change each time to hours by dividing the minutes by 60.

solution.title: Add elapsed time
solution.reason: The whole journey is two rides and one wait. Count the wait once.

solution.title: Find overall speed
solution.reason: Divide the whole distance by the whole time. Round only at the end.

solution.title: Find moving average
solution.reason: Both buses travel at 72 km/h while moving. The wait is what lowers the overall average.

challenges.answer: First leg 95 min; final arrival 02:40 next day. Each bus averages 72 km/h; overall 64.7 km/h; moving average 72 km/h.
challenges.check: From 23:42 to 02:40 is 2 h 58 min=178 min; 72×160/60=192 km checks the moving total.

title: Statistics 3: Presenting Data
intro: A chart turns a table of numbers into a picture. Learn to read each kind of chart, to draw it accurately and to spot one that gives the wrong impression.

lessons.title: Read line plots and bar charts
lessons.goal: Read a line plot, where each dot is one value, and a bar chart, where the height of each bar is a count.

steps.text: The data 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 5 record tries in eight sessions. A line plot stacks repeated values above the same number.
steps.why: Each repeated value gets its own dot, so no value is lost.

quiz.question: In a line plot, four dots above 7 mean…
quiz.hint: Each dot is one observation.
quiz.explanation: Four dots at 7 represent four data values equal to 7.

quiz.question: A bar chart has category frequencies 6, 9 and 5. How many observations are there?
quiz.hint: The height of each bar is a count of observations. Add the three counts.
quiz.explanation: 6 + 9 + 5 = 20 observations.

lessons.takeaway: Ask what one dot or one bar stands for. Then add the counts to find how many values there are.
lessons.mistake: Thinking the tallest bar is the biggest value. It is the category that was chosen most often.

lessons.title: Build and read a pie chart
lessons.goal: Turn each count into an angle to draw a pie chart. Turn an angle back into a count to read one.

steps.text: Twenty pupils choose sports: 10 rugby, 6 football and 4 other. Check that the frequencies add to 20.
steps.why: Each sector is a fraction of the whole group, so you need the total for the bottom of the fraction.

steps.text: Rugby is 10 out of 20, exactly half. Its angle is half of 360°, or 180°.
steps.why: Half the pupils get half the circle. The fraction of the group and the fraction of the circle are always equal.

steps.title: Calculate every sector
steps.text: Football gives 6/20 × 360° = 108°. Other gives 4/20 × 360° = 72°. Draw each angle at the centre, starting where the previous sector ends.
steps.why: The sectors do not overlap and together fill the circle, so their angles must add to 360°.

steps.title: Check and work backwards
steps.text: The three angles total 360°. A 72° sector in a group of 20 represents 72/360 × 20 = 4 pupils.
steps.why: 72° is one fifth of the circle, so the sector stands for one fifth of the 20 pupils.

quiz.question: A category has frequency 15 out of 60. What is its pie-chart angle?
quiz.hint: 15 out of 60 is what fraction? Take that fraction of 360°.
quiz.explanation: 15/60 × 360° = 90°. 15 out of 60 is one quarter, and a quarter of the circle is 90°. The count 15 is not the angle.

quiz.question: A sector is 120° in a chart of 45 people. How many people does it represent?
quiz.hint: 120° is what fraction of 360°?
quiz.explanation: 120/360 × 45 = 15 people. 120° is one third of the circle, and one third of 45 is 15.

lessons.takeaway: A sector is the same fraction of the circle as its count is of the total: count/total = angle/360°.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying the count by 360° and stopping. Divide by the total as well: angle = count/total × 360°.

lessons.title: Make histogram areas tell the truth
lessons.goal: Read a histogram for grouped measurements. Exam histograms have equal class widths. When widths differ (an extension), the area of a bar shows the frequency.

steps.why: The classes do not overlap, so every time belongs to exactly one class.

steps.text: Time is continuous and the classes meet at their boundaries, so histogram bars touch. Category bars in a bar chart usually have gaps.
steps.why: Time runs on without a gap from one class into the next, so the bars have no gaps either.

steps.why: Now width × height gives frequency. A wide class spreads its count over a wider bar; it does not create extra observations.

quiz.question: A histogram class has width 5 and frequency 20. What is its frequency density?
quiz.hint: Divide frequency by class width.
quiz.explanation: Frequency density = 20/5 = 4. Check: width 5 × height 4 gives back the frequency, 20.

quiz.question: In 10 ≤ t < 20, which value belongs to the class?
quiz.hint: 10 ≤ t means t can be 10 or more. t < 20 means t must be less than 20.
quiz.explanation: The class starts at 10 and includes it. It stops just before 20, so 20 belongs to the next class.

lessons.takeaway: Histogram bars touch because the data are continuous. When class widths differ, the area of a bar gives the frequency, not its height.
lessons.mistake: Reading height as frequency when the widths differ. A wide, low bar can hold more values than a narrow, tall one.

lessons.title: Read stem-and-leaf plots
lessons.goal: Read the key, rebuild every value from its stem and leaf, and compare two groups on a back-to-back plot.

steps.title: Choose place values
steps.text: For 12, 17, 21, 23, 23, 29, 34, use tens as stems and units as leaves. The key must explain the value.
steps.why: A stem and a leaf together make one value. The key tells you how.

quiz.question: The key says stem 4, leaf 6 means 4.6 kg. What does stem 5, leaf 2 mean?
quiz.hint: Use the place value shown in the key.
quiz.explanation: The stem is whole kilograms and the leaf tenths, so it means 5.2 kg.

quiz.question: A stem row has stem 3 and leaves 1, 1, 5, 8. How many observations are in that row?
quiz.hint: Count leaves, including repeats.
quiz.explanation: There are four leaves, so four observations.

lessons.takeaway: A stem-and-leaf plot keeps every value. The key tells you what a stem and a leaf mean.
lessons.mistake: Removing a repeated leaf because it looks like a copy. Each leaf is one value, so repeats must stay.

lessons.title: Challenge misleading graphs
lessons.goal: Check where the scale starts, how pictures are sized and what the real change is before you trust a chart.

steps.title: Notice an axis that does not start at zero
steps.text: Sales rise from 100 to 110, but an axis starting at 90 makes one bar appear twice the height of the other.
steps.why: A bar is drawn up from where the axis starts. With the axis starting at 90, the bars only show the amounts above 90, which are 10 and 20.

steps.title: Calculate the actual change
steps.text: The increase is 110 − 100 = 10. Compared with the original 100, this is 10%, not 100%.
steps.why: A percentage change compares the change with the amount you started from.

steps.title: Check the wider context
steps.text: Read the title, units, key, source and sample. A pictogram doubled in both width and height has four times the area, which can exaggerate a twofold change.
steps.why: A fair chart needs fair drawing and fair data. Check both.
steps.math: Question the design and the evidence

quiz.question: A value rises from 50 to 60. What is its percentage increase?
quiz.hint: The increase is 10. Compare it with the starting value, 50.

quiz.question: A pictogram is doubled in both width and height. Its area becomes…
quiz.hint: Area = width × height, and both have doubled.
quiz.explanation: 2 × 2 = 4, so its area quadruples.

lessons.takeaway: Read the scale, the numbers and the source before you trust how a chart looks.
lessons.mistake: Trusting how big the bars or pictures look. A chart can have correct numbers and still give the wrong impression, so read the scale.

reference.name: Pie sector
reference.note: All angles sum to 360°.

reference.name: Histogram
reference.note: JC exams use equal class widths; for unequal widths (extension) area represents frequency.

reference.name: Stem-and-leaf key
reference.note: State the place value explicitly.

reference.name: Graph checks
reference.formula: Read title, axes, units, scale, key and source.
reference.note: A visual impression needs the context of the numbers.

toolkit.strategy: Identify what one mark represents, recover the actual values or frequencies, then choose the summary or display that answers the question. Support every comparison with numbers and a sentence.

methods.title: Read line plots and category bars
methods.when: A graph uses dots at values or separate bars for categories.
methods.rule: Each dot is one observation; bar height is frequency when the frequency axis is labelled as such.
steps: Read title, key, units and scale.
Count repeated marks or read each frequency.
Sum frequencies before calculating shares or comparisons.
methods.example: Frequencies 4,9,7 total 20; the middle category is 9/20 of the sample.
methods.check: Recover the full sample size from the graph.
methods.trap: A high category frequency is not a large numerical data value.

methods.title: Recover a missing value from the mean
methods.when: The sample mean is known but one data value is missing.
methods.rule: Mean=Σvalues/n; total=n×mean; missing value=n×required mean−sum of known values, using the final sample size n.
steps: Count the final number of observations.
Multiply that count by the required mean.
Subtract the sum of the known values.
Recalculate the mean to verify.
methods.example: Nine known values sum to 216; ten values have mean 25 ⇒ missing value = 250−216=34.
methods.trap: Use the final sample size, including the unknown value.

methods.title: Convert between a budget, a share and a pie angle
methods.when: A pie chart gives counts, money, angles or a total.
methods.rule: θ=360°f/N; f=(θ/360°)N; if f and θ are known, N=360°f/θ.
steps: Find or reconstruct the whole.
Use the same fraction for quantity and angle.
Calculate missing categories by subtraction.
Check that all sector angles total 360°.
methods.example: €240 is represented by 72° ⇒ whole budget = 360×240/72=€1200.
methods.trap: A sector angle is a proportion of the whole, not an amount of money.

methods.title: Build and interpret a histogram
methods.when: Data are grouped into continuous intervals, especially of unequal width.
methods.rule: Density=f/w; frequency=bar area=density×class width.
steps: Read endpoints and compute each width.
Divide each frequency by its width.
Draw touching bars over the actual intervals, starting from zero density.
Recover frequencies from areas when reading the graph.
methods.example: A width-20 class with frequency 18 has density 0.9; a width-30 class with frequency 30 has density 1.0.
methods.check: Multiplying each density by its own width recovers the original frequencies.
methods.trap: The widest class can contain most observations without being the tallest bar.

methods.title: Construct and read a stem-and-leaf display
methods.when: Raw numerical values need a display preserving every observation.
methods.rule: Key fixes place value; leaves count observations. Ordered median: position (n+1)/2 if n is odd; mean of positions n/2 and n/2+1 if even. Mode=most frequent value; range=max−min.
steps: Choose stems and leaves with a clear key.
Sort each row and keep repeats.
Read data in order for median, mode and range.
methods.example: For 12,18,18,23,25,25: stem 1 with leaves 2, 8, 8 and stem 2 with leaves 3, 5, 5; median=(18+23)/2=20.5.
methods.check: Six leaves reconstruct the six original values.
methods.trap: For an even count, the median is the mean of the two middle values, not one middle leaf.

methods.title: Compare back-to-back data with a sentence
methods.when: Two groups share stems and a question asks about typical value or consistency.
methods.rule: Median compares centres; range=max−min compares overall spread. Smaller range suggests greater consistency by this measure.
steps: Read both sides using the same key.
Find each median and range independently.
Write a conclusion naming both values and the relevant property.
Separate typical level from consistency.
methods.example: Both medians are 8, but ranges are 5 and 13: the first group is more consistent by range, while their median results are equal.
methods.check: Check the minimum, maximum and middle positions directly in each ordered list.
methods.trap: A smaller range does not mean a larger typical result, and range alone does not describe every feature.

methods.title: Audit the visual claim
methods.when: The graph seems dramatic or supports a claim about change.
methods.rule: Percentage change=(new−old)/old ×100%, with old≠0. A pictogram scaled by k in both dimensions has area factor k².
steps: Read the baseline, equal steps, units and sample.
Calculate the actual numerical change.
Check whether picture size represents length or area.
Qualify conclusions when sampling or context is missing.
methods.example: 100→110 is a 10% increase even if a baseline of 90 makes the visible bars have ratio 1:2.
methods.check: Replot mentally from zero or compare the labelled values.
methods.trap: Correct numbers can still be displayed in a misleading way.

checks: Check totals: dots, leaves, frequencies and pie sectors must represent the whole data set.
State a stem-and-leaf key and preserve repeated values.
Use class boundaries consistently; a value must not be counted twice.
For unequal histogram widths, frequency follows area, not height alone.
A comparison sentence should name a statistic, give both values and explain its meaning.

challenges.title: Raw data, a display and a missing result
challenges.question: Ten training results are 12,18,18,23,25,25,25,31,33,40. (a) Make an ordered stem-and-leaf plot with a key. (b) Find the mean, median, mode and range. (c) An eleventh result makes the mean 26. Find it. (d) Find the new median and explain whether the larger mean forces the median to increase.
hints: The ten given values total 250.
The required total for eleven values is 11×26; then reorder before finding the new median.

solution.title: Arrange the display
solution.math: Stem 1: 2 8 8; stem 2: 3 5 5 5; stem 3: 1 3; stem 4: 0. Key: stem 2, leaf 5 means 25.
solution.reason: The plot preserves every original observation.

solution.title: Find the summaries
solution.reason: Ten values have the 5th and 6th in the middle, and both are 25. The range uses the two ends, 40 and 12.

solution.title: Recover the missing result
solution.reason: Eleven results with mean 26 must add to 11 × 26. Subtract the 250 you already have.

solution.title: Reorder and find the middle
solution.math: Ordered list gains 36 between 33 and 40; sixth value=25
solution.reason: Eleven ordered values have the sixth one in the middle, with five on each side.

solution.title: Interpret
solution.math: Mean rises to 26, while median stays 25
solution.reason: One new high value lifts the total, so the mean rises. The middle value does not have to move.

challenges.answer: Stem rows as shown; original mean 25, median 25, mode 25, range 28. Missing result 36; new median 25.
challenges.check: (250+36)/11=26. The new ordered list has five values on each side of its sixth value, 25.

challenges.title: Turn a club budget into a pie chart
challenges.question: A club budget totals €1200: rent €360, travel €300, equipment €180 and the remainder for refreshments. (a) Find the refreshment budget. (b) Calculate all four pie-chart angles. (c) A different budget has a 72° equipment sector representing €240. Find its total. (d) If the original total rises to €1500 but rent remains €360, find the new rent angle.
hints: The missing category is the total minus the listed amounts.
For part (c), €240 is 72/360 of the unknown total.

solution.title: Complete the budget
solution.reason: The four parts make up the whole budget, so the last part is what is left over.

solution.title: Calculate angles
solution.reason: Multiply each fraction of €1200 by 360°.

solution.title: Reverse a sector
solution.reason: 72° is one fifth of the circle, so €240 is one fifth of the total.

solution.title: Change the denominator
solution.reason: The same rent amount becomes a smaller share of a larger budget.

challenges.answer: Refreshments €360. Angles 108°, 90°, 54°, 108°. Reconstructed total €1200. Revised rent angle 86.4°.
challenges.check: The original angles sum to 360°. The revised rent share is 24%, and 24% of 360° is 86.4°.

challenges.title: Same centre, different consistency
challenges.question: Two squads record these counts across seven sessions. Squad A: 6,7,8,8,9,10,11. Squad B: 3,6,8,8,10,12,16. (a) Make a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot with a shared key. (b) Find each median and range. (c) Compare typical results using the medians and consistency using the ranges in one clear sentence. (d) Find each mean and explain why “more consistent” does not mean “higher average”.
hints: Use stems 0 and 1, and keep the repeated 8s.
Each median is the fourth ordered value; compare the means separately from the ranges.

solution.title: Build shared stems
solution.math: A left: stem 0 leaves 9 8 8 7 6; stem 1 leaves 1 0. B right: stem 0 leaves 3 6 8 8; stem 1 leaves 0 2 6.
solution.reason: On the left side the leaves are written so that the smallest is nearest the stem.

solution.title: Compare centres
solution.reason: Each squad has seven ordered values, so the fourth value is the median.

solution.title: Compare spreads
solution.reason: The range is the largest value minus the smallest.

solution.title: State the interpretation
solution.math: Equal median results; A is more consistent by range because 5<13
solution.reason: Say which measure you used and give both values.

solution.title: Check means separately
solution.reason: B has a higher mean despite a wider range.

challenges.answer: Both medians are 8; ranges A=5 and B=13. A is more consistent by range. Means A=59/7≈8.43, B=9.
challenges.check: Each side contains seven leaves. Totals 59 and 63 confirm the means, while the original extreme values confirm the ranges.

challenges.title: A histogram that cannot use raw frequency as height
challenges.question: Sixty running times are grouped as follows: 0≤t<10 minutes, frequency 12; 10≤t<30, frequency 18; 30≤t<60, frequency 30. (a) Calculate the class widths and frequency densities, then describe the correct histogram. (b) Find the proportion of times below 30 minutes. (c) Explain why the last class has the greatest frequency but not the tallest bar. (d) A student says the exact median is 30 minutes because the cumulative count reaches 30 there. Is that conclusion justified?
hints: Frequency density divides each frequency by its own width.
The exact median of 60 values uses the 30th and 31st values; the grouped table does not reveal those individual values.

solution.title: Find widths
solution.reason: Use upper boundary minus lower boundary.

solution.title: Set bar heights
solution.math: Densities are 1.2,0.9,1.0; draw touching bars over the stated intervals
solution.reason: Each area must equal its frequency.

solution.title: Count below 30
solution.reason: Both first intervals lie below 30; the second excludes 30.

solution.title: Explain height versus area
solution.math: The last bar has width 30 and height 1.0, so area 30; the first height 1.2 is taller but area 12
solution.reason: The widths differ, so you cannot compare frequencies by height alone. Compare areas.

solution.title: Limit the median claim
solution.math: Exact median=(30th value+31st value)/2 is unknown
solution.reason: The 30th is below 30 and the 31st is at least 30; their exact average is not determined.

challenges.answer: Widths 10,20,30; densities 1.2,0.9,1.0. Half the times are below 30. Frequency is area, and the exact median cannot be recovered from this grouped table.
challenges.check: Density×width gives 12,18,30 and total 60. Possible boundary values 29 and 31 give median 30, while 28 and 30 give 29, showing why it is not fixed.

title: Indices, Standard form, Surds
intro: A power is a short way to write the same number multiplied again and again. Once you know what each rule is counting, powers and roots become much easier to simplify.

lessons.title: Use index laws for the right reason
lessons.goal: Know which index rule goes with multiplying, dividing and a power of a power, and why each one works.

steps.title: Multiply matching bases
steps.text: x² means x × x, and x³ means x × x × x. Multiply them and you get two copies of x followed by three more. That is five copies, so the indices add: 2 + 3 = 5.
steps.why: The small raised number, called the index, counts how many copies of x are multiplied together.

steps.title: Divide matching bases
steps.text: Write x⁵ ÷ x² as five copies of x on top and two underneath. Each x underneath cancels one on top. Three are left, so you subtract the indices: 5 − 2 = 3. This needs x ≠ 0.
steps.why: x divided by x is 1, as long as x is not zero. Each cancelled pair just leaves a 1.

steps.title: Raise a power to a power
steps.text: (x²)³ means x² × x² × x². That is three groups, with two copies of x in each. Three groups of two make six copies, so you multiply the indices: 2 × 3 = 6.
steps.why: Equal groups are counted by multiplying, like 3 bags with 2 apples in each.

steps.title: Extend to zero and negative indices
steps.text: Go down the list 8, 4, 2. Each step down divides by 2. Keep going: 2⁰ = 1, 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4. A negative index means one over the power. It does not make the answer negative.
steps.why: This keeps the dividing rule working: 2² ÷ 2² = 2⁰, and any number divided by itself is 1.
