quiz.question: Simplify a³ × a⁴.
quiz.hint: The letters match and you are multiplying. What happens to the indices?
quiz.explanation: Three copies of a times four copies of a is seven copies: a³ × a⁴ = a³⁺⁴ = a⁷. Multiplying the indices to get a¹² is the usual slip.

quiz.question: Evaluate 3⁻².
quiz.hint: A negative index means one over the power. The answer is not a negative number.
quiz.explanation: 3⁻² = 1/3² = 1/9. The minus sign in the index means one over 3². It does not make the answer negative.

lessons.takeaway: With the same base: multiplying adds the indices, dividing subtracts them, and a power of a power multiplies them.
lessons.mistake: Writing a² + a³ = a⁵. The rules are for multiplying and dividing, not adding. With a = 2, a² + a³ is 4 + 8 = 12, but a⁵ is 32.

lessons.title: Translate fractional indices into roots
lessons.goal: Read a fraction index in two parts: the bottom number tells you which root, and the top number tells you which power.

steps.title: Read a half power
steps.text: An index of 1/2 means square root. So 16^(1/2) asks which positive number squared makes 16. The answer is 4, because 4² = 16.
steps.why: Two of them multiply to give 16¹, because 1/2 + 1/2 = 1. A number that does that is the square root.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Root first, then power"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Root first, then power</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">16^(1/2) = √16 = 4</text></svg>

steps.title: Read a third power
steps.text: An index of 1/3 means cube root. Which number, multiplied three times over, makes 27? 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, so 27^(1/3) = 3.
steps.why: Three of them multiply to give 27¹, because 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 1. That is what a cube root does.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Root first, then power"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Root first, then power</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">16^(1/2) = √16 = 4</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">27^(1/3) = ∛27 = 3</text></svg>

steps.title: Use both parts of the exponent
steps.text: For 27^(2/3), use the bottom number first. The 3 says cube root, which gives 3. Then the top number 2 says square it: 3² = 9.
steps.why: Taking the root first keeps the numbers small. Squaring 27 first gives 729, and its cube root is harder to spot.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Root first, then power"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Root first, then power</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">16^(1/2) = √16 = 4</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">27^(1/3) = ∛27 = 3</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">27^(2/3) = (∛27)² = 3² = 9</text></svg>

steps.title: Combine with a negative exponent
steps.text: Take 16^(−3/4) in three small moves. The fourth root of 16 is 2, because 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. Cube it to get 8. The minus sign means one over, so the answer is 1/8.
steps.why: A minus sign in an index always means one over the power. It never makes the answer negative.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Root first, then power"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Root first, then power</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">16^(1/2) = √16 = 4</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">27^(1/3) = ∛27 = 3</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">27^(2/3) = (∛27)² = 3² = 9</text><rect id="row-3" x="35" y="275" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="313" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">16^(−3/4) = 1/(⁴√16)³ = 1/8</text></svg>

quiz.question: Evaluate 81^(1/4).
quiz.hint: Which positive number gives 81 when four of them are multiplied together?
quiz.explanation: 81^(1/4) is the fourth root of 81. Since 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81, the answer is 3. Dividing 81 by 4 to get 20.25 is the usual slip.

quiz.question: Evaluate 8^(2/3).
quiz.hint: Take the cube root first, then square.
quiz.explanation: The cube root of 8 is 2, and 2² = 4. So 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 2² = 4. Multiplying 8 by 2/3 gives 16/3, which is not what the index means.

lessons.takeaway: Bottom of the fraction: which root. Top of the fraction: which power. Minus sign: one over the answer.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying the number by the fraction. 8^(2/3) is not 8 × 2/3. It is the cube root of 8, squared, which is 4.

lessons.title: Solve equations involving indices
lessons.goal: Find an unknown index by writing both sides as powers of the same number.

steps.title: Inspect the bases
steps.text: Solve 2^(x + 1) = 16. The unknown x is up in the index, so dividing both sides by 2 will not free it. Instead, ask which power of 2 makes 16.
steps.why: If both sides are powers of 2, you can compare the indices directly.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Rewrite both sides with the same base"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Rewrite both sides with the same base</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">2^(x + 1) = 16</text></svg>

steps.title: Rewrite the known side
steps.text: Count up the powers of 2: 2, 4, 8, 16. That is four steps, so 16 = 2⁴. Write 2⁴ in place of 16.
steps.why: 2⁴ and 16 are the same number, so swapping one for the other changes nothing.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Rewrite both sides with the same base"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Rewrite both sides with the same base</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">2^(x + 1) = 16</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">2^(x + 1) = 2⁴</text></svg>

steps.title: Equate the exponents
steps.text: Both sides are now 2 to some power, and they are equal. So the two indices must be the same number: x + 1 = 4. Subtract 1 from both sides to get x = 3.
steps.why: Each higher power of 2 is a bigger number. So two powers of 2 are equal only when their indices match.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Rewrite both sides with the same base"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Rewrite both sides with the same base</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">2^(x + 1) = 16</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">2^(x + 1) = 2⁴</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">x + 1 = 4 → x = 3</text></svg>

steps.title: Substitute to verify
steps.text: Put x = 3 back into the equation you were given at the start. 2^(3 + 1) is 2⁴, which is 16. Both sides agree, so x = 3 is right.
steps.why: Checking in the first line catches a slip made in any later line.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Rewrite both sides with the same base"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Rewrite both sides with the same base</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">2^(x + 1) = 16</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">2^(x + 1) = 2⁴</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x + 1 = 4 → x = 3</text><rect id="row-3" x="35" y="275" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="313" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">Check: 2^(3 + 1) = 16</text></svg>

quiz.question: Solve 3ˣ = 81.
quiz.hint: Rewrite 81 as a power of 3.
quiz.explanation: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81, so 81 = 3⁴. Then 3ˣ = 3⁴ gives x = 4. Dividing 81 by 3 gives 27, but that is not the index.

quiz.question: Solve 5^(2x) = 125.
quiz.hint: Write 125 as a power of 5, then compare the indices.
quiz.explanation: 125 = 5³, so 5^(2x) = 5³. The indices match: 2x = 3. Divide both sides by 2 to get x = 3/2. Stopping at 3 forgets the 2 in front of x.

lessons.takeaway: First get the same base on both sides. Then set the indices equal and solve. Last, check in the original equation.
lessons.mistake: Treating the index like a multiplier. 2ˣ = 16 does not mean 2 × x = 16. It asks which power of 2 makes 16, and that is 4.

lessons.title: Simplify and combine surds
lessons.goal: Take square numbers out of a root, and add roots only when the part under the root sign matches.

steps.title: Find a square factor
steps.text: A surd is a root that does not come out as a neat number, like √2. To simplify √72, look for a square number that divides 72. 36 does: 72 = 36 × 2.
steps.why: The root of a product can be split into two roots, and the root of a square number is a whole number.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Use perfect-square factors and like surds"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Use perfect-square factors and like surds</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">√72 = √(36 × 2)</text></svg>

steps.title: Keep the non-square part inside
steps.text: Split the root: √72 = √36 × √2. √36 is exactly 6, and √2 stays as it is. So √72 = 6√2, which means 6 × √2. Check: 6² × 2 = 72.
steps.why: 36 is a square number, so its root is the whole number 6. The 2 is not, so it stays under the root.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Use perfect-square factors and like surds"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Use perfect-square factors and like surds</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">√72 = √(36 × 2)</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">√72 = 6√2</text></svg>

steps.title: Combine only like surds
steps.text: To add √18 + √8, simplify each one first: √18 = 3√2 and √8 = 2√2. Now both are lots of √2, so add them like 3 apples and 2 apples: 5√2.
steps.why: Surds add like letters in algebra. 3x + 2x = 5x, and in the same way 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Use perfect-square factors and like surds"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Use perfect-square factors and like surds</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">√72 = √(36 × 2)</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">√72 = 6√2</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">√18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2</text></svg>

steps.title: Multiply inside one root
steps.text: Multiplying is different. You may multiply the numbers under the roots: √3 × √12 = √36 = 6. Adding does not work this way: √9 + √16 is 3 + 4 = 7, not √25.
steps.why: Roots work with multiplying and dividing. They do not split across a plus or a minus.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Use perfect-square factors and like surds"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Use perfect-square factors and like surds</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">√72 = √(36 × 2)</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">√72 = 6√2</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">√18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2</text><rect id="row-3" x="35" y="275" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="313" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">√3 × √12 = √36 = 6</text></svg>

steps.title: Remove a simple surd denominator
steps.text: A root on the bottom of a fraction is awkward. Multiply the top and the bottom of 1/√2 by √2. The bottom becomes √2 × √2 = 2, and the top becomes √2.
steps.why: Multiplying the top and bottom by the same number is multiplying by 1, so the value does not change.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Use perfect-square factors and like surds"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Use perfect-square factors and like surds</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">√72 = 6√2</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">√18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2</text><rect id="row-3" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">√3 × √12 = √36 = 6</text><rect id="row-4" x="35" y="275" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-4" x="380" y="313" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">1/√2 = √2/2</text></svg>

quiz.question: Simplify √50.
quiz.hint: Find a square number that divides 50.
quiz.explanation: 50 = 25 × 2 and √25 = 5, so √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2. Bringing the 25 outside without taking its root gives 25√2, which is the usual slip.

quiz.question: Simplify 2√3 + 5√3.
quiz.hint: Both terms are lots of √3, so treat √3 like a letter.
quiz.explanation: Two lots of √3 plus five lots of √3 is seven lots: 2√3 + 5√3 = (2 + 5)√3 = 7√3. The number under the root does not change.

lessons.takeaway: Take square numbers out of each root first. Then add or subtract only the surds whose root parts match.
lessons.mistake: Adding the numbers under two roots. √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7, but √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.

lessons.title: Use standard form for scale
lessons.goal: Write very big and very small numbers in standard form, also called scientific notation, and calculate with them.

steps.title: Normalise a large number
steps.text: Standard form is a front number from 1 up to, but not including, 10, times a power of ten. For 45 000 the front number is 4.5. The decimal point moved 4 places, so the power is 10⁴.
steps.why: 4.5 × 10⁴ = 4.5 × 10 000 = 45 000: the power of ten puts the digits back in their original places.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="One non-zero digit before the decimal point"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">One non-zero digit before the decimal point</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">45 000 = 4.5 × 10⁴</text></svg>

steps.title: Represent a small number
steps.text: For 0.00072 the front number is 7.2. The decimal point moved 4 places the other way, so the power is 10⁻⁴. A negative power of ten means a small number, not a negative one.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="One non-zero digit before the decimal point"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">One non-zero digit before the decimal point</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">45 000 = 4.5 × 10⁴</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">0.00072 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴</text></svg>

steps.title: Multiply coefficients and powers
steps.text: To multiply, deal with the front numbers and the powers of ten separately. 3 × 2 = 6, and 10⁵ × 10³ = 10⁸ because the indices add. So (3 × 10⁵)(2 × 10³) = 6 × 10⁸.
steps.why: Everything is multiplied, and the order of multiplying does not matter. So you can pair the front numbers and pair the tens.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="One non-zero digit before the decimal point"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">One non-zero digit before the decimal point</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">45 000 = 4.5 × 10⁴</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">0.00072 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">(3 × 10⁵)(2 × 10³) = 6 × 10⁸</text></svg>

steps.title: Divide and check the final coefficient
steps.text: To divide 8 × 10⁶ by 2 × 10², divide the front numbers: 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Subtract the indices: 10⁶ ÷ 10² = 10⁴. The answer is 4 × 10⁴. Check that the front number is at least 1 and less than 10.
steps.why: If the front number comes out as 10 or more, or below 1, move the decimal point and change the power of ten to match.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="One non-zero digit before the decimal point"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">One non-zero digit before the decimal point</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">45 000 = 4.5 × 10⁴</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">0.00072 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">(3 × 10⁵)(2 × 10³) = 6 × 10⁸</text><rect id="row-3" x="35" y="275" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="313" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">(8 × 10⁶)/(2 × 10²) = 4 × 10⁴</text></svg>

steps.title: Add only after matching the powers
steps.text: Adding is different. First make the powers of ten the same: 2 × 10³ is 0.2 × 10⁴. Now add the front numbers: 3 × 10⁴ + 0.2 × 10⁴ = 3.2 × 10⁴. Subtracting works the same way.
steps.why: This is thirty thousand plus two thousand, which makes thirty-two thousand. You can only add amounts counted in the same unit.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="One non-zero digit before the decimal point"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">One non-zero digit before the decimal point</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">0.00072 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">(3 × 10⁵)(2 × 10³) = 6 × 10⁸</text><rect id="row-3" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">(8 × 10⁶)/(2 × 10²) = 4 × 10⁴</text><rect id="row-4" x="35" y="275" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-4" x="380" y="313" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">3 × 10⁴ + 2 × 10³ = 3.2 × 10⁴</text></svg>

quiz.question: Write 0.0036 in standard form.
quiz.hint: The front number must be at least 1 and less than 10. Then count how many places the point moved.
quiz.explanation: The front number is 3.6. The point moved 3 places and the number is small, so the power is 10⁻³: 0.0036 = 3.6 × 10⁻³. 36 × 10⁻⁴ has the same value, but 36 is not below 10.

quiz.question: Calculate (2 × 10⁴)(4 × 10⁻²).
quiz.hint: Multiply the front numbers. Add the indices, taking care with the minus sign.
quiz.explanation: 2 × 4 = 8, and adding the indices 4 and −2 gives 2. So (2 × 10⁴)(4 × 10⁻²) = (2 × 4) × 10^(4 − 2) = 8 × 10².

lessons.takeaway: Work with the front number and the power of ten separately. Then check that the front number is at least 1 and less than 10.
lessons.mistake: Adding the indices when you add two numbers. 3 × 10⁴ + 2 × 10³ is not 5 × 10⁷. Match the powers of ten first, then add the front numbers.

lessons.title: Round at the correct place
lessons.goal: Tell significant figures from decimal places, and round only once, at the end.

steps.title: Locate the first significant digit
steps.text: In 0.004786, the zeros at the front only show where the decimal point is. They are not significant figures. Start counting at the first digit that is not zero, the 4.
steps.why: Significant figures are the digits that carry the size of the number, starting from the first non-zero one.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the requested digits, inspect the next one"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the requested digits, inspect the next one</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">0.004786: first significant digit is 4</text></svg>

steps.title: Keep the requested count
steps.text: For three significant figures, keep 4, 7 and 8. Then look at the next digit, which is 6. Because it is 5 or more, the 8 goes up to 9.
steps.why: 5 or more means the number is at least halfway to the next value, so you round up.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the requested digits, inspect the next one"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the requested digits, inspect the next one</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">0.004786: first significant digit is 4</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">3 s.f.: keep 4, 7, 8; next digit is 6</text></svg>

steps.title: Preserve the original magnitude
steps.text: Put the front zeros back: the answer is 0.00479. Rounding must not change how big the number is. 4.79 would be a thousand times too big.
steps.why: A rounded number should sit right beside the original on a number line.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the requested digits, inspect the next one"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the requested digits, inspect the next one</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">0.004786: first significant digit is 4</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">3 s.f.: keep 4, 7, 8; next digit is 6</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">0.004786 ≈ 0.00479 (3 s.f.)</text></svg>

steps.title: Distinguish decimal places
steps.text: Decimal places are different. Count digits after the decimal point: 3.14159 to two decimal places is 3.14, because the next digit, 1, is below 5. In longer questions, keep all the digits and round only the final answer.
steps.why: Each early rounding adds a small error, and the errors can build up by the end.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the requested digits, inspect the next one"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the requested digits, inspect the next one</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">0.004786: first significant digit is 4</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">3 s.f.: keep 4, 7, 8; next digit is 6</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">0.004786 ≈ 0.00479 (3 s.f.)</text><rect id="row-3" x="35" y="275" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="313" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">3.14159 ≈ 3.14 (2 decimal places)</text></svg>

quiz.question: Round 0.006284 to 2 significant figures.
quiz.hint: Start counting at the 6.
quiz.explanation: Counting starts at the 6. Keep 6 and 2. The next digit is 8, which is 5 or more, so the 2 goes up to 3: 0.0063. The zeros at the front stay.

quiz.question: Round 12.346 to 2 decimal places.
quiz.hint: Keep two digits after the point, then look at the third.
quiz.explanation: Two decimal places keeps 12.34. The third decimal digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so the 4 goes up: 12.35.

lessons.takeaway: Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit. Decimal places count digits after the decimal point.
lessons.mistake: Rounding in the middle of a calculation. Keep the full calculator value until the last line, then round once.

lessons.title: Use a calculator as a checking tool
lessons.goal: Type a calculation so the calculator groups it the way it is written, and check that the answer makes sense.

steps.title: Read the structure first
steps.text: Look at (8 + 4)/(7 − 3) before you press anything. The fraction line means all of the top is divided by all of the bottom. It acts like brackets around each part.
steps.why: On paper the long fraction line does the grouping. On a calculator you must type the brackets yourself.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Make the calculator follow the written structure"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Make the calculator follow the written structure</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">(8 + 4)/(7 − 3)</text></svg>

steps.title: Protect both groups
steps.text: If you type 8 + 4 ÷ 7 − 3, the calculator divides only 4 by 7. That is a different calculation. Type both pairs of brackets, or work out the top, 12, and the bottom, 4, first.
steps.why: A calculator multiplies and divides before it adds and subtracts, unless brackets tell it otherwise.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Make the calculator follow the written structure"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Make the calculator follow the written structure</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">(8 + 4)/(7 − 3)</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">Numerator = 12; denominator = 4</text></svg>

steps.title: Check the answer independently
steps.text: The top is 12 and the bottom is 4, so the answer is 12 ÷ 4 = 3. Do this in your head as well. If the display shows something far from 3, you mistyped.
steps.why: A rough answer worked out a second way is the quickest way to catch a typing slip.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Make the calculator follow the written structure"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Make the calculator follow the written structure</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">(8 + 4)/(7 − 3)</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Numerator = 12; denominator = 4</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">12/4 = 3</text></svg>

steps.title: Handle powers and roots carefully
steps.text: Put a negative number in brackets before you square it. (−3)² is −3 × −3 = 9. Without brackets, −3² squares the 3 first and then makes it negative: −9.
steps.why: The power is done before the minus sign. The brackets tell the calculator to square the whole of −3.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Make the calculator follow the written structure"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Make the calculator follow the written structure</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">(8 + 4)/(7 − 3)</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Numerator = 12; denominator = 4</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">12/4 = 3</text><rect id="row-3" x="35" y="275" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="313" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">Estimate first; use brackets; round last</text></svg>

quiz.question: Which entry correctly represents (5 + 7)/(9 − 5)?
quiz.hint: All of the top and all of the bottom each need their own brackets.
quiz.explanation: Brackets keep 5 + 7 together and 9 − 5 together, giving 12 ÷ 4 = 3. Without both pairs, the calculator divides only the 7, or divides by only the 9.

quiz.question: What is (−4)²?
quiz.hint: The whole negative number is squared.
quiz.explanation: (−4)² means −4 × −4. A negative times a negative is positive, so the answer is 16.

lessons.takeaway: Read how the calculation is grouped before you type it. Afterwards, compare the display with a rough answer.
lessons.mistake: Trusting the display without thinking. The calculator works out exactly what you typed, even when you left out a bracket.

reference.name: Products and quotients
reference.note: The bases must match; division needs a ≠ 0.

reference.name: Power of a power
reference.note: Multiply the exponents.

reference.name: Fractional powers
reference.note: For these real-number rules use a > 0 and n > 0.

reference.name: Standard form (scientific notation)
reference.note: For a non-zero number; n is an integer.

reference.name: Surd product
reference.note: For a, b ≥ 0 in the real-number system.

reference.name: Rationalise a simple denominator
reference.note: For a > 0. Multiply numerator and denominator by the same non-zero root.

toolkit.strategy: First see what is being done: adding, multiplying, dividing, taking a power or taking a root. Then choose the rule for that operation. Keep exact values until the last line, and use brackets so the calculator sees what is written.

methods.title: Choose the correct index law
methods.when: Powers of the same base are multiplied, divided or raised to another power.
methods.rule: aᵐaⁿ=aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ/aⁿ=aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ=aᵐⁿ; (ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ; (a/b)ⁿ=aⁿ/bⁿ. For integer indices, exclude zero wherever dividing or using a negative power; for these rational-index laws use positive bases.
steps: See what is being done to the powers: multiplying, dividing or raising to a power.
Check that the bases match before you add or subtract the indices.
Multiply the indices only for a power raised to another power.
methods.example: (x³)²/x⁴=x⁶/x⁴=x² for x≠0.
methods.trap: Adding powers is not multiplying them. aᵐ+aⁿ cannot be joined into one power.

methods.title: Interpret zero, negative and fractional indices
methods.when: The index is zero, has a minus sign or is a fraction.
methods.rule: For a≠0: a⁰=1 and a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ. For a>0 and positive integer n: a^(m/n)=(ⁿ√a)ᵐ; the denominator gives the root and numerator the power.
steps: A minus sign in the index means one over the power.
The bottom of a fraction index gives the root, and the top gives the power.
Keep roots exact where you can. Do not turn them into decimals early.
methods.check: Raise your root back to its power. For the fourth root 2, check that 2⁴ = 16.
methods.trap: A negative index does not make the answer negative. It means one over the power.

methods.title: Solve equal-base equations on both sides
methods.when: Both sides can be written as powers of the same number.
methods.rule: For b>0 and b≠1, bᵘ=bᵛ ⇒ u=v.
steps: Write both sides as powers of the same base.
When a base is replaced by a power, multiply the whole index by it.
Set the indices equal and solve the equation.
Check your answer in the original equation.
methods.check: Both original sides become 3⁹.
methods.trap: When 27 becomes 3³, the whole index x−2 is multiplied by 3, not just the x.

methods.title: Simplify and combine like surds
methods.when: A root contains a square number as a factor, or roots are added or subtracted.
methods.rule: √(ab)=√a√b for a,b≥0; p√q+r√q=(p+r)√q.
steps: Take out the largest square number that divides the number under the root.
Simplify each root on its own.
Add or subtract the numbers in front only when the root parts match.
methods.check: Work out both forms on a calculator. They should give the same decimal.
methods.trap: √a+√b is not √(a+b). For example √9+√16 = 7, but √25 = 5.

methods.title: Multiply surds and rationalise a simple denominator
methods.when: Surds are multiplied, or a single square root is on the bottom of a fraction.
methods.rule: √a√b=√(ab) for a,b≥0; √a/√b=√(a/b) for a≥0,b>0. p/√q=p√q/q for q>0. (√a±√b)²=a+b±2√(ab).
steps: To multiply surds, multiply the numbers under the roots, then simplify.
For a root on the bottom, multiply the top and the bottom by that root.
Cancel only a factor that divides the whole top and the whole bottom.
methods.check: Multiply 3√2/2 by √2 to recover 3.
methods.trap: Multiplying only the bottom changes the value of the fraction. Multiply the top as well.

methods.title: Calculate with standard form
methods.when: Very large or small numbers are multiplied or divided.
methods.rule: (a×10ᵐ)(b×10ⁿ)=ab×10ᵐ⁺ⁿ; quotient=(a/b)×10ᵐ⁻ⁿ, b≠0.
steps: Work with the front numbers and the powers of ten separately.
If the front number is 10 or more, or below 1, move the decimal point and adjust the power of ten.
Keep the units with your answer.
methods.trap: A front number such as 25.6 gives the right value, but it is not yet standard form. Write 2.56 and raise the power of ten by one.

methods.title: Add or subtract quantities in standard form
methods.when: Numbers in standard form are added or subtracted, not multiplied or divided.
methods.rule: First write both terms with the same power of ten, then combine coefficients.
steps: Choose one power of ten for both numbers.
Rewrite the other number with that power, keeping its value the same.
Add or subtract the front numbers, then put the answer back in standard form.
methods.trap: Adding or subtracting the indices. That rule is for multiplying and dividing only.

methods.title: Round and estimate deliberately
methods.when: The question asks for a given accuracy, or you want to check that an answer is sensible.
methods.rule: Decimal places count from the decimal point; significant figures start at the first non-zero digit.
steps: Find the last digit you are keeping.
Look at the next digit. If it is 5 or more, round up. Round once only.
To estimate, use easy numbers nearby and say that the answer is approximate.
methods.example: 0.006284 to 2 significant figures is 0.0063; 12.346 to 2 decimal places is 12.35.
methods.check: Count the digits in your answer. It should have the number of significant figures or decimal places asked for.
methods.trap: Zeros at the front of a decimal, as in 0.0063, do not count as significant figures.

methods.title: Enter the whole expression and test a claim
methods.when: A calculation has a fraction, a root or a negative number raised to a power, or a claimed rule needs testing.
methods.rule: Use brackets around compound numerators, denominators and radicands; one valid counterexample disproves a universal claim.
steps: Estimate the size and sign of the answer first.
Type every bracket that the written calculation needs.
Keep all the calculator's digits until the end.
To test a claimed rule, put simple allowed numbers into both sides and compare.
methods.example: For a=3,b=4, (a+b)²=49 but a²+b²=25, so the claimed equality is false.
methods.check: The numbers you test with must be allowed by the question.
methods.trap: One example that works does not prove a rule. One example that fails does disprove it.

checks: The index rules for multiplying and dividing need the same base. The base cannot be zero when you divide or use a negative index.
Use the fraction index rules with a positive base. You cannot take the square root of a negative number.
Simplify surds first. Then add or subtract only the ones whose root parts match.
In standard form the front number is at least 1 and less than 10, and the index is a whole number.
Estimate first. Keep all the digits while you work, and know whether the question wants decimal places or significant figures.

challenges.title: Powers with roots, reciprocals and an unknown on both sides
challenges.question: (a) Evaluate exactly (16^(−3/4) × 27^(2/3)) ÷ 9^(−1/2). Show the root and reciprocal decisions. (b) Solve 3^(2x−1)=27^(x−2). (c) Check the value of x in the original equation without expanding huge integers.
hints: The 4 on the bottom of the index means fourth root. A minus sign in the index means one over the power.
Write 27 as 3³. Then the whole index x − 2 is multiplied by 3.

solution.title: Evaluate each factor
solution.reason: The bottom of each fraction index names the root. Each minus sign turns that power into one over it.

solution.title: Complete the quotient
solution.reason: 1/8 × 9 is 9/8. Dividing by one third is the same as multiplying by 3, which gives 27/8.

solution.title: Match the bases
solution.reason: 27 is 3³, so the right side is 3 to the power 3(x − 2). Multiply out the bracket to get 3x − 6.

solution.title: Solve the exponent equation
solution.reason: Both sides are powers of 3, so the indices must be equal. Then solve the equation in the usual way.

solution.title: Check the original powers
solution.reason: With x = 5 both sides are 3⁹. You do not need to work out that large number to see that they match.

challenges.answer: The expression is 27/8. The equation has x=5, and both sides then equal 3⁹.
challenges.check: Work backwards: 27/8 × 1/3 = 9/8, and 9/8 is 1/8 × 9, the value of the first bracket.

challenges.title: Simplify surds and challenge a false rule
challenges.question: (a) Simplify √72−2√8+√18 exactly. (b) Multiply your answer by √2. (c) Rationalise 3/√2. (d) A student claims √(a²+b²)=a+b for all positive a,b. Use a=3,b=4 to test the claim, then explain why this settles the universal claim.
hints: Take the square numbers 36, 4 and 9 out of the three roots.
A rule that claims to work for all numbers is false if it fails for even one allowed pair.

solution.title: Extract square factors
solution.reason: √72 = 6√2, √8 = 2√2 and √18 = 3√2. All three are now lots of √2.

solution.title: Collect coefficients
solution.reason: The root parts match, so add and subtract the numbers in front, like collecting like terms.

solution.title: Multiply
solution.reason: √2 × √2 = 2, so the answer is 5 × 2 = 10.

solution.title: Rationalise
solution.reason: Multiplying the top and bottom by √2 is multiplying by 1. The value stays the same and the bottom becomes 2.

solution.title: Test the claim
solution.reason: 3 and 4 are allowed values, and the two sides give 5 and 7. One failure is enough to show the rule is not always true.

challenges.answer: (a) 5√2; (b) 10; (c) 3√2/2; (d) the claim is false because 5≠7.
challenges.check: Multiplying the rationalised form by √2 gives 3. Squaring the proposed values 5 and 7 gives 25 and 49, confirming they differ.

challenges.title: Available storage and a transfer estimate
challenges.question: A storage device has capacity 6.4×10⁹ bytes and already holds 7.5×10⁸ bytes. Each new file occupies exactly 2.5×10⁶ bytes. A transfer rate is exactly 3.2×10⁷ bytes per second in this model. (a) Find free capacity in standard form. (b) Find the greatest number of complete new files that fit. (c) Estimate the time to transfer data equal to the free capacity, then calculate it to 3 significant figures.
hints: Rewrite 7.5×10⁸ as 0.75×10⁹ before subtracting.
Divide the free bytes by the bytes in one file to count the files. Divide by the bytes per second to get the time.

solution.title: Find free capacity
solution.reason: You can subtract the front numbers only when both powers of ten are the same, here 10⁹.

solution.title: Find the file count
solution.reason: Divide the front numbers, 5.65 ÷ 2.5 = 2.26, and subtract the indices, 9 − 6 = 3.

solution.title: Estimate the transfer
solution.reason: Round to easy numbers first. The estimate tells you roughly what size the exact answer should be.

solution.title: Calculate precisely
solution.reason: Keep the full value 176.5625 until the end, then round once to three significant figures.

solution.title: Check the maximum
solution.math: 2260 files use 5.65×10⁹ bytes; one more would exceed it
solution.reason: 2260 files fill the free space exactly, so there is no room left for another file.

challenges.answer: Free capacity 5.65×10⁹ bytes; 2260 files; estimate about 200 s, calculated time 177 s to 3 significant figures.

challenges.title: A calculator result that needs brackets and judgement
challenges.question: A rectangle has sides 12.8 cm and 7.6 cm. (a) Estimate its area using 13 cm and 8 cm, then calculate the exact area from the given decimals. (b) Write a correctly bracketed calculator entry for its diagonal and find the diagonal to 3 significant figures. (c) Test the claim (a+b)²=a²+b² with a=3,b=4. Explain what this warns you not to do in part (b).
hints: Pythagoras: square each side first, add the squares, then take the root of the whole sum.
Do not round 12.8² + 7.6² before taking the square root.

solution.title: Estimate and calculate area
solution.reason: The estimate 104 tells you the exact answer should be near 100. It does not replace the exact answer.

solution.title: Structure the diagonal
solution.reason: The diagonal cuts the rectangle into two right-angled triangles, so Pythagoras gives its length.

solution.title: Keep exact intermediate values
solution.reason: Square each side first, then add. Keep every digit of the sum.

solution.title: Round at the end
solution.reason: Only the final root is rounded.

solution.title: Disprove the false expansion
solution.reason: (3 + 4)² is 7² = 49, not 9 + 16. In the same way, you cannot swap √(a² + b²) for a + b in the diagonal.

challenges.answer: Estimated area 104 cm²; calculated area 97.28 cm². Diagonal √221.6 cm≈14.9 cm. The proposed identity is false.
challenges.check: The diagonal must be longer than the longer side, 12.8 cm, and shorter than the two sides together, 12.8+7.6=20.4 cm. 14.9 cm fits, and its exact square is 221.6 cm².

title: Quadratic equations
intro: A quadratic equation has an x² in it and usually has two answers. You can solve it by factorising, or with a formula that always works.

lessons.title: Solve a quadratic by factorising
lessons.goal: Solve a quadratic by factorising it and then setting each bracket equal to zero. The answers are called roots.

steps.title: Put the equation in standard form
steps.text: Solve x² − x − 12 = 0. Before you factorise, make sure one side of the equation is zero. Here it already is.
steps.why: The method only works when the brackets multiply to give zero.

steps.title: Find the factor pair
steps.text: Find two numbers that multiply to −12 and add to −1. They are −4 and +3. So the left side factorises as (x − 4)(x + 3).
steps.why: Multiply out the brackets and you get x² − x − 12 again, so the factors are right.

steps.title: Split the zero product
steps.text: Two things multiply to give zero only when at least one of them is zero. So either x − 4 = 0 or x + 3 = 0.
steps.why: Try it with numbers: you cannot multiply two non-zero numbers and get zero.

steps.title: Keep and check both roots
steps.text: The roots are x = 4 and x = −3. Both make the original left side zero: 16 − 4 − 12 = 0 and 9 + 3 − 12 = 0.
steps.why: A correct root makes the original equation true when you put it in.
