title: Cylinder, Sphere
intro: A cylinder is a stack of equal circles and a sphere is a perfect ball. Learn how much each one holds, how much surface it has, and how long a tank takes to fill.

lessons.title: Build a cylinder from layers
lessons.goal: Find the volume of a cylinder, and work backwards from the volume to find a missing height.

steps.title: Identify the radius and height
steps.text: A cylindrical container has radius 3 centimetres and height 8 centimetres. Its circular cross-section stays the same all the way up.
steps.why: Think of a stack of coins. Every coin is the same circle, so the volume is one circle’s area times the height.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="body" x="270" y="100" width="150" height="200" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="base" cx="345" cy="300" rx="75" ry="23" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><ellipse id="top" cx="345" cy="100" rx="75" ry="23" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="345" y1="100" x2="420" y2="100" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="383" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3 cm</text><line id="height" x1="470" y1="100" x2="470" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text x="555" y="207" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba">h = 8 cm</text></svg>

steps.title: Find one circular layer
steps.text: Square the radius before multiplying by pi. Keep pi in the calculation until the end.
steps.why: The base is a circle, so its area is πr². Only the 3 is squared, not the π.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="body" x="270" y="100" width="150" height="200" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="base" cx="345" cy="300" rx="75" ry="23" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><ellipse id="top" cx="345" cy="100" rx="75" ry="23" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="345" y1="100" x2="420" y2="100" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="383" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3 cm</text><line id="height" x1="470" y1="100" x2="470" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text x="555" y="207" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba">h = 8 cm</text><text id="base-formula" x="135" y="318" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75">base area = 9π cm²</text></svg>

steps.title: Stack the layers
steps.text: Multiply the base area by the height of eight centimetres. Square centimetres times centimetres gives cubic centimetres.
steps.why: Each layer 1 cm thick holds 9π cm³, and there are 8 layers.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="body" x="270" y="100" width="150" height="200" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="base" cx="345" cy="300" rx="75" ry="23" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><ellipse id="top" cx="345" cy="100" rx="75" ry="23" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="345" y1="100" x2="420" y2="100" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="383" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3 cm</text><line id="height" x1="470" y1="100" x2="470" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text x="555" y="207" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba">h = 8 cm</text><text id="base-formula" x="135" y="318" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75">base area = 9π cm²</text><text id="layers" x="135" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#3175ba">8 layers, each 1 cm high</text></svg>

steps.title: Round and reverse if needed
steps.text: The volume is about 226.2 cubic centimetres. If volume and radius were known instead, divide volume by the circular base area to find height.
steps.why: The height was multiplied by the base area to make the volume. Dividing by the base area brings the height back.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="body" x="270" y="100" width="150" height="200" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="base" cx="345" cy="300" rx="75" ry="23" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><ellipse id="top" cx="345" cy="100" rx="75" ry="23" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="345" y1="100" x2="420" y2="100" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="383" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3 cm</text><line id="height" x1="470" y1="100" x2="470" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text x="555" y="207" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba">h = 8 cm</text><text id="base-formula" x="135" y="318" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75">base area = 9π cm²</text><text id="layers" x="135" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#3175ba">8 layers, each 1 cm high</text><text id="result" x="380" y="360" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#087f75">V = 72π cm³ ≈ 226.2 cm³</text></svg>

quiz.question: A cylinder has radius 2 cm and height 5 cm. Its volume is…
quiz.hint: Square the radius, then multiply by height.
quiz.explanation: π × 2² × 5 = 20π cm³. The answer 10π forgets to square the radius.

quiz.question: A cylinder has volume 54π cm³ and radius 3 cm. Its height is…
quiz.hint: Volume = πr² × height. Divide the volume by πr² to get the height.
quiz.explanation: h = 54π/(9π) = 6 cm. Dividing by 3π instead of 9π gives 18, which forgets to square the radius.

lessons.takeaway: Volume of a cylinder = area of the circular base × height, which is πr²h.
lessons.mistake: Using the diameter where the formula needs the radius. Halve the diameter first, or the volume comes out four times too big.

lessons.title: Unroll the surface
lessons.goal: Find the surface area of a cylinder, counting only the parts that are really there: the curved side, and both ends, one end or none.

steps.title: Separate the surfaces
steps.text: A closed cylinder has one curved side and two circular ends. Decide which parts are present before calculating area.
steps.why: Surface area is the material needed to cover the outside, not the space inside.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="body" x="270" y="100" width="150" height="200" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="base" cx="345" cy="300" rx="75" ry="23" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><ellipse id="top" cx="345" cy="100" rx="75" ry="23" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="345" y1="100" x2="420" y2="100" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="383" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3 cm</text><line id="height" x1="470" y1="100" x2="470" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text x="555" y="207" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba">h = 8 cm</text></svg>

steps.title: Unroll the curved side
steps.text: Imagine cutting the side vertically and laying it flat. It becomes a rectangle whose width is the circumference of the base.
steps.why: One full wrap around the circle has length two pi times radius.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="curved" x="190" y="110" width="340" height="170" rx="8" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text x="360" y="204" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba">curved surface</text><text x="360" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba">width = 2πr</text><text x="580" y="201" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#173349">h</text></svg>

steps.title: Count the circular ends
steps.text: Add one circle for an open-topped can, or two circles for a closed can. An end has area pi times radius squared.
steps.why: A lid that is not there needs no material, so it adds no area.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="curved" x="190" y="110" width="340" height="170" rx="8" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text x="360" y="204" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba">curved surface</text><text x="360" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba">width = 2πr</text><text x="580" y="201" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#173349">h</text><circle id="end1" cx="108" cy="195" r="52" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><circle id="end2" cx="652" cy="195" r="52" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text x="108" y="202" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#087f75">πr²</text><text x="652" y="202" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#087f75">πr²</text></svg>

steps.title: Calculate the closed total
steps.text: For radius 3 centimetres and height 8 centimetres, the curved side is 48 pi square centimetres and the two ends total 18 pi. Add those areas.
steps.why: Both parts are measured in square centimetres, so they can be added.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="curved" x="190" y="110" width="340" height="170" rx="8" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text x="360" y="204" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba">curved surface</text><text x="360" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba">width = 2πr</text><text x="580" y="201" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#173349">h</text><circle id="end1" cx="108" cy="195" r="52" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><circle id="end2" cx="652" cy="195" r="52" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text x="108" y="202" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#087f75">πr²</text><text x="652" y="202" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#087f75">πr²</text><text id="result" x="380" y="337" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#087f75">Total area = 2πrh + 2πr²</text></svg>

quiz.question: An open-topped cylinder has radius r and height h. Which area formula includes its base?
quiz.hint: Count one curved side and one circular base.
quiz.explanation: The curved side contributes 2πrh and the single base contributes πr². The formula with 2πr² is for a closed can with a lid.

quiz.question: For r = 2 cm, h = 3 cm, the curved surface area is…
quiz.hint: Use circumference × height.
quiz.explanation: 2π × 2 × 3 = 12π cm²; do not add the ends when asked for curved area.

lessons.takeaway: Unroll the curved side into a rectangle, 2πr wide and h high. Then add a circle for each end that exists.
lessons.mistake: Adding two circular ends to a container that has no lid. An open can has only one.

lessons.title: Sphere or hemisphere?
lessons.goal: Use the sphere formulas, and find the volume, curved area and total area of half a sphere, called a hemisphere.

steps.title: Measure from centre to surface
steps.text: A sphere has radius 3 centimetres. Every point on its surface is the same distance from its centre.
steps.why: The formulas use the radius. If you are given the diameter, halve it first.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><circle id="sphere" cx="250" cy="200" r="125" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="equator" cx="250" cy="200" rx="125" ry="30" fill="none" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/><line id="radius" x1="250" y1="200" x2="375" y2="200" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="308" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3</text></svg>

steps.title: Use the sphere formulas
steps.text: For volume, cube the radius. For area, square it. With r = 3 both come to 36π, so only the units, cm³ for volume and cm² for area, tell the two answers apart.
steps.why: Volume is measured in cubic units; surface area in square units.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><circle id="sphere" cx="250" cy="200" r="125" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="equator" cx="250" cy="200" rx="125" ry="30" fill="none" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/><line id="radius" x1="250" y1="200" x2="375" y2="200" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="308" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3</text><text x="560" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#3175ba">Sphere</text><text x="560" y="161" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba">V = 4πr³/3</text><text x="560" y="202" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba">A = 4πr²</text></svg>

steps.title: Halve the curved object
steps.text: A hemisphere is half a sphere. Its volume and curved surface area are each half the corresponding sphere values.
steps.why: Cutting into two equal halves divides both volume and curved surface equally.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><circle id="sphere" cx="250" cy="200" r="125" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="equator" cx="250" cy="200" rx="125" ry="30" fill="none" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/><line id="radius" x1="250" y1="200" x2="375" y2="200" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="308" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3</text><text x="560" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#3175ba">Sphere</text><text x="560" y="161" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba">V = 4πr³/3</text><text x="560" y="202" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba">A = 4πr²</text><path id="hemisphere" d="M 125 200 A 125 125 0 0 1 375 200 Z" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="flat-base" x1="125" y1="200" x2="375" y2="200" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text x="560" y="264" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">Half the volume</text><text x="560" y="300" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">Curved area: 2πr²</text></svg>

steps.title: Add the flat face if it is included
steps.text: A solid hemisphere also has a circular flat base. Add its area when asked for total surface area.
steps.why: The flat face is a new surface created by cutting the sphere.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><circle id="sphere" cx="250" cy="200" r="125" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="equator" cx="250" cy="200" rx="125" ry="30" fill="none" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/><line id="radius" x1="250" y1="200" x2="375" y2="200" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="308" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3</text><text x="560" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#3175ba">Sphere</text><text x="560" y="161" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba">V = 4πr³/3</text><text x="560" y="202" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba">A = 4πr²</text><path id="hemisphere" d="M 125 200 A 125 125 0 0 1 375 200 Z" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="flat-base" x1="125" y1="200" x2="375" y2="200" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text x="560" y="264" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">Half the volume</text><text x="560" y="300" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">Curved area: 2πr²</text><text id="closed" x="380" y="361" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12">Closed hemisphere: add the flat base → 3πr²</text></svg>

quiz.question: A closed solid hemisphere has radius 2 cm. Its total surface area is…
quiz.hint: The flat base counts as well as the curved surface.
quiz.explanation: Total area = 3πr² = 3π × 4 = 12π cm². The answer 8π is the curved part only.

quiz.question: Doubling a sphere’s radius multiplies its volume by…
quiz.hint: Volume uses the radius cubed: r × r × r.
quiz.explanation: (2r)³ = 8r³, so the volume becomes eight times as large.

lessons.takeaway: Half a sphere has half the volume and half the curved area. Its total area also includes the flat circle.
lessons.mistake: Halving the sphere’s area and stopping there. A solid hemisphere also has a flat circular face, so add πr².

lessons.title: Fill a container at a steady rate
lessons.goal: Find how long a tank takes to fill, by matching the units of its volume to the units of the flow.

steps.title: Work out the capacity
steps.text: A rectangular tank is 0.8 metres long, 0.5 metres wide and 0.6 metres high. First find the space it can hold.
steps.why: For a cuboid, volume is length times width times height.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="tank" x="130" y="85" width="270" height="235" rx="0" fill="#f3f7fb" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="water" x="133" y="287" width="264" height="30" rx="0" fill="#d8eafc" stroke="#d8eafc" stroke-width="2"/><path id="pipe" d="M 500 70 L 500 125 L 330 125 L 330 165" fill="none" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="12"/><text x="560" y="65" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba">12 L/min</text><text x="560" y="220" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75">Find volume</text><text x="380" y="357" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75">0.8 m × 0.5 m × 0.6 m</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">The water level rises as volume enters; the flow rate is volume per time.</text></svg>

steps.title: Match the flow-rate units
steps.text: Water enters at 12 litres per minute. Convert the tank capacity into litres before dividing.
steps.why: One cubic metre contains one thousand litres.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="tank" x="130" y="85" width="270" height="235" rx="0" fill="#f3f7fb" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="water" x="133" y="237" width="264" height="80" rx="0" fill="#d8eafc" stroke="#d8eafc" stroke-width="2"/><path id="pipe" d="M 500 70 L 500 125 L 330 125 L 330 165" fill="none" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="12"/><text x="560" y="65" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba">12 L/min</text><text x="560" y="220" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75">Convert units</text><text x="380" y="357" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75">0.24 m³ = 240 L</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">The water level rises as volume enters; the flow rate is volume per time.</text></svg>

steps.title: Divide volume by rate
steps.text: At a steady rate, every minute contributes another twelve litres. Ask how many groups of twelve fit into two hundred and forty.
steps.why: Time = volume needed ÷ volume arriving each minute.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="tank" x="130" y="85" width="270" height="235" rx="0" fill="#f3f7fb" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="water" x="133" y="172" width="264" height="145" rx="0" fill="#d8eafc" stroke="#d8eafc" stroke-width="2"/><path id="pipe" d="M 500 70 L 500 125 L 330 125 L 330 165" fill="none" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="12"/><text x="560" y="65" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba">12 L/min</text><text x="560" y="220" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75">From empty: 20 min</text><text x="380" y="357" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75">240 ÷ 12 = 20 min</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">The water level rises as volume enters; the flow rate is volume per time.</text></svg>

steps.title: Allow for water already present
steps.text: Picture the empty space, not the full tank. Capacity is 240 litres; 60 litres are already there. Only 240 − 60 = 180 litres need to flow in. Use 180 in the filling-time calculation.
steps.why: The tap fills the remaining space. Water already in the tank does not need to be supplied again.

quiz.question: A 150 L tank receives water at 5 L/min from empty. How long does it take to fill?
quiz.hint: Use volume ÷ rate.
quiz.explanation: 150 ÷ 5 = 30 minutes. Multiplying gives 750, which is far too long.

quiz.question: How many litres are in 0.035 m³?
quiz.hint: Multiply cubic metres by 1000.

lessons.takeaway: Change the units first. Then time = volume still needed ÷ flow rate.
lessons.mistake: Dividing cubic metres by litres per minute. Change the volume to litres first: 1 m³ = 1000 litres.

reference.name: Cylinder volume
reference.note: Use radius, not diameter.

reference.name: Cylinder area
reference.note: Count only the surfaces that exist.

reference.name: Sphere
reference.note: r is the radius.

reference.name: Hemisphere
reference.note: A closed hemisphere includes its circular base.

reference.name: Steady flow
reference.note: Use matching volume and time units.

toolkit.strategy: Decide whether the question asks for a volume, an outside area or a time. Split a joined shape into simple solids, label each one’s own measurements, and change the units before you calculate.

methods.title: Cylinder: volume and missing dimensions
methods.when: A solid or container is the same circle all the way up.
methods.rule: V = πr²h; h = V/(πr²); r = √[V/(πh)], with r,h > 0.
steps: Convert diameter to radius.
Use perpendicular height, then substitute in consistent units.
For an unknown dimension, isolate its power before taking a positive square root.
methods.example: V = 180π cm³ and h = 5 cm give r² = 36, hence r = 6 cm.
methods.check: Substitution gives π(6²)(5) = 180π cm³.
methods.trap: Using the diameter as the radius, or taking a square root before r² is on its own.

methods.title: Cylinder: curved, open and closed area
methods.when: The question asks how much material covers the outside.
methods.rule: Curved A = 2πrh; open top with base: A = 2πrh + πr²; closed: A = 2πrh + 2πr².
steps: Sketch which ends exist.
Unroll the curved side into a circumference-by-height rectangle.
Add only exposed circular ends.
methods.example: An open can with r = 2 cm, h = 7 cm has area 28π + 4π = 32π cm².
methods.check: The curved contribution has dimensions length × length.
methods.trap: Adding a lid that is not there, or mixing up surface area with the amount the container holds.

methods.title: Predict changes before calculating
methods.when: A radius or height changes by a scale factor.
methods.rule: Cylinder V is proportional to r²h; sphere V is proportional to r³. With h fixed, r × k gives V × k².
steps: Identify which dimensions change and which remain fixed.
Apply the appropriate power to each scale factor.
For unchanged volume, solve for the compensating height.
methods.example: Doubling cylinder radius requires height ÷ 4 to preserve volume.
methods.check: Calculate both volumes independently once.
methods.trap: Thinking that doubling any length always doubles the volume. Doubling a cylinder’s radius makes its volume four times bigger.

methods.title: Sphere and hemisphere: choose volume or area
methods.when: The shape is a sphere, half-sphere, or rounded end.
methods.rule: Sphere: V = 4πr³/3, A = 4πr². Hemisphere: V = 2πr³/3; curved A = 2πr²; closed A = 3πr².
steps: Use the common radius.
Halve the sphere volume or curved area for one hemisphere.
For total hemisphere area, add its circular base only if exposed.
methods.example: A closed hemisphere of r = 4 cm has V = 128π/3 cm³ and A = 48π cm².
methods.check: Two hemisphere volumes equal one sphere volume.
methods.trap: Adding a base where a hemisphere joins a cylinder.

methods.title: Capsules and other composite solids
methods.when: A cylinder is joined to two hemispherical ends.
methods.rule: For total end-to-end length L and radius r: h = L − 2r; V = πr²h + 4πr³/3; external A = 2πrh + 4πr², L > 2r.
steps: Mark the two radii along the total length.
Subtract 2r to find the straight cylindrical length.
Add volumes; for external area omit the two internal joining circles.
methods.example: For L = 18 cm and r = 3 cm, h = 12 cm and V = 144π cm³.
methods.check: The cylindrical part must be shorter than the total object.
methods.trap: Using L as the cylinder height.

methods.title: Empty space and complete units
methods.when: A solid sits inside a box, or a capacity must be reported in complete litres.
methods.rule: Empty volume = container volume − enclosed solid volume; 1 L = 1000 cm³; complete litres = the capacity in L rounded down to a whole number.
steps: Find the entire enclosing volume.
Subtract occupied volume without rounding either part early.
Convert to litres if needed, then distinguish approximation from the number of complete litres.
methods.example: A 2200 cm³ box holding a 600π cm³ solid has empty space 2200 − 600π ≈ 315.0 cm³, correct to one decimal place.
methods.check: Occupied plus empty volume must recover the container volume.
methods.trap: Rounding 3.9 litres up to four complete litres.

methods.title: Steady flow and remaining capacity
methods.when: Volume enters or leaves at a fixed rate.
methods.rule: t = remaining volume / net inflow; net inflow = inflow − outflow; use compatible units.
steps: Find capacity minus the volume already present.
Express all rates in one volume-per-time unit.
Divide by net inflow, which must be positive to fill.
methods.example: A 90 L vessel already holding 18 L fills at net 6 L/min in (90−18)/6 = 12 min.
methods.check: Rate × time + starting volume = final volume.
methods.trap: Using full capacity when the vessel is partly full.

methods.title: Convert pipe speed into volume flow
methods.when: Water speed is given in cm/s through a circular pipe.
methods.rule: Q = cross-sectional area × speed = πr²v. For cm and s, Q is cm³/s.
steps: Find the pipe’s internal radius.
Multiply area by water speed to find volume each second.
Convert the tank dimensions to centimetres or the flow to litres before dividing.
methods.example: A pipe of r = 1 cm carrying water at 25 cm/s supplies 25π cm³/s = 0.025π L/s.
methods.check: In one second the water forms a cylinder of length v centimetres.
methods.trap: Treating a speed in cm/s as though it were a flow in litres/s.

methods.title: Convert volume and time units before dividing
methods.when: A tank and pipe use different length, volume or time units.
methods.rule: 1 m³=10⁶ cm³=1000 L; 1 L=1000 cm³; 1 ml=1 cm³; 1 min=60 s. Area conversion squares a length factor; volume conversion cubes it.
steps: Choose one volume unit and one time unit.
Convert every dimension before forming a volume, or convert the completed volume using the cubic factor.
Convert rate and required volume to matching units before finding time.
methods.example: 0.06 m³=60 L; at 250 cm³/s=0.25 L/s, this volume takes 240 s=4 min.
methods.check: 0.25×240=60 L checks both the flow and time conversion.
methods.trap: Saying 1 m³ = 100 cm³. A cubic metre is 100 × 100 × 100 = 1,000,000 cm³.

checks: Radius is half the diameter; a capsule’s straight cylinder length excludes both end radii.
Area uses square units, volume uses cubic units, and flow divides volume by time.
Count exposed surfaces only; an internal join is not part of external area.
Retain π until the final answer; round down only when asked for complete units.

challenges.title: A rounded specimen case
challenges.question: A closed case is a cylinder with a hemisphere attached at each end. Its total length is 26 cm and its diameter is 6 cm. A rectangular box fits it exactly, with internal dimensions 26 cm by 6 cm by 6 cm. (a) Find the length of the cylindrical part. (b) Find the case volume exactly. (c) Find the empty space in the box to the nearest cm³. (d) Find the external area of the case exactly.
hints: Each rounded end is one radius long, so the two ends together take up one diameter of the length.
Use one sphere for the two ends; joining circles are internal.

solution.title: Separate the lengths
solution.reason: Each hemispherical end extends one radius along the length.

solution.title: Add the component volumes
solution.reason: The two hemispheres make one sphere.

solution.title: Subtract occupied space
solution.reason: The space left over is the whole box minus the case.

solution.title: Count exposed surfaces
solution.reason: Only the curved cylinder and sphere surfaces are exposed.

challenges.answer: (a) 20 cm. (b) 216π cm³. (c) 257 cm³ approximately. (d) 156π cm².
challenges.check: 216π ≈ 678.6 cm³, smaller than 936 cm³; adding the unrounded empty space gives 936 cm³.

challenges.title: A hose fills a partly full tank
challenges.question: A tank measures 0.8 m by 0.5 m by 0.6 m internally and initially holds 42 L. A circular hose has internal radius 1.5 cm. Water moves through it at a steady 40 cm/s, with no leaks. (a) Find the inflow in cm³/s and L/s. (b) Find the time to fill the tank, to the nearest second. (c) After exactly 6 minutes, how many complete litres does the tank contain?
hints: A water column passing in one second has length 40 cm.
Capacity is 240 L; convert the hose flow to L/s before finding the filling time.

solution.title: Find capacity
solution.reason: One cubic metre is one thousand litres.

solution.title: Find volume flow
solution.reason: Flow is pipe cross-sectional area times speed.

solution.title: Use the unfilled part
solution.reason: Only the remaining 198 litres need to enter.

solution.title: Count complete litres after six minutes
solution.reason: There are 143 complete litres; the remainder does not make another full litre.

challenges.answer: (a) 90π cm³/s = 0.09π L/s. (b) 700 s approximately. (c) 143 complete litres.
challenges.check: The six-minute volume is below 240 L, and 0.09π × (2200/π) = 198 L exactly.

challenges.title: Same capacity, different cylinder
challenges.question: A closed cylindrical tin has radius 4 cm and height 10 cm. (a) Find its volume and total area exactly. (b) State the volume multiplier if only its radius is doubled; then if only its height is doubled. (c) A redesigned tin doubles the radius but keeps the original volume. Find its height and total area. (d) By what percentage has the total area changed?
hints: Volume depends on radius squared but only on the first power of height.
The volume stays the same, so write πr²h for the old tin and for the new tin and set them equal.

solution.title: Calculate the original tin
solution.reason: A closed cylinder has two circular ends.

solution.title: Apply separate scale changes
solution.reason: Only the radius is squared in πr²h.

solution.title: Preserve the capacity
solution.reason: Doubling the radius forces height to become one quarter.

solution.title: Calculate the new area
solution.reason: The larger ends can outweigh the shorter curved side.

solution.title: Compare like quantities
solution.reason: Percentage change is measured against the original area.

challenges.answer: (a) V = 160π cm³, A = 112π cm². (b) ×4; ×2. (c) h = 2.5 cm, A = 168π cm². (d) 50% increase.
challenges.check: π(8²)(2.5) = 160π verifies unchanged capacity; 168/112 = 1.5 verifies the area increase.

challenges.title: Transfer water between curved containers
challenges.question: A hemispherical bowl has internal radius 6 cm and contains three quarters of its full capacity. All its water is poured into an empty cylindrical measuring jar of internal radius 3 cm and height 15 cm. (a) Find the water volume exactly. (b) Find its depth in the jar. (c) Find the spare capacity of the jar in cm³ and in litres. (d) Find the curved inside area of the bowl; explain why the flat circle is excluded.
hints: Three quarters refers to volume, not to the bowl’s radius or depth.
After the transfer, divide water volume by the jar’s circular base area.

solution.title: Find the bowl’s water volume
solution.reason: A hemisphere is half a sphere; the fill fraction applies to capacity.

solution.title: Find the cylindrical depth
solution.reason: The transferred volume is unchanged.

solution.title: Find spare capacity
solution.reason: The remaining 3 cm of jar height has the same circular cross-section.

solution.title: Choose the correct bowl surface
solution.reason: The bowl is open; its circular opening is not a physical inner surface.

challenges.answer: (a) 108π cm³. (b) 12 cm. (c) 27π cm³ = 0.027π L ≈ 0.0848 L. (d) 72π cm²; no flat lid is present.
challenges.check: Water plus spare volume is 108π + 27π = 135π cm³, equal to the jar’s full capacity.

title: Patterns and Sequences
intro: A sequence is a list of numbers that follows a rule. Spot the rule, write it using n, and you can find any term without listing them all.

lessons.title: Term versus position
lessons.goal: Keep two things apart: where a term sits in the list, and what number it is.

steps.title: Read positions from one
steps.text: Look at the sequence 4, 7, 10, 13. The first term is 4, and its position is 1. We write T₁ = 4, which says the term in position 1 is 4.
steps.why: Think of numbered lockers. The position is the locker number. The term is what is inside.

steps.title: Describe a term-to-term rule
steps.text: Each term is 3 more than the one before it. So you can keep the list going by adding 3 each time: after 13 comes 16.
steps.why: When the jump is the same every time, the sequence is called arithmetic, or linear.

steps.title: Check the rule against every gap
steps.text: Do not trust the first jump alone. Subtract each term from the next one and check that every jump is 3.
steps.why: One matching jump could be luck. The rule is only right if it fits every term you were given.

steps.title: Distinguish two kinds of rule
steps.text: Adding 3 only gets you to the next term. A position rule goes straight to any term. With Tₙ = 3n + 1, put the position in for n: the 10th term is 3 × 10 + 1 = 31.
steps.why: The letter n stands for the position in the list. It is not the value of the term before.

quiz.question: In 8, 13, 18, 23, what is T₃?
quiz.hint: T₃ means the term in position 3. Count along the list.
quiz.explanation: Count along: 8, 13, 18. The third term is 18, so T₃ = 18. The 3 is the position, not the answer.

quiz.question: For Tₙ = 4n − 1, the fifth term is…
quiz.hint: Put 5 in place of n in the rule.
quiz.explanation: Replace n with 5: T₅ = 4 × 5 − 1 = 19. Multiply first, then subtract 1.

lessons.takeaway: The position goes into the rule. The term is the number that comes out.
lessons.mistake: Putting the previous term into the rule in place of n. In Tₙ = 3n + 1, n is the position, so the 5th term is 3 × 5 + 1 = 16.

lessons.title: Find a distant repeating item
lessons.goal: Find any item in a repeating pattern by dividing and looking at the remainder.

steps.title: Identify one full cycle
steps.text: A pattern on a team kit repeats red, blue, blue, gold. After gold the same block of four starts again. One block is called a cycle, and here the cycle length is 4.
steps.why: Once you know one cycle, you know the whole pattern, because it only repeats.
steps.math: R, B, B, G | R, B, B, G | …

steps.title: Count complete cycles
steps.text: To find item 23, divide 23 by the cycle length, 4. It goes in 5 times, which uses up 20 items. There are 3 left over.
steps.why: Each full cycle ends on gold and the next starts fresh. So full cycles do not change where you are in the block.

steps.title: Use the remainder as a position
steps.text: The remainder is 3. So item 23 is the same as the 3rd item in the cycle. Count red, blue, blue: it is blue.
steps.why: After 20 items the pattern starts again at red, and you count on 3 more.

steps.title: Handle a zero remainder
steps.text: Item 24 is 6 full cycles with nothing left over. A remainder of 0 means you stopped at the end of a cycle. So item 24 is the last item, gold.
steps.why: There is no item number 0 in the block. Finishing a cycle exactly means landing on its last item.

quiz.question: A, B, C repeats. What is item 20?
quiz.hint: Divide 20 by 3 and look at the remainder.
quiz.explanation: 20 = 6 × 3 + 2, so item 20 is the second cycle item, B. Rounding 20 ÷ 3 to 7 throws away the remainder, and the remainder is what tells you the item.

quiz.question: Red, blue, green, yellow repeats. Item 32 is…
quiz.hint: Divide 32 by 4. What does a remainder of 0 tell you?
quiz.explanation: 32 = 8 × 4 with remainder 0. That is the end of a full cycle, so item 32 is the last colour, yellow.

lessons.takeaway: Divide the position by the cycle length. The remainder tells you the item, and a remainder of 0 means the last item.
lessons.mistake: Treating a remainder of 0 as the first item. Remainder 0 means a cycle has just finished, so it is the last item.

lessons.title: Spot a linear sequence
lessons.goal: Spot a sequence that goes up or down by the same amount each time, and tell it apart from one that multiplies.

steps.title: Subtract consecutive terms
steps.text: For 5, 9, 13, 17, subtract each term from the one after it. Every answer is 4. These jumps are called the first differences.
steps.why: The same jump every time means the sequence is linear. On a graph its points lie in a straight line.

steps.title: Keep the sign of the difference
steps.text: A sequence that goes down can be linear too. In 20, 17, 14, 11 each term is 3 less than the one before. Next minus previous gives 17 − 20 = −3 every time.
steps.why: Always work out next term minus previous term. Then a falling sequence gives a negative difference.

steps.text: In 2, 6, 18, 54 the jumps are 4, 12 and 36, so it is not linear. But each term is 3 times the one before. A sequence that multiplies like this is called geometric.
steps.why: Adding the same amount grows steadily. Multiplying by the same amount grows faster and faster.

steps.title: Check a candidate rule
steps.text: Back to 5, 9, 13, 17. The jump is 4, so start with 4 times the position: 4, 8, 12, 16. Each is 1 too small, so add 1. The rule is Tₙ = 4n + 1.
steps.why: The jump gives the number in front of n. The added number then lines the rule up with the first term.

quiz.question: Which sequence has a constant first difference?
quiz.hint: Subtract each term from the next one. Are all the answers the same?
quiz.explanation: 12, 9, 6, 3 goes down by 3 every time, so its difference is always −3. The others fail: 2, 4, 8, 16 doubles, 1, 4, 9, 16 has jumps 3, 5, 7, and 16, 8, 4, 2 halves.

quiz.question: For 7, 12, 17, 22, the common difference is…
quiz.hint: Take any term away from the one after it.
quiz.explanation: 12 − 7 = 5, and every later jump is also 5. The first term, 7, is not the difference.

lessons.takeaway: Adding the same amount each time gives a linear sequence. Multiplying by the same amount each time gives a geometric one.
lessons.mistake: Calling every sequence that goes up linear. Check the jumps: 2, 6, 18, 54 goes up, but its jumps are 4, 12, 36.

lessons.title: Build the nth-term rule
lessons.goal: Write a rule for the term in position n of a linear sequence, and use it forwards and backwards.

steps.title: Identify the first term and gap
steps.text: Use the sequence 7, 11, 15, 19. The first term is 7, and we call it a. The jump between terms is 4. It is called the common difference, d.
steps.why: The first term tells you where you start. The difference tells you how far each step goes.

steps.title: Count the jumps
steps.text: To get from term 1 to term 5 you make 4 jumps, not 5. To reach position n you make n − 1 jumps of size d. So the term is the start plus those jumps.
steps.why: You are already standing on the first term before you jump. Like fence posts: 5 posts have only 4 gaps.

steps.title: Substitute and simplify
steps.text: Put a = 7 and d = 4 into the rule. Multiply out the bracket to get 4n − 4. Then 7 − 4 = 3, so the rule is 4n + 3. Check: n = 1 gives 7.
steps.why: Both forms give the same terms. The short form 4n + 3 is quicker to use.

steps.title: Predict or find a position
steps.text: Forwards: the 20th term is 4 × 20 + 3 = 83. Backwards: is 99 in the sequence? Solve 4n + 3 = 99. Subtract 3, then divide by 4, to get n = 24. So 99 is the 24th term.
steps.why: A number is in the sequence only if n comes out as a positive whole number.

quiz.question: The nth term of 6, 11, 16, 21 is…
quiz.hint: The jump gives the number in front of n. Then test the rule with n = 1.
quiz.explanation: The jump is 5, so the rule starts 5n. At n = 1, 5n gives 5 and the first term is 6, so add 1: 5n + 1. Putting the first term, 6, in front of n is the usual slip.

quiz.question: Does 50 occur in Tₙ = 4n + 3, with n a positive integer?
quiz.hint: Solve 4n + 3 = 50. Is n a whole number?
quiz.explanation: 4n + 3 = 50 → 4n = 47 → n = 11.75. A position must be a whole number, so 50 is not in the sequence.

lessons.takeaway: Term = first term + number of jumps × size of jump, and the number of jumps is n − 1.
lessons.mistake: Using n jumps where there are only n − 1. For 7, 11, 15 the rule 7 + 4n gives 11 at n = 1. The correct rule 7 + 4(n − 1) gives 7.

lessons.title: Explain a shape pattern
lessons.goal: Build a rule for a shape pattern by counting what you start with and what each new shape adds.

steps.title: Count the first shape carefully
steps.text: One square needs 4 matchsticks. Put a second square beside it and they share a side. That shared stick is already there, so you do not add it again.
steps.why: The side between two squares is one real stick. Count it once.

steps.title: Count what each extra square adds
steps.text: Each new square needs only a top, a bottom and a far side. That is 3 more sticks every time, so the totals go 4, 7, 10, 13.
steps.why: The near side of the new square is the far side of the one before it.

steps.title: Write a rule from the growth
steps.text: Start with 4 sticks for the first square. Each extra square adds 3, and a row of n squares has n − 1 extra squares. Multiply out and tidy up to get 3n + 1.
steps.why: It is a linear sequence with first term 4 and common difference 3. The picture tells you why.

steps.title: Check with a different count
steps.text: Count a second way. A row of n squares has n sticks along the top, n along the bottom and n + 1 standing upright. Add them and you get 3n + 1 again.
steps.why: Two different ways of counting that agree are strong evidence that the rule is right.

quiz.question: How many sticks make a row of 10 joined squares?
quiz.hint: The first square uses 4 sticks. Each of the other 9 squares adds 3.
quiz.explanation: The rule is 3n + 1, so 10 squares need 3 × 10 + 1 = 31 sticks. Counting 4 for every square gives 40, which counts the shared sides twice.

quiz.question: Why is 4n wrong for joined squares?
quiz.hint: Look at the stick between two squares that touch.
quiz.explanation: Two squares side by side share one stick. Counting 4 for each square counts that shared stick twice.

lessons.takeaway: Count what the first shape needs, then count only what each new shape adds.
lessons.mistake: Counting joined shapes as if they were apart. Three joined squares need 10 sticks, not 3 × 4 = 12, because two sides are shared.

lessons.title: Find a quadratic sequence rule
lessons.goal: When the jumps themselves go up by the same amount, find a rule with n² in it.

steps.title: Calculate first differences
steps.text: Look at 3, 8, 15, 24, 35. The jumps are 5, 7, 9 and 11. They are not all the same, so the sequence is not linear.
steps.why: A linear rule has one fixed jump. Here the jump keeps growing, so you need a different kind of rule.

steps.title: Take differences again
steps.text: Now look at the jumps 5, 7, 9, 11. They go up by 2 each time. This is the second difference. Halve it to get the number in front of n²: 2 ÷ 2 = 1.
steps.why: Try n² itself: 1, 4, 9, 16 has jumps 3, 5, 7, which go up by 2. So one lot of n² gives a second difference of 2.

steps.title: Remove the square part
steps.text: The rule starts with n². Take the square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 away from the terms. What is left is 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. That is 2 times the position, so the rest of the rule is 2n.
steps.why: Once the n² part is removed, what remains is a linear sequence, and you already know how to find its rule.

steps.title: Combine and test
steps.text: Put the two parts together: Tₙ = n² + 2n. Test it. At n = 1 it gives 1 + 2 = 3, and at n = 3 it gives 9 + 6 = 15. Both match, so use it: T₁₀ = 100 + 20 = 120.
steps.why: A rule is only trusted after it gives back the terms you started with.

quiz.question: A quadratic sequence has second difference 6. Its coefficient of n² is…
quiz.hint: The number in front of n² is half the second difference.
quiz.explanation: The second difference is twice the number in front of n². Half of 6 is 3. Using 6 itself is the usual slip.

quiz.question: For Tₙ = n² + 2n, T₄ is…
quiz.hint: Put 4 in place of n. Square it first, then add 2 × 4.

lessons.takeaway: Halve the second difference to get the number in front of n². Take that n² part away from the terms, then find the linear rule that is left.
lessons.mistake: Putting the second difference straight in front of n². A second difference of 2 means 1n², not 2n². Halve it first.

lessons.title: Graph a sequence as separate points
lessons.goal: Plot a sequence as separate points, and read from the shape whether it is linear, quadratic or exponential.

steps.title: Use position on the horizontal axis
steps.text: Put the position n along the bottom and the term value up the side. For 2, 4, 8, 16, position 1 has value 2, so plot the point (1,2). Do the same for each term.
steps.why: Each term gives one point: across to its position, up to its value.

steps.title: Look for the kind of growth
steps.text: These terms double each time: 2, 4, 8, 16. The jumps are 2, 4, 8, so they are not equal. What stays the same is the multiplier, 2. The rule is Tₙ = 2ⁿ.
steps.why: Multiplying by the same number again and again is called exponential growth. It gives a geometric sequence.

steps.title: Compare the graph shapes
steps.text: Compare three shapes. A linear sequence gives points in a straight line. A quadratic one curves upwards. An exponential one starts slowly and then climbs faster than both.
steps.why: Equal jumps make a straight line. Growing jumps make a curve. Jumps that multiply make the steepest curve.
steps.math: linear: constant gaps; geometric: constant ratios

steps.title: Respect the domain
steps.text: The 5th term is 2⁵ = 32. Positions are whole numbers only: 1, 2, 3 and so on. There is no term at position 2.5, so leave the points separate and do not join them.
steps.why: A joined line would say there are terms between the positions. In a sequence there are none.

quiz.question: Which graph convention is best for a sequence at integer positions?
options: Points joined by a smooth curve
quiz.hint: Think about which positions actually exist.
quiz.explanation: Plot one point for each whole-number position. A joined curve would suggest terms at positions such as 2.5, and a sequence has none.

quiz.question: The sequence 3, 6, 12, 24 has nth term…
quiz.hint: Test each rule with n = 1. It must give 3.
quiz.explanation: The terms double, so the rule uses powers of 2. At n = 1, 3 × 2ⁿ⁻¹ is 3 × 2⁰ = 3, which is right. 3 × 2ⁿ would start at 6.

lessons.takeaway: A sequence graph is a set of separate points: position across, term value up.
lessons.mistake: Joining the points with a line. That suggests terms at positions like 2.5, and a sequence only has whole-number positions.

reference.name: Arithmetic sequence
reference.note: a is first term, d is common difference; n begins at 1.

reference.name: Quadratic sequence
reference.formula: Tₙ = an² + bn + c; second difference = 2a
reference.note: Use equally spaced integer positions.

reference.name: Geometric sequence
reference.note: a is first term; r is the constant multiplier.

reference.name: Repeating pattern
reference.formula: Divide the position by the cycle length and use the remainder
reference.note: A zero remainder means the last item in the cycle.

toolkit.strategy: First decide what the pattern does: repeat, add the same amount, multiply by the same amount, or have jumps that grow steadily. Then check which position comes first, usually n = 1, before you write a rule.

methods.title: Separate position from value
methods.when: The question uses Tₙ, term number or stage number.
methods.rule: Tₙ is the value at position n; n is not generally the term value.
steps: Write the position above each term you are given.
Note where the positions start, usually n = 1.
Put the position into the rule, not the previous term.
methods.example: If Tₙ = 2n + 5, then T₄ = 13; 4 is the position and 13 its value.
methods.check: Write the pair as (4,13): position first, value second.
methods.trap: Putting the previous term into the rule in place of the position n.

methods.title: Locate an item in a repeating cycle
methods.when: A fixed block of colours, shapes or actions repeats.
methods.rule: n = qL + r, 0 ≤ r < L; use cycle item r, except r = 0 means item L.
steps: Find the shortest block that repeats and count its length, L.
Divide the position you want by L.
Use the remainder to pick the item. A remainder of 0 means the last item of the block.
methods.example: For the cycle A,B,C,D,E, item 38 matches item 3, C.
methods.check: Positions 35 and 40 both end complete cycles.
methods.trap: Treating a remainder of 0 as the first item. It is the last item of the cycle.

methods.title: Recognise a linear or geometric sequence
methods.when: You need to decide whether a sequence adds or multiplies before choosing a rule.
methods.rule: Arithmetic: Tₙ₊₁−Tₙ = d. Geometric: Tₙ₊₁/Tₙ = r where the denominator is non-zero.
steps: Work out every jump between neighbouring terms.
If the jumps are not equal, test whether each term is the one before times a fixed number.
For a sequence that goes down, keep the minus sign on the difference.
methods.example: 18,14,10,6 has d = −4; 2,6,18,54 has multiplier 3.
methods.check: Use your rule to make the next term and see that it fits the pattern.
methods.trap: Calling every sequence that goes up linear. Check the jumps first.

methods.title: Build and reverse an arithmetic rule
methods.when: The jump between terms is always the same, or you are given a term and asked for its position.
methods.rule: Tₙ = a + (n−1)d; for d ≠ 0, n = 1 + (T−a)/d.
steps: Find the first term a and the common difference d.
Count n−1 jumps from the first term.
For a given value, set the rule equal to it, solve, and check that n is a positive whole number.
methods.example: For 9,14,19,…, Tₙ = 5n+4. Target 74 gives n = 14.
methods.trap: Accepting a value such as n = 14.2 as a position. Positions are whole numbers.

methods.title: Derive a shape rule by counting
methods.when: A growing shape pattern shares sides, or has a fixed part and a repeated part.
methods.rule: Total = fixed part + repeated part; count a shared edge once.
steps: Say exactly what each new stage adds.
Count the first stage, then count what each later stage adds.
Count the picture a second way, such as rows and columns, to check the rule.
methods.example: A row of n edge-sharing pentagons uses 5+4(n−1) = 4n+1 sticks.
methods.check: n = 1 gives 5; each added pentagon contributes four new sticks.
methods.trap: Counting every side of every shape. A side shared by two shapes is one stick.

methods.title: Recover a quadratic nth term
methods.when: The jumps change, but the jumps between the jumps are all equal.
methods.rule: Tₙ = an²+bn+c; constant second difference = 2a for unit-spaced n.
steps: Find the first and second differences.
Halve the second difference to get a, the number in front of n².
Take that n² part away from each term. What is left is a linear sequence.
methods.example: 5,12,23,38,… has second difference 4; subtract 2n² to obtain 3,4,5,6,…, giving Tₙ = 2n²+n+2.
methods.check: Check n = 1 and n = 4 directly.
methods.trap: Using the second difference itself as a. Halve it first.

methods.title: Reverse a quadratic term and test uniqueness
methods.when: You are given a term and asked for its position, or you are given too few terms to fix a rule.
methods.rule: Solve an²+bn+c = target, then retain allowed integer n. Three independent term conditions determine a general quadratic.
steps: Set the rule equal to the given term, rearrange so one side is zero, and factorise if you can.
Reject any n that is negative or not a whole number. It cannot be a position.
With only two terms, show two different quadratic rules that fit. That proves the rule is not fixed.
methods.example: Tₙ = n²+n+2 reaches 44 when (n−6)(n+7)=0, hence n = 6.
methods.check: The rejected root −7 is not a positive position; T₆ = 44.
methods.trap: Thinking that two terms are enough to fix a quadratic rule. You need three.

methods.title: Index exponential stages correctly
methods.when: Each stage multiplies the previous amount by r.
methods.rule: If stage 1 is a: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹. If stage 0 is a: Tₙ = arⁿ. For positive a,r, Tₙ₊k/Tₙ = rᵏ.
steps: Say whether the stages start at zero or at one.
Count how many times the amount has been multiplied since the starting stage.
To find the stage for a given amount, keep multiplying, or list the powers, until you reach it.
methods.example: Stage 1 = 7 and each stage triples: T₄ = 7×3³ = 189.
methods.check: Putting n = 1 must give 7, not 21.
methods.trap: Using the index n when the starting amount belongs to stage 1. Then the index must be n−1.

methods.title: Compare sequence graphs honestly
methods.when: A graph or a comparison of two rules is requested.
methods.rule: Plot (n,Tₙ) at allowed integer n; linear, quadratic and exponential growth have different difference patterns.
steps: Make a table of both rules for the same positions.
Plot both on the same axes with the same scales.
Compare the actual values. To find where one rule first passes the other, check the positions on either side.
methods.example: For n = 1,2,3,4: n² gives 1,4,9,16 while 3n gives 3,6,9,12.
methods.check: The shapes alone are not enough. At n = 3 both rules give exactly 9.
methods.trap: Joining the points, which suggests there are terms between the whole-number positions.

checks: Test every rule with n = 1 and with one other position you were given.
A position must be a whole number, usually 1 or more.
Check all the terms you were given. A rule that fits only two of them may not be the only one.
Plot sequence points separately. Do not join them unless the question says values in between exist.

challenges.title: Find the term and recover its position
challenges.question: A sequence begins 6, 13, 24, 39, 58. Assume it follows a quadratic rule. (a) Find its first and second differences. (b) Find Tₙ. (c) Calculate T₈. (d) Determine the position of the term 81, showing why any other algebraic root is rejected.
hints: Halve the second difference to get the number in front of n².
Take 2n² away from each term to find the linear part. For the last part, set your rule equal to 81 and solve.

solution.title: Take differences twice
solution.reason: The second difference is 4 every time, so the rule is quadratic. Half of 4 is 2, the number in front of n².

solution.title: Remove the quadratic part
solution.reason: Taking 2n² away from the terms leaves 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. That is n + 3, the linear part of the rule.

solution.title: Predict a term
solution.reason: Put the position 8 in for n. Square 8 first, then multiply by 2.

solution.title: Reverse the target
solution.math: 2n² + n + 3 = 81 → 2n² + n − 78 = 0 → (n − 6)(2n + 13) = 0 → n = 6 or n = −13/2; only position 6 is a positive integer
solution.reason: Factorising gives two values of n. A position must be a positive whole number, so −13/2 is rejected and n = 6.

challenges.answer: (a) First differences 7,11,15,19; second differences 4. (b) Tₙ = 2n²+n+3. (c) 139. (d) Position 6.
challenges.check: The rule reproduces all five supplied terms and T₆ = 72+6+3 = 81.

challenges.title: Two terms are not enough
challenges.question: Only the first two terms of a sequence are known: T₁ = 4 and T₂ = 9. (a) Find the unique arithmetic rule fitting them. (b) Show that Qₙ = n²+2n+1 and Rₙ = 2n²−n+3 both fit them. (c) Calculate the third term of all three rules. (d) Explain whether saying “the sequence is quadratic” determines a unique next term.
hints: In an arithmetic sequence the jump never changes, so the two terms give it at once.
Put n = 1, 2 and 3 into both quadratic rules and compare.

solution.title: Find the arithmetic rule
solution.reason: The jump from 4 to 9 is 5, and an arithmetic sequence keeps that jump all the way. So only one arithmetic rule fits.

solution.title: Check two quadratic candidates
solution.reason: Put n = 1 and n = 2 into each rule. Both give 4 and then 9, so both fit what is known.

solution.title: Compare the next values
solution.reason: All three rules agree on the first two terms and then give three different third terms.

solution.title: State the limitation
solution.math: Two known terms do not determine a general quadratic rule
solution.reason: A quadratic rule has three unknown numbers, a, b and c. Two terms give only two equations, so the rule is not pinned down.

challenges.answer: (a) 5n−1. (b) Both quadratic rules fit. (c) 14, 16 and 18 respectively. (d) No unique next term follows.
challenges.check: Qₙ−Rₙ = −(n−1)(n−2). This is zero only at n = 1 and n = 2, so the two rules agree at those positions and nowhere else.

challenges.title: An indexed branching design
challenges.question: A design has 5 branches at stage 1. Each branch is replaced by 3 new branches at every next stage. (a) Give a formula for the number at stage n. (b) Find stages 4 and 7. (c) Which stage has 1215 branches? (d) Compare the number at stage 7 with stage 3 by finding their ratio without calculating both full counts again.
hints: At stage 1 nothing has been multiplied yet. Stage n comes after n − 1 multiplications by 3.
Divide 1215 by 5, then write what is left as a power of 3.

solution.title: Count replacement rounds
solution.reason: Each new stage multiplies the count by 3. Stage n comes after n − 1 of these steps, so the index is n − 1.

solution.title: Calculate the requested stages
solution.reason: Stage 4 is 3 steps after stage 1, and stage 7 is 6 steps after it.

solution.title: Find the target position
solution.reason: Divide both sides by 5 first. Then write 243 as a power of 3 and compare the indices.

solution.title: Compare stage separation
solution.reason: Stage 7 is four steps after stage 3. Four multiplications by 3 make 3⁴ = 81, and the 5 cancels.

challenges.answer: (a) 5×3ⁿ⁻¹. (b) 135 and 3645. (c) Stage 6. (d) Ratio 81:1.
challenges.check: Stage 3 has 45 branches; 45×81 = 3645, and stage 6 has 5×243 = 1215.

challenges.title: Two growing construction patterns
challenges.question: Pattern H is a row of n hexagons made from sticks; each new hexagon shares exactly one complete side with the previous row and creates no other overlap. Pattern R is a rectangle of unit tiles with n rows and n+1 columns. Count sticks in H and tiles in R. (a) Derive a rule for each count. (b) Make a table for n = 1 to 5. (c) Find the first positive stage where R’s tile count exceeds H’s stick count. (d) Explain why R stays ahead at every later stage.
hints: A new hexagon shares one side that is already there, so it adds only 5 sticks.
Look at tiles minus sticks, n(n+1) − (5n+1). Then see how that gap changes from one stage to the next.

solution.title: Count the shared-edge pattern
solution.reason: The first hexagon needs 6 sticks. Each of the other n − 1 hexagons adds 5.

solution.title: Count the rectangle
solution.reason: A rectangle of tiles has rows times columns tiles: n rows with n + 1 in each.

solution.title: Compare the first five stages
solution.reason: Compare the two lists stage by stage. R is behind until stage 5, where 30 is more than 26.

solution.title: Check every later stage
solution.math: Dₙ = Rₙ−Hₙ = n²−4n−1; D₅ = 4; Dₙ₊₁−Dₙ = 2n−3 > 0 for n ≥ 5
solution.reason: The gap is 4 at stage 5. From then on it grows by 2n − 3 at each step, which is positive, so R stays ahead.

challenges.answer: (a) Hₙ = 5n+1 and Rₙ = n²+n. (b) Table as shown. (c) Stage 5. (d) The difference is positive at 5 and increases thereafter.
challenges.check: At n = 6, R = 42 and H = 31, giving difference 11; this is 7 more than the stage-5 difference, agreeing with 2(5)−3.

title: Functions
intro: A function is a rule that turns each number you put in into exactly one number out. You will follow rules forwards, run them backwards, and find a hidden rule from its results.

lessons.title: Follow a function machine
lessons.goal: Read the same rule three ways: in words, as a machine and as a formula.

steps.title: Choose the input
steps.text: Put four into a machine that multiplies by three and then subtracts two. Do the operations in the order given.
steps.why: Change the order and you can get a different answer. Subtracting first would give 6, not 10.

steps.title: Perform the first operation
steps.text: Multiply the input by three to get twelve. This is a halfway value, not the final output.
steps.why: The next box works on twelve, the result so far, not on the original four.

steps.title: Finish the rule
steps.text: Subtract two from twelve to get ten. Both operations are now done, so ten is the output.
steps.why: The output is ready only when every box in the machine has been used.

steps.title: Write and reverse the rule
steps.text: The same machine is described by three x minus two. To work backwards from ten, add two first and then divide by three.
steps.why: Going backwards, you undo each operation, and you undo the last one first. It is like taking off shoes before socks.

quiz.question: A rule multiplies an input by 4, then adds 3. Input 5 gives…
quiz.hint: Do the operations in the order given: multiply first, then add.
quiz.explanation: 4 × 5 + 3 = 20 + 3 = 23. Adding first gives 4 × 8 = 32, which is the usual slip.

quiz.question: The output of y = 5x − 6 is 14. What was the input?
quiz.hint: Work backwards. Undo the subtraction of 6 first, then undo the multiplication by 5.

lessons.takeaway: A function rule turns each allowed input into one output.
lessons.mistake: Stopping one step early and giving the halfway value, such as 12, as the output. Use every box in the machine before you answer.

lessons.title: Reverse a function machine
lessons.goal: Run a rule backwards to get the input back, and see why squaring needs its inputs limited before it can be reversed.

steps.title: Track the forward order
steps.text: The rule three x minus two first multiplies by three and then subtracts two. For input four, the halfway value is twelve and the output is ten.
steps.why: The reverse rule, called the inverse, has one job. It starts from the output and gets the input back.

steps.title: Undo in reverse order
steps.text: Start from an output y. Add two first, then divide the whole result by three.
steps.why: The last operation done is the first one undone.

steps.why: A function must give exactly one output for each allowed input. Reversing is only a function when that rule still holds.

quiz.question: The inverse of y = 4x + 7 is the rule…
quiz.hint: Undo the last operation first: subtract 7, then divide by 4.
quiz.explanation: y = 4x + 7 → y − 7 = 4x → x = (y − 7)/4. Rename the input to write the inverse rule f⁻¹(x) = (x − 7)/4.

quiz.question: Why does squaring on all real numbers fail to have an inverse function?
options: Different inputs can give the same output
quiz.hint: Consider inputs −3 and 3.
quiz.explanation: −3 and 3 both map to 9. Going backwards, 9 would need two outputs, and a function allows only one.

lessons.takeaway: Undo the operations in reverse order. An inverse is a function only if each output comes from just one input.
lessons.mistake: Undoing the operations in their original order. Also, f⁻¹(x) means the reverse rule, not 1 divided by f(x).

lessons.title: Domain, codomain and range
lessons.goal: Read an arrow diagram and decide whether it shows a function.

steps.title: Name the allowed inputs
steps.text: Use the input set containing negative two, zero and two. This set is the domain of the squaring rule.
steps.why: The domain says which inputs are allowed in this particular function.

steps.why: The rule counts arrows leaving each input. It puts no limit on arrows arriving at an output.

steps.text: The codomain is the set of outputs on offer: zero, four and nine. Nine is never reached. So the range, the outputs actually used, is only zero and four.
steps.why: Think of a menu and an order. The codomain is everything on the menu; the range is what was actually ordered.
