quiz.question: Which assignment fails the function test?
quiz.hint: Count arrows leaving one input.
quiz.explanation: Input 1 has two different outputs, so it is not a function.

quiz.question: For domain {−1,0,1}, rule x², and codomain {0,1,2}, the range is…
quiz.hint: Square each allowed input, then list each different result once.
quiz.explanation: The outputs are 1, 0 and 1, so the range is {0,1}.

lessons.takeaway: Every allowed input has exactly one output. The range lists only the outputs that are actually reached.
lessons.mistake: Saying it is not a function because two inputs share an output. That is allowed. Only an input with two different outputs breaks the rule.

lessons.title: Substitute the whole input
lessons.goal: Put a number or an expression into a rule, using brackets so that the whole input is used.

steps.title: Read f of an input
steps.text: Let the rule be x squared minus one. The notation f of three asks for the output when the entire input is three.
steps.why: Function brackets contain the input; they do not mean multiplication by f.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(x) = x² − 1; f(3) = 3² − 1 = 8</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Protect a negative input
steps.text: For negative three, put the negative number inside brackets before squaring. A negative times itself is positive.
steps.why: The square acts on the whole input, minus sign included. Without brackets, −3² would wrongly give −9.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = x² − 1; f(3) = 3² − 1 = 8</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(−3) = (−3)² − 1 = 8</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Protect an expression input
steps.text: For input k plus one, replace every x by the whole bracket. Expand the square using all four products.
steps.why: (k + 1)² means (k + 1)(k + 1). The two middle products add to 2k, which the wrong answer k² + 1 leaves out.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = x² − 1; f(3) = 3² − 1 = 8</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(−3) = (−3)² − 1 = 8</text><rect id="row-2" x="45" y="209" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(k + 1) = (k + 1)² − 1 = k² + 2k</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Distinguish input multiplication
steps.text: For input three k, the entire product is squared. This is different from multiplying the output by three.
steps.why: A multiplier inside the function acts before the rule; one outside acts after it.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = x² − 1; f(3) = 3² − 1 = 8</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(−3) = (−3)² − 1 = 8</text><rect id="row-2" x="45" y="209" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(k + 1) = (k + 1)² − 1 = k² + 2k</text><rect id="row-3" x="45" y="286" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(3k) = 9k² − 1; 3·f(k) = 3k² − 3</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

quiz.question: For f(x) = 2x² + 1, f(−2) is…
quiz.hint: Put −2 in brackets before squaring.

quiz.question: For g(x) = x², g(a + 2) equals…
quiz.hint: Multiply (a + 2)(a + 2).

lessons.takeaway: Replace every variable with the whole input, inside brackets.
lessons.mistake: Squaring only part of the input: writing (k + 1)² as k² + 1, or (3k)² as 3k². The correct results are k² + 2k + 1 and 9k².

lessons.title: Solve for an input from a target output
lessons.goal: When the output is given, write an equation, solve it for the input and check.

steps.title: Identify what the question gives
steps.text: Let f of x equal five x minus two. Solve f of x equals eight: eight is the required output, while x is still unknown.
steps.why: Eight is what comes out of the machine. You still have to work out what went in.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(x) = 5x − 2; f(x) = 8</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Replace the function notation by its rule
steps.text: Write five x minus two equals eight. Add two to both sides to undo the final subtraction.
steps.why: Both sides are equal. Add 2 to both and they are still equal, like adding the same weight to both pans of a balance.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = 5x − 2; f(x) = 8</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">5x − 2 = 8 → 5x = 10</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Undo the multiplication
steps.text: Divide both sides by five. The input that produces the target output is two.
steps.why: Five times x is 10. Dividing both sides by 5 undoes the multiplication and leaves x on its own.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = 5x − 2; f(x) = 8</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">5x − 2 = 8 → 5x = 10</text><rect id="row-2" x="45" y="209" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">x = 10/5 = 2</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Check the original target
steps.text: Substitute the input two into the original rule. Its output is eight, exactly as required.
steps.why: A correct input must give the target output, 8, when you put it back into the original rule.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = 5x − 2; f(x) = 8</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">5x − 2 = 8 → 5x = 10</text><rect id="row-2" x="45" y="209" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">x = 10/5 = 2</text><rect id="row-3" x="45" y="286" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(2) = 5(2) − 2 = 8</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

quiz.question: For f(x) = 3x + 4, solve f(x) = 19.
quiz.hint: Write 3x + 4 = 19, then undo the two operations.

quiz.question: For f(x) = 2x − 1, what does f(x) = 7 ask for?
quiz.hint: Notice that the unknown is inside the brackets.
quiz.explanation: The target output is 7. Solve 2x − 1 = 7 to find the input, x = 4.

lessons.takeaway: Target output → replace f(x) by its rule → solve → substitute to check.
lessons.mistake: Putting the target output into the rule as if it were the input. For f(x) = 8, do not work out f(8); solve 5x − 2 = 8.

lessons.title: Find when two functions agree
lessons.goal: Find the input where two rules give the same output by solving f(x) = g(x).

steps.title: Read both function rules
steps.text: Let f of x equal twice x minus three, and g of x equal three minus five x. Find the input at which their outputs match.
steps.why: The same input x must be used in both functions.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(x) = 2x − 3; g(x) = 3 − 5x</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Set the outputs equal
steps.text: Replace both function names with their expressions. Add five x to both sides, then add three to both sides.
steps.why: f(x) = g(x) says the two outputs are equal. Write the two rules with an equals sign between them and solve as usual.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = 2x − 3; g(x) = 3 − 5x</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">2x − 3 = 3 − 5x → 7x = 6</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Find the common input
steps.text: Divide by seven. Keep six sevenths as an exact fraction so that the check stays exact.
steps.why: An input does not have to be a whole number. A fraction is a perfectly good answer here.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = 2x − 3; g(x) = 3 − 5x</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">2x − 3 = 3 − 5x → 7x = 6</text><rect id="row-2" x="45" y="209" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">x = 6/7</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Check both outputs separately
steps.text: The first rule gives negative nine sevenths. The second rule also gives negative nine sevenths, so they agree at the same input.
steps.why: You need both outputs to match. Checking only one rule tells you nothing about the other.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = 2x − 3; g(x) = 3 − 5x</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">2x − 3 = 3 − 5x → 7x = 6</text><rect id="row-2" x="45" y="209" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">x = 6/7</text><rect id="row-3" x="45" y="286" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(6/7) = −9/7 = g(6/7)</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

quiz.question: If f(x) = 3x + 1 and g(x) = x + 7, solve f(x) = g(x).
quiz.hint: Set 3x + 1 equal to x + 7.

quiz.question: For f(x) = 2x and g(x) = x + 5, f(x) = g(x) is equivalent to…
quiz.hint: Swap f(x) for 2x and g(x) for x + 5.
quiz.explanation: The equality means 2x = x + 5. Solving gives x = 5 and common output 10.

lessons.takeaway: Same input in both rules; equate outputs and check both.
lessons.mistake: Putting different inputs into the two rules. In f(x) = g(x), the same x goes into both.

lessons.title: Keep an outside multiplier outside
lessons.goal: See the difference between k·f(3) and f(3k), then solve for k.

steps.title: Read the location of the multiplier
steps.text: Let f of x equal four x minus five. In k times f of three, the input is three and k multiplies the completed output.
steps.why: The brackets hold what goes into the machine. A multiplier outside the brackets waits, then multiplies what comes out.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">k·f(3) ≠ f(3k) in general</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Evaluate the fixed function values
steps.text: Find f of three and f of ten before solving k times f of three equals f of ten. They are seven and thirty-five.
steps.why: The inputs 3 and 10 are known numbers, so both function values can be worked out before you touch k.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">k·f(3) ≠ f(3k) in general</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(3) = 7; f(10) = 35</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Solve the resulting simple equation
steps.text: Replace the two function values by those numbers. Divide thirty-five by seven to find k.
steps.why: The outside multiplier now multiplies the known number seven.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">k·f(3) ≠ f(3k) in general</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(3) = 7; f(10) = 35</text><rect id="row-2" x="45" y="209" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">7k = 35 → k = 5</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Compare with an input multiplier
steps.text: Compare k × f(3) with f(3k). The first multiplies an OUTPUT by k. The second puts 3k into the function as its INPUT. For f(x) = 4x − 5, f(3k) = f(10) becomes 12k − 5 = 35, giving k = 10/3.
steps.why: Look at the brackets: they show what goes into the machine. A multiplier outside the brackets acts on the result.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">k·f(3) ≠ f(3k) in general</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(3) = 7; f(10) = 35</text><rect id="row-2" x="45" y="209" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">7k = 35 → k = 5</text><rect id="row-3" x="45" y="286" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">k·f(3): k = 5; f(3k): k = 10/3</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

quiz.question: For f(x) = 2x + 1, solve k·f(2) = f(7).
quiz.hint: Evaluate f(2) and f(7) before solving for k.

quiz.question: For f(x) = 2x + 1, f(3k) equals…
quiz.hint: Replace x by the whole input 3k.
quiz.explanation: f(3k) = 2(3k) + 1 = 6k + 1. By contrast, 3·f(k) = 6k + 3.

lessons.takeaway: Find what is inside the function brackets first. Work out that function value, then apply any multiplier outside.
lessons.mistake: Moving an outside multiplier inside the brackets, such as treating 3·f(2) as f(6). For f(x) = 2x + 1, 3·f(2) = 15 but f(6) = 13.

lessons.title: Recover a linear rule from points
lessons.goal: Use two input and output pairs, called couples, to find the two unknown numbers in a straight-line rule.

steps.title: Read each couple as an instruction
steps.text: Suppose a linear rule sends one to five and three to nine. Write the unknown rule as a x plus b.
steps.why: A couple records input first and output second.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(x) = ax + b; (1,5), (3,9)</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Substitute both points
steps.text: The first couple gives a plus b equals five. The second gives three a plus b equals nine.
steps.why: The same a and b must work for both couples, so each couple gives one equation.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = ax + b; (1,5), (3,9)</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">a + b = 5; 3a + b = 9</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Eliminate one coefficient
steps.text: Subtract the first equation from the second. The two b terms cancel, leaving twice a equal to four, so a is two. Put a = 2 back into a + b = 5 to get b = 3.
steps.why: Each equation contains one b. Subtracting one equation from the other removes b and leaves only a.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = ax + b; (1,5), (3,9)</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">a + b = 5; 3a + b = 9</text><rect id="row-2" x="45" y="209" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">2a = 4 → a = 2; b = 3</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Check the recovered rule
steps.text: Use the rule twice x plus three on both given inputs. It produces five and nine as required.
steps.why: Checking both couples catches a wrong number or a wrong sign.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = ax + b; (1,5), (3,9)</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">a + b = 5; 3a + b = 9</text><rect id="row-2" x="45" y="209" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">2a = 4 → a = 2; b = 3</text><rect id="row-3" x="45" y="286" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(x) = 2x + 3; f(1) = 5, f(3) = 9</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

quiz.question: For f(x) = ax + b, the point (0,4) immediately gives…
quiz.hint: Substitute x = 0.

quiz.question: A line passes through (1,4) and (3,10). Its rule is…
quiz.hint: Its output rises 6 when input rises 2.

lessons.takeaway: Each couple you know gives one equation for the unknown numbers a and b.
lessons.mistake: Swapping input and output when you substitute. In the couple (1, 5), 1 goes in for x and 5 is the output.

lessons.title: Recover a quadratic rule
lessons.goal: Use known points to find the missing numbers in a quadratic rule.

steps.title: Identify exactly what is unknown
steps.text: A quadratic rule x squared plus b x plus c passes through the points (0, −3) and (2, 3). Its leading coefficient is already one; only b and c need to be found.
steps.why: Two numbers are missing, b and c, so you need two facts. The two points supply them.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(x) = x² + bx + c</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Translate the first point
steps.text: The point (0,−3) is especially useful. Terms containing x disappear when x is zero.
steps.why: Put in zero and every term with x disappears. Only the constant c is left.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = x² + bx + c</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(0) = −3 → c = −3</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Use the second point
steps.text: The point (2,3) says the output at two is three. Substitute the known constant and solve for b.
steps.why: The same rule must fit both points.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = x² + bx + c</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(0) = −3 → c = −3</text><rect id="row-2" x="45" y="209" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">3 = 2² + 2b − 3 → 2b = 2 → b = 1</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

steps.title: Write and check the result
steps.text: The recovered rule is x squared plus x minus three. Substituting zero and two reproduces both supplied outputs.
steps.why: Check with the original points. A slip made while rearranging would not show up in the rearranged equations.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="row-0" x="45" y="55" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(x) = x² + bx + c</text><rect id="row-1" x="45" y="132" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">f(0) = −3 → c = −3</text><rect id="row-2" x="45" y="209" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#f3f6fa" stroke="#dce5eb" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#173349">3 = 2² + 2b − 3 → 2b = 2 → b = 1</text><rect id="row-3" x="45" y="286" width="670" height="62" rx="8" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75">f(x) = x² + x − 3; f(2) = 3</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Read the highlighted line, then explain why it follows.</text></svg>

quiz.question: For f(x) = x² + bx + c, f(0) = 7 gives…
quiz.hint: All terms containing x become zero.

quiz.question: For f(x) = x² + bx − 2, f(1) = 4. Find b.
quiz.hint: Substitute x = 1, then solve.

lessons.takeaway: Substitute known points, solve the coefficient equations, then check every point.
lessons.mistake: Trying to find three unknown numbers, a, b and c, from only two points. Each unknown needs its own fact.

reference.name: Function
reference.formula: Every allowed input has exactly one output
reference.note: Several inputs may share the same output.

reference.name: Couple
reference.note: First coordinate is input; second is output.

reference.name: Linear rule
reference.note: A point (p,q) gives ap + b = q.

reference.name: Quadratic rule
reference.note: Each known point gives one equation. You need as many separate facts as there are unknown numbers.

reference.name: Domain, codomain and range
reference.formula: Range = {f(x) : x is in the domain}
reference.note: The domain lists allowed inputs; the codomain is the stated target set. The range is the part actually reached.

reference.name: Inverse of a linear function
reference.note: a ≠ 0. Undo the operations in reverse order. In general, an inverse is a function only when each reached output comes from exactly one input.

reference.name: Solve a function equation
reference.formula: f(x) = k: set the rule equal to k
reference.note: For f(x) = g(x), equate the two rules at the same input. An outside multiplier, such as 3·f(x), multiplies the output.

toolkit.strategy: Mark what is inside each pair of function brackets. Evaluate known inputs first; then write an ordinary equation. Keep the stated domain attached to the rule.

methods.title: Translate and reverse a function machine
methods.when: A rule is given in words or ordered operation boxes.
methods.rule: For f(x)=ax+b with a ≠ 0: f⁻¹(x)=(x−b)/a.
steps: Write the forward operations in order.
Undo them in reverse order.
Test a forward-and-backward round trip.
methods.check: An inverse must restore the original input.
methods.trap: Using the original operation order when reversing.

methods.title: Check whether the inverse is a function
methods.when: The rule is to be reversed, especially squaring.
methods.rule: An inverse on the range is a function only when each reached output has a unique original input.
steps: Look for two inputs sharing one output.
If you find them, limit the inputs so that only one of them is allowed.
Then reverse the rule on those limited inputs.
methods.example: x² on all real x is not one-to-one; on x ≥ 0 its inverse is √x on x ≥ 0.
methods.check: Both −4 and 4 square to 16. So 16 has no single way back unless the inputs are limited.
methods.trap: Writing ±√x as though it were a single-valued inverse function.

methods.title: Test function validity and its sets
methods.when: A mapping diagram or set of couples is provided.
methods.rule: Every x in the domain has exactly one output; range = set of reached outputs ⊂ codomain.
steps: List the allowed inputs.
Count arrows leaving each input, not arrows arriving at an output.
List each reached output once. Leave out codomain values that no input reaches.
methods.example: {(−2,4),(2,4),(0,0)} is a function with range {0,4}.
methods.check: Check all domain elements are assigned and no input has two different outputs.
methods.trap: Rejecting many-to-one mappings.

methods.title: Substitute numerical or algebraic inputs
methods.when: You see f(−a), f(k+1), f(2k) or a fractional input.
methods.rule: Replace every x by the whole input u: f(u). In general f(ku) ≠ k·f(u).
steps: Bracket the entire input at every occurrence.
Apply powers and multiplication before addition.
Expand carefully and collect like terms if requested.
methods.check: Test k = 1: f(2)=−2, matching 1−1−2.
methods.trap: Dropping a negative sign or a cross term from a squared bracket.

methods.title: Solve a target output or equality of functions
methods.when: You are asked for x when f(x)=c or f(x)=g(x).
methods.rule: Replace function notation by the corresponding rules; solve in the allowed domain.
steps: Write both output expressions explicitly.
Rearrange and solve the resulting equation.
Substitute the proposed input into the original rule or both rules.
methods.example: If f(x)=4x−1 and g(x)=x+8, equal outputs give 3x=9, so x=3 and output 11.
methods.check: Both rules must give 11 at input 3.
methods.trap: Reporting the common output when the question asks for the input.

methods.title: Handle mixed function equations
methods.when: An equation contains f(k)+f(2k), or t·f(3)=g(t).
methods.rule: Expand each function value separately; evaluate fixed inputs before solving.
steps: Circle fixed inputs such as 3.
Evaluate them once and keep outside multipliers outside.
Substitute variable inputs using brackets, then collect and solve.
methods.check: The outputs are 19/3 and 35/3, totalling 18.
methods.trap: Using f(k)+f(2k)=f(3k) without a valid reason.

methods.title: Model repeated layering
methods.when: Cutting and stacking multiplies layer count by a fixed factor.
methods.rule: With n operations after the original sheet: L(n)=rⁿ; thickness H(n)=h₀rⁿ.
steps: State n=0 for the untouched sheet unless otherwise defined.
Multiply layers and thickness by the same factor per operation.
To find when a target is first reached, compare the values just before and just after it.
methods.example: A 0.2 mm sheet stacked in four pieces per round has H(3)=0.2×4³=12.8 mm.
methods.check: H(n+1)/H(n)=4; thickness divided by 0.2 equals layer count.
methods.trap: Using the cut count as the number of layers or mixing millimetres and centimetres.

methods.title: Recover a linear rule from couples
methods.when: The unknown rule is ax+b and two distinct input-output points are known.
methods.rule: a=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), x₂≠x₁; b=y₁−ax₁.
steps: Turn each couple into an equation.
Subtract to remove b or calculate the slope.
Find b and verify both original couples.
methods.example: Points (2,9),(5,21) give a=4, b=1, hence f(x)=4x+1.
methods.check: Both outputs are reproduced exactly.
methods.trap: Swapping input and output during substitution.

methods.title: Recover and interpret a quadratic
methods.when: Some coefficients in ax²+bx+c are unknown; intercepts or couples are supplied.
methods.rule: f(0)=c; an x-intercept solves f(x)=0. General a,b,c need three independent conditions unless a coefficient is already known.
steps: Translate each point into a coefficient equation.
Use x=0 immediately if available.
Solve, then factorise to find roots when possible; the sign of a gives the opening direction.
methods.example: For f(x)=−x²+bx+c with (0,6),(2,8), c=6 and b=3.
methods.check: Substitution gives f(2)=−4+6+6=8.
methods.trap: Assuming a downward parabola cannot have positive outputs.

checks: Use the entire input in brackets before squaring or expanding.
An outside multiplier acts on the output; it does not automatically move inside the input.
A function allows shared outputs but exactly one output for each allowed input.
Check every recovered coefficient against all supplied points.
In a layering model, say which stage counts as n = 0 and keep the thickness in one unit, millimetres or centimetres.

challenges.title: Two different roles for an unknown
challenges.question: Let f(x)=3x−2 and g(x)=14−2x, with real inputs. (a) Find f(−2) and f(3). (b) Solve f(k)+f(2k)=32. (c) Solve t·f(3)=g(t). (d) Check part (c) by evaluating its two sides separately.
hints: Evaluate f(3) once: its input is fixed even though t is unknown.
For part (b), write (3k−2)+(6k−2)=32. For part (c), use 7t=14−2t.

solution.title: Evaluate the fixed inputs
solution.reason: Put the whole input, sign included, into the rule.

solution.title: Expand the sum
solution.reason: f(k) and f(2k) each bring their own −2, so the constants add to −4.

solution.title: Keep the multiplier outside
solution.reason: t multiplies the output f(3), not the input 3.

solution.title: Check the original equality
solution.reason: Both sides have the same exact value.

challenges.answer: (a) −8 and 7. (b) k=4. (c) t=14/9. (d) Both sides are 98/9.
challenges.check: For part (b), f(4)+f(8)=10+22=32. For part (c), the separate evaluations agree.

challenges.title: Diagnose a mapping, then reverse it
challenges.question: Let D={−3,−1,1,3} and codomain C={0,1,9,16}. The rule is f(x)=x². (a) Write all couples and the range. (b) Explain why the shared outputs do not prevent f being a function. (c) Explain why its reverse is not a function on the whole range. Give a two-element restriction of D that makes the inverse a function and write that inverse’s couples. (d) If the arrow 1→1 is replaced by 1→16, is the new mapping still a function? Is it still the rule x² on D?
hints: Count arrows leaving each input, not the arrows arriving at each output.
For an inverse, choose just one original input for each reached output.

solution.title: List the complete mapping
solution.reason: Unused codomain values 0 and 16 are not in the range.

solution.title: Apply the function test
solution.math: Each of the four inputs has exactly one output
solution.reason: Several inputs may share a reached output.

solution.title: Repair the inverse domain
solution.reason: The unrestricted reverse sends 1 to both −1 and 1, so it is not single-valued.

solution.title: Separate a mapping from a specified rule
solution.math: The changed mapping is a function, but no longer x² on D
solution.reason: There is still exactly one output per input, but 1² is 1 rather than 16.

challenges.answer: (a) Couples above; range {1,9}. (b) One output per input. (c) Not invertible without restriction; {1,3} is one valid choice. (d) Still a function, but not the squaring rule.
challenges.check: The restricted inverse has exactly one output for each of its inputs 1 and 9, and composing the two maps returns 1 and 3.

challenges.title: A downward quadratic from two conditions
challenges.question: A function has rule f(x)=−x²+bx+c and passes through (0,8) and (3,5). (a) Find b and c. (b) Find both x-intercepts and the y-intercept. (c) Show that f(x)=9−(x−1)² and use this to find its greatest output. (d) Solve f(x)=8. Inputs are all real numbers.
hints: The point with input zero reveals c immediately.
After finding b, factorise −x²+2x+8 or complete the square.

solution.title: Recover the coefficients
solution.math: c = 8 and −3² + 3b + c = 5 → c = 8 and −9 + 3b + 8 = 5 → c = 8 and b = 2
solution.reason: Every supplied couple must satisfy the same rule.

solution.reason: x-axis points have output zero; y-axis points have input zero.

solution.title: Expose the maximum
solution.reason: A square is never negative. Taking it away from 9 can only lower the output, so 9 is the greatest.

solution.reason: A quadratic can reach the same output at two different inputs.

challenges.check: The roots are symmetric about x=1; f(3)=−9+6+8=5 verifies the second supplied point.

challenges.title: Cut, stack and compare thickness
challenges.question: A sheet is 0.12 mm thick. In each operation, the whole current stack is cut into three equal pieces and those pieces are stacked, with no air gaps or loss. Let n be the number of operations, so n=0 is the original sheet. (a) Write functions for the layer count L(n) and thickness H(n). (b) Find H(4) in millimetres and centimetres. (c) Find H(6)/H(2) without first evaluating both thicknesses. (d) What is the least whole number of operations making the stack at least 100 mm thick?
hints: Each operation triples both layers and thickness.
For the threshold, compare n=6 and n=7; 3⁶=729 and 3⁷=2187.

solution.title: State the indexed functions
solution.reason: At n = 0 nothing has been cut yet, so there is one layer: 3⁰ = 1.

solution.title: Evaluate and convert
solution.reason: Ten millimetres equal one centimetre.

solution.title: Use the gap in operation counts
solution.reason: The starting thickness cancels in the ratio.

solution.title: Bracket the threshold
solution.reason: Each operation makes the stack thicker. Six operations fall short and seven are enough, so the answer is 7.

challenges.answer: (a) L(n)=3ⁿ, H(n)=0.12×3ⁿ mm. (b) 9.72 mm=0.972 cm. (c) 81. (d) 7 operations.
challenges.check: H(0)=0.12 mm returns the original sheet; 262.44/87.48=3 checks the final step.

title: Drawing and Interpreting Real-life Graphs
intro: A graph tells a story. Read what each axis measures first, then say what the shape of the line means.

lessons.title: Read a journey graph
lessons.goal: Read a journey graph: when the traveller moves away, stops and comes back, and how far they go in total.

steps.title: Read the axis labels first
steps.text: The horizontal axis is time in hours. The vertical axis is distance from home in kilometres, not the total distance travelled.
steps.why: The same line means different things on different axes, so read the labels and units first.

steps.why: A straight segment means the speed stays the same along it.

steps.text: From hour one to hour two, the distance from home stays at ten kilometres. The traveller is stopped for one hour.
steps.why: Time passes but the distance does not change, so the speed is zero.

steps.title: Read the return without losing distance
steps.text: The line comes back to zero because the traveller returns home. The outward journey still counts. Add 10 km out and 10 km back: 20 km travelled. The return takes 2 hours, so its speed is 5 km/h.
steps.why: Distance from home is a position. Distance travelled counts every part of the journey, in either direction.

quiz.question: A distance-from-home graph slopes down. This means…
options: The traveller is returning towards home
quiz.hint: Distance from home is decreasing as time increases.
quiz.explanation: The distance from home is getting smaller, so the traveller is coming back. Speed is never negative: use the size of the slope and ignore its sign.

quiz.question: A traveller goes 6 km out and 6 km back in 3 hours. Average speed is…
quiz.hint: Add the distance out and the distance back, then divide by the total time.
quiz.explanation: Total distance is 12 km, so average speed = 12/3 = 4 km/h. The traveller ends at home, but 0 km/h would ignore the 12 km travelled.

lessons.takeaway: Distance from home is where you are. Total distance travelled is how far you have gone, out and back.
lessons.mistake: Reading the final height of the graph as the total distance. A traveller who is back home is at 0 km but may have travelled 20 km.

lessons.title: Test direct proportion
lessons.goal: Tell from a table, a graph or a rule whether one quantity is directly proportional to another.

steps.title: Compare pairs of values
steps.text: Suppose each training bib costs €3. Then 1, 2 or 4 bibs cost €3, €6 or €12.
steps.why: The price of one bib never changes, so the cost is always 3 times the number of bibs.

steps.title: Check the constant ratio
steps.text: Divide each cost by its number of bibs. The answer is always €3 per bib.
steps.why: If y = kx, then y divided by x is always the same number k.

quiz.question: Which rule represents direct proportion?
quiz.hint: Look for y = kx with no added constant.
quiz.explanation: y = 5x has constant ratio y/x = 5 and passes through the origin. y = 5x + 2 is also a straight line, but it misses the origin.

quiz.question: If y is directly proportional to x and y = 18 when x = 6, then y at x = 10 is…
quiz.hint: First find y ÷ x from the pair you know.
quiz.explanation: k = 18/6 = 3, so y = 3 × 10 = 30. Adding 4 to get 22 is the usual slip: in direct proportion you multiply, you do not add.

lessons.takeaway: Direct proportion means y ÷ x is always the same number, and the graph is a straight line through (0, 0).
lessons.mistake: Thinking every straight-line graph shows direct proportion. It must also pass through (0, 0).

lessons.title: Turn a graph into a story
lessons.goal: Explain why a graph gets steeper or flatter by picturing what is really happening.

steps.title: Identify what is being measured
steps.text: Water pours into two containers at the same steady rate: the same volume every second. The graph shows the height of the water against time.
steps.why: The same amount of water each second does not always raise the level by the same height.

steps.title: Predict the straight-sided container
steps.text: The straight-sided container is the same width all the way up. Each equal amount of water raises the level by the same height.
steps.why: The same width at every level means the same rise every second, so the graph is a straight line.
steps.math: constant area → constant slope of the height graph

steps.title: Predict a container that widens
steps.text: As the level reaches a wider part, the same water spreads over a bigger area. The height rises more slowly, so the graph gets less steep.
steps.why: Picture a cup of water poured into a wide basin: it barely raises the level.

steps.title: Explain before calculating
steps.text: A container that gets narrower does the opposite: the graph gets steeper. Always link the steepness of a graph to what its axes measure.
steps.why: The container explains the shape. Without the axis labels, the same curve could tell many stories.

quiz.question: Water enters a container at a steady rate. If the container widens upwards, the height-time graph…
quiz.hint: The same volume spreads across a larger area.
quiz.explanation: As the container gets wider, the level rises more slowly, so the graph gets less steep.

quiz.question: A straight rising height-time graph suggests…
options: A container of the same width all the way up, filled at a steady rate
A container that narrows towards the top
quiz.hint: A straight line means the height rises by the same amount in every equal time.
quiz.explanation: With a steady inflow, a container of the same width at every level rises by the same height each second. A container that narrows towards the top would give a graph that gets steeper.

lessons.takeaway: Explain a slope by what is happening, not just by how the line looks.
lessons.mistake: Thinking a steady flow always gives a steady rise in height. In a wider part the level rises more slowly.

reference.name: Journey graph
reference.formula: slope = change in distance from start / change in time
reference.note: A negative slope means returning towards the start.

reference.name: Direct proportion
reference.note: A straight line through the origin; y/x is constant for x ≠ 0.

reference.name: Steady filling
reference.formula: rate of height rise = volume flow / cross-sectional area
reference.note: A wider cross-section makes the water level rise more slowly.

toolkit.strategy: Read each axis and its unit before you say what a line means. Split a journey into time intervals, and decide which rule applies in each interval before solving for a meeting or a separation.

methods.title: Read a piecewise journey
methods.when: A position or distance-from-start graph has several straight segments.
methods.rule: On a segment: signed rate = change in position ÷ change in time; speed is the size of this rate with its sign ignored.
steps: Write the coordinates of each corner.
Label each segment as moving away, resting or returning, from its slope.
Work out each speed, using the same time unit throughout.
methods.example: Moving from 2 km to 8 km in 15 min gives speed 6/(15/60)=24 km/h.
methods.check: Speed × time equals the size of the position change.
methods.trap: Treating a flat graph at 8 km as movement at 8 km/h.

methods.title: Separate position, path length and average speed
methods.when: A traveller rests or returns, or begins away from zero.
methods.rule: Total distance = add up the sizes of all the position changes, ignoring signs; average speed = total distance ÷ full elapsed time.
steps: Keep the starting position: do not quietly reset it to zero.
Add the lengths of all the parts travelled.
Include rests in the overall average speed; leave them out only if the question asks for the average while moving.
methods.example: Positions 4→11→11→2 give total distance 7+0+9=16 km, not 2 km.
methods.check: A complete return ends at distance zero from the start but still has a positive total distance.
methods.trap: Calling final position the total distance.

methods.title: Compare two travellers on the same axes
methods.when: Two travellers are graphed on the same axes, on the same road and the same clock.
methods.rule: Meeting: pA(t)=pB(t); separation: the difference between pA(t) and pB(t), taken as a positive number, on the same line.
steps: List every time at which either traveller changes speed or direction.
Use the correct segment rule for each traveller on each shared interval.
Set the positions equal to find a meeting, then test that the time lies inside the interval.
For a separation, find both positions at the same time.
methods.example: pA=3t and pB=2+t meet at t=1 with position 3, if that time lies in both intervals.
methods.check: Substitute the meeting time into both rules.
methods.trap: Accepting an intersection outside its segment.

methods.title: Build a line segment from its endpoints
methods.when: You need an exact value between two plotted corners.
methods.rule: p=p₁+[(p₂−p₁)/(t₂−t₁)](t−t₁), for t₁≤t≤t₂.
steps: Find the slope and keep its sign.
Start from a known end and add slope × time passed since that end.
Write beside the rule the times for which it holds.
methods.check: The expression returns 6 at t=10 and 2 at t=30.
methods.trap: Assuming every segment begins at the origin.

methods.title: Test and use direct proportion
methods.when: You must decide whether one quantity is always the same multiple of another.
methods.rule: y=kx; y/x=k for x≠0; graph passes through (0,0).
steps: Test the ratio y/x for every data point with x not zero.
Check that an input of zero gives an output of zero.
Use k to calculate a value, or divide by k to work backwards.
methods.example: If 4 units cost €14 with no fee, k=3.5 and 10 units cost €35.
methods.check: A zero purchase costs zero in this model.
methods.trap: Calling y=3.5x+6 directly proportional because it is straight.

methods.title: Compare fixed-fee and proportional models
methods.when: A table goes up in equal steps but includes a starting charge.
methods.rule: Linear: y=mx+c; directly proportional only when c=0.
steps: Find the rate m from two points.
Find the fixed fee c using one point.
Set two models equal to find where they cost the same, then compare the costs on each side of that point.
methods.example: Costs €8 at 1 h and €14 at 3 h give C=3h+5, not direct proportion.
methods.check: Use any remaining table rows to test the model.
methods.trap: Scaling a total price while ignoring its fixed fee.

methods.title: Predict water-height graph steepness
methods.when: Water pours in at a steady rate into a container whose width changes.
methods.rule: Height rate = Q/A, where Q is the volume flow rate and A is the cross-sectional area at that level; a larger area gives a smaller height rate.
steps: Keep volume flow and height rise apart: they are different quantities.
Decide whether the container keeps the same width, widens or narrows.
Draw a rising graph whose slope stays constant, decreases or increases to match.
methods.example: An upper cross-section one quarter of the lower area has four times the height-rise rate.
methods.check: Where the width is constant, area × rise in height equals the volume that came in.
methods.trap: Assuming constant flow always gives a straight height-time graph.

methods.title: Construct a piecewise filling graph
methods.when: A container is made of straight-sided parts stacked on top of each other.
methods.rule: Time in each part = part volume ÷ flow rate Q; cumulative height and time give graph corners.
steps: Find how much each part holds.
Divide each volume by the steady flow to get its filling time.
Add up the times and heights to get the corners, then join the corners with straight lines.
methods.example: Areas 20 cm² for 5 cm and 10 cm² for 4 cm, at 10 cm³/s, give (0,0),(10,5),(14,9).
methods.check: 14 s gives incoming volume 140 cm³, matching the two capacities.
methods.trap: Restarting time when the width changes.

checks: A falling position graph means the traveller is returning. It does not mean a negative total distance.
Speed is the size of a segment’s slope, with the sign ignored; convert minutes to hours if required.
Only accept a meeting time that lies inside both time intervals.
Total journey distance adds the sizes of all the position changes; average speed uses the whole time stated.
A direct-proportion graph must pass through the origin.

challenges.title: Two people on one straight road
challenges.question: A and B move along the same straight road; position is in kilometres from a fixed origin and time in minutes. Join each person’s points by straight segments. A: (0,0),(12,3),(18,3),(30,0). B: (0,1),(20,3),(30,3). (a) State each person’s rest interval and moving speed(s) in km/h. (b) Find every meeting time during 0≤t≤30. (c) Find their separation at t=24. (d) Find each person’s total distance.
hints: Split time at every corner of either graph: 0,12,18,20,30.
Initially pA=t/4 and pB=1+t/10. On A’s return pA=7.5−t/4.

solution.title: Find speeds and rests
solution.math: A rests from 12 to 18 min; moving speed 3/(12/60)=15 km/h both ways. B rests from 20 to 30 min; moving speed 2/(20/60)=6 km/h.
solution.reason: Speed uses the size of the position change. During a rest the position does not change.

solution.title: Find the first meeting
solution.reason: 20/3 min is about 6.7 min, which lies inside the first shared interval, 0 to 12 min.

solution.title: Test later intervals
solution.reason: This second meeting lies between 18 and 20 min, while A is returning. They do not meet during A’s rest or after t=20.

solution.title: Find the separation
solution.reason: Compare the two positions at the same time, t = 24.

solution.title: Add path lengths
solution.reason: Coming back adds to the distance travelled, even though the position gets smaller.

challenges.answer: (a) A: 12 to 18 min rest, 15 km/h moving; B: 20 to 30 min rest, 6 km/h moving. (b) 20/3 min and 130/7 min. (c) 1.5 km. (d) A 6 km; B 2 km.
challenges.check: At 130/7 minutes both rules give 20/7 km. Each shared interval has at most one crossing because both rules are linear.
