quiz.question: Can lengths 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm form a triangle?
options: Yes, if the 6 cm side is drawn first
quiz.hint: Lay the 6 cm side flat. Can the 2 cm and 3 cm sides reach each other above it?
quiz.explanation: 2 + 3 = 5, which is less than 6, so they cannot close into a triangle.

quiz.question: In an SSS construction, the third vertex is located by…
options: An arc from the midpoint of the base
The intersection of two compass arcs
Drawing a vertical line from the midpoint only
A protractor reading at each base endpoint
quiz.hint: The third corner must be the right distance from A and the right distance from B.
quiz.explanation: One arc fixes distance from A and another fixes distance from B. Their intersection locates C.

lessons.takeaway: Draw the base first. Then cross an arc from each end, each with its own side length as the compass opening.
lessons.mistake: Using the same compass opening for both arcs when the two sides are different lengths. Reset the compass for each side.

lessons.title: Construct from two sides and their included angle
lessons.goal: Draw a triangle when you know two sides and the angle between them. This is called SAS, for side, angle, side.

steps.title: Identify the included angle
steps.text: The triangle has AB of six centimetres, AC of four centimetres and an angle of sixty degrees at A. Both known sides start at A, so the angle sits between them.
steps.why: The angle between the two given sides is called the included angle. This method only works with that angle.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="base" x1="200" y1="300" x2="560" y2="300" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text x="380" y="337" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349">AB = 6 cm</text><text x="180" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">A</text><text x="580" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">B</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Draw the base and angle ray
steps.text: Draw AB six centimetres long. At A, draw a line that makes sixty degrees with AB. Use a protractor unless the question asks for a compass.
steps.why: The side AC must lie along this line, because the angle at A is sixty degrees.
steps.math: draw ray AC at 60° to AB

steps.title: Locate the second side length
steps.text: Measure four centimetres from A along the new line, or cross it with a compass arc of radius four centimetres centred at A. Mark the point C.
steps.why: You know which way C lies from A and how far. That fixes exactly one point.

steps.title: Join the final side
steps.text: Join C to B to finish the triangle. You did not need the length of the third side. The two sides and the angle between them fixed it.
steps.why: Two sides and the included angle, written SAS, fix the triangle. The only other choice is its mirror image.

quiz.question: In SAS, the given angle must be…
quiz.hint: Included means lying between the two given sides.
quiz.explanation: The included angle is the one where the two given sides meet.

quiz.question: After drawing one given side and the line for the included angle, how is the third vertex fixed?
options: By the second given side length
By an arc from the far endpoint of the base
quiz.hint: The third corner is on the angle line. How far along is it?
quiz.explanation: Measure the second given side along the angle line, starting from the corner where the angle is.

lessons.takeaway: Draw one side, draw the angle at its end, mark the second side along the new line, then join up.
lessons.mistake: Drawing the angle at the wrong end of the base. It goes at the corner where the two given sides meet.

lessons.title: Construct from a side and two angles
lessons.goal: Draw a triangle when you know one side and the angle at each end of it. This is called ASA, for angle, side, angle.

steps.title: Read the endpoint information
steps.text: Draw the base AB six centimetres long. The angle at A is fifty degrees and the angle at B is sixty degrees.
steps.why: Each angle belongs to one end of the base. Swapping them gives a different drawing.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="base" x1="180" y1="305" x2="540" y2="305" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text x="360" y="342" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349">AB = 6 cm</text><text x="160" y="330" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">A</text><text x="560" y="330" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">B</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Draw the first angle ray
steps.text: At A, draw a line that makes fifty degrees with AB, above the base.
steps.why: The third corner C must be somewhere on this line.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="base" x1="180" y1="305" x2="540" y2="305" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text x="360" y="342" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349">AB = 6 cm</text><line id="ray-a" x1="180" y1="305" x2="393.26265556273717" y2="50.8434640669264" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><path id="angle-a" d="M 221.1384070199385 255.97315564038541 A 64 64 0 0 1 244.0 305.0" fill="none" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text x="278" y="280" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba">50°</text><text x="160" y="330" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">A</text><text x="560" y="330" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">B</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Draw the second ray inward
steps.text: At B, measure sixty degrees from the base, turning in towards A. Draw this line above the base too. The two lines meet at C.
steps.why: Each line gives one of the angles. The point where they cross gives both angles at once.
steps.math: ray from B at 60° to BA

steps.title: Check the remaining angle
steps.text: The three angles of a triangle add to one hundred and eighty degrees. So the angle at C should be seventy degrees. Measure it to check your drawing.
steps.why: If the angle at C is not close to seventy degrees, one of the other two angles was drawn wrongly.

quiz.question: A triangle has angles 42° and 68°. Its third angle is…
quiz.hint: Subtract both known angles from 180°.

quiz.question: At endpoint B, the inside angle must be measured from…
options: The ray BA pointing towards A
quiz.hint: The angle must be inside the triangle. Which way does the base run from B?
quiz.explanation: Measure from the base, going from B back towards A, and turn into the triangle. Measuring from the line continued past B gives the outside angle instead.

lessons.takeaway: Draw the base, then a line at the correct angle from each end. The lines cross at the third corner.
lessons.mistake: At B, measuring the angle from the base continued past B. That gives the angle outside the triangle.

lessons.title: Construct a right-angled triangle
lessons.goal: Draw a right-angled triangle from its longest side, called the hypotenuse, and one other side. Or from one side and one of the smaller angles.

steps.title: Separate the hypotenuse from the given perpendicular side
steps.text: The triangle has a right angle at A, side AB of eight centimetres and hypotenuse BC of ten centimetres.
steps.why: The hypotenuse is the side facing the right angle. The right angle is at A, so the hypotenuse is BC.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="base" x1="180" y1="300" x2="500" y2="300" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text x="340" y="337" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349">AB = 8 cm</text><text x="160" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">A</text><text x="520" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">B</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Construct the right-angle ray
steps.text: Draw AB eight centimetres long. Construct a perpendicular at A. The third corner C must be somewhere on that perpendicular.
steps.why: Any point on the perpendicular makes a right angle at A.

steps.title: Use the hypotenuse as a compass radius
steps.text: Set the compass to ten centimetres. Put the point on B and draw an arc that crosses the perpendicular. The crossing point is C.
steps.why: Every point on the arc is ten centimetres from B. C is the one that is also on the perpendicular.

steps.title: Join and check with Pythagoras
steps.text: Join B to C. Check: the third side should be six centimetres, because 10² − 8² = 36. If you are given an angle at B instead of the hypotenuse, draw a line from B at that angle. C is where it meets the perpendicular.
steps.why: Pythagoras checks the drawing. If the side you are given is the hypotenuse BC, draw BC, then the angle at B, then drop a perpendicular from C onto that line.

quiz.question: You have drawn the known shorter side and the perpendicular at one end of it. From the other end, the compass opening for the arc is…
quiz.hint: How far is the third corner from that end of the known side?
quiz.explanation: The hypotenuse joins that end to the third corner. So the compass opening is the given hypotenuse length.

quiz.question: A right-angled triangle has its right angle at A, AB = 6 cm and ∠B = 40°. After drawing AB and the perpendicular at A, how is C found?
options: An arc of radius 6 cm centred at B
A ray from B at 40° to AB, meeting the perpendicular
An arc of radius 6 cm centred at A
A ray from A at 40° to AB
quiz.hint: The given angle is at B. Where must the new line start?
quiz.explanation: The 40° angle is at B, so draw a line from B at 40° to AB. The right angle is at A, so C is also on the perpendicular. C is where the two lines cross.

lessons.takeaway: Draw the known side and construct the right angle at one end. Then find the third corner with a hypotenuse arc, or an angle line, from the other end.
lessons.mistake: Setting the compass to the shorter side for the arc from B. That arc uses the hypotenuse, the longest side.

lessons.title: Construct a rectangle
lessons.goal: Draw a rectangle from its length and width, using two perpendiculars of equal height.

steps.title: Draw the chosen base
steps.text: Construct a rectangle eight centimetres long and four centimetres wide. Draw the eight-centimetre base AB.
steps.why: A rectangle has four right angles and equal opposite sides.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="base" x1="190" y1="300" x2="570" y2="300" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text x="380" y="337" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349">8 cm</text><text x="170" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">A</text><text x="590" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">B</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Construct perpendiculars at both ends
steps.text: Construct a perpendicular at A and another at B. Both go up from the base, on the same side of AB.
steps.why: Both lines are at right angles to AB, so they are parallel to each other.

steps.title: Mark equal widths
steps.text: Set the compass to four centimetres. Mark D on the perpendicular from A and C on the perpendicular from B. Keep the same opening for both.
steps.why: D and C are the same height above the base, so the top side will be parallel to AB.

steps.title: Join the final side and check
steps.text: Join D to C. Check with a ruler that DC is eight centimetres and that the two diagonals are equal. A shape that only looks like a rectangle may be slightly tilted.
steps.why: Right angles at A and B and two equal heights are enough to make ABCD a rectangle.
steps.math: AB ∥ DC; AD ∥ BC; AC = BD

quiz.question: A rectangle’s diagonals are…
options: Always equal to its shorter side
quiz.hint: This holds for every rectangle, not only a square.
quiz.explanation: Both diagonals have length √(length² + width²), so they are equal.

quiz.question: A rectangle is 8 cm by 4 cm. Its perimeter is…
quiz.hint: Add all four side lengths.
quiz.explanation: There are two sides of 8 cm and two sides of 4 cm. 2 × (8 + 4) = 24 cm.

lessons.takeaway: Draw the base, a perpendicular at each end, equal heights on both, then join the top and check.
lessons.mistake: Drawing the second perpendicular below the base when the first goes above it. Both must be on the same side.

reference.name: Translation
reference.note: Every point moves by the same vector (a,b).

reference.name: Axial symmetry, or reflection, in the axes
reference.note: Each point and its image are equally far from the mirror line.

reference.name: Central symmetry
reference.note: A half-turn. The centre is the midpoint of each point and its image.

reference.name: Rotation about origin
reference.note: State centre, angle and direction.

reference.name: Construct a bisector
reference.formula: Equal-radius arcs locate equally distant points
reference.note: Do not change the compass opening between matched arcs.

reference.name: Triangle data
reference.note: RHS uses a right angle, hypotenuse and one other side; a right-angled triangle can also be built from one side and one acute angle.

toolkit.strategy: For a transformation, follow each named point to its image and state every fact the transformation needs. For a construction, start from what you are given, follow the steps in order, leave the arcs on the page and say why the result is right.

methods.title: Translate a point, segment or triangle
methods.when: A shape slides without turning. Every point moves the same distance in the same direction.
methods.rule: Vector (a,b): (x,y)↦(x+a,y+b); image−original=(a,b) for every vertex.
steps: Find how far one point moves across and up to reach its image.
Move every other vertex by the same vector.
Join the image vertices in the same order as the original.
methods.example: Translation (4,−2) maps (−1,3) to (3,1) and (2,5) to (6,3).
methods.check: Image minus original gives the same vector for every vertex.
methods.trap: Finding the vector from one vertex, then moving another vertex by a different amount.

methods.title: Reflect in a specified line
methods.when: A shape is flipped over a mirror line, or you must find the mirror line between a shape and its image.
methods.rule: In x=a: (x,y)↦(2a−x,y); in y=b: (x,y)↦(x,2b−y); in y=x: (y,x); in y=−x: (−y,−x).
steps: Join each point to its image and find the midpoint.
Check that the mirror passes through every midpoint, at right angles to each joining line.
Leave any point on the mirror where it is.
methods.example: Reflection in x=2 maps (5,1) to (−1,1).
methods.check: The midpoint of (5,1) and (−1,1) is (2,1), which is on the line x = 2.
methods.trap: Accepting a mirror line that works for one point and its image but fails for the other vertices.

methods.title: Central and axial symmetry
methods.when: You must decide whether a shape has a centre of symmetry, an axis of symmetry, both or neither.
methods.rule: Central symmetry about (h,k): (x,y)↦(2h−x,2k−y). Axial symmetry means reflection in a line maps the entire shape to itself.
steps: Test every vertex, not just one.
For a centre of symmetry, check that the centre is the midpoint of every point and its partner.
For an axis of symmetry, check that one line is the perpendicular bisector for every point and its partner.
methods.example: Every parallelogram has a centre of symmetry where its diagonals cross. A slanted parallelogram has no axis of symmetry.
methods.check: Fold a slanted parallelogram along any line through its centre. The two halves do not match, so it has no axis.
methods.trap: Treating central symmetry as a reflection in some line through the centre. It is a half-turn about a point.

methods.title: Rotate with complete information
methods.when: A shape turns about a fixed point.
methods.rule: About origin: 90° anticlockwise (−y,x), 90° clockwise (y,−x), 180° (−x,−y). About (h,k), translate to the origin, rotate, then translate back.
steps: State the centre, the angle and the direction.
Measure the distance from the centre to the point and keep it the same.
Turn every point through the same angle.
For 180°, the centre is the midpoint of each point and its image.
methods.example: About (2,1), a 90° anticlockwise turn sends (5,1) to (2,4).
methods.check: Both points are 3 units from (2,1). One is straight to the right of the centre and its image is straight above it.
methods.trap: Saying only “a rotation”, or turning about the wrong centre.

methods.title: Describe and distinguish full transformations
methods.when: You are given a shape and its image and must say exactly which transformation was used.
methods.rule: Translation needs a vector; reflection needs a mirror line; rotation needs centre, angle and direction. An ordered mapping fixes the vertex correspondence.
steps: Write down at least two points and their images.
Test your transformation on every vertex.
Give every fact needed: the vector, the mirror line, or the centre, angle and direction.
If several transformations fit one point, use the other points to choose between them.
methods.example: In a parallelogram ABCD, a half-turn about the point where the diagonals cross maps A to C and B to D.
methods.check: The centre must be the midpoint of both AC and BD.
methods.trap: Deciding from one point and its image. One matching point does not show that the whole shape maps.

methods.title: Perpendicular bisector of a segment
methods.when: You need the midpoint of AB, a line at right angles through it, or the points equally far from A and B.
methods.rule: Use equal radius r>AB/2 from A and B; joining the two intersections gives the perpendicular bisector.
steps: Open the compass to more than half of AB.
From A, draw arcs above and below the segment.
Without changing the opening, draw arcs from B to cross them at P and Q.
Draw the line PQ with a straight edge. It crosses AB at the midpoint M.
methods.example: For AB = 8 cm, an opening of 5 cm works. The bisector crosses AB 4 cm from each end.
methods.check: PA = PB and QA = QB, so P and Q are both equally far from A and B. Measure: AM = MB, and the angle at M is 90°.
methods.trap: Changing the compass opening between A and B.

methods.title: Bisect a given angle
methods.when: You must split a given angle into two equal angles.
methods.rule: From vertex V mark VA=VB; find P with PA=PB using equal arcs; ray VP bisects ∠AVB.
steps: Put the compass point on the vertex V and draw one arc across both arms, at A and B.
From A and from B, draw equal arcs that cross inside the angle at P.
Join V to P with a straight edge.
Leave both sets of arcs on the page.
methods.example: Bisecting a given 70° angle produces 35° and 35°; bisecting one half again gives 17.5°.
methods.check: Triangles VAP and VBP have VA = VB, AP = BP and a shared side VP. They are congruent by SSS, so the two angles at V are equal.
methods.trap: Joining A to B instead of V to P.

methods.title: Perpendicular at a point on a line
methods.when: You need a right angle at a given point P on a line.
methods.rule: Mark PA=PB on opposite sides; a point Q with QA=QB gives PQ perpendicular to AB.
steps: Put the compass point on P and mark A and B on the line, one on each side.
Open the compass wider. From A and from B, draw equal arcs that cross at Q, off the line.
Join P to Q.
methods.example: If PA = PB = 3 cm, equal arcs of radius 4 cm from A and B cross off the line at Q.
methods.check: P and Q are both on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
methods.trap: Placing A and B at unequal distances from P.

methods.title: Perpendicular from a point off a line
methods.when: You need a line at right angles to a given line, through a point P that is not on it.
methods.rule: One circle centred at P cuts the line at A,B with PA=PB; a second equal-distance point Q fixes their bisector PQ.
steps: Put the compass point on P and draw an arc wide enough to cut the line twice, at A and B.
From A and from B, draw equal arcs that cross at Q, on the other side of the line from P.
Draw PQ with a straight edge.
Mark the point where PQ meets the line. It is the foot of the perpendicular.
methods.example: PA = PB and QA = QB, so PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB.
methods.check: PQ should pass through P and meet the line at 90°.
methods.trap: Joining P to A or to B instead of to Q, where the two equal arcs cross.

methods.title: Parallel through a given outside point
methods.when: You need a line through a point P that is parallel to a given line l.
methods.rule: Two distinct lines in the same plane perpendicular to the same line are parallel.
steps: Drop a perpendicular m from P to l, using the construction for a point off the line.
At P, construct a perpendicular n to m, using equal marks and crossing arcs.
Draw and label n. It passes through P.
methods.example: l⊥m and n⊥m give l∥n.
methods.check: The new line must pass through P, and both right angles must be accurate.
methods.trap: Drawing a line that looks parallel but misses the given point.

methods.title: Divide a segment into equal parts
methods.when: You must cut AB into a number of equal parts without measuring it.
methods.rule: Equal steps on an auxiliary ray transfer to equal parts of AB through parallel lines; n is a positive integer.
steps: Draw a sloping helper line from A.
Step off n equal compass lengths along it. Call the last mark C.
Join C to B.
Through each earlier mark, construct a line parallel to CB.
These parallels cut AB at the dividing points.
methods.example: For six parts, mark six equal steps, join the sixth mark to B, and draw five parallels.
methods.check: Measure the parts of AB with a ruler. They should all be equal.
methods.trap: Marking one step too few. For n parts you need n steps on the helper line.

methods.title: Construct a triangle from SSS
methods.when: You are given all three side lengths.
methods.rule: Each side must be positive; the two shorter lengths must sum to more than the longest.
steps: Draw one side, AB, with a ruler.
Set the compass to the length AC and draw an arc from A.
Set the compass to the length BC and draw an arc from B that crosses the first.
Label the crossing point C and join it to A and to B.
methods.example: AB = 7 cm, AC = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm is possible, because 5 + 6 is more than 7. The arcs cross at C, above or below AB.
methods.check: Measure all three sides with a ruler. Each should match the length you were given.
methods.trap: Using one compass opening for both arcs when AC and BC are different lengths.

methods.title: Construct a triangle from SAS
methods.when: You are given two sides and the angle between them.
methods.rule: The angle lies between the two known sides; lengths>0 and 0°<included angle<180°.
steps: Draw the first given side, starting at the vertex of the angle.
At that vertex, draw the given angle.
Mark the length of the second given side along the new arm.
Join the two free ends.
methods.example: AB = 6 cm, AC = 4 cm, ∠BAC = 50°: draw AB, draw a line at 50° at A, then mark C on it, 4 cm from A.
methods.check: The angle must be at the point where the two given sides meet.
methods.trap: Putting the given angle opposite one of the given sides instead of between them.

methods.title: Construct a triangle from ASA
methods.when: You are given one side and the angle at each end of it.
methods.rule: For endpoint angles α,β>0, require α+β<180°; the third angle is 180°−α−β.
steps: Draw the given side AB.
At A, draw a line at the first angle to AB.
At B, draw a line at the second angle to BA, on the same side of AB.
The lines cross at C. Join up and label.
methods.check: The three angles should add to 180°. Measure the angle at C to check.
methods.trap: Measuring the angle at B from the base continued past B, instead of from BA.

methods.title: Construct a right-angled triangle
methods.when: You are given a right angle with the hypotenuse and one other side, or with one side and one of the smaller angles.
methods.rule: Hypotenuse h must exceed the given perpendicular side a>0; the other perpendicular side is √(h²−a²).
steps: Draw the given shorter side AB.
Construct a perpendicular at A, where the right angle is.
Set the compass to the hypotenuse and draw an arc from B. If you are given an angle at B instead, draw a line from B at that angle to AB.
The arc or line meets the perpendicular at C. Join B to C.
methods.example: AB=5, BC=13 cm and right angle at A give AC=12 cm.
methods.check: 5²+12²=13² checks the finished triangle.
methods.trap: Drawing the hypotenuse arc from A, the vertex of the right angle. It must be drawn from B, the other end of the known side.

methods.title: Construct a rectangle and check its diagonal
methods.when: You are given the length and width of a rectangle, or one side and a diagonal.
methods.rule: Opposite sides equal and parallel; all angles 90°; diagonal²=length²+width².
steps: Draw the known base AB.
Construct perpendiculars at A and at B, on the same side of AB.
For a known width, mark it on both perpendiculars. For a known diagonal AC, find C with an arc centred at A.
Through C, construct a line parallel to AB. It meets the perpendicular from A at D.
Check the four right angles, the equal opposite sides and the equal diagonals.
methods.example: Base 9 cm and diagonal 15 cm give width 12 cm by Pythagoras.
methods.check: 9²+12²=15² and the opposite sides agree.
methods.trap: Using the diagonal as the width of the rectangle.

checks: Name a translation’s vector, a reflection’s mirror line, or a rotation’s centre, angle and direction.
One point landing on its image does not prove that the whole shape maps. Test every vertex.
Keep the compass opening the same where the construction needs it, and leave the arcs on the page.
Before you construct a triangle, check that it can exist: the two shorter sides must add to more than the longest.
Check a drawing with coordinates, a ruler or a congruence reason. Looking right is not proof.

challenges.title: Construct two bisectors and verify a distance
challenges.question: Draw an angle BAC of 110° using a protractor, then put the protractor aside. (a) Construct its bisector with ruler and compass, leaving arcs visible. (b) Bisect the angle between AB and the first bisector again. State all resulting angle sizes from AB. (c) Mark P on the first bisector with AP=6 cm. Drop perpendiculars PF and PG to the two original arms. Explain why PF=PG. (d) Find that common distance to the nearest 0.01 cm.
hints: Use equal marks from A, then equal crossing arcs from those marks.
For the distance, each right-angled triangle has hypotenuse AP=6 and angle at A equal to 55°.

solution.title: Construct the first bisector
solution.math: From A mark equal-radius intersections U,V on the arms; equal arcs from U,V meet at Q; draw AQ.
solution.reason: Triangles AUQ and AVQ have three pairs of equal sides, so they are congruent by SSS. Each angle at A is half of 110°, which is 55°.

solution.title: Bisect again
solution.math: Repeat the compass construction inside ∠BAQ: the new ray is 27.5° from AB; AQ is 55° from AB; AC is 110° from AB.
solution.reason: Each bisection halves the angle it is used on. Half of 55° is 27.5°.

solution.title: Justify equal distances
solution.math: Right-angled triangles APF and APG have common hypotenuse AP and equal acute angle 55° at A. Their other acute angles are both 35°, so ASA gives congruence.
solution.reason: The shared side AP sits between the two pairs of equal angles, so the triangles are congruent and PF = PG.

solution.title: Calculate the distance
solution.reason: PF is opposite the 55° angle and AP is the hypotenuse, so use sine: opposite = hypotenuse × sin 55°.

challenges.answer: (a) First bisector at 55°. (b) Second ray at 27.5° from AB; first at 55°, original second arm at 110°. (c) Congruent right-angled triangles give PF=PG. (d) Both distances≈4.91 cm.
challenges.check: The adjacent lengths AF and AG both equal 6cos55°; each right-angled triangle satisfies (6sin55°)²+(6cos55°)²=36.

challenges.title: An outside point and a verified perpendicular
challenges.question: Draw AB=8 cm. Using arcs of radius 5 cm centred at A and B, construct their intersection P above AB and join AP and BP. (a) Construct a perpendicular from P to the line AB using an arc from P and matching arcs from its two crossings; do not simply estimate a midpoint. Call the foot M. (b) Explain why M is the midpoint of AB. (c) Find PM exactly. (d) State two independent checks on the drawing.
hints: The original construction ensures PA=PB. A second point equally far from A and B locates the perpendicular bisector.
Once AM is known, use Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle APM.

solution.title: Construct the perpendicular
solution.math: Centre an arc at P to cross AB in U,V. Draw equal arcs from U,V meeting at Q on the opposite side, then draw PQ; let M=PQ∩AB.
solution.reason: P and Q are each equally far from U and V, so PQ is the perpendicular bisector of UV. It meets AB at a right angle.

solution.title: Use the original equal distances
solution.math: PA=PB=5 cm; P lies on AB’s perpendicular bisector. The perpendicular through P is unique, so AM=MB=4 cm.
solution.reason: There is only one perpendicular from P to AB. P is also on the perpendicular bisector of AB, so the two lines are the same and M is the midpoint.

solution.title: Find the height
solution.reason: Triangle APM is right-angled at M, with hypotenuse AP. So use Pythagoras.

solution.title: Check independently
solution.reason: One check uses lengths and the other uses an angle. They test different parts of the drawing.

challenges.answer: (a) Construction route above. (b) M is the midpoint, with AM=MB=4 cm. (c) PM=3 cm. (d) For example equal 5 cm sloping sides and a right angle at M.
challenges.check: Both right-angled triangles have sides 3,4,5; their combined base is 8 cm as required.

challenges.title: Which transformation maps the whole shape?
challenges.question: Parallelogram ABCD has A=(0,0), B=(6,0), D=(2,4) and C=(8,4). (a) Describe completely a translation mapping the ordered segment AD to BC. (b) Describe completely a rotation mapping triangle ABD to triangle CDB, in that order. (c) Could one reflection map A→B and D→C simultaneously? Prove your answer using the candidate mirror lines. (d) Under the rotation in part b, find the image of E=(1,1).
hints: Check at least two corresponding pairs rather than one point alone.
The mirror for A→B must perpendicularly bisect AB; compare it with the mirror required for D→C.

solution.title: Find the translation
solution.reason: A and D both move 6 to the right, so one translation maps the whole segment.

solution.title: Find the half-turn centre
solution.math: Midpoint of AC=(4,2); midpoint of BD=(4,2). A 180° rotation about (4,2) maps A→C, B→D, D→B.
solution.reason: A half-turn swaps any two points whose midpoint is the centre. For 180°, clockwise and anticlockwise give the same result.

solution.title: Test a reflection on both pairs
solution.math: A→B requires mirror x=3; D→C requires mirror x=5
solution.reason: A reflection has only one mirror line. These two pairs need different mirrors, so no single reflection does both.

solution.title: Apply the complete rotation
solution.reason: The centre is the midpoint of E and its image.

challenges.answer: (a) Translation vector (6,0). (b) 180° about (4,2), either direction. (c) No: required mirrors are x=3 and x=5. (d) E′=(7,3).
challenges.check: Midpoint of (1,1) and (7,3) is (4,2), and the vectors from that centre are opposites.

challenges.title: Build a rectangle, divide and rotate
challenges.question: Construct rectangle ABCD in cyclic order with AB=6 cm and diagonal AC=10 cm, choosing C above AB. (a) Give and carry out a ruler-and-compass construction from these data, leaving arcs. (b) Calculate BC exactly as a check. (c) Divide AB into three equal parts by an auxiliary ray and parallels; call the division point nearer A, E. (d) Let O be the rectangle’s diagonal intersection. A 180° rotation about O sends E to E′. Locate E′ precisely on side DC, stating its distances from D and C.
hints: Construct the perpendicular at B, then use an arc centred at A with radius 10 cm to find C.
For part d, you may use the coordinates A=(0,0) and B=(6,0), with the height you calculated.

solution.title: Construct the rectangle
solution.math: Draw AB=6. Construct a perpendicular at B. An arc centred at A, radius 10, meets it above AB at C. Construct a parallel to AB through C and a perpendicular to AB through A; their intersection is D.
solution.reason: The arc makes AC equal to 10 cm. The perpendicular and the parallel give the right angles and the parallel sides of a rectangle.

solution.title: Check the missing side
solution.reason: ABC is a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse AC.

solution.title: Divide the base accurately
solution.math: From A draw an auxiliary ray; step off three equal compass lengths U₁,U₂,U₃. Join U₃B and construct parallels through U₁,U₂ to meet AB. AE=2 cm.
solution.reason: The parallels copy the three equal steps onto AB as three equal parts. One third of 6 cm is 2 cm.

solution.title: Apply the half-turn
solution.reason: A half-turn about O(3,4) sends (x, y) to (6 − x, 8 − y), because O is the midpoint of each point and its image.

solution.title: State the location on the requested side
solution.reason: E′ is on DC because its y-coordinate is 8. It is 4 from D(0,8) and 2 from C(6,8).

challenges.answer: (a) Construction route above. (b) BC=8 cm. (c) AE=2 cm. (d) E′ lies on DC, 4 cm from D and 2 cm from C.
challenges.check: The rectangle has diagonal √(6²+8²)=10. O is the midpoint of E=(2,0) and E′=(4,8), verifying the rotation.
